articles.title: Diagnostic yield of cancer predisposition in a nationwide prospective childhood acute leukemia cohort.
articles.authors: Taylan F, Staffas A, Sjögren S, Lagerstedt-Robinson K, Kuchinskaya E, Poluha A, Ivarsson S, Hellberg M, Klar J, Abel F, Abrahamsson J, Pronk CJ, Belander Strålin K, Harila A, Vogt H, Norén-Nyström U, Grillner P, Palmqvist L, Arvidsson L, Pandzic T, Bondeson ML, Mu N, Ekholm K, Anderlid BM, Golovleva I, Maya-González C, Gideonsson P, Tham E, Barbany G, Lähteenmäki P, Sandgren J, Rosenquist R, Wirta V, Ljungman G, Gisselsson D, Palle J, Tesi B, Nordgren A.
articles.abstract: The utility of whole-genome sequencing (WGS) for detecting childhood leukemia predisposition remains unclear. We perform a nationwide, prospective, population-based study of 181 children with acute leukemia to assess diagnostic yield and clinical utility of a uniformly applied three-pronged strategy, including systematic phenotyping, germline WGS-based 189-gene panel and tumor sequencing of positive cases. Trio-WGS is performed in 11 high-suspicion families. Nine patients have pathogenic germline alterations: six (3.3%) with leukemia predisposition syndromes ( TP53, CEBPA, DNMT3A , trisomy 21) and three (1.6%) with solid tumor predisposition syndromes ( MSH6, PALB2, SDHA ). Trio-WGS identifies one likely-pathogenic de novo DNMT3A variant. Six of nine diagnoses are previously unrecognized. Findings lead to tailored surveillance in 8/9 patients and treatment modifications in 4/9. Here, we show that this strategy gives a modest diagnostic yield. Nevertheless, the actionability of the findings supports its feasibility and validity in practice. Whether to restrict analysis to leukemia-relevant genes or broaden the panel should reflect local resources and counseling capacity.
paragraphs: The utility of whole-genome sequencing (WGS) for detecting childhood leukemia predisposition remains unclear. We perform a nationwide, prospective, population-based study of 181 children with acute leukemia to assess diagnostic yield and clinical utility of a uniformly applied three-pronged strategy, including systematic phenotyping, germline WGS-based 189-gene panel and tumor sequencing of positive cases. Trio-WGS is performed in 11 high-suspicion families. Nine patients have pathogenic germline alterations: six (3.3%) with leukemia predisposition syndromes ( TP53, CEBPA, DNMT3A , trisomy 21) and three (1.6%) with solid tumor predisposition syndromes ( MSH6, PALB2, SDHA ). Trio-WGS identifies one likely-pathogenic de novo DNMT3A variant. Six of nine diagnoses are previously unrecognized. Findings lead to tailored surveillance in 8/9 patients and treatment modifications in 4/9. Here, we show that this strategy gives a modest diagnostic yield. Nevertheless, the actionability of the findings supports its feasibility and validity in practice. Whether to restrict analysis to leukemia-relevant genes or broaden the panel should reflect local resources and counseling capacity.

The potential of germline whole-genome sequencing (WGS) in detecting childhood leukemia predisposition remains to be elucidated. Here the authors show that a three-pronged diagnostic strategy including systematic phenotyping, germline WGS based 189-gene panel and tumor sequencing of positive cases may be feasible and clinically useful for cancer predisposition screening in childhood acute leukemia.

Leukemia represents the most common pediatric malignancy, accounting for approximately one-third of all childhood cancer cases worldwide 1 , 2 . Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) comprises approximately 80% of cases, with incidence peaking between two and five years of age 2 – 5 , while acute myeloid leukemia (AML) represents approximately 15-20% of pediatric leukemia cases, with a bimodal age distribution in childhood 6 . In Sweden, approximately 100 children are diagnosed with leukemia each year 7 .

While most leukemia cases arise sporadically, large-scale genomic studies involving analysis of 100 or more genes in cohorts exceeding 50 cases of pediatric leukemia have estimated that germline predisposition underlies 4–10% of pediatric hematological malignancies 8 – 12 . The prevalence varies significantly by subtype, with germline variants identified in 12–19% of childhood AML, compared to approximately 3% of childhood ALL 13 – 15 . Whether this discrepancy reflects true biological differences or arises from methodological factors -such as study design, cohort size, gene selection, or variant interpretation criteria—remains to be determined 8 – 11 .

To date, 45 genes have been associated with childhood leukemia predisposition 16 . These genes commonly affect core cellular pathways, including DNA repair (e.g., ATM, NBN , Fanconi anemia genes), apoptosis and cell cycle regulation (e.g., TP53 ), cellular signaling (e.g., CBL, NF1, SOS1 ), and hematological cell differentiation (e.g., ETV6, RUNX1, IKZF1, PAX5 ) 16 – 20 . Constitutional trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) confers elevated risk for both acute lymphoblastic and myeloid leukemias mediated by dosage-sensitive effects on hematopoiesis and cooperating somatic mutations 21 , 22 . Predisposing variants can be categorized as overt cancer predisposition syndromes (CPSs) which are associated with recognizable phenotypic features or as covert syndromes which present with subtle or no distinctive features 16 . Recognition of these genetic syndromes has led to their classification as distinct entities in the fifth editions of the World Health Organization (WHO) Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumors and WHO Classification of Pediatric Tumors, as well as in the 2022 International Consensus Classification of Myeloid Neoplasms and Acute Leukemias 5 , 23 , 24 . Consequently, recent clinical perspectives emphasize the systematic integration of germline testing into standard pediatric oncology workflows to ensure these patients receive optimized surveillance and personalized therapeutic interventions 25 .

Despite increasing recognition of germline predisposition in childhood leukemia, prospective population-based studies remain essential to study diagnostic strategies and clinical implications in routine care. The nationwide Genomic Medicine Sweden (GMS) Childhood Cancer Predisposition (ChiCaP) study is designed to evaluate the diagnostic yield and clinical utility of a three-pronged diagnostic strategy - systematic phenotyping, germline WGS-based analysis of a 189-gene panel, and tumor sequencing of positive cases - uniformly applied across Sweden and offered to all children at cancer diagnosis in Sweden 26 . Here, we show that our three-pronged diagnostic strategy is feasible and clinically valid for universal cancer predisposition screening in childhood acute leukemia. In the Swedish nationwide, population-based, prospective, multi-center study of 181 patients, this integrated approach identifies pathogenic germline alterations in nine patients (5%; 3.3% leukemia predisposition, 1.7% solid tumor predisposition), six of whom are previously unrecognized, prompting tailored surveillance in eight and treatment modification in four. Although the diagnostic yield is modest, the findings are clinically actionable and support implementation of this strategy in routine clinical practice.

Between 17 December 2021 and 30 April 2024, 181 children diagnosed with acute leukemia across all six pediatric oncology centers in Sweden were consecutively enrolled and investigated through our three-pronged diagnostic strategy (Fig. 1 ). Median age at diagnosis was 5 years (range 0–17), and 74 (41%) were female (Table 1 ). The most common diagnoses were B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (BCP-ALL; n = 138, 76%), followed by acute myeloid leukemia (AML; n = 22, 12%), T-cell ALL (T-ALL; n = 18, 10%), and acute leukemias of ambiguous lineage (ALALs) ( n = 3, 2%) (Table 1 , Fig. 2a ). Distribution of ages showed a peak at 2–3 years which is driven by BCP-ALLs (Fig. 2b ). At study enrollment, we collected family history of cancer, malignancy type, and clinical features suggestive of ChiCaP using the structured ChiCaP criteria form described in detail by Tesi et al. 26 and in the Supplementary Information. Complete ChiCaP criteria forms were available for 174 of the 181 enrolled patients (96%) (Table 1 ). Fig. 1 Three-pronged diagnostic strategy. The strategy combines systematic phenotyping, germline WGS-based analysis of a 189-gene panel, and analysis of tumor sequencing data of positive cases. Children with newly diagnosed acute leukemia ( n = 181) were prospectively enrolled and evaluated through three parallel arms. Systematic clinical phenotyping was performed in 176 patients using the childhood cancer predisposition (ChiCaP) criteria. Germline whole-genome sequencing was undertaken in 181 patients and analyzed with an in silico 189-gene panel. Trio-WGS was performed in 11 cases with a high suspicion of a predisposition. In parallel, tumor WGS (90x coverage) was performed alongside standard-of-care diagnostic testing in the same patients; somatic findings suggestive of an underlying germline variant triggered reflex testing. Phenotypic, germline, and reflex-derived data were jointly considered during germline variant interpretation to identify pathogenic (P) or likely pathogenic (LP) variants. In patients harboring a P/LP variant, integrated tumor-germline analysis was performed to refine clinical actionability, informing genetic counseling, treatment adjustment, and long-term surveillance recommendations for patients and at-risk relatives. All samples were analyzed for variants in 189 established ChiCaP genes 26 (Supplementary Data 1 ). Germline DNA was obtained primarily from cultured skin fibroblasts ( n = 175, 97%). In six patients, a peripheral blood ( n = 2) or bone marrow ( n = 4) sample drawn at remission was used. To evaluate the diagnostic benefit of broader genetic testing, patients with negative analysis results but a strong clinical suspicion of ChiCaP (family history of any cancer ( n = 6); non-malignant features suggestive of an underlying syndrome ( n = 3); family history of cancer with multiple primary tumors ( n = 1); and family history of cancer and non-malignant features ( n = 1)), trio WGS - sequencing of proband (i.e., the child diagnosed with leukemia) alongside both parents —was performed in 11 cases (6 BCP-ALL, 3 T-ALL, 2 AML).

The Swedish Childhood Cancer Registry (SCCR) which captures ≥93% of cancer diagnoses in patients <16 years 7 was used only for comparison of population coverage and representativeness. According to the SCCR, there were 213 first diagnoses of leukemia in children during the study period, while only 181 patients were included in the study, mainly due to logistic challenges in obtaining written informed consent. However, the age- (Fig. 2c ) and disease-group (Fig. 2d ) distribution of GMS ChiCaP participants closely matched the SCCR distribution for the study period, supporting that the cohort is broadly representative of the national childhood leukemia population.

The overall germline analysis workflow and the pathogenic (P)/likely pathogenic (LP) findings in our cohort are summarized in Fig. 3a . In silico analysis using the 189-gene ChiCaP panel revealed a germline P/LP variant in 5 of 181 (2.76%; 95% CI 1.2-6.3%) cases. Additionally, trio WGS identified a de novo heterozygous variant in DNMT3A ( NM_022552.5 : c.2635 A > G, p.(Asn879Asp)), absent in both parents and classified as LP according to ACMG criteria. Three patients had already been diagnosed with Down syndrome at enrollment, including one with mosaic trisomy 21. A cancer predisposition syndrome was identified in 9 of 181 patients, corresponding to an overall diagnostic yield of 5.0% (95% CI 2.6–9.2%) (Table 1 , Fig. 3b , Supplementary Data 2 ). Six patients (6/181, 3.3%; 95% CI 1.5–7.0%) carried genetic aberrations associated with established leukemia predisposition syndromes (Fig. 3b ), whereas three patients (3/181, 1.7%; 95% CI 0.5–4.8%) harbored heterozygous P/LP variants in ChiCaP genes associated with adult-onset predisposition to solid tumors (Table 1 ). ChiCaP diagnoses were identified in 2 of 22 AML cases (9.1%; 95% CI 1.6–27.8%), 1 of 18 T-ALL cases (5.6%; 95% CI 0.3–25.8%), and 3 of 138 BCP-ALL cases (2.2%; 95% CI 0.6–6.2%) (Fig. 3b ). Due to small sample sizes in the AML and T-ALL subgroups, statistical comparison of prevalence across subtypes was not feasible. A second BCP-ALL patient (SE_AL120) had a Li–Fraumeni syndrome caused by a heterozygous germline NM_000546.6 ( TP53 ):c.325 T > A (p.Phe109Ile) variant (Table 2 ). No P/LP germline variants were identified in any of the six cases who were analyzed in blood/bone marrow remission samples with the 189-gene panel. However, 30x WGS analysis performed in one remission sample (SE_AL029) could not detect trisomy 21 mosaicism, previously found in approximately 90% of fibroblasts and in all leukemic cells. Three other BCP-ALL patients carried heterozygous P/LP variants in MSH6, PALB2 , and SDHA - genes known for adult-onset solid tumor predisposition but not previously linked to childhood leukemia. The MSH6 variant was maternally inherited with limited family cancer history (one colorectal cancer after age 50 years in a second-degree relative), while the PALB2 variant was paternally inherited. On the paternal side, family history included breast cancer in the father’s cousin at age 50 and cervical, prostate, and colon cancers in different paternal relatives, all diagnosed after age 50. The SDHA variant was not considered actionable given its low penetrance and absence of family history of pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma, and no segregation analysis was performed.

Eight patients were offered genetic counseling. In addition to the individuals with Down syndrome, two children had de novo variants in CEBPA and DNMT3A respectively, while the TP53 variant was inherited from a sperm donor 27 . In two families with inherited variants in PALB2 and MSH6 , family members were offered cascade testing, with surveillance offered to carriers.

Across ChiCaP-positive cases, WGS performed on leukemia cells identified large structural variants and canonical, subtype-specific drivers that were consistent with karyotypic abnormalities detected in standard-of-care investigations (details in Table 3 ). In the AML case (SE_AL154) with a germline heterozygous CEBPA , a somatic second hit causing a biallelic CEBPA disruption was observed. In the Down syndrome-associated AML (SE_AL144), the leukemic clone showed trisomy 21 with a truncating GATA1 variant. In the T-ALL case (SE_AL119) harboring the germline DNMT3A variant, somatic focal 9p loss (including PAX5 , and CDKN2A / B) , loss of IKZF1 on 7p and partial ETV6 deletion were detected. The Down syndrome BCP-ALL case (SE_AL037) harbored multiple somatic copy-number alterations, including CDKN2A/CDKN2B deletions, without any known driver SNV/indel. All leukemic cells in the individual (SE_AL029) with trisomy 21 mosaicism, harbored +21 in combination with BTG1 and IKZF1 deletions, consistent with the molecular landscape of Down syndrome-associated BCP-ALL 28 – 30 . This patient had been diagnosed with AML and mosaic trisomy 21 at age two, four years prior to BCP-ALL diagnosis. The genetic profile of the BCP-ALL - harboring IKZF1 and BTG1 deletions without KMT2A rearrangement - is inconsistent with a therapy-related origin and instead supports a predisposition-driven second primary leukemia. Although the mosaicism was undetectable in peripheral blood and remission bone marrow, analysis of 24 informative SNPs across chromosome 21 confirmed duplication of the same chromosome 21 parental homolog in fibroblasts, AML, and BCP-ALL, which is in line with a shared constitutional origin, although an independent recurrent event involving the same homolog cannot be formally excluded.

In the TP53 -related low-hypodiploid BCP-ALL case (SE_AL120), leukemic cells exhibited extensive whole-chromosome losses and copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity (CN-LOH), including monosomy 17 with biallelic loss of TP53 , together with deletions of CDKN2A / B , IKZF1, EBF1, PAX5 , and RB1 . The germline TP53 variant had a variant allele frequency (VAF) of 81%, consistent with loss of the wild-type chromosome 17.

Cases harboring germline variants in MSH6 , SDHA , or PALB2 each exhibited different BCP-ALL subtypes: the MSH6 case was classified as high hyperdiploid ALL, the SDHA case as iAMP21 ALL, and the PALB2 case as KMT2A -rearranged ALL. The somatic profiles in these cases also included recurrent secondary alterations typical of BCP-ALL, such as deletions at PAX5 and CDKN2A / CDKN2B . No second hit was identified in the respective cancer predisposition genes; case-level specifics are provided in Table 3 .

The child with Down syndrome and AML (SE_AL144) was treated according to the Myeloid Leukemia of Down Syndrome 2006 protocol without modifications and the patient with CEBPA -associated familial AML (SE_AL154) received standard treatment with the NOPHO-DBH-AML-2012 regimen without adjustment (Table 3 ). Patient SE_AL119 with T-ALL underwent trio-WGS following negative results from the 189-gene ChiCaP panel, prompted by clinical suspicion of an underlying syndrome. The patient presented with hydrocephalus, Chiari-1 malformation, hydrocele, developmental delay, hypotonia, nystagmus, and recurrent infections. Trio WGS identified a de novo LP DNMT3A variant that explained both the syndromic features, establishing a diagnosis of TBRS, and the predisposition to T-ALL 31 – 34 . This association is consistent with reports of a 4% prevalence of hematopoietic malignancies in TBRS, representing a > 250-fold increased risk compared to the general population 33 . The patient was treated according to the ALLTogether intermediate-high-risk protocol without modifications (Table 3 ). The two BCP-ALL patients, Down syndrome (SE_AL037) and trisomy 21 mosaicism (SE_AL029), were both stratified to intermediate risk and treated according to the ALLTogether Down IR protocol. The patient (SE_AL120) with Li–Fraumeni syndrome was classified as high-risk based on somatic genetic findings (low hypodiploidy) and enrolled in the ALLTogether high-risk treatment protocol (Table 3 ).

Among the 174 patients with completed ChiCaP criteria forms 26 , 45.4% (79/174; 95% CI 38.2–52.8%) met at least one ChiCaP criterion, and 5.7% (10/174; 95% CI 3.2–10.3%) fulfilled two criteria (Table 1 and Fig. 4a ). No patients met three or more criteria (Fig. 4a ). Among patients with BCP-ALL, 41.8% (56/134; 95% CI 33.8–50.3%) fulfilled at least one criterion, and only 3.0% (4/134; 95% CI 1.2–7.4%) met two criteria (Fig. 4a ). Positive family history of cancer was reported in 29.1% of patients (50/172; 95% CI 22.8–36.3%) across leukemia subtypes (Fig. 4b ). Specifically, childhood cancer in a close relative (parent, sibling, or half-sibling) was noted in 10% (17/172; 95% CI 6.3–15.3%), and hematological malignancies in family members of any age were reported in 10.5% (18/172; 95% CI 6.7–15.9%). Consanguinity was present in 4.6% (8/172; 2.4–8.9%), and 7% of patients (12/172; 95% CI 4.0–11.8%) had a parent diagnosed with cancer before the age of 50 (Fig. 4b ). Among patients with BCP-ALL, a positive family history of cancer was reported in 24.2% of patients (32/132; 95% CI 17.7–32.2%) (Fig. 4b ). Childhood cancer in a close relative was noted in 9.8% (13/132; 95% CI 5.8–16.1%), and hematological malignancies in family members of any age were reported in 9.1% (12/132; 95% CI 5.3–15.2%). Consanguinity was present in 5.3% of cases (7/132; 95% CI 2.6–10.5%). Additionally, 3.8% of patients (5/132; 95% CI 1.6–8.6%) had a parent diagnosed with cancer before age 50.

Multiple primary malignancies were documented in 3/174 patients (1.7%; 95% CI 0.5–4.9%). The first patient (SE_AL001) was initially diagnosed with BCP-ALL at 2 years of age and subsequently developed therapy-related acute myeloid leukemia (t-AML) 5 years later, at 7 years of age. The second patient (SE_AL060) was initially diagnosed with neuroblastoma at 5 years of age and subsequently developed t-AML during the same year, remaining 5 years of age at the time of the second diagnosis. The third patient (SE_AL029) was diagnosed with AML at age 2 and BCP-ALL four years later, at age 6. We conducted a comprehensive “tip-to-toe” clinical review to identify congenital malformations and other non-cancer symptoms using the ChiCaP criteria form. Among the 173 patients with a completed ChiCaP criteria form, at least one non-malignant feature was present in 16.8% (29/173; 95% CI 11.9–23.0%), and 4.6% (8/173; 95% CI 2.4–8.9%) had more than one. The most frequent features were cognitive or behavioral disorders (6.9%, 12/173; 95% CI 4.0–11.7%), congenital malformations (4.0%, 7/173; 95% CI 2.0–8.1%), and skin manifestations (3.5%, 6/173; 95% CI 1.6–7.4%). The two patients with non-mosaic Down syndrome were diagnosed prior to leukemia onset, while the patient with BCP-ALL was diagnosed with mosaic trisomy 21 at age 2 when the AML diagnosis was established. One patient had a known genetic condition, X-linked deafness type 2 (OMIM 304400) caused by a POU3F4 variant, which has not been associated with cancer predisposition. This patient had no additional ChiCaP findings.

Among the six patients with genetically confirmed ChiCaP findings in leukemia-associated genes, four met the ChiCaP criteria based on syndromic features (trisomy 21, DNMT3A , TP53 ) (Table 3 ) and one also met the criteria due to a previous primary malignancy (AML in the child with mosaic trisomy 21).

The individual with a germline TP53 variant presented with hypodiploid ALL and somatic TP53 aberrations. This child also met the ChiCaP criteria due to an abnormal thorax shape, which we consider an incidental finding with no apparent relation to the TP53 variant. Although the individual with familial CEBPA -associated AML did not meet ChiCaP criteria, paired tumor–normal analysis identified a pathogenic somatic CEBPA p.(Lys313dup), and subsequent testing revealed a germline CEBPA p.(Gln83Serfs*77).

In contrast, none of the three individuals with variants in established solid tumor predisposition genes met the ChiCaP criteria (Table 3 ). Notably, no child with leukemia and a positive family history carried a pathogenic variant in the ChiCaP 189-gene list.

In this nationwide prospective cohort of 181 children with newly diagnosed acute leukemia 3.3% (6/181; 95% CI 1.5–7.0%) harbored a childhood leukemia predisposition syndrome and 1.7% (3/181; 95% CI 0.5–4.8%) harbored pathogenic variants in solid tumor predisposition genes. Using a three-pronged approach uniformly applied across Sweden, we identified cancer predisposition syndromes in 5.0% (9/181; 95% CI 2.6–9.2%) of leukemia patients overall, often previously unrecognized and with direct clinical implications. These findings indicate a modest but clinically actionable yield in an unselected population of childhood acute leukemias.

Previous pan-cancer pediatric studies have reported overall cancer predisposition syndrome prevalences of 7–18% 8 – 10 , 18 , 26 , 35 – 38 , but most of these estimates derive from targeted panels or pre-selected cohorts. Also, these figures encompass all tumor types and varying definitions, including adult-onset cancer predisposition syndromes, variants without established causality to the child’s neoplasm, and in some studies, heterozygous carriers of autosomal recessive genes 8 – 11 . When the comparison is restricted to P/LP variants in genes with an established association with childhood leukemia and matching inheritance pattern—the definition used for ChiCaP syndromes in our study -, the prevalence across studies narrows to 0.5–8.1%, and drops further to 0.5–4% when Down syndrome is excluded, with our 1.7% falling within both of these ranges (Supplementary Table 1 ). Overall, current data seem to point to a relatively low ChiCaP prevalence in childhood leukemia. In our cohort, prevalence appeared to vary by leukemia type, with AML showing a higher rate (2/22 cases) compared with BCP-ALL (2.2%, 3/138), although the small sample sizes preclude definitive conclusions.

Although the number of children diagnosed with a ChiCaP syndrome was modest, the clinical benefit of identifying a leukemia predisposition at the individual level was substantial. Only 3/9 ChiCaP diagnoses (constitutional and mosaic trisomy 21) were known prior to leukemia diagnosis. The ChiCaP findings directly influenced treatment in 4/9 of the cases, with management aligned to established protocols for Down syndrome and TP53 -related cancer predisposition disorders and led to gene specific implementation of surveillance recommendations in 88% (8/9) of cases (Table 3 ). In addition, the ChiCaP results complemented somatic genetic findings; integrating germline data with leukemia karyotypes and clinical phenotypes revealed associations that refined risk assessment and guided genetic counseling. An illustrative example is the TP53 (c.325 T > A) variant, previously reported in five pediatric patients across malignancies, including hypodiploid BCP-ALL 27 . Li–Fraumeni syndrome is associated with poor treatment outcome in ALL and an elevated risk of therapy-related secondary malignancies 39 , 40 . Similarly, detection of a somatic CEBPA variant should prompt germline assessment to exclude hereditary predisposition 41 – 45 . These findings underscore the clinical value of routine germline evaluation even when overall prevalence is modest.

A separate category of findings comprised three patients carrying P/LP variants in solid-tumor predisposition genes ( MSH6, SDHA, PALB2 ) who met no ChiCaP criteria; their family cancer histories, where present, exceeded the age-of-onset thresholds, and these patients would have been missed, had patient selection relied solely on phenotype-driven triage with reflex testing. A review of the existing literature reveals no confirmed leukemia-associated monoallelic germline variants in these three genes. Hematological malignancy associated with MSH6 and PALB2 has predominantly been described in the context of biallelic inactivation 46 , 47 , whereas evidence for childhood leukemia in monoallelic carriers is limited to isolated case reports 10 , 48 , 49 and a comprehensive review of germline SDHA variants across cancer types found no cases of hematological malignancy among affected individuals 50 , 51 . Taken together with the absence of second hits in the leukemias of these patients, the lack of established evidence linking heterozygous variants in these genes to childhood BCP-ALL supports the interpretation that these findings are likely unrelated to leukemia development 52 . Larger cohorts and functional studies are required to establish whether leukemia falls within the phenotypic spectrum associated with these solid tumor predisposition genes. Importantly, identifying the MSH6 and PALB2 variants nonetheless conferred immediate clinical benefit through risk-appropriate surveillance for the associated solid tumor predisposition syndromes and by facilitating genetic counseling with cascade testing of at-risk relatives.

Restricting attention to the leukemia-associated ChiCaP syndromes, all six genetically confirmed cases would have been triaged for germline analysis under a phenotype-driven diagnostic strategy, either through fulfillment of established clinical criteria or through somatic findings prompting reflex testing, in accordance with current diagnostic guidelines and published recommendations 23 , 24 , 40 , 45 , 53 – 56 . However, this observation is contingent on systematic somatic profiling of the leukemia at diagnosis, since reflex testing depends on the detection of informative somatic variants. We did not perform a direct prospective comparison between phenotype-driven triage and phenotype-agnostic germline sequencing, an analysis recently undertaken by Bakhuizen and colleagues in a pediatric pan-cancer cohort 11 , who demonstrated phenotype-driven genetic testing and phenotype-agnostic CPS gene panel sequencing to be complementary. These considerations support a phenotype-driven strategy as a pragmatic and resource-efficient framework, particularly in settings where universal germline sequencing is not feasible, provided that it is coupled with thorough somatic workup of the leukemia. However, several limitations of a phenotype-driven approach nevertheless warrant emphasis: variants are expected to escape detection in patients with (i) de novo variants without supportive family history, (ii) variants in low-penetrance genes, (iii) absent or as-yet-unrecognized phenotypic features, and (iv) insufficient tumor material for somatic analyses. Heterozygous variants in genes associated with adult-onset predisposition - findings beyond the scope of the analysis would also be missed by a phenotype-driven approach. On the other hand, a universal genotype-first approach, in which sequencing is performed without prior phenotypic anchoring, may result in lower-quality variant interpretation, which depends critically on detailed phenotypic information. Instead, phenotypic information is integral to our three-pronged strategy, ensuring high-quality variant interpretation.

Several observations in our cohort indicate that the spectrum of leukemia predisposition extends beyond what current ChiCaP gene panels capture. Approximately 10% of children in our cohort had a reported family history of childhood cancer and 9% had relatives with hematological malignancies at any age, suggesting undiagnosed predisposition in a proportion of cases. In our previous study of the children with solid/CNS tumors, 66% (194/293) met at least one ChiCaP criterion and among those 17% (33/194) received a ChiCaP diagnosis using the same gene panel as we have used in this study 26 . In the present leukemia cohort, 45.4% (79/174) met at least one ChiCaP criterion and 6.3% (5/79) of these had a confirmed leukemia-associated ChiCaP syndrome. The lower yield among criteria-positive leukemia patients, combined with the family history data, supports the interpretation that ChiCaP syndromes caused by currently known ChiCaP genes are infrequently identified in leukemia and that undiscovered leukemia predisposition syndromes likely exist. The low overall prevalence in BCP-ALL (2.2%) may, however, be consistent with previous hypotheses that most cases arise from somatic events—chromosomal rearrangements, aneuploidy, and gene fusions - during early development or in response to environmental factors, including infections during immune maturation in early childhood 57 , 58 .

The identification of a de novo LP DNMT3A variant in a patient with T-ALL and a clear TBRS phenotype is in line with emerging evidence that germline DNMT3A variants may predispose to hematological malignancies in children 31 , 33 , 34 and illustrates the value of trio-WGS in patients with syndromic features of undetermined etiology, where panel-based approaches remain constrained by the timeliness of gene content updates and may fail to capture clinically relevant variants in genes not yet incorporated into curated lists. The patient with mosaic trisomy 21 and BCP-ALL illustrates how low-level mosaicism in the hematopoietic compartment can confer clinically significant leukemia predisposition that may be overlooked when only single tissue is analyzed, underscoring the importance of examining multiple tissues with appropriate methodologies when the clinical phenotype or somatic findings raise suspicion of ChiCaP.

A key strength of this study lies in its three-pronged diagnostic strategy uniformly applied across centers, integrating systematic clinical phenotyping, germline WGS analyzed through the 189-gene panel, and analysis of tumor data of cases harboring candidate predisposing variants. This multimodal framework was applied to nearly all children diagnosed with acute leukemia in Sweden during the study period, reflecting the unselected, prospective, and nationwide design of the GMS-ChiCaP cohort. The use of fibroblast-derived DNA as the germline source in the majority of cases further strengthens the analytical validity of our findings. Although the pathogenic variants identified in this study were confined to exonic regions and would have been detectable by exome sequencing or targeted panels, WGS enables detection of variant classes beyond the reach of exome-based approaches.

Limitations include reliance on a predefined in silico gene panel, which may miss relevant variants outside the curated list; failure to detect mosaic variants present at levels below approximately 20%; and the exclusion of novel gene discovery approaches apart from the 11 patients in whom trio WGS was performed even though this was not within the scope of our study. Reasons for declining study participation were not systematically recorded during the consent process, limiting our ability to fully characterize non-participation. The small T-ALL and AML cohort sizes constrain statistical power. In approximately 3% of the cohort, germline DNA was derived from remission blood or bone marrow rather than fibroblasts, which in principle carries a risk of somatic-to-germline misclassification; apart from the case with mosaic trisomy 21, none of these patients harbored a germline finding. Although cultured skin fibroblasts remain the preferred germline source in hematological malignancies because the culture process eliminates contaminating hematopoietic cells, cultures typically require 3–4 weeks from biopsy to DNA extraction 59 , contributing to the inherent delay in germline analysis in this clinical setting.

Looking ahead, trio WGS remains particularly advantageous, for resolving previously undiagnosed syndromes and sequencing of parents supports segregation analysis that reduces the interpretive burden associated with the large number of variants of uncertain significance. Large, harmonized multicenter studies pairing standardized phenotyping with comprehensive omics—including long-read trio-WGS, deep exome sequencing for mosaicism detection, transcriptomics, epigenomics, functional assays and proteomics—combined with systematic somatic-germline integration, will be essential to advance ChiCaP diagnostics, refine risk stratification, and identify new leukemia predisposition genes.

In conclusion, we demonstrate that our three-pronged diagnostic strategy is feasible in clinical practice and valid for universal cancer predisposition screening in childhood acute leukemia, and we therefore advocate its implementation where resources allow. Because the genetic basis of leukemia predisposition is highly heterogeneous, focused germline gene panels restricted to actionable cancer predisposition genes are unlikely to capture the full spectrum of ChiCaP diagnoses. The choice of testing strategy should accordingly reflect local policies and resources, including the capacity for pre-test genetic counseling, as well as the decision of whether to restrict analysis to genes directly relevant to the child’s cancer or to extend it to a broader set encompassing solid tumor predisposition genes.

Ethical approval was obtained from the Swedish Ethical Review Authority (Etikprövningsmyndigheten), the single national authority responsible for ethical review of research involving human participants in Sweden. Under Swedish law (the Ethical Review Act, SFS 2003:460), approval from this authority applies to all participating sites; no separate site-specific approvals are required or issued by individual hospitals or regions. Accordingly, the following permits cover sample and data collection at all six participating pediatric oncology centers (Astrid Lindgren Children’s Hospital, Karolinska University Hospital; Akademiska Children’s Hospital, Uppsala University Hospital; Crown Princess Victoria Children’s Hospital, Linköping University Hospital; Queen Silvia Children’s Hospital, Sahlgrenska University Hospital; Childhood Cancer Center, Skåne University Hospital; and Norrlands University Hospital, Umeå): 2021-04135 (tumor–normal WGS analysis) and 2019-04746 (trio WGS analysis). Register data were analyzed under ethical permits 2018/1849-32 and 2023-06901-01. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants, either from legal guardians or for patients aged ≥15 years, directly from the patients themselves. Participants received no compensation. Study information and counseling were provided by trained clinicians in pediatric hemato-oncology and clinical genetics. Consent included the disclosure of germline findings consistent with ChiCaP syndromes, as well as other actionable incidental findings when identified.

Children under 18 years of age (median age at diagnosis 5 years, IQR [3.0-8.5]; [ n = 74 female, n = 107 male]) diagnosed with acute leukemia between 17 December 2021 and 30 April 2024 at one of the six pediatric oncology centers in Sweden were eligible for inclusion. Families were approached for participation at the time of leukemia diagnosis. Participation required written informed consent and the availability of germline DNA from either cultured skin fibroblasts (from skin biopsy), remission blood, or remission bone marrow sample. In addition, blood samples from both parents were collected. To account for the possibility of dual diagnoses, all children diagnosed with cancer during the study period were included regardless of pre-existing genetic predisposition syndromes, as patients may harbor additional, previously unrecognized pathogenic germline variants. Not all eligible patients could be enrolled primarily due to logistic challenges in obtaining written informed consent.

Baseline characteristics were recorded for all participants, including sex, age at diagnosis and diagnosis type. Sex was obtained from medical records and verified using sex-chromosome dosage from WGS. Sex and gender were not analyzed as variables, as germline cancer-predisposition variants were evaluated irrespective of sex and gender.

At enrollment, pre-test genetic counseling was performed and a standardized clinical assessment for potential underlying ChiCaP was conducted using a form adapted from established screening tools for all types of childhood cancers, as described by Tesi et al. 26 and in the Supplementary Information . Information was categorized into four ChiCaP criteria: (1) family history, including familial cancer or parental consanguinity; (2) multiple primary malignancies and/or severe toxicity to treatment in the child; (3) other features, including non-malignant phenotypes suggestive of a predisposition syndrome; and (4) malignancy type, based on tumor types known to be enriched for genetic predisposition 26 . Positive family history of cancer was defined as meeting at least one of the following criteria across three generations (parents, siblings, parents’ siblings, cousins, grandparents, and grandparents’ siblings): consanguinity of the child’s parents; at least one relative with cancer before age 18; a parent or sibling/half-sibling with cancer before age 50; at least two relatives on the same side of the family with cancer before age 50; at least one relative with multiple cancers; or at least one relative with the same type of cancer/tumor as the child. For this study, only criteria 1, 2, and 3 were evaluated. A supplementary ChiCaP criteria form was completed exclusively for children who exhibited an unusually severe toxicity reaction or were diagnosed with one of the following conditions: AML or MDS with karyotype monosomy 7/7q-, BCP-ALL with low hypodiploidy (31–39 chromosomes), or BCP-ALL with iAMP21. Fulfilling at least two of the main criteria, one main criteria with two or more sub-criteria or a somatic variant triggering reflex testing was regarded as high-risk clinical criteria.

While patients were recruited across six centers, germline and tumor genomic analyses were centralized to four regional genomics nodes—Gothenburg, Lund, Stockholm, Uppsala - following local protocols. Results were returned in written form to the treating physicians and documented in patients’ medical records. If ChiCaP was diagnosed, the patient was referred for genetic counseling. Clinical follow-up data were obtained from chart review.

Primary dermal fibroblasts were isolated from skin punch biopsies obtained simultaneously with diagnostic bone marrow sampling. Biopsies were enzymatically dissociated with collagenase type II (Worthington Biochemical Corporation) prior to plating. Fibroblasts were cultured either in AmnioMAX-II Complete Medium (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific) or in an in-house medium comprising RPMI 1640 (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and Ham’s F-10 Nutrient Mix (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific), according to site-specific routine practice. Genomic DNA was extracted from cultured fibroblasts, remission blood, or bone marrow using standard protocols.

Germline WGS was performed at 30x coverage using clinical bioinformatic pipelines established for rare disease diagnostics across four national Clinical genomics nodes. Pipelines used in all nodes (Stockholm, Lund, Gothenburg and Uppsala) were described in detail in the Supplementary Information . Depending on local protocols, sequence alignment was performed to either the hg19 or hg38 human reference genome. In general, our bioinformatic pipelines for WGS were designed to detect SNVs, indels, CNVs, and SVs. For SNV and indel calling, the Stockholm and Uppsala nodes employed DeepVariant (v.1.2.0-v.1.6.0) 60 , a deep neural network-based germline variant caller, was employed. During candidate variant generation, DeepVariant requires a minimum of two reads supporting the alternate allele and a minimum variant-supporting read fraction of 0.12 for both SNVs and indels (the vsc_min_fraction_snps and vsc_min_fraction_indels parameters). While this means that variants with a VAF as low as approximately 12% may be considered as candidates, DeepVariant is trained on germline data where expected allele fractions cluster around 50% (heterozygous) or 100% (homozygous). Consequently, its sensitivity for mosaic variants decreases at lower VAFs and may vary with variant type and genomic context. The Gothenburg and Lund nodes used Sentieon DNAscope (version 202308.01), a machine learning-based germline variant caller. In the Lund pipeline, a hard VAF filter of 20% was applied, excluding any variant below this threshold; no such hard filter was applied in the other pipelines. As all callers used in this study are designed and trained for germline variant detection, reliable detection of mosaic variants below approximately 20% VAF cannot be guaranteed, and sensitivity may further vary with variant type, genomic context, and local sequencing coverage.

Variant filtering was restricted to 189 established cancer predisposition genes (Supplementary Data 1 ) included in the ChiCaP panel, which was designed in 2020 based on stringent evidence criteria. The gene list followed certain rules such as replicated links to cancer risk, high or well-documented penetrance, and supporting segregation or functional data, as well as supporting evidence from at least five unrelated affected individuals 61 . The panel was version-locked in 2020 and applied unchanged to all samples. Evidence for leukemia risk in TBRS was only emerging, with three hematological cases reported by 2021 32 , 33 ; therefore, DNMT3A was not included. Variant assessment followed routine clinical diagnostic practice at each center, focused on coding and splice-region variants within the gene panel. Predicted splice effects were assessed using in silico tools, including SpliceAI (generated as a separate annotation within the analysis pipelines where available) and the splice-prediction algorithms implemented in Alamut TM Visual Plus (SOFiA GENETICS), alongside population allele frequencies (gnomAD). Review was extended to deeper intronic regions on a case-by-case basis where clinical suspicion warranted, or where variants had previously been reported as (likely) pathogenic in ClinVar. No clinically significant deep intronic variants were identified.

SNVs, insertions/deletions (INDELs), CNVs and structural variants (SVs) were interpreted by clinical laboratory geneticists and clinical geneticists according to guidelines from the American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG)/Association for Molecular Pathology (AMP) or gene-specific guidelines, considering the syndrome’s known inheritance pattern 62 , 63 . We established harmonized stringent variant reporting criteria to be used for variants identified in the ChiCaP study: P and LP variants scored as ACMG class 4 (LP) and 5 (P) were reported if: (1) they fitted the known inheritance pattern for the specific ChiCaP syndrome (e.g., biallelic P/LP variants in ATM ) or constituted heterozygous P/LP variants in genes causative of high-risk dominant adult-onset cancer predisposition syndromes (e.g., BRCA1/2 , Lynch syndrome, PTEN , etc.). Heterozygous variants in moderate-risk genes for adult-onset cancers (e.g., heterozygous P/LP variant in ATM ) were not reported. Variants of uncertain significance defined as ACMG class 3 were reported only when both the variant characteristics indicated pathogenicity (i.e., not present in normal variation databases, high local ranking, compound variant present for autosomal recessive genes) and the patients´ phenotype had clinical presentation in line with the phenotype described for the affected gene. In these cases, segregation analysis with parental samples was performed—e.g., to prove de novo origin of the variant - prior to variant classification as P/LP.

For the six patients where a remission blood or bone marrow sample was used as the germline DNA source, candidate germline variants were cross-referenced against paired leukemia WGS data. Variant origin was assessed using variant allele fraction information to distinguish true germline variants from potential somatic contamination.

In patients with positive ChiCaP criteria but a negative 189-gene panel result, trio WGS was performed where parental samples were available, extending the analysis a broader set of disease-associated genes comprising all OMIM 64 Morbid genes known at the time of analysis (Supplementary Data 3 ). WGS was performed at Clinical Genomics, Stockholm, Sweden using the Illumina HiSeq X Ten or NovaSeq 6000 platforms, employing a 30x PCR-free paired-end WGS protocol. Genomic variants (SNVs and INDELs) were called using the Mutation Identification Pipeline (MIP; https://github.com/Clinical-Genomics/MIP ) 65 , with DeepVariant as the variant caller, aligned to the GRCh37 (hg19) reference genome. In addition to SNVs and INDELs, the pipeline includes analysis of structural variants (deletions, duplications, and inversions), short tandem repeat expansions, and SMN1 copy number assessment. Variants were filtered per family for de novo events, X-linked inheritance, autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive inheritance (homozygous or compound heterozygous). For autosomal recessive inheritance, two variants in trans in the same gene were required. Only sequence variants with an allele frequency below 1% in the general population, affecting exons or exon-intron boundaries, were considered. Called variants were annotated and prioritized using an in-house pathogenicity scoring system, genmod ( https://github.com/Clinical-Genomics/genmod) , that assigns a rank score based on multiple parameters including allele frequency, predicted protein impact, gene intolerance, inheritance model compatibility, variant consequence, evolutionary conservation, variant call quality, predicted deleteriousness, clinical significance, and splicing predictions. Variants classified as P/LP in ClinVar with a gold star review status were always retained regardless of frequency or consequence. A detailed description of the trio WGS analysis pipeline used here has been reported previously 65 – 67 . Confirmatory testing of identified variants was carried out using orthogonal methods, following established procedures at each participating laboratory.

DNA extracted from diagnostic bone marrow specimens underwent WGS analysis at 90x coverage using clinical bioinformatic pipelines established for tumor diagnostics across four national clinical genomics nodes. Pipelines used in all nodes (Gothenburg, Lund, Stockholm and Uppsala) were described in detail in the Supplementary Information .

A somatic finding with VAF above 40% in genes associated with leukemia predisposition triggered a reflex testing. Second-hit analysis was conducted on tumor samples from patients harboring P/LP germline variants in tumor suppressor genes. Second hits were categorized into three groups: (1) second mutations, comprising somatic SNVs and INDELs affecting the same gene; (2) CN-LOH, defined as LOH detected through B-allele frequency analysis or variant allele frequency exceeding 70% for the germline variant in the absence of copy-number alterations; and (3) SVs. Somatic tumor findings were limited to P/LP variants of diagnostic and/or prognostic relevance defined by study protocols ALLTogether for ALL and NOPHO-DBH-AML-2012 for AML 68 , 69 and through an additional analysis using the ChiCaP gene panel for second-hit detection.

Standard-of-care diagnostic tests for acute leukemia were performed alongside WGTS according to ongoing study protocols (mentioned above). Standard-of-care diagnostic tests for pediatric ALL and AML in Sweden comprise various cytogenetic and molecular genetic analyses, including chromosomal G-banding analysis, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis, targeted analysis, gene panel sequencing, chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) or multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) according to well-established standard protocols. The analyses were performed in five Swedish university hospital laboratories in Gothenburg, Lund, Stockholm, Uppsala and Umeå.

Systematic germline predisposition testing was not conducted. Reflex germline testing was performed when the leukemia karyotype (i.e., monosomy 7/7q-, low hypodiploidy (31-39 chromosomes), iAMP21) indicated an underlying germline predisposition.

To determine whether the same parental chromosome 21 was duplicated across tissues and malignancies in SE_AL029, we identified 24 informative single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) distributed across chromosome 21. SNPs (hg19) were selected based on a biased signal on the SNP array in the skin fibroblast sample (array ratio 2.0), indicating allelic imbalance consistent with trisomy. Genomic positions were translated to the GRCh38 reference assembly. For the ALL sample, variant allele frequencies (VAFs) were extracted from WGS data. For the fibroblast sample, the allelic ratio was calculated from SNP array signal intensities as “alternative signal”/(“alternative signal”+“reference signal”) for the corresponding allele. Concordance of the duplicated allele was assessed across all available sample types.

To assess the population coverage of the GMS-ChiCaP study and address potential sources of bias, we conducted a comparative analysis using aggregated data from the Swedish Childhood Cancer Registry (SCCR) 7 . The SCCR is a National Quality Registry used to evaluate treatment outcomes for children diagnosed with cancer. No individual-level registry data were analyzed. For comparison with data from the GMS-ChiCaP study, we extracted aggregated data on cancer diagnoses registered between 17 December 2021 and 30 April 2024. Patients were included in the study cohort based on the date when their sample (e.g., skin biopsy or remission blood) for germline analysis reached the Department of Clinical Genetics, not on the date of leukemia diagnosis. Therefore, the cohorts differ slightly at the beginning and end of the study period.

Data collected through the ChiCaP criteria form were manually reviewed and assessed for fulfillment of ChiCaP criteria developed by Tesi et al. 26 and detailed in Supplementary Information. Additional conditions were added specifically for familial history of hematological malignancies: FDR_SDR_blood_cancer (first- and second-degree relative with hematological malignancy regardless of age at diagnosis); FDR_blood_cancer (first-degree relative with hematological malignancy regardless of age at diagnosis); SDR_blood_cancer (second-degree relative with hematological malignancy regardless of age at diagnosis); TDR_blood_cancer (third-degree relative with hematological malignancy regardless of age at diagnosis). All the conditions used to evaluate the family history and the non-cancer medical history in the ChiCaP criteria form are available in Supplementary Information.

No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size; all eligible patients who consented were included. No data were excluded from the analyses. As this was an observational cohort study, randomization and blinding were not applicable. Data were analyzed as recorded, without imputation. Proportions are reported using the number of patients with available data for the variable in question as the denominator; denominators therefore vary between variables and are reported throughout as n / N (%) or % ( n / N ). Germline sequencing results were available for all 181 patients, so the denominator for the primary diagnostic yield estimate is complete. Descriptive statistics were used for demographic and clinical characteristics: categorical variables are presented as frequencies and percentages, and continuous variables as medians with interquartile ranges (IQR). No inferential hypothesis testing was performed. Binomial 95% confidence intervals for proportions were calculated using the hybrid Wilson/Brown method. All analyses and figure visualizations were performed using GraphPad Prism version 10.5.0 or 11.0.2 and can be reproduced using the Source Data and Supplementary files.

The study is reported in accordance with the STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) statement for cohort studies. The completed STROBE checklist is provided with this article.
Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

articles.title: Broadly neutralizing antibodies target the coronavirus fusion peptide.
articles.authors: Dacon C, Tucker C, Peng L, Lee CD, Lin TH, Yuan M, Cong Y, Wang L, Purser L, Williams JK, Pyo CW, Kosik I, Hu Z, Zhao M, Mohan D, Cooper AJR, Peterson M, Skinner J, Dixit S, Kollins E, Huzella L, Perry D, Byrum R, Lembirik S, Drawbaugh D, Eaton B, Zhang Y, Yang ES, Chen M, Chen M, Leung K, Weinberg RS, Pegu A, Geraghty DE, Davidson E, Douagi I, Moir S, Yewdell JW, Schmaljohn C, Crompton PD, Holbrook MR, Nemazee D, Mascola JR, Wilson IA, Tan J.
articles.abstract: The potential for future coronavirus outbreaks highlights the need to broadly target this group of pathogens. We use an epitope-agnostic approach to identify six monoclonal antibodies that bind to spike proteins from all seven human-infecting coronaviruses. All six antibodies target the conserved fusion peptide region adjacent to the S2' cleavage site. COV44-62 and COV44-79 broadly neutralize alpha and beta coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2 Omicron subvariants BA.2 and BA.4/5, albeit with lower potency than RBD-specific antibodies. In crystal structures of Fabs COV44-62 and COV44-79 with the SARS-CoV-2 fusion peptide, the fusion peptide epitope adopts a helical structure and includes the arginine at the S2' cleavage site. COV44-79 limited disease caused by SARS-CoV-2 in a Syrian hamster model. These findings highlight the fusion peptide as a candidate epitope for next-generation coronavirus vaccine development.
paragraphs: The potential for future coronavirus outbreaks highlights the need to broadly target this group of pathogens. We use an epitope-agnostic approach to identify six monoclonal antibodies that bind to spike proteins from all seven human-infecting coronaviruses. All six antibodies target the conserved fusion peptide region adjacent to the S2' cleavage site. COV44-62 and COV44-79 broadly neutralize alpha and beta coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2 Omicron subvariants BA.2 and BA.4/5, albeit with lower potency than RBD-specific antibodies. In crystal structures of Fabs COV44-62 and COV44-79 with the SARS-CoV-2 fusion peptide, the fusion peptide epitope adopts a helical structure and includes the arginine at the S2' cleavage site. COV44-79 limited disease caused by SARS-CoV-2 in a Syrian hamster model. These findings highlight the fusion peptide as a candidate epitope for next-generation coronavirus vaccine development.

Coronaviruses consist of four genera of viruses that infect birds and mammals ( 1 ). Seven coronaviruses are known to cause human disease: the alphacoronaviruses HCoV-229E and HCoV-NL63, as well as the betacoronaviruses HCoV-OC43, HCoV-HKU1, SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2. While the first four coronaviruses generally cause mild disease, the latter three have caused serious outbreaks in recent years. In particular, the ongoing coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic by SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in more than six million deaths since the first cases were identified in 2019 ( 2 ). The currently dominant SARS-CoV-2 Omicron BA.2, BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/BA.5 subvariants are at least partially resistant to most available vaccines and antibody therapeutics ( 3 – 6 ). Furthermore, two coronaviruses previously linked only to animal infection were recently detected in individuals with flu-like symptoms ( 7 , 8 ). These developments highlight the importance of targeting conserved and functionally essential sites on coronaviruses.

Coronavirus infection is a multi-step process that involves enzymatic cleavage and rearrangement of the surface spike protein ( 9 ). The SARS-CoV-2 spike contains two cleavage sites: a furin cleavage site at the boundary of the S1 and S2 subunits, and an S2' site that is conserved in all coronaviruses. The spike protein is thought to be cleaved at the S1/S2 site during virus assembly, leaving the S1 and S2 subunits non-covalently linked. During entry, the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein uses the receptor-binding domain (RBD) on the S1 subunit to engage angiotensin-converting enzyme-2 (ACE2) on target cells. Following receptor binding, the S1 subunit is shed and the S2' site is cleaved by the membrane enzyme transmembrane serine protease 2 (TMPRSS2) or endosomal cathepsins ( 1 ), leading to the insertion of the fusion peptide into the cell membrane and viral fusion.

Much of the protection provided by COVID-19 vaccines arises from neutralizing antibodies that target the RBD ( 10 ). Likewise, all currently available therapeutic monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) target this domain ( 3 ). However, spike elements that participate in the subsequent stages of infection involve the more complex S2 fusion machinery with many moving parts and these elements are more conserved than the RBD, which so far has been capable of retaining or even increasing binding to ACE2 despite a variety of mutations ( 11 ). Therefore, these sites are worth exploring as targets for novel COVID-19 vaccines and therapeutics that retain efficacy against new variants and protect against a wider range of coronaviruses. Progress in this direction has started with recent studies identifying several mAbs that target the conserved stem helix ( 12 – 16 ) and using unbiased approaches to screen for mAbs of interest ( 17 – 20 ). Here we undertake a large-scale survey of the binding landscape of broadly reactive mAbs against coronaviruses.

To identify individuals likely to harbor B cells that produce broadly reactive mAbs, we used a multiplex bead-based assay to examine plasma samples of 142 donors from a previously described cohort of COVID-19 convalescent individuals ( 20 ). We assessed plasma immunoglobulin G (IgG) reactivity toward spike glycoproteins of the seven human coronaviruses: SARS-CoV-2 (Wuhan Hu-1), SARS-CoV-1, MERS-CoV, HCoV-HKU1, HCoV-OC43, HCoV-NL63 and HCoV-229E. Nineteen donors were selected for mAb isolation and characterization based on plasma IgG reactivity to the spike proteins of SARS-CoV-2 and at least two other betacoronaviruses (fig. S1A).

We next interrogated human IgG + memory B cells (MBCs) from the selected donors using a two-stage screen to prioritize isolating mAbs with the greatest possible breadth of reactivity. First, we screened supernatants from 673,671 stimulated IgG + B cells for binding to the coronavirus spike panel used in the plasma screen. Supernatants from only 2% ( n = 211) of the MBC culture wells met our criteria for broad reactivity by binding at least three betacoronavirus spike proteins ( Fig. 1A ). Next, we developed an optofluidics assay to isolate individual MBCs of interest using the Berkeley Lights Beacon system (fig. S1B). Candidate MBCs identified in the supernatant screen were sorted individually into nanoliter-volume pens and assessed in real-time for secretion of mAbs that bound to beads coated with a cocktail of MERS-CoV and HCoV-OC43 spikes, followed by beads coated with SARS-CoV-2 spike. Double positive MBCs were exported for single-cell reverse transcription-PCR (RT-PCR) and antibody production as recombinant IgG1. In total, we obtained 60 IgG mAbs with reactivity to at least three coronaviruses.

( A ) Analysis of the frequency of MBCs expressing broadly reactive antibodies from n = 19 donors. Values in parentheses represent the percentage of SARS-CoV-2 reactive supernatants that also bind the specified subsets of non-SARS coronavirus spikes. A total of 10,356 MBC culture supernatants (50-100 B cells/well) was screened. ( B ) Phylogenetic relationships across the coronavirus spike proteins targeted by the broadly reactive mAbs were inferred by the Neighbor-Joining method in MEGA11 using full-length amino-acid sequences of CoV spike proteins. Branch lengths are drawn to scale and bootstrap values from 500 samplings are shown on the branches. The scale bar represents the number of amino acid substitutions per site. ( C ) Heat map representing the binding of broadly reactive mAbs to spike proteins from coronaviruses across the alpha, beta and deltacoronavirus genera. H1 hemagglutinin was included as a negative control for mAb binding experiments and area under the curve (AUC) values for each antigen are shown after subtraction with values for the negative control antigen CD4. ( D ) Values represent antibody titer at 50% neutralization (NT 50 ) against SARS-CoV-2 Wuhan Hu-1, SARS-CoV-1, MERS-CoV, HCoV-NL63 and HCoV-229E envelope-pseudotyped lentivirus, as well as authentic HCoV-OC43. For Assay Scripps , values are average of two experiments. For values with the † symbol, one NT 50 was determinable and one was not (i.e., >100 μg/mL), and the determinable NT 50 is shown. Negative controls mAbs were anti-CoV-2 RBD CV503 (for OC43 assay) ( 20 ), anti-influenza HA CR9114 (for Assay NIH except OC43) ( 41 ) and anti-dengue DEN3 (for Assay Scripps ) ( 42 ). NT50 values were calculated using the dose-response-inhibition model with 5-parameter Hill slope equation in GraphPad Prism 9. ( E ) Neutralization of SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern (pseudovirus) by COV44-62 and COV44-79.

To fully interrogate their breadth, we tested the 60 mAbs for binding to spikes from the seven human coronaviruses. Only six mAbs, COV91-27, COV44-62, COV44-79, COV77-04, COV77-39 and COV78-36, bound to spike proteins from all seven coronaviruses ( Fig. 1, B and C ). Notably, four of the six also bound to spike from two new coronaviruses recently associated with human disease: Canine CoV HuPn-2018 (CCoV-HuPn-2018) and Porcine Deltacoronavirus 0081-4 (PDCoV-0081-4) ( 7 , 8 ) ( Fig. 1C ). The six broadly reactive mAbs were isolated from four different donors and were encoded by four different heavy chain variable (VH) genes (VH1-2, VH3-30, VH4-59, VH5-10-1) (table S1). Five mAbs were highly mutated, with VH nucleotide mutation frequencies ranging from 10 to 13% (fig. S1C). Given that these mAbs were isolated from COVID-19 convalescent individuals in New York approximately one month after the first outbreak in March 2020, these mutation levels suggest that the B cells were primed during an earlier seasonal coronavirus infection and possibly reactivated during SARS-CoV-2 infection.

We assessed the neutralizing potency of the six mAbs against SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV-1, MERS-CoV, HCoV-NL63 and HCoV-229E envelope pseudotyped viruses, as well as authentic HCoV-OC43. COV44-62 and COV44-79 showed the broadest functional reactivity, neutralizing the betacoronaviruses SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV-1 and HCoV-OC43, as well as the alphacoronavirus HCoV-NL63 and HCoV-229E ( Fig. 1D and fig. S1D). Moreover, both mAbs neutralized SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern, including the Omicron BA.2 and BA.4/5 subvariants, as well as authentic SARS-CoV-2 ( Fig. 1E and fig. S1E). COV44-62 also neutralized MERS-CoV, whereas no other mAbs neutralized this virus within the concentrations tested.

To determine the domain of SARS-CoV-2 spike that was targeted by the six broadly reactive mAbs, we assessed mAb binding to the SARS-CoV-2 S2 subunit, as well as the RBD and N-terminal domain (NTD) of the S1 subunit. All six mAbs bound only to the S2 subunit ( Fig. 2A ). VJ germline-reverted versions of the broadly neutralizing mAbs COV44-62 and COV44-79 showed weaker binding to S2 than the mutated versions (fig. S2A), suggesting that somatic mutations were important for improving binding to the target site. A surface plasmon resonance (SPR) kinetics assay determined the binding affinity of antigen-binding fragments (Fabs) derived from these mAbs for pre-fusion stabilized whole SARS-CoV-2 spike (2P, with an intact S1/S2 cleavage site) and the unmodified S2 subunit. The Fabs bound with low-to-moderate nanomolar affinity to both proteins, but their affinity for the S2 subunit was 3- to 76-fold higher than their affinity for whole spike ( Fig. 2B and fig. S2A). There were no substantial differences between the six Fabs in their affinity for the S2 subunit. The mAbs showed reduced binding to a form of S2 that had been stabilized with two proline mutations (S2-2P) and bound more poorly still to a further stabilized version with six proline mutations (S2-HexaPro) ( Fig. 2C ). SPR-based competition showed that the six mAbs competed for the same binding site on the S2 subunit ( Fig. 2D ), but none competed with S2P6, a control mAb targeting the stem helix region ( 12 ), indicating their specificity for a distinct site on S2.

( A ) Titration curves for mAb binding to selected regions within the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein: the receptor binding domain (RBD), N-terminal domain (NTD) and the S2 subunit. Interconnected data points are shown without curve fitting. L9 is a malaria-specific mAb used as a negative control ( 43 ). ( B ) On-rates, off-rates and dissociation constants of the six fusion peptide Fabs for binding to SARS-CoV-2 pre-fusion stabilized spike (2P) with an unmodified furin cleavage site and the non-stabilized S2 subunit. ( C ) Fusion peptide mAb binding (AUC) to wild-type SARS-CoV-2 S2 subunit and S2 subunit constructs modified with two (2P) or six (HexaPro) stabilizing proline mutations. ( D ) Epitope binning of broadly reactive antibodies versus the S2 stem-helix targeting mAb S2P6. All included antibodies were tested as both ligands and analytes. Solid lines indicate two-way competition while hashed lines indicate one-way competition. Red boxes indicate competing antibody pairs, green boxes indicate non-competing antibody pairs and hashed filling indicates self-competition.

To further interrogate the specificity of these mAbs, we performed SPR-based peptide mapping using an array of 15-mer overlapping peptides that spanned the entire SARS-CoV-2 S2 subunit (Ser686 to Lys1211, Accession # YP_009724390.1 ). All six mAbs bound to peptides 42-44, which share the 815 RSFIEDLLF 823 motif ( Fig. 3A ). This motif is located within the SARS-CoV-2 fusion peptide region, directly C-terminal to the S2' cleavage site. To determine the diversity of this region across coronaviruses, we selected 34 viral isolates representing each of the coronavirus genera – alpha , beta , gamma , and delta ( Fig. 3B ). Each amino-acid position in the 815 RSFIEDLLF 823 motif was conserved in >90% of all viruses selected except F 817 , which was conserved in <50% of isolates examined ( Fig. 3, B and C ). The fusion peptide appears partially surface-exposed in a range of coronavirus spike proteins, including SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV and MHV ( 21 , 22 ) ( Fig. 3C and fig. S3A). However, antibody access to this site may be partially occluded by the S1 subunit on an adjacent protomer, consistent with their stronger binding to the S2 subunit relative to SARS-CoV-2 spike ( Fig. 2B and fig. S3B).

( A ) Heat map of SARS-CoV-2 S2 peptide array. Binding responses were assessed by SPR using a 15-mer peptide array with 12 aa overlay covering the entire S2 subunit. Each column within the map represents a single peptide. The white triangle shows the S1/S2 cleavage site and the black triangle indicates the S2' cleavage site. FP, fusion peptide; HR1, heptad repeat 1; C helix, central helix; CD, connector domain; SH, stem helix; HR2, heptad repeat 2. ( B ) Sequence alignment of the fusion peptide from 34 viral isolates representing a diverse group of coronaviruses across four genera. Performed using MAFFT v7.450 using a BLOSUM62 scoring matrix and the L-INS-I algorithm. ( C ) Sequence conservation of pre-fusion SARS-CoV-2 spike protein (PDB 6VSB) with the fusion peptide (aa 816-843) highlighted in a black outline. Inset shows a magnified view of this region. ( D ) Alanine scan evaluating the binding of COV44-62 and COV44-79 to the SARS-CoV2 fusion peptide. Responses were normalized to the wild-type sequence. A cut-off of 20% (brown hashed line) was used to identify residues that were critical for binding. ( E ) Sequence logo plot of diversity within the fusion peptide region of coronaviruses from 34 isolates, built using WebLogo 3. Height is proportional to the probability of an amino acid at a given position and amino-acid residues are colored by charge. Narrow stacks (amino acids) indicate deletions or gaps in the sequences. Numbering is based on the SARS-CoV-2 Wuhan-Hu-1 sequence. The key residues in the epitope footprints of mAbs COV44-62 (red) and COV44-79 (blue), based on peptide alanine scanning, are highlighted above the logo plot. ( F ) Amino acids critical for the binding of COV44-62 and COV44-79 identified by shotgun alanine mutagenesis of S2 residues on whole spike protein. Only fusion peptide residues are shown here. Key residues were identified based on a <20% signal relative to wild-type spike (brown hashed line), with no corresponding loss of signal for a control mAb, which targets the spike protein but does not bind to this site (see fig. S3C).

That these mAbs target the fusion peptide is consistent with their reduced binding to the HexaPro S2 construct ( Fig. 2C ), which includes a non-conservative F817P mutation at this site ( 23 ). To identify critical amino acids for mAb binding, we performed an alanine scan on a peptide encompassing residues 810 to 830 and focused on residues targeted by the broadly neutralizing mAbs COV44-62 and COV44-79 ( Fig. 3D ). Four amino acids, E819, D820, L822 and F823, were important for binding of COV44-62, where mutation of the F823 residue abolished binding. Similarly, critical residues for the binding of COV44-79 were E819, D820 and F823, but also included R815 at the S2' cleavage site ( Fig. 3D ). All five residues identified as important for COV44-62 or COV44-79 binding are among the most conserved residues in the coronavirus spike protein. D820 and L822 are completely conserved, while R815, E819 and F823 are conserved in 34 out of 35 coronaviruses ( Fig. 3, B and E ). Amino-acid mutations at the peptide level may have different effects from mutations in the intact spike protein, where modified interactions with surrounding residues may also affect antibody binding. Therefore, we screened the six mAbs using a shotgun alanine mutagenesis approach, whereby every amino acid in the S2 subunit of intact spike was individually mutated to generate a panel of spike mutants ( Fig. 3F and fig. S3, C and D). In general, this assay identified a greater number of residues as important for mAb binding, including some with a more intermediate phenotype. For COV44-62, D820, L822 and F823 were again crucial for binding, while K825 and D830, as well as R815, were also identified as important ( Fig. 3F ). For COV44-79, the results closely matched the peptide alanine scan, with the same four amino acids, R815, E819, D820 and F823, identified as the most critical. When the six mAbs were analyzed as a group, we found that only the four broadest neutralizing mAbs were negatively affected by the R815A mutation (fig. S4, A and B), suggesting that binding to the S2' cleavage site may be a distinguishing property of broadly neutralizing mAbs against this site.

To elucidate the molecular characteristics of anti-fusion peptide antibodies that neutralize SARS-CoV-2, the Fabs of the three broadest neutralizing mAbs COV44-62, COV44-79, and COV91-27 were complexed with 15-mer peptides containing the fusion peptide sequence ( Fig. 4 ). Crystal structures were determined to 1.46 Å, 2.8 Å and 2.3 Å resolution, respectively ( Fig. 4 , fig. S5 and table S2). Fourteen of the 15 peptide residues were visible in the electron density map for COV44-62 (fig. S5A), 13 of which have a buried surface area (BSA) >0 Å 2 in complex with antibody. For COV44-79, 12 of the 15 peptide residues were visible (fig. S5A), 10 of which have a buried surface >0 Å 2 . Similarly, in COV91-27, 12 peptide residues had interpretable density ( Fig. 4C and fig. S5A), with nine exhibiting a buried surface >0 Å 2 . The fusion peptide forms a helix as in the prefusion state of the SARS-CoV-2 spike (fig. S5B). All three complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) of the heavy chain (HC) of all three Fabs are involved in peptide recognition whereas CDR1 and CDR3 of the light chain (LC) of COV44-62 and only LCDR3 of COV44-79 and COV91-27 contact the peptide ( Fig. 4, A to C ). The BSA on each Fab is dominated by the heavy chain and is 791 Å 2 for COV44-62 (627 Å 2 by HC and 164 Å 2 by LC), 573 Å 2 for COV44-79 (505 Å 2 by HC and 129 Å 2 by LC), and 573 Å 2 for COV91-27 (447 Å 2 by HC and 126 Å 2 by LC). The fusion peptide makes side-chain and backbone H-bonds and salt bridges with COV44-62 mainly through K814, R815, E819, D820, L822, F823 and N824, and hydrophobic interactions through I818, L822, and F823 ( Fig. 4D ). These residues include the key residues, E819, D820, L822 and F823 identified by site-directed mutagenesis ( Fig. 3D ). The fusion peptide did not form as many interactions with COV44-79 and COV91-27 ( Fig. 4, E and F ). However, R815, E819, and D820 contributed H-bonds and salt bridges, and I818, L822, and F823 made hydrophobic interactions. In all three antibodies, R815, S816, I818, E819, D820, L822, and F823 contributed the most buried surface area to the interaction ( Fig. 4, G to I ). There was partial overlap between the residues of COV44-62 and COV44-79 that interacted with the fusion peptide and those that were mutated from germline (fig. S6), consistent with the reduction in binding of germline-reverted versions of these mAbs (fig. S2A). The structural results are consistent with the mutagenesis data with peptide and spike protein that identify the key binding residues ( Fig. 3, D to F , and fig. S3D). Importantly, the arginine at the S2' cleavage site is involved in recognition by these anti-fusion peptide antibodies. Although the antibodies all interact with one face of the fusion peptide helical structure (fig. S5D), their approach angles to the peptide differ. Superimposition of the fusion peptide structures onto an intact SARS-CoV-2 spike trimer structure in the pre-fusion state showed a potential clash with the S protein, suggesting that a conformational change or conformational dynamics around the fusion peptide is required to accommodate antibody targeting (fig. S5C). Notwithstanding, these antibodies have neutralization activity against SARS-CoV-2 and therefore are able to interact with the fusion peptide on the virus ( Fig. 1D ).

Cyan and yellow represent the heavy and light chains of the Fabs. Peptides are shown in green. H1, H2, H3, L1, and L3 denotes CDRs in the heavy (H) and light (L) chains. The resolution of the crystal structures are 1.46 Å, 2.8 Å, and 2.3 Å for the COV44-62, COV44-79, and COV91-27 complexes. Peptide residues observed in the crystal structure are in bold and residues involved in interaction with antibody (buried surface area >0 Å 2 ) are in red. ( D to F ) Details of the interactions between (D) COV44-62, (E) COV44-79, and (F) COV91-27 with the fusion peptide. V H and V L indicate the variable domains of the heavy (H) and light (L) chains. ( G to I ) Buried surface area (in gray) and accessible surface area (in white) of each residue of the fusion peptide in complex with antibody are shown in the stacked bar chart. Residues that form polar interactions with COV44-62, COV44-79, and COV91-27 are denoted with “H” if they form a hydrogen-bond or “S” for a salt bridge on top of the corresponding bar. Buried and accessible surface areas were calculated with PISA ( 44 ).

We compared the binding of polyclonal IgG from mRNA-1273-vaccinated donors (fig. S7A), COVID-19 convalescent individuals, and COVID-19-naïve individuals to the SARS-CoV-2 fusion peptide (peptide 43) ( Fig. 3A and fig. S7B). All COVID-19-naïve donors showed minimal binding to the peptide, indicating a minor contribution by previous seasonal coronavirus infections to circulating fusion peptide-specific IgG. While there was an increased response in several vaccinees after the 2nd vaccine dose ( P = 0.025), this was not enhanced by the administration of a booster. The COVID-19 convalescent donors did not have significantly higher responses than vaccinated donors ( P = 0.864 versus post-2nd dose). However, several convalescent donors had the highest responses in all three cohorts, suggesting that SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers a strong fusion peptide-specific antibody response in some individuals.

Spike-mediated cell fusion relies on insertion of the fusion peptide into the target cell membrane and thus might be inhibited by antibody binding to the fusion peptide. Consistent with this, COV44-62 and COV44-79 inhibited the fusion of cells expressing SARS-CoV-2 spike and cells expressing the ACE2 receptor in an imaging-based assay ( Fig. 5A ). We further tested the six fusion peptide-specific mAbs in a more quantitative assay wherein fusion would trigger the release of an enzyme that cleaves a chromogenic substrate. Only the mAbs that neutralized SARS-CoV-2 were able to strongly inhibit fusion ( Fig. 5B ).

( A ) Images of fusion between HeLa cells stably expressing SARS-CoV-2 spike (RFP) and HeLa cells stably expressing the ACE2 receptor (GFP) after counter-staining with Hoechst (blue). Cells were co-cultured in the presence of COV44-62, COV44-79 or without a mAb (control). Scale bar, 500 μm. ( B ) Fusion inhibition of six fusion peptide-specific mAbs in a quantitative assay. ( C ) Weight change for SARS-CoV-2 naïve animals versus virus-exposed animals that were mock-treated or treated with 16 mg/kg of mAb.
