This indicates a robust upper 2000 m OHC increase since 1955 of 449 [385, 519] ZJ. Quality-Control (QC) has become a primary error source recently, due to the difficulties detecting outliers in eddy-rich regions. Trend uncertainty sources differ from annual OHC: for 2005–2023, the upper 2000m trend is 10.9 [9.2, 11.4] ZJ yr −1 (0.68 [0.57, 0.71] Wm −2 ), with uncertainties from spatial gaps, mapping, QC, and climatology choice. The ocean warming rate increase from 2005–2023 is small but robust: 0.34 [0.19, 0.46] Wm −2 dec −1 . These comprehensive uncertainty estimates guide future improvements in the global ocean observing system.
Subject terms: Ocean sciences, Climate change

This study presents a comprehensive quantification of ocean heat content uncertainty since 1960 and shows a six-fold reduction in the global upper-2000m uncertainty in the last decade and a robust ocean warming.

Oceans store ~90% of Earth’s energy imbalance (EEI), making ocean heat content (OHC) change a critical climate indicator 1 – 4 . Observations show that the OHC has broken its warming record nine years in a row from 2017 to 2025 (ref. 5 ), and has a long-term acceleration since 1960 6 – 9 . The rapid ocean warming has become a significant concern for the ocean’s biological systems and for human society 3 , 10 . For example, thermal expansion contributes ~40% of the contemporary sea level rise and poses significant risks to low-lying coastal communities 2 . Ocean warming reduces the solubility of oxygen in the sea water and contributes to the ocean deoxygenation, threatening ocean life and marine fisheries 11 . Increase of ocean heat also super-charges tropical cyclones and increases their intensity and rainfall 12 . As an essential climate variable, OHC plays a crucial role in the interactions among Earth’s energy, water, and carbon cycles 3 , 13 , 14 .

Given its importance, substantial efforts have been made to estimate and understand OHC changes 3 , 4 , 9 , despite differences existing among different available OHC estimates 2 – 4 , 9 , 15 . For instance, a synthesis of 21 available datasets 15 reveals that the trend of global OHC from 2005 to 2020 ranges from 0.40 to 0.96 Wm −2 with an acceleration rate from −0.03 Wm −2 dec −1 to 1.11 Wm −2 dec −1 , revealing a substantial spread among the available estimates. Therefore, understanding the sources of errors and quantifying uncertainty is crucial to refining the OHC estimates over time and is important for improving the current global ocean observing system (GOOS). Additionally, as previous investigations reveal a critical mismatch of inter-annual variations between most in situ observation-based OHC estimates and net radiation imbalance (EEI) observed by satellite at the top of the atmosphere (TOA) 4 , 9 , understanding the sources of uncertainty will provide important clues for reconciling these EEI differences.

Several previous efforts have indeed been dedicated to comprehensively quantifying the OHC uncertainty, but have limitations of considering neither some important error sources nor the error covariances. The first comprehensive estimate of the OHC (0–700 m) uncertainty budget is Lyman et al. 16 , where four error sources from 1993 to 2008 were considered: combined quality-control and eXpendable BathyThermographs (XBT) bias correction, sampling, mapping, and climatology choice. That work identified XBT bias correction as the major source of error (with a maximum standard deviation of ~24 ZJ around 2000), whereas mapping played a secondary, but important, role (~9 ZJ).

As different approaches are used to estimate different error sources, inconsistencies occur and the uncertainties for each error source are not necessarily comparable. To resolve these issues, an international coordinated effort 16 used a set of consistent sensitivity experiments to quantify errors from three sources separately: XBT bias correction, mapping, and the choice of climatology from 1970 to 2008. Several alternative methodologies were used for each, and then the standard deviation of their resultant OHCs was calculated as a quantification of uncertainty. The regional uncertainty was then investigated in a follow-on study with the same experiments 17 . The mapping method to fill in inevitable sampling gaps was identified as the primary source of error in OHC calculation (mean standard deviation of 16.5 ZJ from 1970-2008), and the XBT bias correction uncertainty ranged from 8.0 to 17.9 ZJ since 1970. However, the overall uncertainty has not been defined because only parts of error sources were considered and the error covariances were not analyzed.

Limitations of previous efforts have made it unclear what contributes most to the uncertainty of OHC estimates and what the total uncertainty is. OHC uncertainty comes mainly from the following ten error sources: instrumental error 18 , quality control procedure 19 , biases in various instruments (XBT 20 , mechanical bathythermographs -MBT 21 , Bottle—BOT 22 , Autonomous Pinniped Bathythermographs -APB 23 ), vertical interpolation methods 24 , 25 , choices of climatology 26 , 27 , and data sampling/mapping 16 , 17 , 26 , 28 – 30 . Additionally, these uncertainty sources are not independent; for example, different QC systems flag and remove various amounts of data, which in turn impact ocean sampling and mapping accuracy. Furthermore, the uncertainty for different time scales (e.g., annual mean, inter-annual, decadal to multi-decadal changes, and long-term trends) should be different, as the errors are manifested differently at various time scales as the observing system has evolved or because different types of errors are correlated on different time scales (see results of this study). A comprehensive assessment of these error sources, accounting for error covariances, is the goal of this study.

To assess all the identified error sources and the error covariance, a Large-Ensemble approach is used for OHC uncertainty estimation. Briefly, for each major group of error sources (8 groups in total with 10 different error sources considered), we employed the three most up-to-date alternative techniques used in the literature for their estimation, and then these techniques were cross-used to derive final OHC estimates, allowing for a large ensemble to be constructed with ~900 members (Data and Methods). The ensemble is used to derive global and regional OHC uncertainty and the major contributors for different periods since 1955 (slightly before the International Geophysical Year when global OHC trend can be derived 3 , 31 ). The uncertainty and the error sources for estimating the OHC annual mean, trend and variability are quantified separately.

Global upper 2000 m OHC (OHC0-2000m) estimates suggest a robust increase since 1955 (449 [385, 519] ZJ, and 314 [281, 370] ZJ for 0–700 m; 468 [386, 535] ZJ for full-depth) with larger uncertainty in earlier periods revealed by the Large-Ensemble (Fig. 1a ). The overall OHC0-2000m uncertainty, represented by the range of the [5%, 95%] quantile of the Large-Ensemble, is reduced from ~111 ZJ for 1955–1965 to ~19 ZJ for 2014–2023 for the annual mean OHC, indicating a nearly six-fold reduction in uncertainty and an increased precision in the OHC estimate.

a Global upper 300 m, 700 m and 2000 m OHC estimate by IAP (Institute of Atmospheric Physics—IAP) data (central estimate) and its uncertainty envelope (5%-95% quantile of the large ensemble computed on an annual basis), relative to a 2010-2023 baseline (Unit: ZJ); b OHC0-2000 m uncertainty from 8 major error contributions (colored lines) and the total uncertainty estimated from the large-ensemble (5%–95% quantile range estimated on an annual basis, solid black line), compared with the ±1.64 standard deviation range (dashed grey line, Unit: ZJ); c Global OHC0-2000m variance and covariance time series from 1955 to 2023 calculated by Eq.( 1 ), including the variance of various error sources (colored lines), their sum (magenta line), the total variance of the large ensemble (black line), and the covariance term (pink line) (Unit: ZJ 2 ); d Fractional contributions of different error sources (positive colored shadings) and covariance (negative pink shading) to the total variance of global OHC0–2000 m estimates. The sum of contributions from all error sources and the covariance equals 100. (Unit: %).

The dramatic reduction of the uncertainty is attributed primarily to the decrease in mapping uncertainty (a combination of mapping/sampling and instrumental errors), which is progressively reduced from ~97 ZJ within 1955–1964 to ~7 ZJ for 2015–2023 (Fig. 1b, d ; Supplementary Figs. 4 , 6 ). The mapping uncertainty decrease is mainly linked to the substantial improvement of data coverage and sampling over time 28 , including the establishment of the Argo network since the beginning of this century which achieves a near-global open ocean coverage at upper ~2000 m 32 . The instrumental errors 18 are much smaller than the mapping error.

Before ~1980, the vertical interpolation method was the second largest source of OHC0-2000m uncertainty, on average ~60 ZJ from 1955 to 1980 (Fig. 1b, c, d ), associated with relatively lower vertical resolution of earlier temperature profile observations 24 , especially in the deep ocean below 700 m (Supplementary Fig. 4 ). There is a decadal-scale fluctuation of the vertical interpolation uncertainty, also mainly associated with the change of data resolution (Fig. 1c ). However, the impacts of vertical resolution also depend on other factors such as spatial distribution; for instance, if a low-resolution profile is located in a data-sparse area, the impacts will be much bigger than when it is surrounded by many high-resolution data. The large vertical-sampling uncertainty is revealed by a notable difference between the PCHIP and RR approaches; the former yields larger OHC long-term trends than the RR method 24 , 25 , 33 . PCHIP considers the shape of the typical ocean temperature profiles and is considered to be more physically sound 25 , 33 .

The choice of climatology is the third largest uncertainty before ~1980, reducing from ~34 ZJ within 1955–1965 to ~6 ZJ for 2014–2023 (Fig. 1b ). The climatology makes an impact because it is used to calculate the regional temperature anomalies that are input to the mapping procedure, and the impact of climatology is much larger in the deep ocean below 700 m, probably associated with less data there to estimate the climatology (Supplementary Fig. 4 ).

For the most recent period (after 2010), it is surprising that the total uncertainty increases from 2015 to 2023. Data QC has become the major source of error (~13 ZJ on average from 2010 to 2023), overwhelmingly dominating the OHC uncertainty (Fig. 1b ). Specifically, the QC uncertainty is ~1.7 times larger than mapping. An additional test using removing one of the two QC systems suggests a substantial reduction of the uncertainty range (e.g., CODC-QC only ensemble spread is ~10 ZJ within 2015–2023, compared with total uncertainty range of ~19 ZJ) and a reduced increasing trend since ~2015, confirming that QC is mainly responsible for the recent uncertainty increase. An investigation indicates that the WOD local climatological range in its QC check, which is constructed by all historical data, mainly represents the historical ocean conditions and thus removes more positive temperature anomalies in the eddy-rich regions (such as Boundary currents and Antarctic Circumpolar Currents) than CODC 34 (Supplementary Figs. 5 , 6 ).

Unlike previous assessments where instrumental biases are the major error source 16 , 26 , this study finds a moderate contribution of four instrumental biases, implying a substantial reduction in uncertainty after bias correction (i.e., there is a better agreement among the three correction schemes, which leads to a smaller spread among corrected data, indicating biases can be well corrected). The OHC0-2000m uncertainty due to bias correction is notable from the late 1970s to ~2000, exhibiting peaks exceeding 70 ZJ in certain years and contributing an average of ~35 ZJ (XBT) and ~24 ZJ (MBT) over 1980–2000 (Fig. 1b, d ). Although XBT data became a dominant data source from the late 1960s to 1980, the XBT data uncertainty is relatively small during 1960-1980 (~10 ZJ, Fig. 1b , d), indicating a consistent performance of the three XBT bias correction schemes 26 . Similarly, MBT bias correction uncertainty is only ~12 ZJ before 1980 (Fig. 1b, d ), suggesting consistent corrections of MBT data by different schemes. In addition, APB bias correction uncertainty is <1 ZJ since ~1997, where APB data become available (Fig. 1b, d ). The small APB bias uncertainty is because they are predominantly in the polar regions, and the impact on global OHC is not as large as other bias corrections (XBT/MBT). Moreover, the BOT bias correction is ~3 ZJ before 1990 and becomes near zero afterward because of the dismissal of BOT in recent decades (Fig. 1b, d ).

As the error sources are not independent, the sum of all uncertainties is larger than the total OHC0-2000m uncertainty (Fig. 1c ). This is expected because each technique uses the output from the other procedures or provides an input to another procedure, thus linking error sources. Interestingly, the total covariance changed over time, being larger in the earlier periods (Fig. 1c , d). This effect is induced by the smaller number and less precise measurements in the earlier periods, in particular before the deployment of Argo floats. The variance–covariance matrix of the global OHC0-2000m change (Fig. 2a ) shows substantial long-term covariances, which are dominated by multi-decadal scale covariances (>30 years) over decadal (10 – 30 years) and inter-annual scale covariances (<10 years) (Fig. 2 ), in particular before 2005 and the deployment of the Argo network. Hence the OHC errors are mainly manifested on decadal/multi-decadal scales. This large multidecadal covariance in global OHC is likely due to much less sampling before than after 2005 (in particular in regions far from trade routes like the Southern and the Arctic oceans or in regions with highly variable OHC as in western boundary currents, see Fig. 3 ). Less sampling led to notable errors in quality control, the climatology and also in mapping which are correlated in time (and eventually in space as well, see Fig. 4 and Supplementary Figs. 7 - 14 ). The sampling/mapping error (in particular below 700 m depth) before 2005 is also likely a contributor to these large multidecadal error covariances (Supplementary Fig. 4 ). The inter-annual scale covariances are larger before than after 2000 (Fig. 2d ) probably for similar reasons. By contrast, the error covariance matrix for the derivative of OHC ( d O H C / d t , ocean heat rate) is dominated by error covariances on interannual time scales. This is caused by the amplification of high-frequency errors/noise when doing the time derivative for the annual mean time series of OHC.

The spatial maps of uncertainty indicate that uncertainty reduction has occurred in most ocean regions over the past six decades, with different patterns over time (Figs. 3 , 4 , Supplementary Figs. 7 - 14 ). In the earlier periods, the OHC0-2000m uncertainty distribution is characterized by larger errors in the Southern Hemisphere (2.4 × 10 9 J m -2 and 2.0 × 10 9 J m -2 on average from 1955–1964, 1965–1974, respectively, Fig. 3 ) than in the Northern Hemisphere (1.4 × 10 9 J m -2 and 1.2 × 10 9 J m -2 on average from 1955–1964, 1965–1974 respectively), primarily due to fewer observations and thus mapping uncertainty, Supplementary Fig. 7 ). Indeed, there are more cruises and human activities in the Northern Hemisphere. Hence, mapping is the largest source of uncertainty for almost all regions and across all decades (Fig. 4 ), so that sampling and associated mapping techniques remain the major limitation for a more accurate OHC estimate.

The choice of climatology was the second-largest source of error in at least half of the ocean area over the past 60 years (Fig. 4 , Supplementary Fig. 8 ), owing to differences in regional anomaly calculations. The climatology-induced uncertainty can reach a maximum of > 1.3×10 9 J m -2 in the eddy-rich regions. However, these regional climatology-induced errors do not seem to contribute substantially to global mean and trend estimates (see other sections of this study), indicating regional compensation.

The uncertainty in mid-latitude OHC0-2000m has been reduced since the mid-1960s due to the widespread use of XBT data (Fig. 3 ). Meanwhile, XBT and MBT bias corrections became the second-largest source of uncertainty in the mid-latitude Pacific Ocean from 1965 to 2004 (Fig. 4 , Supplementary Figs. 9–10 ). The MBT/XBT bias correction uncertainty is more important in the Pacific Ocean than the Atlantic Ocean because there is also a large amount of more accurate CTD data in the Atlantic, while MBT/XBT dominates the Pacific Ocean observing system during these periods 28 , 32 (Fig. 4 , Supplementary Figs. 9 – 10 ). BOT bias is critical for the North Pacific and Atlantic Oceans before the 1990s (Supplementary Fig. 11 ).

The tropical OHC uncertainty has been reduced since the 1980s (Fig. 3 ), largely due to the establishment of the tropical moored buoy system designed to track El Niño. Indeed, the tropical ocean within 10 o S ~ 10 o N is the region with the smallest OHC uncertainty in the recent decade (2015–2023, <0.3×10 9 J m -2 ), highlighting the importance of maintaining the tropical observing system.

The vertical interpolation has become the second largest source of uncertainty in the North Pacific from 1955 to 1974, tropical and subtropical Atlantic Ocean from 1955 to 2014 (up to 1 × 10 9 J m -2 , Supplementary Fig. 12 ), owing to a significant amount of low-resolution data 24 . Vertical interpolation is also critical in ACC and boundary current regions, where strong vertical gradients are present.

In earlier periods, QC impacts (Figs. 3 , 4 ) were primarily observed in the middle parts of the Pacific and Indian Oceans and the Southern Ocean (before 2004), where XBT, MBT, and BOT data dominated and often contained more erroneous data than other instruments, such as CTD and moored observations. Since ~2005, QC impacts are substantial in the eddy-rich regions (Fig. 5 ) where the handling of the large anomalies associated with eddies becomes critical (Supplementary Figs. 5 , 6 , 13 ).

OHC trends and variability uncertainty are separated from the annual mean estimates in previous sections, because the precision of the trend and variability estimates are impacted by both annual OHC uncertainty and its time variation and time correlation. The trend of OHC0-2000m from 1960 to 2023 is estimated to be 6.4 [5.5, 7.4] ZJ yr -1 (equivalent to 0.40 [0.34, 0.46] Wm -2 over the global surface area), with the error range represented by [5%, 95%] quantile of all ensemble members (Fig. 5a ). The first and second sources of error in 1960–2023 OHC0-2000m trend are mapping (1.6 ZJ yr -1 , hereinafter calculated by 2 × 1.64-sigma based on ensemble members fixing other techniques) and vertical interpolation (1.0 ZJ yr -1 ), respectively, followed by climatology choice (0.7 ZJ yr -1 ) and QC (0.3 ZJ yr -1 ). Again, the sum of errors is two times larger than the total trend uncertainty, implying strong error covariance impacts on trend estimate (Fig. 5a ).

The OHC0-2000m trend has increased over time: 2.8 [2.0, 4.3] ZJ yr -1 (equivalent to 0.18 [0.12, 0.27] Wm -2 over the global surface area) from 1960 to 1990, 9.9 [8.5, 10.6] ZJ yr -1 (0.61 [0.53, 0.66] Wm -2 ) from 1991 to 2023, and 10.9 [9.2, 11.4] ZJ yr -1 (0.68 [0.57, 0.71] Wm -2 ) from 2005 to 2023 (Fig. 5a ). As their error ranges do not overlap, the rate changes are statistically significant, increasing the robustness of the multidecadal ocean warming acceleration 3 , 6 – 8 . For all time periods, the regional OHC0-2000m trend uncertainties are larger in the Southern Ocean (78-30S), western Indian, Arctic, and boundary currents regions than in other regions (Fig. 6 ), probably associated with higher variability in these regions and also greater noise. However, the primary contributions of error sources vary across different periods. For instance, the mapping is more important for 1960–1990 than 1991–2023 because of the improved sampling in recent decades (Fig. 5a ). Similarly for the vertical interpolation impact, because of the increased vertical resolution of ocean profile data over time (Fig. 5a ). Since 2005, QC has substantially impacted the trends, suggesting the need to address better eddy-rich regions where anomalies are large, often associated with significant thermocline variations in eddies (Fig. 5a ).
The time periods are 1960–2023, 1960–1990, 1991–2023, and 2005–2023. Colored shading represents the magnitude of the trend error.

The centered difference of the OHC time series ( d O H C / d t , full-depth) is often used to calculate ocean and Earth’s heating rate (Fig. 5b ). But there is substantial month-to-month variability of the ocean heating rate 8 , 35 . Because the first-time derivative can amplify noise/errors in time series, the uncertainty can be substantial and is assessed in this section. With this approach, the monthly ocean heating rate uncertainty (5–95% quartile range of annual d O H C / d t ) is estimated to be ~1.54 Wm -2 from 1955 to 1975, which is reduced by over 2-fold in this century, which is 0.67 Wm -2 from 2005 to 2023 (Fig. 5c ). Vertical interpolation is the primary source of error that generates uncertainty in the inter-annual scale OHC change before ~1975 (Fig. 5c ), as the vertical sampling of ocean temperature profiles exhibits substantial year-to-year differences. The second largest error source is mapping, followed by QC and XBT bias corrections (Fig. 5c ). In the recent decade, mapping is the dominant error source, followed by the choice of climatology (Fig. 5c ). This big impact of climatology is a surprise, and it seems to be because of the impacts on the eddy-rich regions, probably associated with the poor definition of a mean state in these regions. Overall, trend errors are larger in recent decades, owing to the short record length as well as larger underlying trends and variability (Fig. 6 ).

Ocean heating dominates the EEI from inter-annual to multi-decadal time scales 4 , 8 , 14 , 36 , thus dOHC/dt is compared with 90% of CERES-EEI and FS derived from CERES and atmospheric reanalysis (Fig. 5b ). The dOHC/dt is correlated with CERES-EEI by 0.61 from 2005 to 2023, suggesting a reasonably good closure of the global energy budget. From 2005–2023, satellite CERES (FS) suggests an ocean heating rate of 0.48 ± 0.13 Wm -2 dec -1 (0.38 ± 0.28 Wm -2 dec -1 , mean of ERA5 and ERA-Interim), slightly stronger than the estimated d O H C / d t trend of 0.34 [0.19, 0.46] Wm -2 dec -1 based on IAP central estimate (Fig. 5b, c ). The IAP central estimate is closer to the upper end of the ensemble members because it used CODC-QC, which yields stronger trends than the results using WOD-QC. Adding atmospheric heat content 37 into d O H C / d t further increases the correlation with CERES-EEI, which becomes 0.7, indicating a substantial contribution from the atmosphere 38 . However, CERES also has sampling, diurnal cycle and satellite/instrument changes uncertainties. Nevertheless, the year-to-year variability of OHC and EEI requires further investigation 39 . Furthermore, as calculating time derivatives exacerbates noise, we integrate EEI and FS time series and compared the detrended ∫ E E I and ∫ F s data with detrended OHC (Fig. 5d ). This comparison shows better consistency. This indicates that the data processing techniques (in particular, derivation techniques) also matter for an OHC and EEI comparison 40 .

This study carried out a large-ensemble approach to quantify the OHC uncertainty from all major error sources. The methods used techniques developed by many international groups, thus reflecting the international community’s progress over the past decade. The results indicate a substantial reduction in OHC estimate error since the 1950s, from ~111 ZJ from 1955–1965 to ~19 ZJ from 2015 to 2023. The uncertainty reduction seems obvious because of the establishment of Argo and other networks in this century 41 . However, given the caveat that WOD-QC removes more realistic positive anomalies in eddy-rich regions 42 , the QC uncertainty is likely to be overestimated in recent decades. If taken CODC-QC as a single choice of QC, the OHC uncertainty since 2015 is ~10 ZJ on average. Long-term increase of ocean warming rate (OHC0-2000m) is robust, indicating a multi-decadal scale ocean warming acceleration.

However, the annual ocean heating rate is more uncertain due to data and methodological uncertainties, including those associated with the calculation of the first derivative. From 2005–2023, the annual full-depth d O H C / d t time series shows a trend of 0.34 [0.19, 0.46] Wm -2 dec -1 (5%-95% uncertainty range calculated by the Large-Ensemble), smaller than satellite CERES estimate during the same period (0.48 ± 0.13 Wm -2 dec -1 ), but the uncertainty range overlaps. All ocean regions show a substantial reduction in OHC uncertainty over the global ocean in the past half-century, especially in the Southern Hemisphere, owing to improved data coverage and quality. In the recent decade, eddy-rich regions have shown greater OHC uncertainty than other regions, highlighting critical areas for improving OHC and its trend estimates. Changes in error sources over time demonstrate how the dominant sources of uncertainty evolve and depend on changes in observational platforms and methodologies, and underscore the importance of properly accounting for both individual error sources and their correlations.

The strength of the Large-Ensemble approach lies in its ability to revisit and integrate all known techniques to examine the spread, given our current understanding of the problem. The covariance among various error sources can also be quantified. However, the weakness of ensemble approaches is that they cannot investigate the “unknown unknowns” (for instance, the not-yet-identified instrumental biases). In this regard, the consequence is that the ensemble approach might provide a lower bound for the real uncertainty. Therefore, when any new error sources are discovered, they should be incorporated into this effort. Even if systematic errors and unknown unknowns are omitted, their impact is likely small on the variability and the trend of the OHC, as it shows reasonable agreement, mostly within error bars, with an independent estimate based on CERES and atmosphere reanalysis. An additional caveat of this study is that the mapping uncertainty is quantified with the IAP ensemble approach in a different framework than other sources. We acknowledged the challenge of quantifying sampling/mapping uncertainty: the truth in data gaps will not be known, and a mapping approach is used to fill the gaps.

Besides, the uncertainty quantified in this study only presents an in-situ observation-based OHC estimate 3 , where a similar protocol is used for various groups 31 , 43 , 44 . However, there are other approaches for OHC estimation, such as an indirect approach based on geodetic techniques using satellite altimetry and gravity to derive OHC 15 , 41 , 45 or hybrid approaches using both in-situ profiles and geodetic techniques. The uncertainty budget associated with these indirect approaches is different and requires separate treatment.
A closer look at the uncertainty in the current decade has critical implications for improving the current GOOS and OHC/EEI estimate:

The eddy-rich regions, including boundary currents and ACC regions, should be better dealt with, because they contribute much larger uncertainty than the other regions (Figs. 3 , 4 , 6 ). Critical improvements include increasing data coverage (improving data sampling), mapping technique (including improving resolution to resolve meso-scale eddies), improving climatology and QC procedure in these regions, and also utilizing other sources of information, such as altimetry, and other satellite observations 46 , 47 .

The global data coverage should be increased over the global ocean where practicable, as mapping is still the dominant uncertainty source in most of the ocean area (Figs. 3, 4, 6). Specifically, the Global Argo network contains ~4000 floats with an average resolution of 3° by 3° and 1 month. This network should be extended horizontally and vertically to reduce mapping uncertainty 32 . Besides Argo, ship-based observations, Moorings, Animal Borne Ocean Sensors also needs to be sustained and expanded to fill the critical gaps and build a resilient GOOS 48 .

The data quality and QC procedure should be further improved (Figs. 1 , 5 ), including a way to investigate why QC leads to recent substantial uncertainty, what the best QC practices are, and how to remove the systematic errors in ocean observations. The exploration could also extend to the ocean conditions under extreme events such as tropical cyclones and marine heat waves, where anomalous large but realistic values occur.

Closure of the Earth’s energy budget using CERES radiation, land, cryosphere and atmosphere data would be critical to test the validity of the GOOS and will provide clues for its improvements. The closure of sea level budget provides an important check for OHC given that the altimetry and GRACE observations provide reliable changes in global mean sea level and its mass component 49 .

Comparing OHC with EEI and surface flux data shows notable differences on the inter-annual scale, although the warming acceleration agrees between these 2 totally independent estimates meaning it is robust. Integrating ocean in situ ocean data with other observations, such as altimetry, satellite gravity data, CERES, and ocean color data using data merging techniques, data assimilation, and Artificial Intelligence methods, seems a promising way forward. Furthermore, as the atmosphere and ocean circulations move heat around, the regional pattern of OHC is distinct from EEI. The OHC and EEI can be better understood and reconciled through an integrated understanding of Earth’s energy budget and there is a heat redistribution between ocean and atmosphere, land, and cryosphere 50 , 51 .

The main data sources come from the in-situ temperature profile data in the World Ocean Database (WOD) downloaded in August 2024, which is then organized in the CODC database after adding more in situ observations from other data sources 52 . Measures from all instruments are used, including Conductivity/Temperature/Depth (CTD), XBT, MBT, Argo, BOT, moorings (MRB), gliders (GLD), APB, and others. The OHC calculation procedure follows the IAP group system 53 , which is similar to those used elsewhere 43 , 44 , 54 .

TOA net radiative flux timeseries data is from the CERES Energy Balanced and Filled (EBAF) Ed4.2 product 55 . CERES instruments have provided continuous broadband radiation measurements since March 2000. The CERES EBAF Ed4.2 record delivers consistent monthly mean shortwave, longwave, and net radiative fluxes at the TOA, and is widely regarded as the reference dataset for studies of Earth’s radiation budget. In our comparisons with d O H C / d t , we consider the period from January 2005 to December 2023. However, it contains noise on monthly time scales owing to limited sampling of the diurnal cycle 56 .

The surface net heat flux ( FS ) products can be derived from observations of net energy budget observations at the TOA, the atmospheric energy storage and the convergence of the vertically-integrated atmospheric energy fluxes from different atmospheric reanalysis products 57 – 59 . Two FS products are used in this study: The first FS product is obtained by combining DEEPC v5.0 TOA fluxes 59 for 1985–2000, adjusted to match CERES EBAF Ed4.2 (Ref. 55 ) by adding the mean annual cycle difference between CERES EBAF Ed4.1 and Ed4.2 (estimated over 2001–2018), and CERES EBAF Ed4.2 thereafter, combined with ERA5 (Ref. 37 ) for January 1985- December 2023. The second FS product is obtained by combining CERES v4.0 TOA radiation and ERA-Interim 60 for March 2000-December 2016 (ref. 61 ).

The atmospheric heat content (AHC) data is computed based on data from the fifth generation of European ReAnalysis (ERA5, Ref. 37 ) monthly single-level reanalysis produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). In this study, we use the total column vertically integrated total energy, which represents the vertically integrated sum of internal, potential, kinetic, and latent energy over the full atmospheric column.

Many steps must be used to calculate OHC from in situ observations, and all contribute to the uncertainty of the final OHC estimate. On this basis, we developed a large-ensemble approach to quantify uncertainty. For each given step, the three most up-to-date techniques (developed by the many international ocean data groups over the world) are used to give three different estimates whose standard deviation serves as the error estimate associated with the given step (except for mapping, as discussed later), as outlined below. Three techniques are used because 1) the computational power is limited, and 2) only the state-of-the-art knowledge is considered to avoid overestimating the uncertainty. An example is XBT bias correction schemes; there are more than 10 correction schemes available, many of which have been investigated in previous efforts 16 , 26 . But recent investigations 20 , 62 have revealed caveats for many correction schemes. For example, some correction schemes only considered part of the XBT biases. The choices of each error source at each step are briefly discussed below (Fig. 7 ), and one of them (Fig. 7 , marked as blue texts) is used to derive the IAP central estimate, which is assessed as the state-of-the-art estimate for the IAP dataset (see Ref. 53 ):

QC: WOD 42 and Chinese Academy of Sciences Ocean Data Center (CODC) 34 . The two systems use very different QC checks and represent different strategies for QC of ocean data. One of the major differences is the local climatology range change. While WOD-QC uses a static climatological range constructed from all historical data to filter out outliers, CODC-QC uses a time-varying range which considers the long-term trends of ocean changes 63 that are non-trivial. For QC, only two systems are used because of the limited access to other systems but the two are representative.

Three best XBT correction schemes are used: Cheng et al. (Ref. 63 ., CH14); Levitus et al. (Ref. 31 ., L09) and Gouretski and Reseghetti (Ref. 64 ., GR10) following the evaluation in previous studies 62 and community-recommendations 20 . CH14 introduces a time- (annual mean), probe-type and temperature- dependent correction scheme, while L09 is a global mean time-varying scheme and GR10 considers the bias dependence on probe-type and time.

Bottle bias correction: the central estimate and an upper and lower bound of the correction developed in Gouretski et al. (ref., 22 GCB22). The upper and lower bounds represent conservative and aggressive estimates of the bottle bias.

APB bias correction: the central estimate, an upper and lower bound of the correction are used based on Gouretski et al. (Ref. 23 ., GRC23). Similar to bottle bias correction, GRC23 is the only correction scheme for APB bias, and the upper and lower bounds represent a conservative and aggressive estimate of the correction.

MBT bias correction: the central estimate is Gouretski and Cheng 21 , with two additional approaches: Gouretski and Reseghetti (ref., 64 GR10) and Ishii et al. (ref., 65 IK09). Another MBT bias correction scheme is available 66 but is not used here as an assessment 63 indicates a substantial suspicious deviation from the other schemes.

Choice of climatology: Three different methods of computing the climatology are used namely the World Ocean Atlas 2023 method (ref., 54 WOA), the Institute of Atmospheric Physics method (ref., 53 IAP); World Ocean Circulation Experiment-Argo Global Hydrographic Climatology method (ref. 67 , WAGHC).

Vertical interpolation: Three methods are used namely: the Reiniger and Ross method(Ref. 68 ., RR), the Piecewise Cubic Hermite Interpolating Polynomial (ref., 33 PCHIP) applied to the temperature profiles, and the RR approach applied to temperature anomaly profiles after subtracting IAP climatology.

Mapping and instrumental error: only IAP mapping 69 , 70 was used because the codes of other approaches are not publicly available. But IAP mapping can provide a reasonable estimate of mapping uncertainty, because it is an Ensemble Optimal Interpolation (EnOI) approach with the CMIP5 multi-model ensemble (30 models) as prior to represent our current understanding of the ocean changes (the larger spread in models, the poorer understanding of physical changes, especially in regions with large data gaps where there is no observational information to estimate uncertainty). The observation accuracy set by IQuOD 18 is used to constrain the model spread and derive the final ensemble of the analysis field. Thus, the more data and the higher quality, the smaller the ensemble spread in the final analysis, representing smaller uncertainty in reconstruction. Besides, in this approach, the instrumental, sampling, and mapping uncertainties are combined and are represented by the ensemble spread of the derived analysis field. An alternative approach to assess sampling/mapping errors is to resample the data in data-rich periods according to historical observation masks and assess the reconstruction error 69 – 71 , which provides reasonably consistent uncertainty estimates compared with the EnOI approach.
The techniques with blue colors are used to derive the IAP (Institute of Atmospheric Physics—IAP) central estimate, as they are assessed as the most up-to-date or best choices.

As introduced in mapping and instrumental error analysis, the mapping uncertainty (defined by the EnOI approach) is treated differently from the other error sources (defined as the differences between different techniques). We merged the mapping uncertainty with the other sources of error by randomly selecting one ensemble member derived from the EnOI ensemble (see Fig. 7 ).

Ideally, all combinations of error sources (first seven in Fig. 7 ) yield a large ensemble of 2*3 7 = 4374. But in practice, there is limited computational power, and calculations show that the ensemble spread and the 10% quantile actually stabilize after only a few hundred members (Supplementary Fig. 1 ), meaning not all the 4374 members need to be computed to derive the actual spread of the ensemble and the estimate of the total uncertainty. We eventually made 908 ensemble members to satisfactorily derive the uncertainty and error covariances (Supplementary Fig. 2 ).

Throughout the paper, the overall uncertainty is defined as the [5%, 95%] quantile range among ensemble members and is close to that obtained if the distribution was assumed as gaussian (see Supplementary Fig. 3 ), meaning the error distribution is likely not far from a gaussian distribution, as expected. For each error source, as only three different choices are made, the quantile is not feasible; instead, the uncertainty is represented by the 1.64 standard deviation (approximately equal to [5%, 95%] range assuming a gaussian distribution), calculated by the mean variance of the 2 or 3 choices of techniques with other error technical choices fixed.
The error covariance is inferred from the differences among the variance of all ensemble members and the sum of all variances of individual error sources:

Throughout this study, the “covariance” includes both linear and nonlinear relationships among variables. In addition, we derive the variance-covariance matrix for global OHC0-2000m time series using the Large-Ensemble to describe the time correlation in errors 72 . The ensemble OHC0-2000m time series ( T S i ) are directly used to calculate the time-covariance between each time series as follows:
where E is the mean operator. This approach is reliable when the ensemble is large enough to describe the dispersion between ensemble members adequately, as is the case with 908 members.

For each OHC member, d O H C / d t is calculated by using the central derivative of the annual (Jan.-Dec. average) OHC time series, and the long-term OHC trend is calculated by a LOWESS approach 73 . Then the uncertainty range is derived through the results of all ensemble members, through which the error covariance can be accounted for. An alternative approach using the variance-covariance matrix 72 yields very similar results (Supplementary Table 1 ).

articles.title: Direct observation of glycans bonded to proteins and lipids at the single-molecule level.
articles.authors: Anggara K, Sršan L, Jaroentomeechai T, Wu X, Rauschenbach S, Narimatsu Y, Clausen H, Ziegler T, Miller RL, Kern K.
articles.abstract: Abstract Proteins and lipids decorated with glycans are found throughout biological entities, playing roles in biological functions and dysfunctions. Current analytical strategies for these glycan-decorated biomolecules, termed glycoconjugates, rely on ensemble averaged methods that do not provide a full view of positions and structures of glycans attached at individual sites in a given molecule, especially for glycoproteins. Here we show single molecule analysis of glycoconjugates by direct imaging of individual glycoconjugate molecules using low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy. Intact glycoconjugate ions from electrospray are soft-landed on surface for their direct single molecule imaging. The sub-molecular imaging resolution corroborated by quantum mechanical modeling unveils the entire structures and attachment sites of glycans in glycopeptides, glycolipids, N-glycoproteins, and O-glycoproteins densely decorated with glycans.
paragraphs: Proteins and lipids decorated with glycans are found throughout biological entities, playing roles in biological functions and dysfunctions. Current analytical strategies for these glycan-decorated biomolecules, termed glycoconjugates, rely on ensemble averaged methods that do not provide a full view of positions and structures of glycans attached at individual sites in a given molecule, especially for glycoproteins. Here we show single molecule analysis of glycoconjugates by direct imaging of individual glycoconjugate molecules using low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy. Intact glycoconjugate ions from electrospray are soft-landed on surface for their direct single molecule imaging. The sub-molecular imaging resolution corroborated by quantum mechanical modeling unveils the entire structures and attachment sites of glycans in glycopeptides, glycolipids, N-glycoproteins, and O-glycoproteins densely decorated with glycans.

Glycan (also known as carbohydrate) is one of the four essential organic building blocks found in all forms of life ( 1 – 7 ). Glycans play key roles in cellular functions ( 7 , 8 ), growth and development ( 2 , 9 ), identification ( 2 – 4 ), shapes ( 10 , 11 ), and energy storage ( 12 ). In biological systems, glycans are predominantly found attached to other biomolecules such as proteins and lipids. These glycan-decorated biomolecules, termed glycoconjugates, are produced via complex enzymatic glycosylation events – the most common and diverse post translational modification (PTM) that greatly expands the functions of biomolecules ( 13 , 14 ). The abundance of glycoconjugates in biological systems and their roles in health and disease make them attractive targets in basic and translational research for new therapeutic and diagnostic strategies ( 1 – 3 , 15 , 16 ). However, despite the ubiquity and importance of glycoconjugates, research to unveil their structure-property relationships has been challenging ( 17 – 19 ).

Glycoconjugates possess extensive structural heterogeneity (i.e. multiple variants of sequence) and structural isomerism (i.e. structures with equal masses), which pose a challenge for today’s analytical methods ( 17 – 19 ). Glycoconjugates are presently analyzed by a combination of chemical labeling, chemoenzymatic digestion, and ensemble averaged methods to indirectly obtain the most likely structures present in a sample ( 18 , 19 ). Ensemble averaged analysis of structurally heterogeneous and isomeric glycoconjugates however obscures the position and structures of glycans bonded to a biomolecule, particularly for proteins with multiple glycans attached. As a result, insights into the structures of individual molecules are lost with ensemble averaged analysis, which hinders structure-property relationship studies of glycoconjugates. Preventing the loss of structural information for individual molecules requires glycoconjugate molecules to be analyzed at single molecule level.

Here we realize single molecule analysis of glycoconjugates by performing direct, label-free, spatial imaging on individual glycoconjugate molecules. We show that imaging single glycoconjugates at sub-nanometer resolution reveals the primary structure of each molecule, by unveiling how its constituent amino acid, lipid, and monosaccharide subunits connect to one another. As a result, our imaging method establishes glycan sequences at every glycan attachment site in a glycoconjugate by locating every monosaccharide in the glycoconjugate molecule discriminated by its stereoconfiguration and side group. We demonstrate our method for a wide range of glycoconjugates, starting from simple glycopeptides and glycolipids, up to complex glycoproteins with more than 20 attached glycans. Our work shows that single molecule imaging provides a direct access to all glycan structures bonded to the complex glycopeptides, glycolipids, and glycoproteins at single molecule level.

We accomplished direct imaging of single glycoconjugate molecules by combining soft-landing electrospray ion beam deposition (ESIBD) ( 20 , 21 ) and scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) (see Methods for details). We show STM imaging of single glycoconjugates on Cu-surface at cryogenic temperatures corroborated by Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations provides direct access to their structural information ( Fig. 1 ). We imaged glycoconjugate ions obtained from nanoelectrospray ionization (nESI) ( 22 ) ( Fig. S1 ), whose usage was critical to lower the amount of sample required to ~1 nanomole, given that glycoconjugates, unlike proteins ( 23 , 24 ) and glycans ( 25 ), are more limited in sample quantity. In cases of sulfated molecules ( Fig. S2 ), we deposited the molecules on a more inert Ag-surface to preserve the labile sulfate groups on surface ( Fig. S3 ).

( A ) Schematic of the experiment: glycoconjugate or GAG ions generated by nESI were mass-selected, soft-landed intact on surface held at 120 K, and imaged by STM at 11 K (see Methods ). STM images of glycopeptides, Glc-Glc-AsnPheAla ( B ) and Gal-Glc-AsnPheAla ( C ), reveal the glycan and the peptide domains of the molecule and differentiate each monosaccharide in the glycan domain i.e. glucose (Glc) vs galactose (Gal). Imaging GAGs ( D-F ) reveals the positions of N-Acetyl groups on all N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) monosaccharides, differentiating them from the glucuronic acid (GlcA) monosaccharides as well as the sulfated GlcNAc6S, GalNAc6S, and GlcNS6S monosaccharides. The GAGs in ( D ) and ( F ) are terminated by para-nitrophenyl (pnp), while in ( E ) the GAG is terminated by para-(6-azidohexanamido)phenyl (pap). STM images were interpreted by STM simulation of molecular structures computed by DFT. Scale bar is 0.5 nm. Glycan icons follow the SNFG standard ( 56 ).

We first highlight the capabilities of STM imaging and DFT modeling in characterizing monosaccharide structures of glycans. We imaged two glycopeptides ( 26 ) ( Fig. 1b,c ) composed of a disaccharide (cellobiose, Glcβ1–4Glc, or lactose, Galβ1–4Glc) linked to a tripeptide, and three glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) ( Fig. 1d-f ). STM imaging of the glycopeptides was found to differentiate the glycan and peptide moieties by their heights: tall/bright for the glycan and low/dim for the peptide ( Fig. 1b,c ), which allowed the DFT calculations to yield the primary structure of the glycopeptides, resolving the order by which amino acid and monosaccharide subunits in the molecule are connected to one another. In addition, STM imaging was found to discriminate glucose from its epimer, galactose (i.e. they differ only in the stereoconfiguration of their C4-atoms), given that the glucose ( h = 2.1 ± 0.2 Å, N = 45) was observed consistently taller than the galactose ( h = 1.7 ± 0.3 Å, N = 75). STM imaging was also found to locate and identify side groups and sulfate moieties present in every monosaccharide, as exemplified by the imaging of GAGs ( Fig. 1d-f ). Each GlcNAc monosaccharide was observed with a dim protrusion corresponding to the N-Acetyl (NAc) moiety, clearly distinct from the GlcA monosaccharides ( Fig. 1d ). Interestingly, each GlcNAc6S and GalNAc6S monosaccharide was observed with its sulfate moiety (a dim protrusion encircled with a dark ring) on the opposite side from its NAc moiety (a dim protrusion without dark ring) ( Fig. 1e,f ); whereby GlcNS6S was observed with two sulfate moieties, each appearing as a dim protrusion with a dark ring ( Fig. 1e ). We further ascertained the STM appearance of sulfate moiety on the same surface as a dim protrusion encircled with a dark ring by imaging simple aryl sulfates ( Fig. S3 ). Our findings show that STM imaging and DFT modeling have sufficient sensitivity and resolution to locate glycans in molecules, and discriminate the constituent monosaccharides based on their stereoconfigurations and side groups.

We show the perspectives of our direct single molecule analysis by determining structures of entire glycans present in complex glycopeptides, glycolipids, and glycoproteins at single molecule level. For glycopeptides, we examined an egg yolk sialoglycopeptide derivative ( Fig. 2a ), which is widely used in biochemical applications ( 27 ). For glycolipids, the GM3 and GD3 gangliosides ( Fig. 2b,c ) were chosen due to their roles as cancer antigens ( 5 , 15 ). For N-glycoproteins, we chose the widely studied pancreatic RNase B ( 28 ). Finally, as a representative for O-glycoproteins, we chose a fragment of human mucin MUC1, one of the most complex glycoproteins in biological systems, which is also overexpressed with aberrant O-glycans in cancer, and a promising cancer biomarker and immunotherapeutic target ( 29 , 30 ). In all cases, there is a clear height contrast between the bright glycan domain and the dim peptide or lipid domains that establishes their respective primary structures. For the N-glycopeptide ( Fig. 2a ), the height contrast discriminated the GlcNAc and Fuc monosaccharides ( h = 2.2 ± 0.4 Å, N = 132) from the mannose ( h = 1.9 ± 0.4 Å, N = 66); while, in the glycolipids ( Fig. 2b,c ), the height contrast differentiated glucose (one lobe, h = 2.1 ± 0.3 Å, N = 158), galactose (one lobe, h = 1.9 ± 0.2 Å, N = 158), and sialic acid (Neu5Ac) (two or more lobes) from one another. The imaging was found to distinguish glycosidic bonds by the characteristic angle formed between monosaccharides when their pyranose rings adsorb horizontally on surface (experimentally verifiable by their respective heights). For example, the Siaα2–3Gal β1–4Glc in GM3 and GD3 (Sia = Neu5Ac monosaccharide) was observed to form an obtuse 141 ± 22º angle ( N = 158), while the Glcβ1–4Glcβ1–4Glc in cellohexaose was observed to form a straight 180 ± 25º angle ( N = 204) ( 31 ). In addition, the imaging of single glycolipids revealed their molecular conformations ( Fig. S4 ) and allowed discrimination of the ceramide moiety with varied lipid chain lengths ( Fig. S5 ), both of which may provide additional information towards structural studies of lipids. Interestingly, we observed the ‘open’ conformation of the lipid moiety in glycolipids ( Fig. 2c and S4 ), which has been discussed in relation to mechanisms of membrane fusions and protein-membrane interactions ( 32 , 33 ).

STM images of an N-glycopeptide (biantennary N-glycan NGA2F on the KVANKT peptide) ( A ), and glycolipids, GM3 ganglioside ( B ) and GD3 ganglioside ( C ), reveal the glycan, peptide, and ceramide (Cer) domains in the respective molecules (Cer consisted of varying length fatty acid chains and sphingosine). STM imaging differentiates individual monosaccharides in the glycoconjugate i.e. glucose (Glc), galactose (Gal), sialic acid (Sia = Neu5Ac), N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc), mannose (Man), and fucose (Fuc). STM images were interpreted by structures computed by DFT. Scale bar is 0.5 nm.

Direct imaging of single a N-glycoprotein, RNase B, revealed the structure and the location of the N-glycan bonded to the protein backbone ( 28 ) ( Fig. 3 ). We examined RNase B by imaging individual proteins in their fully unfolded state, which we prepared by exclusively depositing the highly charged protein ions on surface ( 24 ) ( Fig. S6 ). Given that RNase B has five glycoproteoforms ( 28 ) (each featuring one of five distinct N-glycan structures from Man 5 GlcNAc 2 to Man 9 GlcNAc 2 ), our single protein imaging allowed the glycoproteoforms of RNase B to be determined one-molecule-at-a-time, as shown in Figure 3b for Man 6 GlcNAc 2 and in Figure 3c for Man 5 GlcNAc 2 – the two most abundant glycoproteoforms of RNase B ( Fig. S1g ). The STM imaging clearly revealed the glycan attachment site by locating the intersection between the N-glycan and the protein backbone (red dots in Fig. 3b,c ). Analysis of 33 individual N-glycoproteins confirmed residue 34 (± 2) as the glycan attachment site, consistent with Asn34 as the known glycan attachment site for RNase B ( 28 ).

( A ) Sequence of RNase B (124aa) with one N-linked glycan at Asn34. Imaging single unfolded RNase B molecules reveals the N-glycan position along the protein backbone and the N-glycan structure found on individual glycoproteoforms one-molecule-at-a-time, as shown in ( B ) for Man 6 GlcNAc 2 and in ( C ) for Man 5 GlcNAc 2 . The position of Asn34 is estimated by a red dot along the protein backbone (white dashed line). Scale bar is 1 nm.

To illustrate the full perspective of single glycoprotein imaging, we examined an O-glycoprotein fragment derived from the large mucin MUC1. Mucins are considered one of the last frontiers in glycoanalytics that has remained unexplored to a large extent ( 34 – 36 ), despite their wide importance in mucosal biology and host-pathogen interactions ( 37 ). Structural analysis of mucins and their multiple glycosylation sites is challenging due to their enormous size and dense decoration of O-glycans, resulting in heterogeneity and resistance to protease digestion ( 34 – 36 ). Here we show that it is possible to analyze such heavily O-glycosylated proteins one-molecule-at-a-time ( Fig. 4 ) by using the soft deposition and imaging of single glycoproteins on surface ( Fig. S7 ).

( A ) Sequence of MUC1 reporter (148aa) containing 6.5 tandem repeats of 20 amino acids (GV TS APD T RPAPG ST APPAH) decorated with O-glycans at the Ser ( S ) and Thr ( T ) residues (total of 34 potential O-glycosites). Imaging single MUC1 proteins reveals the number, the structure, and the attachment site of O-glycans decorating the protein, as shown for a glycoproteoform with 27 O-glycans in ( B ), 21 O-glycans in ( C ), and 20 O-glycans in ( D ). The positions of S and T residues are indicated by red dots along the protein backbone (white dashed line). The unannotated STM images are given in Fig. S8 . Scale bar is 1 nm.

We imaged a representative fragment of the densely O-glycosylated tandem repeat region of human MUC1 mucin as an O-glycoprotein reporter with relatively homogeneous trisaccharide O-glycans (ie. ‘core 3’: Galβ1-4GlcNAcβ1-3GalNAcα1-O-S/T) ( Fig. 4 ). For this, we employed our recently developed cell-based strategy using genetically glycoengineered HEK293 cells for recombinant production of mucin reporter glycoproteins with custom-designed O-glycosylation ( 35 ) ( Fig. 4a ) (see Methods ). The MUC1 O-glycoprotein reporter, featuring 34 potential O-glycosylation sites, was analyzed by intact and bottom-up mass spectrometry, and profiling of released O-glycans, which revealed a relatively homogeneous mixture of O-glycans (mainly ‘core 3’) and number of O-glycans (mainly 19 – 23 glycans) ( 35 , 38 ) (see also Fig. S1h and Fig. S9 for MUC1 sample used in single molecule imaging experiments).

Imaging single MUC1 O-glycoproteins allows direct observation of the variation in number, structure, and attachment sites of O-glycans on the protein backbone, as shown in examples with 27, 21, and 20 O-glycans ( Fig. 4b,c,d ). On the individual MUC1 molecules, we found the O-glycans mainly to be the ‘core 3’ trisaccharides with the occasional sialylated ‘core 3’ tetrasaccharide (Siaα2-3Galβ1-4GlcNAcβ1-3GalNAc) in agreement with the glycoprofiling analysis ( 35 , 38 ) ( Fig. S9 ). Most importantly, the direct imaging of MUC1 clearly revealed the positions of each O-glycan at S and T sites along the protein (red dots in Fig. 4b,c,d ) (see Fig. S10 for an example). Analysis of the O-glycan positions on 18 MUC1 O-glycoproteins observed (Table S1) revealed three prevalent patterns of O-glycan distribution on the MUC1 tandem repeats as - TS -T- ST - ; - T S- T - ST - ; and - T S-T- ST - (bold underlined indicates glycosylated, see Table S2 ). These patterns are largely in agreement with the predicted O-glycosylation sequence of the MUC1 from both in vitro ( 39 ) and in vivo ( 38 ) enzyme specificity analysis. The O-glycosylation process is a complex event with multiple isoenzymes (polypeptide GalNAc-transferases) each attaching O-glycans at select positions in proteins, and the O-glycosylation of the five possible sites in the MUC1 tandem repeat requires sequential orchestrated action of multiple isoenzymes ( 39 ). Further analysis of the STM results (Table S1) revealed on average 3.4 O-glycans per tandem repeat with preferred positions at T in VTSA (87% occupied) and ST in GSTA (78% and 83% occupied respectively) and less preferred positions at S in VTSA (44% occupied) and T in PDTR (55% occupied). These results corroborate our previous studies of the MUC1 reporter protein with ‘core 3’ O-glycans ( 35 , 38 ), for which we found reduced occupancy of O-glycans at S in VTSA and T in PDTR ( 38 , 40 , 41 ). Direct STM imaging thereby yields detailed snapshots of single molecule glycoproteoforms that can unveil potential interplay between glycosylation at different positions in proteins and the glycan structures that may be assembled at these positions (Table S2). In addition, STM imaging allows direct observation of glycan-glycan interactions dictating the overall shape of the protein backbone. We expect the single molecule analysis approach to be widely applicable to glycoproteins that can be electrosprayed in unfolded states, regardless of size and numbers of attached glycans. In case of increasingly dense glycans causing proteins to unfold incompletely, the STM tip could be used to further unfold the protein to clarify its primary structure ( Fig. S11 ).

Our combination of electrospray deposition and scanning tunnelling microscopy analysis provides an opportunity to look directly at the primary structures of complex glycoconjugates, including glycoproteins with multiple glycans attached. This technology, corroborated by DFT modeling, should enable direct observation of diverse post-translational modifications (PTMs) on biomolecules ( 42 , 43 ), as well as structures of glycoconjugates that are well beyond today’s analytical capabilities, such as proteoglycans ( 44 ), glycoRNAs ( 45 ), lipopolysaccharides ( 46 ), and carbohydrate vaccines ( 16 ). While the present work demonstrates that prior knowledge of the amino acid sequence of the glycoproteins is advantageous to enable interpretation of the STM images, we recognize that STM imaging can still be further improved to identify each amino acid and monosaccharide in a molecule and thus identify single proteins/glycoproteins in complex biological mixtures. These improvements include the use of a functionalized tip to resolve and distinguish covalent bonds in a molecule ( 47 ), as well as the use of tunneling spectroscopy ( 48 ), nuclear spin detection ( 49 ), or optical fingerprinting ( 50 – 52 ) to identify electronic signatures of specific atoms or functional groups in molecules. With these improvements, we expect STM can contribute to identification of unknown glycoproteins or glycolipids, which may ultimately lead to the discovery of individual glycoproteins and glycolipids in a complex cellular mixtures, particularly in the context of glycoproteomics and glycolipidomics studies. Complementing these improvements with automated structure solvers ( 53 – 55 ) or tip preparation will increase the throughput of scanning probe microscopy and create opportunities to solve previously intractable problems in single molecule (bio)analytical chemistry.
Single molecule imaging of glycan-decorated proteins and lipids unveils all glycan structures bonded to the host molecules

articles.title: Termination of the integrated stress response.
articles.authors: De Miguel C, Thorkelsson SR, Fatalska A, Hodgson G, Dalglish M, Wang C, Bertolotti A.
articles.abstract: Abstract Stress responses enable cells to detect, adapt to, and survive challenges. The benefit of these signalling pathways depends on their reversibility. The integrated stress response (ISR) is elicited by phosphorylation of translation initiation factor eIF2, which traps and inhibits rate-limiting translation factor eIF2B thereby attenuating translation initiation. Termination of this pathway thus requires relieving eIF2B from P-eIF2 inhibition. Here, we found that eIF2 phosphatase subunits PPP1R15A and PPP1R15B (R15B) bound P-eIF2 in complex with eIF2B. Biochemical investigations guided by cryo-EM structures of native eIF2-eIF2B and P-eIF2-eIF2B complexes bound to R15B demonstrated that R15B enabled dephosphorylation of otherwise dephosphorylation-incompetent P-eIF2 on eIF2B. This sheds light on ISR termination, revealing that R15B rescues eIF2B from P-eIF2 inhibition, thereby safeguarding translation and cell fitness.
paragraphs: Stress responses enable cells to detect, adapt to, and survive challenges. The benefit of these signalling pathways depends on their reversibility. The integrated stress response (ISR) is elicited by phosphorylation of translation initiation factor eIF2, which traps and inhibits rate-limiting translation factor eIF2B thereby attenuating translation initiation. Termination of this pathway thus requires relieving eIF2B from P-eIF2 inhibition. Here, we found that eIF2 phosphatase subunits PPP1R15A and PPP1R15B (R15B) bound P-eIF2 in complex with eIF2B. Biochemical investigations guided by cryo-EM structures of native eIF2-eIF2B and P-eIF2-eIF2B complexes bound to R15B demonstrated that R15B enabled dephosphorylation of otherwise dephosphorylation-incompetent P-eIF2 on eIF2B. This sheds light on ISR termination, revealing that R15B rescues eIF2B from P-eIF2 inhibition, thereby safeguarding translation and cell fitness.

Attenuation of protein synthesis to maintain homeostasis is a rapid and evolutionary conserved response to changes in the cellular environment, essential for survival. It mostly occurs at the level of translation initiation, upon phosphorylation of serine 52 (S52) of the alpha subunit of trimeric eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 (eIF2α) ( 1 , 2 ). Phosphorylation of eIF2 is central to cellular fitness and has emerged as a therapeutic target for a broad range of diseases, from cancer to neurodegeneration ( 3 , 4 ). This essential regulation, also known as the integrated stress response (ISR) ( 5 ), has been studied for decades ( 6 ), yet how phospho-eIF2 signalling is terminated has remained unclear. This is an important fundamental question because persistent stress signalling is lethal ( 7 , 8 ).

eIF2 is a trimeric (α, β, γ) GTPase that, when bound to GTP, recruits initiator Met-tRNA to the translation preinitiation complex and leaves after GTP hydrolysis ( 1 , 2 ). For a new round of translation, eIF2-GDP needs to be recycled into eIF2-GTP by its guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) eIF2B. P-eIF2 binds to eIF2B, sequestering it in an inhibited state ( 9 ). In human cells, there is a ~ 30-fold molar excess of eIF2 relative to eIF2B ( 10 ). Thus, only minute amounts of eIF2 phosphorylation are required to inhibit eIF2B and protein synthesis. This molecular principle establishes the power of this signalling event.

eIF2B is a decamer composed of two copies of 5 subunits, eIF2B α, β, γ, δ and ε ( 9 ). eIF2B α, β and δ form the regulatory core, flanked by eIF2Bγ and the catalytic subunit eIF2Bε on each side ( 11 ). Recent structures of human recombinant eIF2-eIF2B and P-eIF2-eIF2B complexes have revealed the mechanism of P-eIF2 inhibition: the substrate eIF2 and the inhibitor P-eIF2 bind to two different sites on eIF2B, defining two structurally different complexes, one catalytic and one inhibited ( 12 , 13 ).

The phosphatases of eIF2 have been identified through genetic screens in mammalian cells ( 14 , 15 ). They are composed of the PP1 catalytic subunit, bound to one of two non-catalytic subunits, PPP1R15A (R15A) or PPP1R15B (R15B) ( 14 , 15 ). Biochemical reconstitutions of eIF2α holophosphatases indicate that R15A and R15B are substrate receptors, conferring selectivity to the holoenzyme ( 16 – 18 ). Most studies of eIF2α phosphatases have been conducted with the N-terminal fragment of eIF2α ( 16 , 19 ). Recently, we reconstituted an R15B-eIF2 complex with recombinant proteins, revealing that R15B binds to eIF2 at the far end of the complex relative to S52 of eIF2α ( 18 ). Studies with R15A yielded similar results ( 20 ). There are no structures of R15A or R15B bound to their full substrate.

Free P-eIF2α can be dephosphorylated in vitro by recombinant eIF2 phosphatases ( 16 , 20 ). However, in cells, eIF2 and P-eIF2 are not always free but bound to other translation factors ( 1 , 2 ). The structures of human P-eIF2 bound to eIF2B indicate that P-S52 of eIF2α is engaged in intramolecular electrostatic interactions ( 12 , 13 ), most likely inaccessible to dephosphorylation on eIF2B. This raised an important question: How is eIF2B relieved from this inhibition by P-eIF2 for translation to resume?

Knowing that the N-terminal 413 residues of R15B are dispensable for eIF2 recruitment and dephosphorylation ( 17 , 18 ), we expressed FLAG-tagged R15B 414-713 in human cells and immunopurified native complexes for structural studies ( Fig. 1A ). R15B co-purified with several proteins, which we identified by mass spectrometry ( Fig. 1B and table S1 ). As expected ( 17 , 18 ), these included the three subunits of eIF2 (α, β, γ), as well as PP1 ( Fig. 1B and table S1 ). Notably, R15B 414-713 also co-purified with all 5 subunits of eIF2B (α, β, γ, δ, ε) ( Fig. 1B and table S1 ). This was confirmed by immunoblot analyses ( fig. S1A ). The paralog R15A also co-purified with eIF2, PP1 and eIF2B ( fig. S1B ). Furthermore, affinity purification of endogenously FLAG-tagged R15B also yielded eIF2, PP1 and eIF2B, establishing the biological relevance of the findings ( fig. S1C ).

( A ) Cartoon illustrating the R15B 414-713 fragment used for purification. H1, H2 and H3 are helical elements important for eIF2 recruitment ( 18 ); KVTF: PP1-recruiting motif. ( B ) Coomassie stained gel of an eluate of immunopurified FLAG-R15B 414-713 expressed in Expi293 cells. Indicated proteins were identified by mass spectrometry ( table S1 ). * Hsp70 1A. ( C ) Representative size exclusion chromatography (SEC) of FLAG-R15B 414-713 eluate (B). ( D ) Coomassie-stained gel of large and small complex peak fractions from SEC (C). Indicated proteins were identified by mass spectrometry ( table S2 ). * Hsp70 1A. ** ANM5. Immunoblots with FLAG antibody (bottom). ( E ) Cartoon depicting the control of translation initiation by P-eIF2. P-eIF2 binds and sequesters eIF2B in an inhibited state. Because eIF2B is rate-limiting, it is not the abundance of free P-eIF2 but the unavailability of eIF2B that controls translation inhibition. Thus, translation recovery requires the rescue of eIF2B from P-eIF2 inhibition. How this occurs is unknown.

The eluate from the R15B 414-713 immunoprecipitation separated on size exclusion chromatography (SEC) in two distinct peaks: A large complex composed of R15B, eIF2 and eIF2B and a small complex containing R15B and eIF2 ( Fig. 1C and D and table S2 ). PP1 was detected in both complexes ( Fig. 1D and table S2 ). This showed that R15B bound both free eIF2 and eIF2 bound to eIF2B. This suggested that this eIF2-eIF2B complex might be a physiological substrate of the eIF2 phosphatases.

These findings revealed both a problem and its solution. The substrate of eIF2 phosphatases was previously thought to be free P-eIF2 ( 14 – 16 , 19 ). However, it is not the abundance of P-eIF2 per se that dictates the rates of translation initiation, but the availability of rate-limiting eIF2B, which is sequestered in an inhibited state upon binding to P-eIF2 ( Fig. 1E ). Thus, unless eIF2B is rescued from P-eIF2, translation initiation remains inhibited. We then took a structural and biochemical approach to evaluate the possible function of R15B in this process.

While the small R15B-eIF2 complex could not be structurally studied, possibly due to high flexibility, the large complex was resolved by single particle electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM) analysis ( fig. S2 and table S3 ). 2D and 3D classification revealed recognizable features of eIF2-eIF2B complexes ( Fig. 2A ). Excluding low resolution classes, 67% of 3D particles displayed typical features of catalytic eIF2-eIF2B complexes ( Fig. 2A and fig. S2 ). The remaining 33% of 3D particles exhibited a distinct, raised conformation that didn’t reach high resolution ( Fig. 2A and fig. S2 ). Non-uniform refinement of the catalytic particles resulted in a structure of eIF2-eIF2B with an overall resolution of 2.7 Å ( Fig. 2, B and C ). eIF2B was a two-fold symmetric heterodecamer: two copies of eIF2B α, β and δ formed the core and eIF2Bγ and the catalytic subunit eIF2Bε flanked each side ( Fig. 2, B and C ). The two catalytic sites of this eIF2B decamer were bound to eIF2 ( Fig. 2 B and C ). The N-terminus of eIF2α bound an interface between eIF2Bβ and eIF2Bδ and eIF2γ was sandwiched between the core and the GEF domains of eIF2Bε ( Fig. 2, B and C ). This native complex resembled catalytic complexes prepared with recombinant eIF2 and eIF2B ( fig. S3A ), with eIF2B in the active state ( fig. S3B ) ( 12 , 13 , 21 ). S52 of eIF2α was resolved and unphosphorylated, forming hydrogen bonds with each sidechain oxygen of E139 of eIF2Bβ ( Fig. 2D ).

( B ) Cryo-EM map of eIF2-eIF2B in catalytic conformation (2.7 Å overall resolution). eIF2Bα (navy blue), eIF2Bβ (dark green), eIF2Bγ (yellow), eIF2Bδ (grey), eIF2Bε (purple), eIF2α (pink); eIF2β (lime); eIF2γ (cyan). The nucleotide pocket of eIF2γ was empty ( fig. S3C ). eIF2γ coordinates nucleotide binding via a series of G-motifs: G4 and G5 coordinate the nucleotide base, G1/P-loop coordinates the phosphates ( 22 ) and the conformation of G2/switch loop 1 and G3/switch loop 2 defines the GTP or GDP bound states ( 23 ). The diameter of the P-loop in our eIF2γ structure was 5.3 Å, too narrow to accommodate a nucleotide ( fig. S3, C and D ). The absence of GDP and the conformation of eIF2γ in this eIF2-eIF2B catalytic complex suggested that GDP dissociation from eIF2γ precedes GTP loading.

The binding sites of previously reported chemical or natural activators of eIF2B, ISRIB and sugar phosphates ( 24 , 25 ), were also unoccupied in this native complex ( fig. S3, E and F ). Notably, we found a GTP molecule bound to each eIF2Bγ in the native eIF2-eIF2B complex ( Fig. 2C ). This was not observed with previous structures of recombinant human eIF2-eIF2B nor yeast eIF2-eIF2B complexes ( 12 , 13 , 26 , 27 ) although GTP can bind and activate purified eIF2B in vitro ( 28 – 30 ). eIF2Bγ bound GTP via several highly conserved residues in its N-terminal domain ( Fig. 2E ). Two eIF2B loss-of-function mutants were reported in residues K66 and D173 of yeast eIF2Bγ ( 29 ), corresponding to human residues K25 and D107 respectively. These directly bound GTP in our native eIF2-eIF2B complex, each forming a hydrogen bond with a hydroxyl group in the pentose sugar of GTP ( Fig. 2E ).

In humans, mutations in eIF2B subunits cause vanishing white matter disease ( 9 ) by unclear mechanisms ( 31 ). We found that a third of the reported EIF2B3 (encoding eIF2Bγ) pathogenic missense mutations mapped to the GTP-binding pocket ( Fig. 2F ). The pathogenic mutations G11V, S14P, S14F, K25R, D107N, R225Q, R225P ( 32 ) affected highly conserved residues that directly contacted the GTP ( Fig. 2F ). Four other disease-causing mutations, A87V, R91H, D201G, A202T ( 32 ) also mapped to highly conserved residues that formed the scaffold of the GTP-binding pocket ( Fig. 2F ). Thus, missense mutations associated with vanishing white matter disease mapped to the conserved GTP-binding pocket of eIF2Bγ.

This structure of endogenous eIF2-eIF2B revealed detailed native features. However, no densities for R15B were observed. Our previous study identified interaction sites between recombinant R15B and recombinant eIF2 ( 18 ). In the native structure, these sites on eIF2 were either bound to eIF2Bε, inside eIF2γ and thereby inaccessible, or devoid of densities ( fig. S3G ). Thus, in this eIF2-eIF2B complex, R15B was not bound to its predicted site but to an alternative site, unresolved probably because of high flexibility. Identifying R15B by cryo-EM was expected to be difficult because it is mostly unstructured ( 18 ).

The remaining 33% of R15B 414-713 particles ( Fig. 2A ) resembled recombinant inhibited P-eIF2-eIF2B complexes ( fig. S3H ) with a notable distinguishing feature regarding the position of eIF2: eIF2γ was raised against the body of eIF2B in our R15B-bound complex, whereas it flails out in a recombinant P-eIF2-eIF2B complex ( 13 ) ( fig. S3H ). We thus refer to this native complex as the raised conformer. Although it could not be resolved to high resolution ( fig. S2 ), we suspected that this conformation was caused by R15B binding to the P-eIF2-eIF2B complex and aimed to purify it by enriching for P-eIF2. Based on our previous work ( 17 , 18 ), we designed a minimized R15B substrate-trap fragment, R15B 411-511 , which contained key eIF2-binding helices H1 (421-431) and H2 (474-480) ( 18 ) ( Fig. 3A ). FLAG-R15B 411-511 immunopurified with the 3 subunits of eIF2 and the 5 subunits of eIF2B ( Fig. 3B ). The SEC profile of the R15B 411-511 eluate revealed that it was predominantly composed of the large R15B-eIF2-eIF2B complex ( Fig. 3, C and D , and tables S4 to S6 ). As expected, the levels of P-eIF2α were increased compared to that of complexes purified with dephosphorylation-competent R15B 414-713 ( Fig. 3E ). Thus, P-eIF2 bound to eIF2B may indeed be a relevant substrate for its phosphatase.
