paragraphs: Selective defluorination of perfluoroalkyl chains remains challenging because of the strength of C–F bonds and the inertness of perfluoroalkyl groups. Here, the authors report a zipper reaction that completely defluorinates perfluoroalkylated alkenes into synthetically useful linear alkyl boranes while preserving the carbon backbone. The reaction is scalable and allows the recovery of fluoride in the form of LiF by simple filtration. It can be further applied to gem -difluoroalkenes, which are concluded to be intermediates of the underlying iterative fluoride removal process.
Subject terms: Synthetic chemistry methodology, Pollution remediation, Organic chemistry

Selective defluorination of perfluoroalkyl chains remains challenging because of the strength of C–F bonds and the inertness of perfluoroalkyl groups. Here, the authors report a zipper reaction that completely defluorinates perfluoroalkylated alkenes into synthetically useful linear alkyl boranes while preserving the carbon backbone.

The removal and substitution of fluoride substituents in organic molecules is particularly challenging due to the strength of C–F bonds, and thus the development of C–F activation methods has been a major research topic during the past decades 1 – 7 . In particular, perfluorinated alkyl groups are chemically inert and highly apolar, which makes them notoriously difficult to defluorinate and renders perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) persistent and bioaccumulating with numerous associated negative environmental and health effects 8 – 11 . While most research on aliphatic C–F activation using molecular reagents and catalysts has focused on fluorinated benzylic, allylic, and α-carbonyl carbons that facilitate the cleavage through stabilization of ionic or radical intermediates 12 , 13 , the defluorination of longer perfluorinated alkyl chains is significantly more difficult and less explored. One main reason is that the oxidative addition of a PFAS C–F bond to a transition metal reagent or catalyst is thermodynamically and kinetically hindered. Nevertheless, the defluorination of perfluoroalkyls has been reported via several alternative activation modes shown in Fig. 1a together with state-of-the-art examples: i) Strong Lewis acids such as silylium cations can abstract a fluoride, which leads to reactive carbocations that are then prone to rearrange, as was shown by the Ozerov group for the defluorination of a nonafluorohexane, giving various hexane isomers 14 . ii) The base-induced (decarboxylative) generation of a carbanion followed by an E1cB fluoride elimination is the basis of several previously reported PFAS destruction and mineralization methods 15 – 20 . For example, perfluoroalkanoic acids undergo fragmentation in the presence of base at elevated temperatures to form a range of carboxylates and fluoride 17 . The recovery and reuse of fluoride is an important aspect of such approaches and recent examples featuring mechanochemical and reductive strategies that achieve high fluoride yield and purity 19 – 23 . Alternative pathways that avoid the destruction of the carbon backbone are iii) the β-F-elimination from metalated intermediates that have previously been explored in the form of titanocene- and zirconocene-promoted partial defluorinations 24 – 26 and more recently as part of the shown nickel-catalyzed exhaustive defluorination of 1-(pentafluoroethyl)naphthalene 27 . iv) Single-electron transfer reagents or photoreductive conditions can be harnessed to defluorinate via a homolytic C–F cleavage. For example, radical defluorinations with stoichiometric zirconium reagents have been reported 28 , and more recently, the photocatalytic hydrodefluorination of various PFAS substances has been demonstrated 29 . While these are impressive examples, these methods typically suffer from either long reaction times, low conversion for extended perfluoroalkyl chains, or fragmentation of the carbon backbone. Moreover, the outcome is often reported as conversion determined by gas or ion chromatography of the reaction mixture and not as the yield of isolated products. Hence, there is a great need for operationally simple and quantitative defluorination methods that are scalable and allow the recovery of both fluoride and the organic molecular skeleton 30 . Even more desirable would be the conversion into synthetically useful building blocks through the introduction of a new functional group, which would lead to new directions in the field.

a C–F activation modes for the defluorination of perfluoroalkyl chains and corresponding state-of-the-art methods. BPI = benzo[ghi]perylene monoimide. b Precedence of defluorination in the presence of diborane in gas phase reactions. c The polydefluorination-borylation strategy explored in this work. Drawn hydrogen atoms indicate removed fluorides.

More than 60 years ago, it was reported that exposing polyfluoroethylenes or 3,3,3-trifluoropropylene in the gas phase to diborane (B 2 H 6 ) leads to mixtures of defluorinated products as well as defluorination-borylation products (Fig. 1b ) 31 , 32 . Although unselective and incomplete, these examples demonstrated intriguing defluorination reactivity of a borane. Defluoroborylations have further been reported by means of transition metal catalysis, but only for fluoroarenes and alkenes, and rarely for more than a single fluorine atom at a time 33 – 35 . Our group has been engaged for several years in the development of heterodefunctionalizations of alkenes and alkene-tethered alkyls using zirconium catalysis 36 – 38 . We now disclose a strikingly simple, exhaustive polydefluorination-monoborylation reaction that addresses all of the above-stated challenges and converts alkene-bound perfluorinated alkyls and gem -difluoroalkenes into alkyl pinacolboronates (Fig. 1c ). Moreover, it allows the straightforward recovery of fluoride as LiF by filtration on a gram scale.

While investigating zirconium-catalyzed defluorinations in the presence of mild hydride transfer agents, we discovered that β-trifluoromethylstyrene 1a underwent an exhaustive poly-defluorination with pinacol borane (HBpin) and LiOMe at 85 °C in the absence of a transition metal catalyst (Table 1 , entry 1). A concomitant borylation took place, which resulted in an overall 95% conversion of the perfluoroalkylated alkene to linear alkylborane product 2a as determined by 1 H NMR. Reducing the amount of LiOMe or attempting the reaction in the absence of it led to lower conversion or no product formation, respectively (entries 2, 3). Furthermore, the lithium cation was important as sodium methoxide did not promote the reaction (entry 4), and other lithium alkoxides were inferior to LiOMe. While LiOEt still gave 85% conversion to the product, bulky LiO t -Bu reduced the amount to 7% (entries 5, 6). Lowering the reaction temperature to 60 °C or changing the solvent from the sustainable 2-MeTHF to THF slightly diminished the product formation to 72% and 86%, respectively (entries 7, 8). Moreover, 2.5 equiv of HBpin with respect to each fluorine and the final hydroboration were required to achieve full conversion to the desired product, as was demonstrated by lowering the overall amount to 8 equiv (entry 9). Increasing the concentration from c = 0.2 M to c = 0.4 M also led to a slight decrease in conversion to the product (entry 10). Importantly, borane 2a was the only product received under the optimal conditions, besides a small amount (~5%) of the branched isomer (entry 1). A corresponding substrate without the alkene functionality did not undergo the defluorination-borylation reaction (see Supplementary Fig. 1 ).
Variation of the reaction conditions
a Determined by 1 H NMR of the crude reaction mixture with benzyl benzoate as internal standard.

We then explored the polydefluoro-monoborylation reaction on a range of perfluoroalkylated E -alkenes (<10% Z -isomer content) on a 0.5 mmol scale and determined the yield of the isolated borylation product (Fig. 2a ). In all cases, the linear alkyl borane was received as the main product in high regioselectivity. Methoxystyrene 1a gave an excellent 97% yield in 2a after 18 h. Other β-trifluoromethyl styrene derivatives, as well as a corresponding naphth-2-yl alkene, gave good yields of 70–80% ( 2b – d ). Here, substrates 1b and 1d had a higher 29% and 33% Z -isomer content, which did not seem to affect the yield. Gratifyingly, substrates with longer perfluoroalkyl chains attached to an alkene moiety also smoothly underwent the reaction, as is shown for n- perfluorobutyl alkene 1e , which gave 84% of alkylborane 2e . Even a primary alcohol function was tolerated, and exhaustive defluorination occurred, giving 59% yield in product 2f . Moreover, a tertiary amine as well as a trisubstituted alkene were well-tolerated, giving products 2g and 2h in 56% and 84%. Even n -perfluorohexyl and n -perfluorooctyl groups were quantitatively defluorinated and gave the corresponding products 2i and 2j in 81% and 90% yield, respectively. In the case of the latter, this corresponded to an outstanding defluorination performance of 99.4% per fluorine. Importantly, terminal alkenes smoothly underwent the polydefluorination-monoborlyation as well. Primary alkenes with perfluoroalkyl chains, such as 1k and 1l , are common precursors of PFAS polymers, and both gave the desired borane in high yield. In addition, a 1,1-disubstituted alkene (α-trifluoromethylstyrene, 1m ) gave product 2m in 61% yield with the linear hydroboration product (3,3,3-trifluoro-2-phenylpropyl)pinacolborane as a major byproduct. This successful polydefluorination-monoborylation of longer perfluoroalkyl chains (products 2e – 2l ) also pointed towards an iterative mechanism ( vide infra ).

Drawn hydrogen atoms indicate removed fluorides, and brackets show linear-branched product ratios. All yields refer to isolated material. a Perfluoroalkylated alkenes. n = number of removed fluorides. Conditions: substrate 1 (0.5 mmol), HBpin (3 n + 1 equiv), LiOMe ( n + 1 equiv), 2-MeTHF ( c = 2.0 M based on HBpin), 85 °C, 18 h. b gem -Difluoroalkenes. Conditions: substrate 3 (0.5 mmol), HBpin (10 equiv), LiOMe (4 equiv), 2-MeTHF ( c = 2.0 M based on HBpin), 85 °C, 18 h. a (3,3,3-Trifluoro-2-phenylpropyl)pinacolborane was observed as a major byproduct.

Since gem -difluoroalkenes are readily available and versatile synthesis building blocks 39 , 40 , we investigated the transfer of our method towards this compound class and tested the performance in the presence of various functional groups under the optimized conditions of Table 1 , entry 1 (Fig. 2b ). Besides biphenyl substrate 3a , electron-donating thioether and ether functions as well as electron-withdrawing fluoride, trifluoromethyl, and pinacolboryl groups were well-tolerated, resulting in yields of 47–81% ( 4a – 4g ). Here, 0–5% of the branched product was observed, with the exception of products 4e – g , which contained electron-withdrawing aryl substituents that affected the final hydroboration selectivity ( vide infra ) and raised the amount of the branched isomer to 13–20%. Product 4f further showed that a chemoselective conversion occurred in the presence of a benzylic trifluoromethyl group. ortho -Methyl- and methoxy-substituted phenyls were tolerated as well, as is shown for products 4h , 4i that were obtained in good yields. Further examples included a benzothiophene ( 4j ), a ferrocene ( 4k ), and a branched aliphatic compound ( 4l ) with yields of 54%, 86%, and 84%, respectively, all of which gave the linear product with high selectivity. Importantly, allylic gem -difluoroalkene 3m was smoothly converted into 4m (77% yield), indicating that such gem -difluoroalkenes are potential intermediates in the reaction of PFA substrates 1 .

It is noteworthy that substrates 1a–j were synthesized in one or two steps from perfluoroalkyl iodides or TFA, respectively 41 , 42 , and substrates 3 were directly accessible from sodium chlorodifluoroacetate 43 , all of which are commonly used PFAS or precursors thereof.

The scalability of the reaction and the recovery of fluoride were demonstrated by subjecting perfluoroalkene 1e to the optimized conditions on a 5 mmol scale (Fig. 3a ). For all examples in Fig. 2 , it was observed that a white solid formed, which was now conveniently isolated by filtration followed by washing with methanol. It was identified as LiF by powder X-ray diffraction analysis (PXRD) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The purity of the LiF obtained from two experiments was further determined by XPS and was found to be at least equal to a commercial sample of 99.98% purity (trace metal basis). In addition, the 7 Li and 19 F NMR (in D 2 O) spectra matched a commercial sample, and organic and boron-containing material was absent as determined by 1 H and 11 B NMR, respectively. The average yield in LiF was 84% (755% based on 1e ). In one of the experiments, no MeOH was added in the workup, and a short path distillation of the mother liquor was carried out, which allowed the recovery of 2.7 g of HBpin (15%) and the isolation of 1.5 g of MeOBpin (19% based on LiOMe), a byproduct of the reaction. Purification of the remaining material gave 2e in an average yield of 74%.

All yields refer to isolated material. a An experiment on a 5 mmol scale with isolation of LiF by filtration and optional isolation of HBpin and MeOBpin by distillation. b Defluorination-oxidation and sequential Suzuki coupling reactions. c Two-step conversion of a commercially used fluorotelomer alcohol into a primary borane. a An average of two experiments.

To further demonstrate the usefulness of our approach, we demonstrated the direct conversion of 1e into primary alcohol 5 by changing to an oxidative workup (Fig. 3b ). Separately, following the purification of 2e , the Suzuki coupling with 4-bromoanisole gave 6 in an overall yield of 59% from 1e . Finally, fluorotelomer alcohol 7 , an industrially used PFAS, was converted into borane 2k by elimination of the alcohol followed by polydefluorination-borylation in an overall 50% yield.

We then carried out preliminary investigations to probe the reaction mechanism. The defluorination of 3,3,3-trifluoropropylene (see Fig. 1b ) was first proposed to proceed via a syn -β-F-elimination after hydroboration 32 . But later, related 1,2-deborochlorination and 1,2-deborobromination reactions after hydroboration have been reported, for which an E2-type anti -elimination mechanism was established if a boron-ate complex-forming base, such as n -BuLi, or a Lewis acid was present 44 , 45 . We therefore suspected that the defluorination steps in our reaction also occurred via a similar anti -elimination mechanism and that the overall polydefluorination-monoborylation reaction resulted from iterative repetition of hydroboration-elimination events.

In order to probe this iterative mechanism, an experiment with 1e and a reduced amount of borane (conditions A) was carried out and the reaction mixture was analyzed by GC-MS (Fig. 4a ). In addition to still unreacted 1e (10%), multiple partially defluorinated alkenes 8 – 10 (24%) and, in smaller quantity, borane (7%) species 12 – 15 were identified based on their mass and fragmentation pattern. Product 2e was the main compound (54%), and 1% of the branched isomer was detected as well. The detailed composition of detected species is shown in the gray box in Fig. 4a . In a second experiment, both reagents, borane and lithium methoxide, were reduced (conditions B), which, in contrast, led to mainly borylated intermediates being present (69%) and only traces of fluorinated alkenes. Although not all expected intermediates could be detected, these two experiments support the iterative mechanism, and that lithium methoxide promotes the 1,2-deboro-defluorination.

a Experiments with reduced HBpin (conditions A) and reduced HBpin/LiOMe (conditions B) followed by GC-MS analysis of the reaction mixture. Alkenes 8 – 10 were assigned to be the shown Z -isomers based on their lower relative energy. b Defluoro-deuteroboration of 1a with DBpin. c Experiment with a deuterated fluorostyrene and 2.0 equiv HBpin proving the anti -elimination. d Reaction time course plot from individual reactions stopped after a certain time, followed by GC-MS analysis. e Proposed mechanism featuring iterative hydroboration/ anti -F-elimination steps. Calculated Hirshfeld partial charges indicate the expected hydroboration regioselectivity. a A small amount of the minor E -isomer ( 9’ ) was detected. b Combined amount of two regioisomers 12 / 12’ that could not be assigned. c Amount of the branched product regioisomer.

In a separate experiment, trifluoromethyl styrene 1a was reacted with deuterated pinacolborane DBpin. NMR analysis revealed 50% deuterium incorporation in the benzylic and homobenzylic position as well as full deuteration at the former trifluoromethyl carbon (Fig. 4b ). This deuterium distribution matched the expected distribution from an iterative hydroboration-elimination mechanism (see Supplementary Fig. 18 ). A second deuterium study was then carried out using selectively cis -monodeuterated fluoroalkene 16 - d 1 and a reduced amount of HBpin (Fig. 4c ). This allowed the observation of alkene intermediate 17 - d 1 in the crude reaction mixture after 48 h, which was again cis -monodeuterated. Since the alkene hydroboration is well-known to proceed with syn selectivity, the elimination step that removes the boryl and fluoride substituents must proceed via an anti mechanism to be in agreement with the observed cis -deuterated product.

Due to the strength of the B-F bond, a boron Lewis acid-assisted C–F cleavage followed by rapid fluoride-methoxide exchange was a possible scenario, in particular because FBpin readily interconverts into MeOBpin and LiF in the presence of LiOMe (see Supplementary Notes 9 ), which would explain the absence of B-F byproducts. However, using a separately prepared α-trifluoromethyl alkylborane, we could experimentally confirm that the 1,2-elimination is triggered by the addition of LiOMe without the requirement of a boron-based Lewis acid (see Supplementary Notes 9 ). Hence, a fluoride abstraction mechanism under direct formation of LiF and without intermediary B-F species is most likely.

We then recorded a time-course plot of the reaction of 1e using both NMR and GC-MS analysis, which showed that the reaction reached completion already after 4h and revealed alkenes 8 and 9 as main intermediates. The other species 10 – 15 were detected in relative amounts of <5% and are not plotted for reasons of clarity. More intriguing, however, is the observation of a sigmoid curve for the substrate conversion and thus an initiation period. In the past, it was proposed that alkene hydroborations with HBpin require a catalytic amount of BH 3 to be present, and the slow formation of the latter could explain this behavior 46 , 47 . However, distilling HBpin, which may remove trace amounts of BH 3 , did not affect the reaction outcome. Neither did the addition of BH 3 •THF (10 mol%) improve the initial conversion rate. Instead, it was discovered that pre-stirring HBpin and LiOMe for 1 h at 85 °C led to a dramatically improved conversion to 2e within the first 30 min (50% vs 0%). 11 B NMR revealed the formation of [(MeO)HBpin] – together with MeOBpin and BH 4 – during the pre-stirring at 85 °C, without detection of BH 3 (or B 2 H 6 ). Presumably, this ate complex has a stronger hydricity than HBpin and is the active hydroboration agent. We further suspect that this premature conversion of HBpin into non-productive MeOBpin and BH 4 – leads to the requirement of an excess of borane reagent. It should be further noted that for alkenes in conjugation with an arene such as 2a , the overall reaction was significantly slower, requiring 18 h to reach completion (see Supplementary Fig. 29 ).

Altogether, these results are in agreement with the mechanism shown in Fig. 4d . It starts with the hydroboration of the alkene function, which is accelerated by the presence of LiOMe through boron-ate complex formation. The regioselectivity is governed by the increased charge density at the CF 3 -bearing alkene carbon, favoring the borylation at this position and leading to intermediate A 48 , 49 . This is supported by the Hirshfeld charge density values at these alkene carbons (for R = 4-MeOPh) 50 that were calculated at the RI-TPSS-D4-CPCM(2-MeTHF)/def2-TZVP level with Orca 6 51 – 56 . The lithium cation then activates one of the fluorine atoms in the β-position, which facilitates the anti −1,2-elimination via the shown transition state to give gem -difluoroalkene intermediate B . Hydroboration then leads to the formation of C , which is in agreement with the species observed by GC-MS and by NMR in the time-course experiment. Repeated elimination and hydroboration events then result in the formation of fully defluorinated alkene D , which undergoes a final hydroboration with usual linear selectivity to give the final product. The reaction entries in Fig. 2b with gem -difluoroalkenes as substrates strongly support B as an intermediate.

In conclusion, a straightforward, exhaustive defluorination-monoborylation has been developed that “zips off” all fluorine atoms from linear perfluoroalkyls attached to an alkene function and transforms them into linear alkyl pinacolboranes. The reaction is concluded to proceed via an iterative hydroboration/ anti -defluoroborylation mechanism with gem -difluoroalkenes as intermediates that by themselves undergo the polydefluorinative borylation as well. The reaction is a unique example of a PFAS defluorination reaction that keeps the carbon framework intact, gives high yields even for longer perfluoroalkyl chains, and installs a new functional group. The newly introduced terminal boryl group enables further utilization in synthesis, rendering this work the first example of the conversion of environmentally problematic long-chain PFAS into useful synthesis building blocks. While this addresses the problem of a selective chemical conversion of certain PFAS, the method is likely transferable to other perhalogenated linear alkyls that present environmental hazards as well.

articles.title: A dual A-to-Y and G-to-Y base editor and a four-base concurrent hypermutator in mammalian cells.
articles.authors: Zhao N, Olajide JS, Guan Z, Huang J, Zou X, Ou F, Lin J, Tao T, Zhou T, Gao Z, Ren Z, Shi X, Huang X, Wang G.
articles.abstract: Abstract Current dual base editors and hypermutators exhibit limited types of base conversion and constrained mutational diversity. To address this challenge, we engineer a compact dual base editor “A&GBE” by fusing a deaminase and glycosylase with nickase Cas9 (nCas9) to enable concurrent adenine and cytosine editing. Furthermore, we develop quadruple base mutating modules (QBMM) by fusing nickase or dead Cas9 with engineered thymine-DNA glycosylase (TDG), N-methylpurine DNA glycosylase (MPG) and TadA8e, together with MS2-MCP system recruited activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID). This QBMM enables simultaneous mutation of all four types of nucleotide bases (A, T, G, C) within an approximately 100 base pair (bp) sequence surrounding the gRNA target site. This platform generates hyper diverse multi-nucleotide variants, establishing a powerful tool for accelerated protein evolution, functional genomics, and disease modeling. Subject terms: CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing

Current base editors exhibit limited types of base conversion and constrained mutational diversity. Here the authors develop a dual base editor for A-to-Y and G-to-Y changes, and a quadruple base mutating module (QBMM) that mutates all four DNA bases in mammalian cells.

Several single-nucleotide base editors (BEs) have been developed, including cytosine base editors (CBEs) for C-to-T conversion 1 , adenine base editors (ABEs) for A-to-G transition 2 , C-to-G base editors (CGBEs) 3 , 4 , adenine-to-pyrimidine base editors (AYBEs) 5 , guanine-to-pyrimidine base editors (GYBEs) 6 , and T-to-G base editors (TGBEs) 7 – 9 . To broaden their editing capability, several dual base editors have been developed to enable a simultaneous editing of two distinct base types, such as A-to-G and C-to-T 10 – 13 , A-to-G and C-to-G 14 , 15 , or A-to-G/C/T and C-to-T/G/A 16 . These dual base editors have great potential for creating or reverting multi-nucleotide variants (MNVs) 17 , 18 , an emerging category of sequence variants associated with genetic diseases. While current AYBE and GYBE facilitate targeted pyrimidine transversions, they have a restricted editing scope that limits their applications and therefore require multiplexed editing for the correction of diverse mutations. To address this, we engineer a dual-functional adenine and guanine base editor (A&GBE), which achieves simultaneous A-to-Y and G-to-Y conversions within a single editing window. However, even the most advanced dual base editors, including A&GBE, are inherently limited to modifying only two nucleotide types, thereby leaving the majority of possible base substitutions inaccessible.

Beyond generating or reverting MNVs, dual base editors and hypermutators represent powerful tools for directed evolution in mammalian systems. However, there are no optimal mutators available for directed evolution in mammalian cells that satisfy two fundamental parameters—high mutation rates and an unbiased mutational spectrum. Two CRISPR-activation-induced cytosine deaminase (CRISPR-AID)-based hypermutators have been demonstrated with high mutation rates for genomic diversification in mammalian cells 19 , 20 . However, their utility remains restricted due to pronounced C/G bias—predominantly converting cytosine and guanine bases while largely preserving adenine and thymine nucleotides 19 , 20 . Although emerging dual base editors partially address the limitation through expanded editing profiles, the current systems still fail to achieve comprehensive diversification across all four DNA bases. Thus, the field urgently needs a single tool capable of simultaneously targeting all nucleotides to achieve unbiased, high-efficiency mutagenesis.

To overcome these challenges, we develop a quadruple-base-mutating module (QBMM), which uniquely integrates an adenine deaminase (TadA8e), a thymine-DNA glycosylase (TDG), a cytosine deaminase (AID), and an engineered guanine excision protein (MPG) to concurrently mutate adenine, thymine, cytosine, and guanine within a single editing window. In marked contrast to existing base editors that are confined to specific base transitions or transversions, and unlike hypermutators that exhibit strong nucleotide bias, QBMM achieves a comprehensive and well-balanced mutational spectrum across all four DNA bases. This design directly addresses the two critical bottlenecks in CRISPR-based base editing—limited editing scope and skewed mutational profiles—and fulfills the long-standing need for a mutator that simultaneously delivers high mutation rates and unbiased diversification. QBMM therefore serves as a transformative platform for directed evolution and protein engineering in mammalian cells.

AYBE 5 enables A-to-Y(C/T) editing via a fusion protein comprising an adenine deaminase (TadA8e), nCas9, and an engineered hypoxanthine excision protein MPG3.0 (MPG carrying G163R, N169S, S198A, K202A, G203A, S206A and K210A mutations). Additionally, GYBE 6 mediates G-to-Y editing using nCas9 fused to a further engineered version, MPG6.3 (MPG3.0 carrying S169G, D175R, C178N, and Q294R mutations), which excises guanine. Given the structural similarity between deoxyinosine (the deamination product of adenine) and guanine, we hypothesized that MPG6.3 could catalyze the excision of both deoxyinosine and guanine. This dual-substrate capability would enable a single editor to simultaneously target both A and G bases, thereby expanding the scope of base editing for concurrent A and G conversions. To test this, we engineered a dual base editor, A&GBE, by fusing TadA8e, nCas9, and MPG6.3 (Fig. 1a ). Comparative analysis at 12 endogenous loci in HEK293T cells revealed that A&GBE maintained robust dual-activity, achieving both A-to-Y and G-to-Y editing at all tested sites (Fig. 1b ). In contrast, control editors (AYBE and GYBE) exhibited strictly mono-specific activities, consistent with prior reports 5 , 6 . Further comparison revealed that AYBE exhibited higher A-to-Y editing activity than A&GBE at most genomic sites (except ABE site 13, FANCF site 2), whereas A&GBE displayed higher G-to-Y editing activity than GYBE at most genomic sites (except ABE site 27, HBG), implying enhanced guanine excision when coupled with TadA8e. Notably, at TAG motifs, A&GBE outperformed AYBE in A-to-Y editing, while at TGA and CGA motifs, it exhibited even more pronounced G-to-Y editing relative to GYBE (Supplementary Fig. 1 ). Compared with AYBE, A&GBE showed lower A-to-T and A-to-C editing activity and a narrower editing window, but higher A-to-G editing. Compared with GYBE, A&GBE displayed higher overall G editing, particularly G-to-A and G-to-C (Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3 ). The elevated indel frequencies observed with AYBE and GYBE are consistent with the established mechanism 6 , whereby MPG-mediated base excision and subsequent AP endonuclease cleavage, combined with the nCas9-induced nick, produce DNA double-strand breaks. Consistent with this mechanism, A&GBE also induced substantial indels, likely reflecting the robust deoxyinosine (from A deamination) and guanine excision activity of MPG6.3. Notably, the overall indel frequencies of A&GBE were slightly lower than those of AYBE (Supplementary Fig. 4 ).

a Schematic architectures of AYBE, GYBE, and A&GBE. b Editing activities of AYBE, GYBE, and A&GBE at 12 endogenous genomic sites. c Cumulative indel frequencies across all sites (see Supplementary Fig. 4 for detailed indel information). Values and error bars reflect the mean and s.d. of three biological replicates performed on separate days. Source data are provided as a Source Data file.

Narrowing the editing window enables exclusive targeting of a single base, thereby ensuring precise modification of the intended base. To constrain the broad editing window of AYBE and A&GBE (both employing the TadA8e 21 adenine deaminase, which has a broad editing window), we generated six variants by replacing the TadA8e domain with our previously characterized adenine deaminase variants—E4-TadA, E14-TadA, and E11-TadA 22 , yielding E4-AYBE, E14-AYBE, and E11-AYBE for AYBE, and E4-A&GBE, E14-A&GBE, and E11-A&GBE for A&GBE (Supplementary Fig. 5a ). We first evaluated the editing profiles of all six variants alongside the original AYBE, A&GBE, and ABE8e at six genomic loci (Site 13, Site 17, HBG, Site 5, Site 6, Site 26) (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 5b ). All AYBE-based variants (E4-, E14-, and E11-AYBE) exhibited a narrowed adenine-editing window compared with parental AYBE (Fig. 2b ), consistent with our previous observations 22 . Among these variants, E14-AYBE maintained editing efficiency comparable to AYBE, whereas E4-AYBE and E11-AYBE showed reduced activity. Similarly, all three A&GBE variants (E4-, E14-, and E11-A&GBE) exhibited a narrowed adenine-editing window relative to parental A&GBE. Among them, E14-A&GBE largely maintained editing activity, whereas E4-A&GBE and E11-A&GBE showed compromised efficiency. To further verify these editing properties across a broader set of targets, we tested the two best-performing variants, E14-AYBE and E14-A&GBE, together with the original AYBE and A&GBE, at an additional six loci (Site 3, Site 2, Site 27, FANCF site 2, Site 11, and VEGFA site 3) (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Figs. 5c ). At these loci, both E14-AYBE and E14-A&GBE maintained narrowed adenine-editing windows. Notably, across 8 out of the total 12 genomic sites examined (Site 13, Site 17, HBG, Site 5, Site 3, Site 2, Site 27, and VEGFA site 3), the E14-A&GBE showed higher guanine editing activity and a broader editing window than the parental A&GBE (Fig. 2a, b ).

a Editing profiles of AYBE, E14-AYBE, A&GBE, and E14-A&GBE at 12 genomic sites. Values and error bars represent the mean and s.d. from three biological replicates performed on separate days (see Supplementary Fig. 6 for indel information). b Cumulative frequencies of A to other bases and G to other bases across the protospacer at the edited sites (PAM located at positions 21–23). Source data are provided as a Source Data file.

The previously characterized AYBE 5 and GYBE 6 were based on nCas9, which is largely due to the fact that the nicking property of nCas9 mediated higher base editing compared to that of dCas9, as initially demonstrated for CBE and ABE. However, nCas9 also induced a higher indel rate, an aspect that poses a challenge to therapeutic applications. The performance of dCas9-derived AYBE and GYBE remained unexplored. To address this, we investigated whether replacing dCas9 with nCas9 in AYBE, GYBE, and our dual-base editor A&GBE would similarly reduce indels. We constructed three dCas9-derived editor variants (dGYBE, dAYBE, and dA&GBE) and compared their editing profiles with nCas9-derived variants, with ABE8e included as a control, in HEK293T cells. As with prior studies 5 , 6 and our earlier findings, AYBE, GYBE, and A&GBE showed adenine, guanine, and concurrent adenine and guanine editing activity respectively, at six genomic sites (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Figs. 7 – 9 ). dGYBE exhibited significantly reduced guanine-editing efficiency relative to GYBE and showed markedly lower indel frequencies. dAYBE demonstrated lower adenine-editing activity than AYBE, yet achieved a pronounced reduction in indel rates. dA&GBE displayed decreased dual-base-editing efficiency, but substantially reduced indels compared with A&GBE. Overall, all three dCas9-derived editors exhibited significantly lower indel frequencies than their nCas9 counterparts. In addition, we observed diverse editing profiles for A&GBE and dA&GBE (Supplementary Fig. 10 ), which could be leveraged to develop a hypermutator.

a Editing activities of AYBE and A&GBE at six genomic sites. b Cumulative indel frequencies across all sites (see Supplementary Fig. 9 for detailed indel information). Values and error bars reflect the mean and s.d. of three biological replicates performed on separate days. Source data are provided as a Source Data file.

Based on A&GBE and dA&GBE, we sought to develop an advanced base mutator capable of simultaneously editing adenine, guanine, and cytosine. Given that AID (hyperactive cytosine deaminase) is known to primarily mutate cytosine and guanine 19 , 20 , we hypothesized that combining A&GBE or dA&GBE with AID could achieve this goal. Unlike A&GBE or dA&GBE, AID was recruited to the target site via the MS2-MCP system (Fig. 4a ). We evaluated the mutation activity of dA&GBE + AID and A&GBE + AID in a GFP-integrated HEK293T cell line (Fig. 4a , see Supplementary Fig. 11 for workflow). dCas9+AID, A&GBE, and dA&GBE were also included for testing (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 12 ). With minimal substitution frequencies (mostly <0.1%) for the blank control, dCas9+AID displayed 1-5% substitution frequencies across all five tested GFP target sites (gGFP1-5), consistent with a previous report 20 . Within the protospacer regions (position −20 to 0, where position 0 is adjacent to the PAM) of the five gRNAs, we observed varying nucleotide substitution frequencies for A&GBE editors. Both dA&GBE + AID and A&GBE + AID induced comparable levels of mutagenesis throughout the target region, exceeding the activity of dA&GBE, A&GBE, and dCas9+AID at the majority of positions. Interestingly, constructs with AID showed higher substitution frequencies in a 40-bp PAM-adjacent flanking region (position 0 to 40) across all five gRNAs targeting sites.

a Schematic of mutator design. b Distribution of base substitution frequencies along the GFP sequence. Frequency (freq.) at each base was calculated as the percentage of reads containing substitutions relative to the total reads covering that base (%). Each dot represents a nucleotide. Data from the first of three independent biological replicates are shown (see Supplementary Fig. 12 for all three repeats). c The total base substitution frequency (Mock-subtracted at each nucleotide position) within the protospacer (−20 to 0) and flanking regions, as well as for the flanking region alone. Each data point represents one of five independent GFP target sites from one of three biological replicates ( n = 15 independent transfections). Horizontal bars indicate the median. Source data are provided as a Source Data file.

Next, we analyzed the mutational signatures of each construct by quantifying base conversion frequencies across the protospacer and flanking regions (Fig. 4c ). Consistent with prior reports 19 , dCas9+AID preferentially converted C or G to other bases. In contrast, A&GBE and dA&GBE primarily induced A or G conversions, aligning with our earlier findings. Strikingly, A&GBE + AID and dA&GBE + AID generated high-frequency substitutions at A, C, and G, demonstrating triple-base-editing capability. To assess mutational patterns beyond the protospacer, we calculated the median frequencies of base conversions in the flanking regions (Fig. 4c ). Here, dCas9+AID maintained elevated C/G substitutions, whereas A&GBE and dA&GBE showed stronger A-specific activity without significant G editing. Notably, A&GBE + AID and dA&GBE + AID outperformed all other constructs in C/G substitution rates but exhibited unexpectedly low A editing in these regions. Both A&GBE + AID and dA&GBE + AID exhibited more evenly distributed C and G mutations to other bases compared with A&GBE and dA&GBE (Supplementary Fig. 13 ). Given the advantages of dA&GBE + AID for downstream applications, we selected it for further development of a quadruple-base mutation system.

Although thymine-DNA glycosylase (TDG) has been engineered as a T-to-G base editor (TGBE) 7 – 9 , its activity also induces T-to-A and T-to-C conversions through thymine excision followed by base excision repair (BER). We hypothesized that integrating engineered TDG 8 into the dA&GBE + AID module could further expand both mutagenic scope and efficiency. Based on TadA8e-dCas9-MPG, we generated two mutator constructs (TDG-TadA8e-dCas9-MPG + AID and TadA8e-TDG-dCas9-MPG + AID, abbreviated as dTAGBE+AID and dATGBE+AID respectively). We assessed the editing efficiency of the three mutator groups in GFP-integrated HEK293T cells (Fig. 5a , see Supplementary Fig. 9 for workflow). Deep sequencing results showed that A&GBE + AID and dTAGBE+AID exhibited comparable substitution frequencies across all five targeted protospacer and flanking regions, and both were generally higher than those of dATGBE+AID (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 14 ).

Frequency at each position was calculated as the percentage of reads containing a substitution relative to all reads covering that base. Each dot represents a nucleotide. Data from the first repeat of three independent biological replicates are shown (see Supplementary Fig. 14 for all three repeats). c Total base substitution frequency (Mock-subtracted at each nucleotide position) calculated for the protospacer region (positions −20 to 0) plus flanking regions, and for the flanking regions alone. Each data point represents one of five independent GFP target sites from one of three biological replicates ( n = 15 independent transfections). Horizontal bars indicate the median. d Proportions of A, C, G, and T mutated to other bases by dTAGBE+AID (see Supplementary Fig. 15 for other mutators). Data are from three independent experiments. Source data are provided as a Source Data file.

We then analyzed the mutational profiles of these mutator groups in detail for the protospacer and flanking regions (Fig. 5c ). Compared with dA&GBE + AID, dTAGBE+AID and dATGBE+AID introduced higher levels of T substitution in both the combined protospacer and flanking regions and in the flanking regions alone, confirming functional TDG integration. dTAGBE+AID demonstrated superior editing efficiency compared with dATGBE+AID in both region sets, indicating that the relative positioning of the deaminase and glycosylase significantly influenced editing outcomes. Although dTAGBE+AID generated less A, C, and G editing than dA&GBE + AID in the combined protospacer and flanking regions, it unexpectedly generated higher A and T substitutions in the flanking regions. Overall, dTAGBE+AID produced a more balanced mutational spectrum across all four bases, with particularly A-to-other base conversions compared with dA&GBE + AID (Fig. 5d and Supplementary Fig. 15 ). Collectively, dTAGBE+AID achieved high substitution frequencies with an expanded activity window, enabling comprehensive mutagenesis of all four bases. dTAGBE+AID is therefore recommended for future applications.

To evaluate whether stacking multiple modules (AID, TadA8e, TDG, MPG) exacerbates BER-related genotoxicity, we compared cell viability among AID, AGBE, dA&GBE, A&GBE + AID, dA&GBE + AID, and dTAGBE using the CCK8 assay at 72 h post-transfection, with the mock group set to 100% (Supplementary Fig. 16 ). AID alone exhibited negligible cytotoxicity. While all A&GBE-containing constructs led to reduced cell viability, dA&GBE and dA&GBE + AID showed improved viability compared with their A&GBE and A&GBE + AID counterparts respectively, indicating that dCas9-based configurations confer lower cytotoxicity than those utilizing nCas9 alone. dTAGBE +AID displayed the lowest viability among the tested groups.

We sought to apply QBMM to perform functional mutagenesis in endogenous coding sequences. We initially screened for mutations within MEK1 (also known as MAP2K1 ) that promote resistance to small-molecule drug inhibition. MEK inhibitors target the MAPK-ERK (extracellular signal-regulated kinase) pathway, which is aberrantly upregulated in one-third of all cancers 23 . We used QBMM to diversify exons of the MEK1 gene in A375 cells, with deep sequencing confirming a saturated mutational spectrum (Supplementary Fig. 17 ), a melanoma line sensitive to MEK inhibition. After 3 days of mutagenesis, we selected cells for resistance to selumetinib (Fig. 6a ). We targeted exons 2, 3, and 4, which contain previously identified mutation hotspots 24 , 25 . Nine gRNAs targeting MEK1 exon were designed to introduce saturation mutagenesis, and exons with high mutation frequencies were identified by deep sequencing (Fig. 6b ). We recovered drug-tolerant mutants and identified MEK1 mutations by targeted amplicon sequencing (see Methods). We identified four candidate mutations (Q46R, Q56P, K57E, and G75A) (Table 1 ). Comparison of pre- and post-selection allele frequencies showed marked enrichment of all four identified variants (Supplementary Fig. 18 ).

a Workflow of the QBMM MEK1 inhibitor–resistance screen. A375 cells were transfected with QBMM and diversified for 3 days. The genomically diversified cells were then selected with selumetinib for 20 days. Genomes of resistant clones were harvested and subjected to deep sequencing. b Schematic showing the distribution of sequencing reads across part of MEK1 exon 2. c Growth inhibition curves of parental A375 cells and A375 cells expressing either wild-type MEK1 or the indicated possible MEK1 inhibitor-resistant alleles. Data are presented as mean ± s.d. from three biological replicates. d Structure of MEK1 in complex with selumetinib (PDB code: 7JUZ). MEK1 is depicted in blue. Selumetinib is shown in orange. Source data are provided as a Source Data file.
Table of candidate hits identified in the MEK1 inhibitor-resistance screen

To validate the candidates, we constructed five expression plasmids: one expressing wild‑type MEK1 and four expressing MEK1 with each of the individual mutations. The ability of these mutations to confer selumetinib resistance was then evaluated using growth inhibition assays (Fig. 6d ). A375 cells expressing wild‑type MEK1 (MEK‑wt) or MEK1 G75A exhibited GI₅₀ values comparable to that of parental A375 cells (≈29 nM; Fig. 6d ). In contrast, MEK1 Q46R, Q56P, and K57E increased selumetinib GI₅₀ values by 3.8‑fold, 40.9‑fold, and 35.1‑fold respectively. Notably, the Q56P mutation has previously been reported to confer selumetinib resistance 24 , and all three mutations (Q46R, Q56P, and K57E) have also been shown to confer resistance to the clinically relevant MEK inhibitor trametinib 25 , further supporting their functional significance as MEK1 hotspot resistance alleles. G75A likely represents a concurrent passenger mutation, as it was co‑detected with K57E in several cDNA clones.

Structural analysis revealed that all three resistance‑conferring mutations cluster in or near the N‑terminal helix A of MEK1, a well‑characterized autoinhibitory element that normally restrains kinase activity by packing against the core kinase domain (Fig. 6e ). Q56P introduces a helix‑breaking proline residue, thereby disrupting the helical conformation of helix A. K57E reverses the charge of a key lysine in the negative regulatory domain 26 , which likely weakens the autoinhibitory interaction. Q46R, located immediately upstream of helix A, introduces a bulky, positively charged side chain that likely perturbs the N-terminal autoinhibitory segment. Consequently, all three mutations relieve the autoinhibitory constraint, leading to elevated basal MEK1 kinase activity and sustained ERK signaling even in the presence of allosteric MEK inhibitors, thereby conferring strong (Q56P, K57E) or moderate (Q46R) resistance. Overall, these results demonstrate that, by generating an unbiased mutational spectrum, QBMM enables the identification of drug resistance-conferring mutations.

The development of versatile base editors capable of conducting all possible base conversion not only expands the genome-editing toolbox for basic research but also holds significant therapeutic potential for treating diseases caused by genetic mutations. In this study, we engineered a compact dual base editor A&GBE with a single MPG domain, which could simultaneously mediate A-to-Y and G-to-Y editing. This strategy eliminated the need for separate MPG3.0 5 and MPG6.3 6 constructs. This design not only simplifies delivery but also facilitates the integration of additional effector proteins for broader mutagenesis applications.

To enhance the editing precision of AYBE and A&GBE, we refined their adenine-editing window by replacing the TadA8e adenine deaminase with our previously evolved TadA variants (E4/E14/E11-TadA) 22 , which constrains deamination activity to a narrower range. Notably, the guanine editing activity of A&GBE substituted with E14-TadA was improved slightly compared with A&GBE (Fig. 2b ). We propose that the reduced DNA-binding affinity of these TadA mutants—attributed primarily to charge-neutralizing or reversing substitutions (e.g., N38D, R39G, R107G)—may alleviate steric hindrance with MPG, thereby facilitating the substrate engagement of MPG. This observation is consistent with earlier reports indicating that TadA (V106W) and nCas9 compete for DNA access 21 . Our results demonstrate a practical strategy for constructing functional fusion proteins without compromising the activity of individual components.

Existing targeted hyper mutators in mammalian cells are constrained by a narrow mutational spectrum, primarily yielding C-to-T or G-to-A substitutions 19 , 20 . Recent advances, including T7 polymerase-driven continuous editing (TRACE 23 /TRIDENT 24 ) and helicase-assisted continuous editing (HACE 27 ), have extended the editable range to over 1000–2000 bp. However, these systems remain limited to C-to-T or A-to-G substitutions mediated by AID or TadA respectively. In contrast, our strategy—which could combines multiplexed gRNAs—enables long-range, all-four-base diversification in endogenous mammalian genomes. QBMM therefore provides unique opportunities for disease analysis. For instance, it can recapitulate multi‑nucleotide variants found in cancer (e.g., concurrent mutations in oncogenes and tumor suppressors) or in neurological disorders such as Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease. It also enables saturation mutagenesis to functionally annotate variants of uncertain significance in disease‑linked genes, such as MYH7 in cardiomyopathies. These capabilities bridge unbiased hypermutation with clinically relevant disease analysis. We anticipate that QBMM will deliver key advances in high-resolution sequence-function mapping, systematic analysis of genetic regulation and disease, and efficient directed evolution in mammalian cells.

Lentiviral plasmid expressing AYBE (Lv-AYBE-Cas9n-Puro) and GYBE (Lv-Cas9n-MPGv6.3_Puro) were made by cloning AYBE and GYBE gene sequences from AYBEv3 (Addgene, #193967) and gGBEv6.3-SpCas9 (Addgene, #202629) respectively. Lv-AGBE-Puro was constructed through the exchange of MPGv3.0 with MPGv6.3 gene in gGBEv6.3-SpCas9 plasmid (Addgene, #202629).

DNA ligation was performed using ClonExpress® II One Step Cloning Kit (Vazyme), and all clones were transformed into home-made Stbl3 Competent E. Coli . Individual colony was grown at 37 °C (non-lentiviral plasmid) or 30 °C (lentiviral plasmid) at 220 rpm for ~16–22 h. Plasmids were purified with HiPure Plasmid Mini/midi Kit, HiPure Plasmid EF Midi Kit (Magen, #P1002-02, #P1003-02, and #P1113-02). All constructs were validated by Sanger sequencing, and sequence alignment was conducted with CodonCode Aligner.

A375 melanoma cells (donated by Dr. Jing Yang, Gannan Medical University) and HEK293T cells (purchased from National Collection of Authenticated Cell Cultures) were grown in a humidified 37 °C incubator with 5% CO 2 using DMEM media supplemented with 100 I.U./mL penicillin and 100 µg/mL streptomycin (Thermo Fisher, #15140163).

Transfection experiment for functional validation: HEK293T cells were seeded into 24-well plates and transfected with 1500 ng BE and 500 ng gRNA plasmids per well using EZtrans (Life iLAB, China) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Protospacer sequences for all mammalian genomic sites targeted in this study are provided in Supplementary Data 1 . Twenty-four hours after transfection, the culture media were exchanged with fresh culture media supplemented with 2 µg/ml puromycin (Solarbio, China) and 20 µg/ml blasticidin (Solarbio, China). 3 days after transfection, genomic DNA was extracted for PCR amplification, and the resultant PCR products were subjected to deep sequencing.

Genomic DNA extraction for base editing test assay: The harvested cells were mixed with 30 μl lysis buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 50 mM KCl, 1.5 mM MgCl 2 , 0.5% Nonidet P-40, 0.5% Tween−20, and 100 μg/ml proteinase K (Roche)) and incubated under the following procedure: 68 °C for 30 min, 16 °C for 2 min and 98 °C for 5 min. The lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 3 min and the supernatant was collected as template. The target genomic loci were amplified from genomic DNA using Phanta® Max Super-Fidelity DNA Polymerase (Vazyme) using the following program: 95 °C for 5 min, 35 cycles of 95 °C for 30 s, 56 °C for 30 s, 72 °C for 20 s, and 72 °C for 5 min. The purified PCR products were subjected to Sanger sequencing or targeted deep sequencing. Sanger sequencing data were analyzed by EditR for base-editing activity.

Endogenous target sites of interest were amplified from genomic DNA as previously described 9 . Genomic DNA was extracted, and the regions of interest in the target sites were amplified by PCR using site-specific primers (Supplementary Data 2 ). In brief, the amplicons were ligated to adapters, and sequencing was performed on the Illumina platforms. The targeted amplicon sequencing reads were processed using fastp with default parameters, and further amplicon sequencing analyses were performed by CRISPResso (Supplementary Data 3 ).

PCR products were purified by the VAHTS DNA clean Beads (Vazyme) and then subjected to library construction and high-throughput sequencing on an Illumina Nova 6000 with PE150 mode (Annoroad, Beijing, China). The numbers of sequencing reads obtained for each amplicon are provided in Supplementary Data 4 . The amplicon sequencing data were analyzed using CRISPResso2 (v.2.0.3) in the batch mode, with parameters “--q 30 --base_edit --wc -8 --fastq_output --base_editor_output --write_cleaned_report --place_report_in_output_folder.” Editing efficiency was quantified from the “Quantification_window_nucleotide_percentage_table.txt” table. Indels were quantified from the “Alleles_frequency_table_around_sgRNA_*.txt” table. The results including A-to-Y conversion rates, C-to-non-Y (A-to-G) conversion rates, G-to-Y conversion rates, G-to-non-Y(G-to-A) and indel rates were calculated. Sum of base substitution frequency were calculated with the formula: Sum of N Nucleotide substitution feq.= sum (N mutated to other bases) of specific treatment-sum (N mutated to other bases) of untreated cells.

A375 cells grown in the absence of antibiotics were seeded into 6-well plates (Biofil, China). At 12–14 h post-seeding, cells at approximately 70% confluency were transfected with 12 μL of Lipofectamine 2000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 4.5 μg of dTAGBE+AID plasmids, 1.5 μg of MS2-sgRNAs-AID targeting MEK1 exons 2, 3, and 4, following the manufacturer’s instructions. Three days later, cells were split into three wells of a 6-well plate and selected with selumetinib (TargetMol, Cat#6218) at 100 nM for 20 days. A portion of preselection cells was harvested as a control. Cells were passaged every 3 days to maintain confluency below 70%. After selection, the total RNA was extracted from cells using an RNAsimple Total RNA Kit (Tiangen Biotech, Beijing, China, Cat#DP419) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The cDNA was synthesized by reverse transcription using HiScript II 1st Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (Vazyme). The MEK1 was amplified by forward primer CGACGGCTCTGCAGTTAAC and reverse primer GTCTGACTGCACAGAGTAATG. Sequencing libraries for cDNA were generated using the S-1.2× TN5 library enrichment Mix. Libraries were subsequently sequenced using the SaluSeq Nimbo sequencing kit on the SaluSeq Nimbo sequencer.

The full-length MEK1 coding sequence was amplified from cDNA of the post-selection cells under the following program: 95 °C for 5 min, 30 cycles of 95 °C for 30 s, 56 °C for 30 s, 72 °C for 20 s, and 72 °C for 5 min. The purified PCR products were ligated into an expression plasmid using ClonExpress® II One Step Cloning Kit (Vazyme). Plasmids were purified with HiPure Plasmid EF Midi Kit (Magen, cat#P1113-02). All constructs were validated by Sanger sequencing, and sequence alignment was conducted with CodonCode Aligner.

Cell viability was assessed using an Enhanced CCK-8 Cell Counting Kit (Genesand, CCK102-500) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. In brief, ~3 × 10 5 A375 cells in 2.5 ml of growth medium were seeded in a six-well plate. The cells were transfected with 6 μg of the respective MEK1 expression plasmids. One day after transfection, cells were transferred to 48‑well plates and cultured in 250 μL of medium containing 5% FBS and various concentrations of selumetinib. After 7 days, cells were washed with DPBS and incubated with 200 μL medium containing CCK‑8 reagent for 1.5 hours. Afterward, 100 μL cell culture medium was replaced in the 96-well plate for measuring at 450 nm to assess cell viability. Cell viability was then calculated by comparing the absorbance of treated samples to that of control (untreated) samples, typically using the formula: Percentage of cell viability = (Atreatment − Ablank)/(Acontrol − Ablank) × 100%. Final values can then be obtained by averaging results from triple biology replicates for plotting.

GraphPad Prism 9 software was used to analyze the data. All numerical values are presented as mean ± s.d, as noted otherwise. Data from the targeted deep sequencing were corrected for between-session variation using Factor Correction. No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. No data were excluded from the analyses. The experiments were not randomized. The Investigators were not blinded to allocation during experiments and outcome assessment.

articles.title: Model-free pattern separation of two-color ultrafast X-ray diffraction.
articles.authors: Hecht L, Ovcharenko Y, Lægdsmand AØ, Bastian B, Baumann TM, Colombo A, De S, De Fanis A, Dold S, Fennel T, Hartmann R, Kolatzki K, Krishnan S, Kruse B, Laforge AC, Langbehn B, Mandal S, Mazza T, Medina C, Peltz C, Pfeifer T, Senfftleben B, Sishodia K, Stienkemeier F, Tanyag RMP, Tümmler P, Usenko S, Heidenreich A, Meyer M, Rupp D, Mudrich M.
articles.abstract: Abstract Two-color X-ray imaging with Free Electron Laser pulses offers a powerful approach for probing ultrafast structural dynamics in nanoscale systems, combining (near-)atomic spatial resolution with femtosecond temporal precision. The first X-ray pulse captures the object’s initial state, while the second, time-delayed pulse records its subsequent evolution. A key challenge lies in disentangling the two patterns simultaneously recorded by the same detector. We demonstrate the realization of this approach on structurally varying nanoscale particles using two X-ray pulses of different photon energies, 1 and 1.2 keV. Sub-micrometer helium nanodroplets generated in vacuum are irradiated by the two X-ray pulses separated in time by up to 750 femtoseconds. Taking advantage of the high photon-energy resolution of the imaging detector, we separate the overlapping diffraction signals by analyzing individual pixel counts and applying pattern recognition. The helium nanodroplets’ spherical shape allows us to cross-validate this approach by fitting the radial scattering profiles with Mie solutions for abichromatic field. The excellent agreement between the two methods, particularly in the sparsely illuminated outer regions of the diffraction patterns where high-resolution structural information is encoded, highlights the quality of this approach and its potential for future advanced X-ray movie techniques. Subject terms: Imaging techniques, Imaging and sensing, Nanoparticles, X-rays
