Current AI systems for leukemia detection typically rely on costly whole-slide scanners, limiting accessibility in low-resource settings. Here, the authors present ALLocate, a low-cost, AI-driven microscope plugin that enables self-driving microscopy for accurate and affordable leukemia detection without whole-slide scanners.

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a hematologic malignancy caused by the proliferation of hematopoietic stem cells and accounts for approximately 28% of leukemia-related deaths worldwide 1 – 3 . Diagnosis typically requires identification of ≥20% leukemic blasts in bone marrow or peripheral blood 4 – 7 , a process that depends on manual examination of 200–500 cells per smear under light microscopy. This task, typically performed by trained pathologists or hematologists, is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and inherently variable due to its subjective nature 7 , 8 . As clinical volumes rise, the need for faster, standardized diagnostics grows, especially in resource-constrained settings with limited access to expert hematologists or pathologists. For instance, countries in sub-Saharan Africa have only 0.1 to 1.3 hematopathologists per million people, creating substantial barriers to the timely diagnosis of hematologic malignancies 9 .

Recent deep learning approaches have shown considerable promise in automating bone marrow histologic evaluation, particularly for single-cell classification 10 , 11 . Matek et al. applied convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to over 170,000 single-cell images from marrow smears, achieving high performance across cell types 12 . Sun et al. introduced a deep ensemble model for bone marrow morphometry that demonstrated expert-level accuracy and strong generalizability on an independent dataset 13 . Incorporating object detection techniques, Chandradevan et al. developed a two-stage pipeline combining Faster R-CNN and VGG16, reporting an AUC-ROC of 96% for detection and 98% for classification using scanned images from 17 patients 14 . Lewis et al. proposed a three-part framework consisting of a region classifier, Fast R-CNN, and CNN-based classification, achieving accuracies ranging from 62% to 96% across various cell types 15 . Nakamura et al. applied semi-supervised learning and segmentation strategies, reaching 98% accuracy in region classification 16 . Beyond region proposal-based models, YOLO architectures have also been explored in hematology; however, most applications have focused on peripheral blood 17 , 18 . To date, only a limited number of studies have applied YOLO models specifically to bone marrow smears 19 , 20 .

While these studies have shown encouraging results, most rely on expensive high-end whole-slide imaging (WSI) systems, which are prohibitively expensive, often exceeding $300,000 USD, and are not readily available in many hospitals or small clinics 14 , 15 , 20 . This challenge is even greater in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where diagnostic infrastructure and specialist availability are severely limited. WSIs enable large-scale data generation and model training but limit deployment due to cost and technical requirements. Manual images captured with light microscopes are more accessible and more common in LMICs’ clinical laboratories, but remain inefficient and impractical for AI deployment due to laborious field selection. This creates a diagnostic gap, where timely leukemia diagnosis is hindered by the lack of affordable imaging tools and automated analysis systems. Overall, an affordable, automated method for capturing and analyzing marrow smears without relying on whole-slide scanners is urgently needed. Despite ongoing advances in deep learning applications to assist in the diagnostic evaluation of leukemia, there remains a need for an AI system that is low-cost, fully automated, and capable of generalizing across real-world smear variability. Recent efforts have explored low-cost and edge-based microscopy platforms for hematologic and cytologic applications. For example, Li et al. developed an autonomous, low-cost microscopy system (~$250–$500) capable of detecting infectious agents in peripheral blood smears, including Loa loa , Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense , and malaria 21 , 22 . Similarly, Maturana et al. introduced a 3D-printed robotic add-on with smartphone-based imaging for malaria detection 23 . While these approaches, together with other low-cost digital microscopy frameworks, demonstrate the feasibility of inexpensive automated microscopy 24 , 25 , they are primarily focused on infectious disease detection and peripheral blood analysis, with limited evaluation for leukocyte classification in bone marrow smears.

In this work, we present ALLocate (Acute Leukemia Locate), a relatively low-cost, AI-powered self-driving microscope system enabling blast detection for leukemia evaluation. It integrates an inexpensive, 3D-printed programmable microscope scanner with two deep learning modules: a CNN-based region classifier and a YOLOv8-based, one-step cell detection and classification model. Designed to operate without reliance on expensive whole-slide imaging infrastructure, ALLocate enables rapid, accurate, and affordable leukemia diagnosis. We evaluated its performance across three core tasks: ROI identification, blast cell detection, and full slide-level diagnosis and quantification on both digital and glass slides. This study leverages a large-scale annotated dataset comprising more than 11,000 marrow regions and 130,000 individual cells, and includes extensive validation on independent cohorts, including a multi-institutional set of 165 physical bone marrow smear slides. Overall, we evaluated a computational pathology framework across both digital slide analysis and real-time glass slide assessment using a self-driving microscope platform. Our evaluation validates ALLocate's robustness, precision, and generalizability, underscoring its potential as a less costly solution for AI-assisted leukemia diagnosis in resource-limited clinical settings.

An integrated deep learning model system was developed for automatic bone marrow slide evaluation without the need to digitize slides using a whole-slide scanner or viewer (Fig. 1 ). The smear will first pass through the ALLocate Automated Microscope Scanning System (AAMSS), which was implemented in accordance with an existing proof-of-concept design 26 . AAMSS transforms the smears into digital images automatically using stepper motors and a program to automatically control the movement of the microscope stage (Fig. 1A ). It consists of two NEMA 14 motors that are mounted into a 3D-printed shell adjacent to the existing knobs for manual control of the microscope stage. Customizable 3D-printed fittings are mounted to the X and Y knobs of the stage and connected to the stepper motors ( Supplementary Dataset 1 ). Through a program, the scanning duration and path can be controlled and uploaded to the Arduino control board, enabling automated capture of a representative region of the smear. Further details on the implementation of AAMSS and its controller are included in the Methods section. Fig. 1 Fully integrated system design of ALLocate. A The ALLocate hardware consists of a RepRap Arduino Mega Polulu Shield (RAMPS) control board shield on an Arduino Mega 2560 board (5), 3D-printed parts (1, 3), and two NEMA 14 motors (2, 4). The ALLocate cost ($150, $1150 with microscope) is significantly lower than WSI scanners. B The smear is scanned by ALLocate hardware connected to the microscope and then processed through an image sampling system, which segments the image into smaller tiles and passes them through a region classifier. YOLOv8 is applied to the adequate regions, giving precise detection within selected regions. C Workflow validation across multiple levels, including region-of-interest identification, blast cell detection, validation on an independent digital-slide cohort, and end-to-end evaluation on physical glass slides.

Downstream of the hardware module, the integrated AI modules deliver the diagnostic power of ALLocate. Each of the captured images is passed through a trained region classifier to select the adequate marrow regions. Furthermore, a trained cell detection module is applied on the diagnostic regions, giving a precise detection of blasts and normal cells (Fig. 1B ). Model development was performed exclusively using data from the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), while validation experiments were conducted on independent cohorts from both UCSF and Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC) to ensure robust assessment of generalizability (Table 1 and Table S1 ). D Model accuracy and AUC score on the MSKCC whole-slide dataset with regions evaluated per slide ranging from 1 to 50, demonstrating the performance of ALLocate with varying sample sizes. Lines represent mean values across five independent folds, and error bands represent ±1 standard deviation ( n = 5 folds) across the 40-slide cohort. Source data are provided as a Source Data file.

Box plots show the median as the center line, the 25th and 75th percentiles as the lower and upper bounds of the box, and whiskers extending to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range (mean blast ratio: 0.41% normal, 40.28% AML). The ALLocate system starts by finding diagnostic regions from digitized slide images. The whole bone marrow aspirate smear contains a variety of complex areas, which can be grouped into three typical categories: clotted areas within the spicules (clot regions), mononuclear cell-enriched areas (adequate regions) and areas with mostly red blood cells (blood regions) (Fig. 2A and Fig. S1 ). Pathologists routinely scan marrow smears at low magnification to identify mononuclear cell-enriched areas for further cell-level classification. To emulate this process, a CNN-based region classifier was developed to identify suitable regions for further classification, thereby reducing the pipeline's overall processing time and streamlining the detection workflow. The model was trained on 9149 region tiles and evaluated on 2286 region tiles, which were labeled by hematopathologists as either adequate, blood, or clot regions (TR, ER).

Figure 2B shows the model’s performance using ROC curves, with AUC reported for each class. The model demonstrates excellent performance across all region types, with AUCs of 0.992 for adequate regions, 0.998 for blood regions, and 0.997 for clot regions. Validation performance across different hyperparameter settings, as well as detailed evaluation and training logs on a randomly sampled 10% subset of the training data, are provided in Table S2 . The high performance (Table S3 and Fig. S2 ) enables our framework to accurately identify the diagnostic regions prior to downstream blast cell quantification. In addition to numerical performance analysis, a visualization is presented in Fig. 2C to show the reliability of our region classification model, with areas in green representing adequate regions. Overall, the high-performing ROI identification provides a solution for the classification of adequate diagnostic regions as suitable for cell-level analysis.

Given the need to balance accuracy and speed, the YOLOv8 architecture was selected for blast cell detection and classification. The model was trained using hematopathologist-annotated bounding boxes of nucleated cell instances, distinguishing blast cells (indicative of AML in this study) from normal cells (TC, EC; Fig. 3A ). Across the dataset, 109,825 cell instances were used for model training (TC), and 26,533 cell instances were used for evaluation (EC). The evaluation metrics used were precision, recall, and mAP50. Detailed training logs on 20% of the training data are provided in Table S4 . Overall, our model achieved precision, recall, and mAP50 of 0.84, 0.85, and 0.90, respectively, with consistent performance across cross-validation folds (Fig. 3B ).

A comparative analysis between hematopathologists and ALLocate was conducted on a dataset from an external institution (MSKCC). Trained exclusively on UCSF data, the cell detection model was applied to 99 normal regions and 87 AML regions from MSKCC data (EVC). Pathologists also annotated the same set of images. At the region level, ALLocate achieved an AUROC of 0.9012 for distinguishing normal regions from AML-associated regions, compared to 0.9359 for the hematopathologist, using blast ratio as the continuous prediction score (Fig. 3E ). Quantitative analysis of blast counts showed that, in normal regions, ALLocate detected a similar number of blasts as the pathologist (mean 0.75 vs. 0.60 blasts per tile; Fig. 3F , Fig. 3G , Table S5 , Table S6 ) without significant statistical difference ( P = 0.07). In AML regions, the model produced comparable blast counts (mean 10.54, range 0–41) to those of the pathologist (mean 11.13, range 0–37; Fig. 3F , Fig. 3G , Table S5 , Table S7 ), with no statistically significant difference ( P = 0.12). However, the evaluation time vastly differed, with ALLocate requiring, on average, less than 1 minute for evaluation compared to more than 4 hours for a hematopathologist to manually perform blast counting in 200 regions. Overall, these results demonstrate the effective performance of the local cell-detection model on pre-tiled region samples. Furthermore, Fig. 3C, D provide visual examples showing that ALLocate can successfully distinguish between normal and blast cells in both the UCSF and MSKCC datasets. ALLocate’s high accuracy on both the in-domain (UCSF) and external (MSKCC) test sets underscores its reliability and robustness across platforms.

While validation of individual AI components, including external validation, is essential, it is insufficient to demonstrate this system’s utility as a practical diagnostic tool. To address this, we conducted an end-to-end evaluation of the complete AI pipeline using digitized slides from MSKCC. To assess the performance of the full deep learning system at the slide level in a clinically realistic setting, we curated a testing cohort consisting of 40 digitized bone marrow aspirate slides from MSKCC, comprising 20 normal and 20 AML cases (EVS; Fig. S3 ). As shown in Fig. 4A , despite being trained exclusively on UCSF data, the model reliably identified diagnostically adequate regions on whole-slide images. With the successful integration of the blast cell detection module (Fig. 4B ), the AI pipeline enabled automated slide-level analysis on external samples.

To mimic the human diagnostic workflow, we randomly selected 10 diagnostically adequate regions per slide and performed blast cell counting, yielding a minimum of 200 cells per slide, comparable to manual clinical assessments. All AML slides exhibited higher blast percentages than normal slides, allowing ALLocate to fully distinguish AML from normal cases under an ideal threshold (Fig. 4C and Table S8 ). To further assess robustness, we varied the number of regions evaluated per slide from 1 (highly underrepresentative) to 50 (highly overrepresentative) (Fig. 4D , Table S9 , Table S10 ). The model achieved near-perfect AUC with as few as 5 regions, demonstrating strong potential as a diagnostic tool. Even when applying a more stringent textbook threshold, which dictates ≤5% blasts for a benign diagnosis and ≥20% for AML, the system achieved 93% accuracy. Together, these results demonstrate the robustness and generalizability of the ALLocate AI algorithm, even when evaluated on a completely external dataset.

To comprehensively evaluate the entire ALLocate pipeline, including both hardware components and AI modules, we processed a total of 165 glass bone marrow smear slides, including 36 glass bone marrow smear slides (SDM, UCSF) from UCSF and an additional 129 glass slides (SDM, MSKCC) from MSKCC through the complete system (Table S11 ). Moving from the region to the slide level, we applied the diagnostic logic of ALLocate in a manner that mimics the pathologist’s evaluation process (Fig. 5A ). ALLocate was installed on a microscope and applied to the physical slides, with its AI component generating blast percentages. Each clinical sample was first digitally captured by the ALLocate hardware. The captured images were then filtered by a region classifier to produce representative images with at least 500 cells for analysis. On AML slides, ALLocate efficiently highlighted blast cells (Fig. 5B and Fig. S4 ). Compared to the hematopathologist’s evaluation, ALLocate demonstrated strong and consistent performance across both internal and external cohorts. Benign slides exhibited low blast percentages, as confirmed by both AI-based and clinician diagnoses (Fig. 5D, F ). The difference in blast percentage between AML and normal samples was highly significant in both the UCSF and MSKCC cohorts ( P = 4.72 × 10⁻¹⁰ and P = 1.77 × 10⁻²³, respectively). In addition to statistical analysis, we applied clinically established thresholds ( ≤ 5% blasts for benign and ≥20% blasts for AML). On the internal UCSF cohort, ALLocate correctly classified 17 out of 18 AML cases (94.4%) and 18 out of 18 normal cases (100%), corresponding to an overall accuracy of 97%. Importantly, performance remained robust on the fully independent external MSKCC cohort, where ALLocate correctly classified 53 out of 56 AML cases (94.6%) and 58 out of 73 normal cases (79.5%), achieving an overall accuracy of 86.0%. This modest decrease in performance on the external cohort is expected due to differences in slide preparation, imaging conditions, and institutional workflows, and further underscores the model’s robustness under real-world variability. Consistent with the separation observed in Fig. 4 , the two categories are linearly separable, resulting in an AUC approaching 1.0 (Fig. 5G and Fig. S5 ). High performance (88% overall accuracy) across the internal (97% accuracy) and external (86% accuracy) SDM datasets highlights the system’s strong diagnostic performance.

For quantitative comparison, pathologists randomly annotated three AML and three normal slides, with 10 diagnostic regions per slide. A strong correlation was observed between the blast counts from ALLocate and the manual annotations across all annotated AML and normal slides, indicating the robustness of ALLocate both overall and at the individual slide level (Fig. 5E and Fig. S6, S7 ). Overall, on actual physical slides, ALLocate not only excelled in diagnostic accuracy but also achieved pathologist-level performance in quantifying blast counts at a fraction of the time (Fig. 5C ).

In this work, we present ALLocate, a study that integrates a deep learning system with a low-cost automated microscope scanner for leukemia detection in whole-marrow smears. We tested ALLocate on different sets of whole marrow smears, including both normal and AML marrows, to show its real-world clinical applicability. To enable cross-institutional generalization, ALLocate was developed using data from the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) and Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC). The models were trained and validated using UCSF data and then tested on several cohorts of images from MSKCC taken by commercial scanners. Beyond comprehensive software testing, the complete ALLocate pipeline, including the ALLocate Automated Microscope Scanning System, was then applied to 165 physical glass slides, which demonstrated the strong reliability of ALLocate. This intensive testing routine shows ALLocate’s clinical generalizability across multiple hospitals and multiple image capture methods.

A key strength of our approach is its low cost, with a total system cost of less than $150 compared to approximately $300,000 for commercial whole-slide scanners. Together with other emerging low-cost digital microscopy frameworks 23 , 25 , this work highlights the growing interest in accessible diagnostic imaging platforms. Combined with a CNN-based region classifier and YOLOv8-based cell detection, the proposed system provides an end-to-end solution for automated analysis of bone marrow smears and can be deployed in resource-limited clinical settings. Importantly, both the region classification model and the object detection model are lightweight and can operate entirely on CPU. In cases where high-end hardware is unavailable, the models can be run locally, albeit with slightly longer processing times, or easily executed using cloud-based resources. Beyond cost savings, the system can augment the capacity of overburdened pathologists and hematologists by automating time-consuming tasks such as ROI selection and blast quantification. In regions with few expert personnel, it can serve as a triage tool to prioritize high-risk cases for expert review, or as a training and educational resource for clinicians in diagnostic hematology. By incorporating this design, scanners that cost hundreds of thousands of dollars may not be needed after the successful implementation of this pipeline.

Our approach parallels human pathologists' workflows for bone marrow smear analysis. Whereas the pathologist’s first step is to examine the whole bone marrow smear at low magnification for suitable regions, a CNN-based region classifier breaks a large smear into processing tiles, searching for the most optimal regions. In usable regions, the pathologist examines individual cells and distinguishes between normal and leukemia cells, typically evaluating 200–500 cells to establish the final differential count. Similarly, these qualified regions will be processed by a real-time one-step localization and classification system for leukemia cell detection, mirroring the steps a pathologist would take. The developed region classifier can identify the usable regions in the aspirate smear with an accuracy of 96%, while the YOLOv8 model was developed and optimized to detect marrow cells with a mAP of 90%. The real-time detection using YOLOv8 was also demonstrated in regions as well as whole-slide images. When tested on scanned tiled marrow regions, whole scanned images, and whole marrow slides, ALLocate demonstrated excellent leukemia detection results, but faster than a clinical expert. As an assistive tool, ALLocate can significantly improve the efficiency of leukemia detection from aspirate smears in real-world settings and can potentially be used for clinical screening. Results can be relayed to a qualified expert pathologist for verification, including captured region and cell images.

To contextualize ALLocate’s performance, we compared it with several published deep learning models for bone marrow analysis 12 , 14 – 16 , 19 , 20 , 27 (Table S12 ). Previous studies have demonstrated impressive achievements using very large datasets. For example, Matek et al. trained a ResNeXt-50 on 171,374 expert-annotated cells from 945 patients, reaching 79% precision for blast detection 12 . Tayebi et al. reported 84% mAP50 using YOLOv4 on data from 1,247 patients 20 , while Lewis et al. built a general differential counting pipeline with 1.5 million cells, achieving 92% mAP50 in AML detection 15 . In comparison, ALLocate achieves 90% mAP50 for blast detection while relying on only one stage of detection, which is computationally more efficient than traditional two-stage systems. It is important to note, however, that while our dataset captures a range of AML subtypes, the sample size within each subtype remains limited, and future studies with larger, subtype-balanced cohorts are needed to fully evaluate model performance across AML variants. In addition, many of these earlier studies addressed the broader and more challenging task of full differential classification, encompassing dozens of bone marrow cell types. While ALLocate focuses specifically on blast detection, these pipelines deserve recognition for the breadth of classes they successfully distinguish. Our work thus complements this body of research by demonstrating that high blast-level accuracy can also be achieved with a streamlined and computationally efficient pipeline.

Although the ALLocate system achieved strong performance, several limitations should be noted. First, while the current hardware enables automated XY stage scanning for slide pre-screening, it lacks automated Z-axis focusing, which, without human input, may result in focal variability across regions. Second, a dedicated graphical user interface for streamlined visualization, case management, and integrated pathologist review has not yet been implemented. Future work will focus on incorporating autofocus functionality and developing a unified interface to facilitate clinical integration. Also, although glass-level validation was performed on both the UCSF dataset (including an independent test set) and the MSKCC external validation cohort, the overall number of physical glass slides remains relatively limited. Larger, multi-center studies will be necessary to further improve statistical power and confirm generalizability across diverse clinical settings. In addition, to our knowledge, there are currently no publicly available bone marrow aspirate smear datasets with blast-level bounding box annotations suitable for object detection tasks. This reflects a broader limitation in the field rather than a constraint specific to this study and highlights the need for standardized, publicly available datasets for benchmarking and future model development. Finally, we observed occasional misclassification of immature granulocytes as blasts, particularly in reactive marrow conditions. These errors most frequently occurred when immature granulocytes exhibited prominent nucleoli, a feature that can overlap morphologically with leukemic blasts and challenge the model’s discriminative capacity. Future work will incorporate a more diverse set of reactive marrow samples to better capture the spectrum of granulocytic maturation and improve model robustness.

Regarding real-world deployment considerations, the algorithm design intentionally reflects a trade-off between sensitivity, precision, and operational speed. The system is intended as a rapid triage and screening tool integrated with an automated microscope, where missed blasts would be clinically more consequential than moderate increases in false positives. Therefore, the detection threshold was tuned to maintain high sensitivity for blast identification while preserving acceptable precision, thereby avoiding an excessive downstream review burden. In practical settings, ALLocate operates as an assistive system rather than a standalone diagnostic replacement: detected regions and cell counts are reviewed in aggregate, and outputs can be verified by a clinician. This design prioritizes rapid identification of potentially malignant regions, efficient slide prescreening, and reduction of manual workload while maintaining clinically meaningful accuracy.

In addition, the current study focuses on distinguishing AML from normal marrow and does not explicitly evaluate performance on other hematologic or metastatic disease categories. For out-of-distribution samples, ALLocate would still generate blast detection outputs and quantitative blast proportion estimates; however, these outputs alone are insufficient for definitive diagnosis and should be interpreted as screening indicators requiring expert review. Furthermore, prediction confidence is inherently provided within the pipeline: the cell-level detector outputs class probabilities, while the blast proportion serves as a continuous, slide-level score that can be used for threshold-based decision-making.

Overall, our study presents a relatively low-cost, end-to-end system for the detection of acute myeloid leukemia, combining two deep learning models with a self-driving microscope controlled by 3D printed adapter hardware. The system costs less than $150, offering a practical alternative to commercial whole-slide scanners priced around $300,000. This affordability, combined with its automation, makes it especially valuable for clinical screening in real-world low-resource settings, where access to advanced imaging infrastructure is limited.

This study complies with all relevant ethical regulations. The study protocols involving de-identified human bone marrow smear samples were reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of California, San Francisco, and the Institutional Review Board of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. The requirement for informed consent was waived because the study used de-identified retrospective samples. The bone marrow smear slides were obtained from archived clinical collections at UCSF and MSKCC. The slides were not destroyed during or after analysis and remain stored at the respective institutions in accordance with institutional policies. Participant sex, gender, and age were not considered in the study design because the study evaluated image-based detection performance using de-identified, retrospectively collected smear slides, and these demographic variables were unavailable across all cohorts. No sex- or gender specific analyses were performed because the model was not designed to predict or evaluate sex- or gender-dependent outcomes.

The ALLocate automated stage was integrated with an Olympus BX40 microscope and Olympus EP50 camera based on a previously described design 26 . For external validation on MSKCC glass slides, images were acquired using an Olympus BX46 microscope equipped with an Olympus DP27 camera and CellSens software.

The system consists of custom 3D-printed components, including motor mounts, couplings, gear assemblies, and linear support structures. Two NEMA 14 stepper motors (1.8° per step, 0.4 A rated current) were used for actuation and controlled via a RAMPS 1.4 shield connected to an Arduino Mega 2560 microcontroller (Fig. 1A ). The motors were powered by a 12 V, 10 A supply and driven using A4988 stepper motor drivers configured to match motor voltage requirements. The total hardware cost of the system is approximately $150 (excluding the microscope).

The system leverages the microscope stage's existing manual XY translation knobs for motorized actuation. Custom 3D-printed couplings were designed to interface with the X- and Y-axis control knobs and were secured using a combination of friction-fitting and mechanical fasteners to ensure stable torque transmission. The X-axis motor is directly coupled to the stage control shaft, whereas the Y-axis motion is achieved through a geared coupling due to the coaxial arrangement of the stage controls. Both motors are mounted within a 3D-printed housing that translates with the stage and is supported by steel guide rods to maintain alignment. Automated image acquisition is performed using a unidirectional raster scanning pattern. The stage translates along the X-axis to capture sequential image tiles, followed by an incremental Y-axis shift before scanning the next row in the opposite direction. This alternating scanning sequence enables systematic coverage of the selected slide region and is controlled by a custom Arduino C + + script. The current implementation does not include Z-axis motorization or autofocus functionality, which will be addressed in future work.

The dataset used for training, validation, and evaluation of the deep learning models was acquired from de-identified bone marrow smear whole-slide images provided by the Department of Laboratory Medicine at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) 13 . All slides were scanned at 40× magnification using Aperio AT2 and GT450 scanners without additional Z-axis focusing.

For region classification, a total of 9,149 region tiles were used for training (TR), with an additional 2,286 tiles reserved for evaluation (ER), derived from 70 patient slides (n_slides = n_patients) (Table S13 ). For cell detection, 109,825 annotated cell instances were used for training (TC), and 26,533 instances were used for evaluation (EC), derived from 170 patient slides (n_slides = n_patients). Model development (training and validation) for both tasks was performed at the region level, as annotations were generated at the tile level and multiple regions were extracted from each slide. The AML cohort included a diverse range of molecular and morphological subtypes encountered in routine clinical practice, including AML with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 fusion, AML with CBFB::MYH11 fusion, AML with KMT2A -rearrangement, AML with NPM1 -mutation, AML with TP53 -mutation, therapy-related AML, AML transformed from myeloproliferative neoplasms, and AML with myelodysplasia-related changes. A detailed subtype distribution is provided in Table S14 .

External validation was performed using de-identified datasets from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC), scanned at 40× equivalent magnification using Hamamatsu S360 and S20 scanners. This included 186 region tiles (99 normal, 87 AML) for partial pipeline evaluation (EVC), derived from 95 patient slides (49 AML, 46 normal), where each slide corresponds to a unique patient (i.e., n_slides = n_patients), and 40 digital slides (20 normal, 20 AML) for full pipeline evaluation (EVS).

To evaluate the end-to-end performance of the integrated hardware-AI system, physical glass slides were tested using the self-driving microscope platform. Internal evaluation at UCSF included 36 slides (18 normal, 18 AML), while external evaluation at MSKCC included 129 slides (73 normal, 56 AML). All slide-level evaluations were performed at the patient level, with each slide corresponding to a unique patient (i.e., n_slides = n_patients), and all external validation cohorts were fully independent and not used during model training. These experiments assessed system performance under realistic clinical workflow conditions, including automated scanning and blast quantification.
This study develops two deep learning models incorporated with ALLocate: a CNN region classifier (Fig. S8 ) and a YOLOv8 blast cell detector (Fig. S9 ).

The CNN region classifier is formulated as a multiclass classification problem. The network was trained using a softmax output layer with cross-entropy loss, which enforces a probability distribution across the three classes (summing to 1). During inference, the predicted class label is obtained using the argmax of the softmax probabilities, and precision-recall metrics were computed based on these discrete class predictions rather than thresholded binary outputs.

The CNN model was implemented using PyTorch 28 , featuring an architecture with one input layer, three convolutional layers with corresponding max pooling layers, and three fully connected layers (Figure S8A ). Each convolutional layer uses the rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation function, with the final fully connected layer using a softmax activation function. Prior to training, oversampling was performed on the clot class to ensure balanced data across all region classes. Model optimization was initially performed on a 10% subset of the total training data. A second model architecture was also tested, which included two convolutional and max pooling pairs instead of three. With these architectures, training was conducted with a batch size of 64 images, experimenting with different epochs (5, 7, 10, 20, 50) and alternating learning rates of 0.001 and 0.0005, using the Adam optimizer for stochastic gradient descent (SGD). The final classifier on the full dataset was trained at 10 epochs with a learning rate of 0.0005.

Building on the one-step detection and classification advantages of the YOLO model, the YOLOv8 model was chosen for this study (Fig. S9A ) 29 . In addition to the normal and blast cell classes, an artifact class was also utilized during training in order to prevent false positive detections of artifacts as normal or blast. The total number of images used for the YOLOv8 model training and validation was 1633. To ensure robust model selection and avoid overfitting, the dataset was first split into a hold-out evaluation set and a training set. A five-fold cross-validation strategy was then applied exclusively within the training set. To achieve an optimal performance in cell detection, the YOLO model was extensively optimized and fine-tuned through multiple configurations of parameters on a 20% subset of the training data. This model was trained with both small and medium default architectures, with the medium configuration featuring additional layers. The learning rate varied from 0.001 to an automatic mode where the model adjusts the rate dynamically. Epochs were tested at 20, 50, 100, and 200, and the model was trained using both the “auto” and SGD optimizers with a batch size of 4. Final training was conducted at 100 epochs with the automatic optimizer.

After training the models, data validation was performed as an initial evaluation of the models’ performance post-training. The CNN and YOLOv8 models were quantitatively assessed on the validation dataset using standard metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. Precision and recall for the YOLOv8 model were computed on the validation set using standard object-detection evaluation protocols at a predefined confidence threshold (confidence = 0.25), selected based on optimal performance on the validation cohort. Once an object was detected, class assignment was determined by the argmax of class probabilities (blast vs. normal).

Balanced composite metrics were not used because performance was evaluated at the cell level and reported separately for each class. This approach is consistent with object-detection practice and avoids obscuring clinically relevant behavior (e.g., sensitivity to blasts) that could be masked by aggregated or class-balanced metrics. Additional evaluation was performed using mean average precision (mAP50). Loss graphs were generated for all training iterations of the two models, and a precision-recall curve also generated for the YOLOv8 model (Fig. 3B and Fig. S8B, 9B ). For the YOLOv8 model, image labeling and preprocessing were performed utilizing the Roboflow image annotation platform, where bounding boxes were manually applied to all cell instances.

After development, ALLocate was used for clinical testing. A total of 186 regions (EVC), including 99 from the normal bone marrow region dataset and 87 from an AML region dataset, were sourced from Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center. This dataset was distinct from the training and validation datasets sourced at UCSF. Normal regions are defined as regions captured from slides of patients without AML, and AML regions are taken from slides of patients with AML. The YOLOv8 object detection model performs inference on individual regions and outputs the detection of the cells and its labels (blast cells vs. normal cells). Region-level ground-truth labels (AML-associated vs. normal) were established by expert hematopathologists. A region was labeled as AML-associated only when the reviewing hematopathologist determined it to contain leukemic features and the assessment was consistent with the corresponding slide-level clinical diagnosis. Regions without leukemic features and concordant with benign slide-level diagnosis were labeled as benign. These curated region-level annotations served as the reference standard for AUROC evaluation.

In addition to training based on regions, a testing cohort of 20 normal and 20 AML whole slide images (EVS) was also used. First, these whole slides were tiled using the OpenSlide Python library. These tiles were then processed through the CNN-based region classification pipeline, which selected 10 regions per case for subsequent analysis by the YOLOv8 detection framework; the final model differential counts were evaluated on a case-by-case basis. For each slide, the performance of the model was compared to the reported pathologist’s review, and accuracy designations were decided using the clinical thresholds of ≤5% blasts for normal cases and ≥20% blasts for leukemia cases.

Moreover, another testing cohort of 91 normal and 74 AML whole-slides images was collected using the AAMSS (SDM), including 18 normal and 18 AML bone marrow smear slides from UCSF and 73 normal and 56 AML marrow smear slides from MSKCC, as opposed to the slides scanned by commercial hardware in the previous test. The images captured were then processed through the CNN region classification pipeline and subsequently processed by the YOLOv8 detection framework; the final model differential counts were evaluated on a case-by-case basis. For each slide, the performance of the model was compared to the reported pathologist’s review, using the clinical thresholds of ≤5% blasts for normal cases and ≥20% blasts for leukemia cases.

Model training and primary validation were performed on a desktop workstation equipped with an AMD Ryzen 9 7900X CPU, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 Ti SUPER GPU, and 32 GB RAM (Windows 11), utilizing GPU acceleration.

External validation and evaluation of the automated microscopy system were conducted on a laptop computer with an Intel Core Ultra 185H CPU, NVIDIA RTX 4070 Laptop GPU, and 16 GB RAM (Windows 11), also using GPU acceleration.

Statistical analyses were performed to evaluate agreement between ALLocate and pathologist assessments, as well as overall model performance. Differences in blast counts between ALLocate and pathologist evaluations on the same regions were assessed using two-tailed paired t-tests. Differences in blast percentage between AML and normal slides were assessed using two-tailed independent t-tests. Correlation analysis was performed to quantify agreement between automated and expert-derived blast counts.

Classification performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, with area under the curve (AUC) reported. For cell detection tasks, standard object detection metrics were used, including precision, recall, and mean average precision at an intersection-over-union threshold of 0.5 (mAP50). All statistical analyses were performed using standard scientific computing libraries. A p -value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant where applicable.

articles.title: SPL13 controls a root apical meristem phase change by triggering oriented cell divisions.
articles.authors: Yang B, Sun Y, Minne M, Ge Y, Yue Q, Goossens V, Mor E, Callebaut B, Bevernaege K, Winne JM, Audenaert D, De Rybel B.
articles.abstract: Oriented cell divisions are crucial to determine the overall morphology and size of plants, but what controls the onset and duration of this process remains largely unknown. Here, we identified a small molecule which activates root meristem expression of SQUAMOSA PROMOTER BINDING-LIKE13 , a known player in the shoot juvenile to adult transition. This leads to oriented cell divisions in the root meristem via SHORT ROOT and cell-cycle regulators. We further show that the root meristem has distinct juvenile and adult phases typed by morphological and molecular characteristics and that SPL factors are crucially required for this transition in Arabidopsis and rice. In summary, we provide molecular insights into the age-dependent morphological changes occurring in the root meristem during phase change.
paragraphs: Oriented cell divisions are crucial to determine the overall morphology and size of plants, but what controls the onset and duration of this process remains largely unknown. Here, we identified a small molecule which activates root meristem expression of SQUAMOSA PROMOTER BINDING-LIKE13 , a known player in the shoot juvenile to adult transition. This leads to oriented cell divisions in the root meristem via SHORT ROOT and cell-cycle regulators. We further show that the root meristem has distinct juvenile and adult phases typed by morphological and molecular characteristics and that SPL factors are crucially required for this transition in Arabidopsis and rice. In summary, we provide molecular insights into the age-dependent morphological changes occurring in the root meristem during phase change.

Plants modulate organ size, shape and tissue patterning via oriented cell divisions. These are made possible via differential cell expansion and changes in cell wall anisotropy ( 1 ). For brevity, we will refer to the process of modulating cell expansion and cell wall anisotropy resulting in oriented cell divisions as ‘oriented cell divisions’ throughout the text. Several molecular factors that direct these cell proliferation processes in distinct cell populations in the root apical meristem (RAM) have been identified in Arabidopsis over the past few years ( 2 – 5 ). One example operating in the vascular tissues is the heterodimer complex formed by the basic helix-loop-helix transcription factors TARGET OF MONOPTEROS5 (TMO5) and LONESOME HIGHWAY (LHW). This protein complex is required and sufficient to modulate oriented cell divisions by locally activating multiple classes of enzymes all leading to higher levels of active cytokinin in the xylem cells ( 6 – 13 ). This cytokinin is thought to move to the surrounding procambium cells and trigger cell proliferation in the primary root meristem. Downstream of TMO5/LHW, the cytokinin-inducible DOF2.1 transcription factor is also sufficient to affect oriented cell divisions in a subset of procambium cells ( 14 ). The closely related mobile PHLOEM EARLY DOF ( PEAR ) genes are also induced by cytokinin and the respective proteins diffuse through plasmodesmata forming a short-range concentration gradient peaking in the protophloem sieve elements ( 15 ). The PEAR proteins lead to oriented cell divisions in and around the phloem pole sieve elements. Furthermore, in the root apical meristem, the mobile transcription factor SHORT ROOT (SHR) has been elaborately shown to move to the endodermis where it interacts with SCARECROW (SCR) to activate expression of CYCD6;1 , thereby controlling oriented cell divisions in the ground tissues ( 16 – 21 ). Additionally, TMO5/LHW was shown to induce SHR expression in xylem cells. In the neighboring procambium cells, the mobile SHR protein triggers expression of CYTOKININ OXIDASE3 ( CKX3 ), thereby balancing the induction of active cytokinin levels and cell proliferation ( 9 ).

Oriented cell divisions are also a prominent feature during vegetative development in the shoot apical meristem (SAM) which can be divided into four phases: a seedling stage, a juvenile stage, and a transitional stage leading to an adult stage. The transition between the juvenile and adult stage is termed vegetative phase change ( 22 ) and is controlled by the miR156-dependent SQUAMOSA PROMOTER BINDING PROTEIN-LIKE (SPL) transcription factors ( 23 – 25 ). Amongst the many reported morphological changes occurring during this process, there is a gradual increase in SAM size by oriented cell divisions ( 26 , 27 ). Recently, SPL9 was shown to directly activate the expression of CYCD3 family genes, thereby controlling cell cycle duration during the different stages of leaf development ( 28 ). More abrupt changes include the appearance of trichomes on the abaxial side and leaf serrations ( 29 ). Although the concept of transitions between distinct juvenile and adult phases of development have not been extrapolated to the RAM as such, there are several parallels that can be drawn. For example, there is a very prominent but so far underexplored increase in cell division activity between the first and third week after germination ( 30 ). This process is distinct from the general activation of the root meristem during the first week after germination in the seedling stage ( 31 – 33 ), the developmental state generally used to study root biology. Although the morphological changes occurring in the first week of growth have been suggested to represent a phase change in the root apical meristem ( 34 ), this process seems unrelated to the dramatic increase in root meristem width which has been observed during the following two weeks of growth of the primary root meristem ( 30 ). Although a role for WOX5 has been shown ( 30 ) during this later occurring process, the overall surge in cell divisions in the meristem has not been explored in detail and molecular regulators remain unknown. In contrast, a well-studied difference between young and older meristems is the appearance of an additional ground tissue layer called the middle cortex ( 35 – 39 ). This process is controlled by a regulatory network involving gibberellic and abscisic acid ( 36 , 37 , 40 – 43 ) and a handful of transcription factors including SHR and SCR ( 17 , 36 , 37 , 40 , 43 – 45 ), but it remains unclear how the onset of this developmental process is controlled.

Here, we identified a small molecule capable of reorienting cell divisions in the root apical meristem. By analyzing the set of genes induced by this chemical, we identified that the transcription factor SPL13 and its homologs are necessary and sufficient to control cell division orientation via SHR and cell cycle regulators. These oriented cell divisions are a hallmark of a phase change of the root apical meristem from a juvenile to an adult state which is conserved in both Arabidopsis and rice.

To identify chemicals specifically affecting cell division orientation in plants, we engineered a Tobacco Bright Yellow-2 (BY2) cell culture system, which allows tracking cell divisions and their orientation over the course of several days in a miniaturized format. Cell-based systems have been successfully used for chemical genetics approaches in plants for screening, for example molecules affecting protein sorting ( 46 , 47 ) or the cytoskeleton ( 48 ). However, these systems have not been adopted for studying cell division orientation. Thus, to follow the divisions over time, we first generated a dual color reporter in BY2 cell cultures by co-transformation of a nuclear (p 35S ::H2B-mCherry) and a plasma membrane (p 35S ::CPK17-YFP) marker ( Fig. S1A ). After careful optimization of growth conditions and adapting it to 96-well plate format (see Fig. S1B and materials and methods section for details), this reporter allows cell divisions to be followed over the course of 2 days in an automated screening platform ( Fig. 1A-E ). In this way, we were able to observe the orientation of the newly formed cell plate in individual BY2 filaments. Based on this system, we conducted screening of a commercial library of 15,040 small molecules at 50 μM final concentration and recorded images at 0, 24 and 48 hours after small molecule addition. We identified 747 molecules that were toxic to the BY2 cells ( Fig. S1C-D ). After manual analysis of over 45,000 images in a primary screen, we carefully categorized all observed cellular phenotypes for each of the small molecules ( Fig. S1E-L and Data S1 ) and found that 51 molecules affected cell division orientation in BY2 cells. We next performed a secondary screen on these 51 molecules, which we termed coral1 - coral51 for c ell division or ientation al tering chemical, using high-resolution confocal imaging to confirm their effect on cell division orientation. After excluding those molecules affecting cytokinesis, we observed a very specific effect on cell division orientation without affecting division potential in general for 33 small molecules ( Data S1 ).

To determine if any of these molecules were able to affect cell division orientation in planta , we transferred Arabidopsis thaliana seedlings harboring a dual color reporter line (p 35S ::FH6-GFP and p 35S ::H2B-RFP) ( 49 ) to medium supplemented with these molecules at 50 μM concentration and evaluated cell division orientation in the root apical meristem at 24 and 48 hours after transfer. For clarity, we distinguish between three types of oriented divisions in plants: anticlinal, radial and periclinal ( Fig. S1M ). From our selection, finally four small molecules (coral7, coral8, coral11 and coral13) with unrelated chemical structures were able to trigger periclinal and radial cell divisions both in BY2 cell cultures ( Fig. 1F-I and Fig. S2A-D ) and in the cortex cell layer of the root apical meristem ( Fig. S3A-J ) which normally only undergoes anticlinal divisions ( 14 ). Given that coral7 treatment resulted in more strict 90 degree switching in cell division orientation ( Fig. 1J-K and Fig. S3C-D and K-P ) as seen for genetic cues such as e.g. TMO5/LHW ( 8 ), DOF2.1 ( 14 ) or PEAR1 ( 15 ), rather than the more oblique divisions observed for coral8, coral11 and coral13 ( Fig. S3E-J ), we focused our attention on coral7 for further analyses. Coral7 treatment increased the number of cells in the root meristem (quantified on a radial section halfway between the quiescent center and the elongation zone) ( Fig. 1L-N ). Coral7 treatment increased auxin signaling ( Fig. S4A-G ) ( 50 ), but we did not observe obvious changes in the expression patterns or levels of well-known reporter lines for microtubules (p 35S ::TUA6-GFP ( 51 )), cell plate formation (p KNOLLE ::GFP-KNOLLE ( 52 )), actin (p 35S ::lifeact-Venus ( 53 )), polarity protein (p PIN2 ::PIN2-GFP ( 54 ) and p SOK2 ::SOK2-GFP ( 55 )), vacuoles (p RPS5A ::VAMP711-GFP ( 56 )) ( Fig. S4H-V ), or factors leading to oriented divisions in the vascular cells ( Fig. S5A-F ). Moreover, coral7 treatment was still able to re-orient cell divisions in vascular cells of the higher order tmo5 loss-of-function mutant ( 8 , 15 ) ( Fig. 1O-Q , Fig. S5G-H ). These results suggest that coral7 affects cell division orientation in the root meristem through a non-canonical pathway. Taken together, our BY2 cell culture-based screening method was successful in identifying small molecules that specifically control cell division orientation in planta .

Despite the highly specific effect on cell division orientation of coral7, a dose-response experiment showed this molecule was only functional at high micromolar concentrations (50 μM) and after a prolonged treatment of 48 hours ( Fig. S6A-E ), suggesting that this molecule might not be taken up very efficiently or might need to be metabolized before exerting its activity. We thus performed a structure-activity relationship (SAR) analysis to determine the active sites and potentially generate a more potent analog. We generated 12 structural variants of coral7 named var1-var12 ( Fig. S7 and Data S2 ) and tested the capacity of these modified molecules to induce oriented cell divisions in the root meristem by growing 5 days after germination (DAG) seedlings on 50 μM of each of these variants for 48 hours. The SAR analysis showed that none of the variants was more potent compared to coral7. Most modifications proved deleterious to the bioactivity of the compound, and even a slightly truncated var9 analog lacking only a single methyl group showed no activity. Its isosteric replacement with a bromine atom (var8) did however retain activity. Alkylation of the reactive alpha-position of the sulfonamide was tolerated to some extent, allowing the installation of a clickable group at that position (var12, Fig. S7 ). This analysis suggested that the chemical structure is overall very sensitive to modifications and that the interaction with its molecular target must be specific. Indeed, biotin labeling at the clickable site in the active analog var12 ( Fig. S6F ), resulted in a non-functional coral7-biotin conjugate ( Fig. S6G-N ), as did alkylation with a sterically more demanding group (var12) suggesting that a biochemical assay to find the molecular target of this small molecule is not possible using such modified affinity probes, as its binding is too easily perturbed.

To understand the mechanism by which coral7 triggers oriented cell divisions in the root apical meristem, we next examined the whole genome transcriptional changes induced by treatment of Arabidopsis thaliana root apical meristems with coral7 in a time series experiment for 6, 12, and 24 hours via bulk RNA-sequencing ( Fig. 2A and Data S3 ). We first overlapped the list of differentially expressed genes (DEG) upon coral7 treatment with similar datasets of known transcription factors of oriented cell divisions in the root apical meristem such as TMO5/LHW ( 7 ) and DOF2.1 ( 14 ). No overlap was found ( Data S3 ), providing further evidence at a molecular level that coral7 affects oriented cell divisions through a non-canonical pathway. After selecting the top 10 DEG upon coral7 treatment ( Fig. 2A , Data S3 ), we constructed ectopic misexpression lines using the strong meristematic RPS5A promoter ( 58 ) to evaluate the ability of these genes to trigger oriented cell divisions in the root apical meristem as observed upon coral7 treatment. SQUAMOSA PROMOTER-BINDING PROTEIN LIKE 13A ( SPL13A/AT5G50570 referred to as SPL13 ) was upregulated around 100-fold at 12 hours in the RNA-seq dataset ( Data S3 ). Misexpression of SPL13 , but not the other differentially expressed genes tested ( Fig. S8A-I, Fig. S9A-I ), triggered additional oriented divisions in root meristem cortex cells with ( Fig. 2B and Fig. S8J ) and without ( Fig. S9J ) GFP tag, similar to a coral7 treatment ( Fig. 1J-K ). Fitting with the concept of SPL13 being one of the genes induced by coral7 treatment, spl13 mutant backgrounds reduced the effect of coral7 treatment ( Fig. S10 ). Although it is unlikely that SPL13 is a direct target protein of coral7, these results suggest that SPL13 likely acts downstream of coral7 to trigger oriented cell divisions in the root apical meristem.

SPL transcription factors are well-studied for their important role in the aerial parts of the plant during the transitions from a juvenile to adult shoot apical meristem and from a vegetative to a flowering meristem ( 25 , 59 – 62 ). In the root, SPL9, SPL10 and miR156 have been shown to be involved in root branching and root meristem length determination ( 34 , 63 , 64 ). To analyze a putative role for SPL13 in the cellular changes leading to cell division orientation in the root meristem, we first examined SPL13 levels in the root. No localization was observed in the root meristem of a miR156 sensitive translational reporter line (p SPL13 ::sSPL13-GUS ( 60 ) ( Fig. S11A ) or in a previously generated scRNA-seq expression dataset of the root meristem ( 65 ). Given SPL transcripts are repressed by miR156 ( 59 ), we next analyzed a miR156 resistant version of the translational SPL13 reporter line (p SPL13 ::rSPL13-GUS ( 60 )) and observed most pronounced localization in the procambium cells ( Fig. 2C-D ). Upon treatment with coral7, both sSPL13 and rSPL13 protein levels were induced ( Fig. S11A-B , Fig. 2E compared to Fig. 2C ), which is consistent with our bulk RNA-seq results ( Data S3 ). Taken together, these results confirm that both transcripts and SPL proteins are detected in the root meristem and levels are increased by coral7 treatment.

We next analyzed the root phenotype of the newly generated p RPS5A ::SPL13-GFP misexpression line in more detail. Consistent with previous reports on the function of SPLs ( 34 , 63 , 64 ), increasing SPL13 expression levels led to longer root meristems ( Fig. 2K-M ), an increased root length ( Fig. 2N and Fig. S11G-H ) and reduction in lateral root density ( Fig. 2P ). In addition to these phenotypes, the most striking effect of increasing SPL13 expression levels were ectopic radial and/or periclinal divisions in all cell types of the root apical meristem ( Fig. 2F-H, K-L ), leading to a strong increase in root meristem width. Notably, an additional ground tissue layer was observed ( Fig. 2F-H ) as seen using the p SCR ::H2B-YFP ( Fig. 2I-J ) and p CO2 ::H2B-YFP ( Fig. S11C-D ) reporter lines for endodermis and cortex, respectively. Most likely, this additional ground tissue layer corresponds to middle cortex formation ( 37 – 39 ). The combination of increased root meristem size, increased root length and reduction in the lateral root density modified the overall root system architecture into a steeper and deeper branching pattern ( Fig. S11E-F ). These root-related phenotypes were largely correlated to the relative expression levels of SPL13 ( Fig. 2O and Fig. S11I ), showing that SPL13 expression levels need to be tightly controlled during normal development. Congruent with this conclusion, mir156/157 loss-of-function lines phenocopied the effects of increasing SPL13 levels ( Fig. S12 ). Moreover, like a coral7 treatment, raising SPL13 levels affected auxin signaling as reported previously ( 66 ), but caused no obvious changes in the expression patterns or levels of well-known reporter lines ( Fig. S13 ). Taken together, we found that increasing SPL13 expression levels leads to changes in the normal cell division orientation patterns in root meristem cells resulting in a strong increase in the root apical meristem width. Given these SPL13 misexpression phenotypes are still present in a tmo5 tmo5-like1 double mutant ( t5t5l1 ) background ( Fig. S14A-I ) and triggering TMO5/LHW does not induce an SPL13 reporter line ( Fig. S14J-K ), it is likely that SPL13 functions independent from the TMO5/LHW pathway ( 8 ).

To further understand the function of SPL13 during root meristem development, we analyzed roots of seedlings at 5 DAG of the available spl13-1 single mutant for cell division related phenotypes ( 60 ). No significant changes were observed in the overall root growth, nor the number of vascular cells compared to Col-0 wild type plants ( Fig. 3A-B, F and Fig. S15 ). Considering that SPL13 belongs to a family with functional redundancy ( 60 ), it is possible other SPL proteins have similar functions. We thus analyzed the localization of root expressed SPL proteins ( 60 ) in more detail. SPL2, SPL9, rSPL10, SPL11, SPL13 and SPL15 were all localized in root vascular cells or more broadly in the root meristem under normal growth conditions ( Fig. 2C-D , Fig. 3G-J and Fig. S16 ). To examine functional redundancy due to a similar function in cell division orientation, we generated p RPS5A -driven misexpression lines for seven additional SPL transcription factors, fused to GFP. Optical confocal cross sections through the root meristem showed that misexpression of all tested SPL transcription factors are able to trigger cell division orientation changes, resulting in an increased root thickness ( Fig. S17 ). Based on the above results, SPL family members have redundant functions during this developmental process. Hence, we analyzed 5 DAG seedlings of an available spl2 spl9 spl10 spl11 spl13 spl15 ( spl hextuple or spl hext .) mutant ( 60 ) in more detail. Even in this higher order mutant or in the miR156 overexpression line in which all miR156 sensitive SPL transcripts are repressed (p 35S :: MIR156A ( 60 )), no significant changes were observed at 5 DAG compared to the wild type Col-0 plants when quantifying several phenotypical characteristics in the root meristem ( Fig. 3C-D, F and Fig. S15 ), likely due to miR156 levels being high at this developmental stage ( 34 , 63 ). We confirmed this by measuring transcript levels of MIR156 in root meristems over time and evaluating expression of a miR156 sensor ( 67 , 68 ) ( Fig. S18 ). As this sensor was not affected by a coral7 treatment, coral7 is unlikely to be involved in the miRNA156 silencing function ( Fig. S18K-O ).

Considering that SPL13 transcripts are targeted by miR156 in early stages of plant growth in the shoot meristem ( 60 ), we investigated the tissue specific expression domains of the different miR156 isoforms ( MIR156A, MIR156B, MIR156C and MIR156D ) in more detail by generating transcriptional reporter lines (p MIR156A-D ::nYFP-GUS) using previous described promoter sequences ( 69 ) and analyzing their spatiotemporal expression patterns in 5 DAG root meristems. The different miR156 isoforms exhibited tissue-specific expression with MIR156A being expressed in phloem cells, MIR156C in root epidermis, cortex, QC and vascular initial cells, and MIR156D in xylem and columella cells ( Fig. S19 ). QC and columella expression was detected in the root meristem for MIR156B ( Fig. S20B ). We however cannot exclude that sequences in the transcribed region of miR156 isoforms might affect these expression patterns ( 70 ). Moreover, miRNA mobility might make the precise expression domains less decisive for the final location of their function. To understand whether the SPL13 protein itself might also be mobile, we drove SPL13 from multiple tissue specific promoters ( Fig. S21 ). In all lines, we observed SPL13 protein in cells neighboring to those where the promoter was active, suggesting SPL13 protein is mobile between cells. Considering the overlapping expression patterns and the cell-to-cell mobility, these results imply a complex spatial interaction between miR156 isoforms and SPLs will eventually define the expression levels of SPL13 at a specific location in the root meristem.

To investigate the temporal dynamics of this complex regulation, we next examined SPL13 levels and expression of MIR156 in root meristems over time. Similar to previous reports ( 63 ), expression levels of MIR156 isoforms decreased over time which was shown to influence timing of meristem growth and lateral root emergence ( 34 ) ( Fig. S20 ). During this process, levels of SPL13 ( Fig. 3G-J ) and other miR156 sensitive SPL reporters ( Fig. S16 ), increased over time and became strongly expressed at 20 DAG. This increase in SPL13 and other SPL levels was accompanied by a gradual increase in the number of vascular, endodermis and epidermis cells in a wild-type background ( Fig. 3M-Q and Fig. S22 ). Although cortex cell divisions and differentiation of the middle cortex are suppressed in the first week after germination, the number of cortex cells and the newly emerged middle cortex cells showed a more discrete increase starting around 15-20 DAG and 10 DAG, respectively, and plateauing at later time points ( Fig. 3R-S and Fig. S22 ). These growth patterns observed in a wild type Col-0 root meristem both in in vitro and soil conditions ( Fig. S22 ) resemble the transition from the juvenile to the adult phase of shoot development which is also characterised by both discrete and continuous patterns of development ( 29 , 71 ). All the additional divisions contributed in a general increase in meristem size in both length and width ( Fig. 3K-L ). The increase in meristem size over time has been reported before ( 30 , 34 , 37 , 72 ), but the exact molecular mechanisms triggering this event remained unexplored. Collectively, these results suggest that root apical meristems undergo a growth transition over time from a juvenile state towards an adult state which is characterized by an increase in the number of cells, middle cortex formation and a general increase in both width and length of the meristem.

Based on its expression during meristem maturation, SPL13 likely plays an important role in the later stages of root meristem development, we next analyzed mature root meristems of the spl13-1 single mutant, the spl hextuple mutants and the miR156 overexpression line at 20 DAG in comparison to the wild type Col-0 control and the SPL13 misexpression line. In contrast to the wild type situation, the spl hextuple mutant and the miR156 overexpression line did not show any of the above mentioned features characterizing the juvenile to adult transition ( Fig. 3U-Y ). Indeed, the number of cells in the spl hextuple mutant and the miR156 overexpression line did not show the strong increase at 20 DAG compared to 5 DAG as seen for the Col-0 control lines ( Fig. 3F, U and Fig. 15B ). Moreover, primary root length was reduced in these lines ( Fig. S15A ). This indicates that SPL factors are required for juvenile to adult transition in the root meristem. Increasing the relative amount of SPL proteins in the SPL13 misexpression line further increased the characteristics associated with the juvenile to adult transition, resulting in even more cells and an overall increase in meristem size at any of the analyzed timepoints ( Fig. 3E-F, U, Z and Fig. S15 ). Fitting with these results, and similar to previous reports ( 28 ), increased SPL13 levels induced expression of cell cycle regulators ( Fig. 4A-E and Fig. S23A-D ). Collectively, this indicates that SPL transcription factors are not only required for, but also sufficient to convey a juvenile to adult transition in the root apical meristem of Arabidopsis thaliana . The onset of this transition is most notably marked by the formation of the middle cortex ( 37 – 39 ). Although the pathways controlling middle cortex formation have been well characterized ( 17 , 36 , 37 , 40 , 44 , 45 , 73 , 74 ), the molecular networks controlling the onset of these divisions remained unclear. Our results suggest that the SPL13 is required for middle cortex formation via the canonical SHR pathway ( Fig. 4F-K ). Similar to previous observations ( 37 ), the first ground tissue periclinal divisions always originate at those endodermal cells at the protoxylem poles and next extended throughout the endodermis until an entire additional layer was formed ( Fig. S24A-D ). From 25 DAG onwards, even a third cortex layer started to form ( Fig. S24E-F ).

To examine whether vascular plants might share a similar mechanism in root juvenile-to-adult transitions, we examined the changes in the meristematic zone and its relationship with SPLs in the monocot crop rice ( Oryza sativa ). We first observed that, similar to our observations in Arabidopsis thaliana ( Fig. 3M-Q ), wild type rice (ZH11) root meristems undergo a transition characterized by an enlarged root meristem and an increase in the number of cells at 27 DAG in comparison to 5 DAG ( Fig. 5A, F, K-M ). Additionally, overexpression of SPL transcription factors in multiple plant species have been shown to lead to a larger tissue size ( 66 , 75 , 76 ). The rice SPL gene family contains 19 members ( 77 ), of which OsSPL14 belongs to the class II of miR156 sensitive SPL proteins ( 78 , 79 ). Unlike the taproot system in Arabidopsis, rice has as fibrous root system characterized by many adventitious roots. We thus analyzed the newly emerged adventitious root meristem characteristics associated with the juvenile to adult transition in the Osspl14 single ( 80 ), the Osspl14 17 double, the Osspl7 14 17 triple mutants and the OsmiR156 overexpression line ( 66 ) at 5 DAG and 27 DAG and found that already in the Osspl14 single mutant, but more pronounced in the higher order mutants and the OsmiR156 overexpression line, these meristem phase transition characteristics are significantly reduced ( Fig. 5B-E, G-J ). These results show that also in the rice root apical meristematic, cell proliferation during aging is controlled through miR156-SPL module.

The miR156-SPL pathway has been implicated in a wide range of developmental processes in plants ( 22 , 81 – 83 ). In most cases, these are linked to age-related processes during vegetative phase transitions in the areal part of the plant, which makes them important targets for breeding and biotechnological applications ( 84 – 86 ). In recent years, it has become clear that the functions of the miR156-SPL pathway are not limited to the shoot region. Indeed, lateral root development, root length and overall root system architecture seem to be dependent on miR156 and SPL expression levels as well ( 34 , 63 , 64 ). Here, we show that plant root apical meristems undergo a marked transition from a juvenile state (first week of growth) to a mature state (reached around 3 weeks after growth) which can be typed by specific characteristics, including an increase in the number of cells and middle cortex formation. We thus provide the first molecular insights into this poorly studied conserved developmental process in the root apical meristem ( 30 ) by showing that SPL transcription factors are crucially required for and sufficient to control the onset of the transition from a juvenile to an adult state of the root meristem by triggering oriented cell divisions. This is highly similar to the vegetative transition from a juvenile to an adult shoot apical meristem ( 24 , 60 , 87 ). In both cases, there is a clear transition from one phase of development to another, each typed by specific morphological and molecular characteristics related to expression levels of MIR156 and SPL transcription factors. As such, perhaps this gradual transition from a juvenile to a mature vegetative state after the first week of growth comprises a true phase change in the root apical meristem. Despite the obvious similarities between the phase change transitions in root and shoot apical meristems, increased SPL activity has been reported to decrease shoot apical meristem size ( 88 – 90 ), while it leads to a larger root apical meristem. This suggests some level of divergence in the SPL regulatory networks between the shoot and root apical meristems. It would be intriguing to investigate whether the onset of transitions in the shoot and root apical meristem are connected via a shoot-to-root signal ( 34 ).

Our results also show that precise control of the expression levels of SPL transcription factors, previously characterized as having an important role in vegetative phase change in the shoot apical meristem, appears also crucial to determine the root apical meristem size and the juvenile to adult characteristics in the root. The exact amount of SPL13 is defined by an age-dependent temporal control mechanism in the root meristem driven by miR156 isoforms and cell-to-cell mobility. The SPL13 misexpression phenotypes characterized by an increased root meristem size and activity can in this context be interpreted as a premature or faster transition from the juvenile to the adult state. In the same line of thought, the reduced SPL13 transcripts in loss-of-function mutants or the miR156 overexpression line can be considered as a delayed or absent transition, respectively. A final important consideration is that SPL13 localization is not visible in the juvenile root meristems, although this is the most common stage for root biologists to perform experiments on, as the meristem is already considered steady-state at this moment in time ( 91 – 94 ). As such, perhaps other regulators currently hallmarked as controlling shoot apical meristem or vegetative phase change have additional roles during root apical meristem development, but they are simply not expressed during the juvenile state. Indeed, our results imply that understanding root meristem development will require a more holistic approach taking into account these dynamic changes in gene expression associated with the juvenile to adult state transition and might require re-evaluating previous results at later stages of development. Moreover, given the evolutionary conservation of SPL function, precise spatiotemporal modulation of SPL expression levels might be an interesting avenue to modulate root growth in general and root system architecture in crop species specifically.
