Group II intron RNPs are elaborately organized retroelements that can recognize the shape and sequence of their structured DNA target.

Group II introns are self-splicing retroelements that have played a key role in shaping eukaryotic genomes as the ancestors of spliceosomal introns and non-LTR retroelements ( 1 ). They remain important for gene expression in plants, fungi, yeasts, and many bacteria ( 2 , 3 ). Group II introns encode a specialized reverse transcriptase (maturase or intron-encoded protein (IEP)), that binds its parent intron and facilitates self-splicing, releasing a well-folded lariat ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex ( 4 ). The liberated RNP functions as a retrotransposon, targeting DNA that contains spliced exon junction sequences and inserting via a two-step transesterification reaction known as reverse splicing ( Fig. 1A ) ( 5 ). The resulting DNA-RNA chimera is copied into cDNA by the reverse transcriptase (RT) activity of the multifunctional IEP in a process known as target primed reverse transcription (TPRT) ( 6 ). Host repair pathways complete the downstream DNA copy-and-paste steps needed to achieve total intron integration ( 4 ).

There are three main classes of group II introns, IIA, IIB and IIC, which share a conserved secondary structure and a similar tertiary organization around a ribozyme active site ( 7 ). Group IIC introns are an ancient class of bacterial introns that recognize both the sequence and three-dimensional structure of their DNA recognition sites ( 8 ). Unlike their larger IIA and IIB counterparts, group IIC introns are almost completely dependent on their IEPs to facilitate intron excision through lariat formation, thereby forming the functional RNP that serves as the minimal element for retrotransposition ( 8 ). Compared to their more evolved counterparts, group IIC IEPs lack an endonuclease domain for generating TPRT primers and instead exploit the lagging strands at DNA replication forks ( 4 ).

Recent structural and biochemical studies of IIA and IIB introns have provided important insights into strategies for IEP recognition of intron RNA ( 9 – 11 ). However, available RNP structures have not revealed a specific mechanistic role for the IEP during RNP assembly, DNA recognition, or chemical catalysis. At present, the mechanism by which group IIC introns recognize DNA structures, and not just DNA sequences, remains unclear. Furthermore, there are no available structures of the free RNP retroelement before it has bound DNA. These open questions preclude a clear understanding of group II intron retrotransposition and its evolutionary role in shaping modern genomes. To address these problems, we solved cryoEM structures of a group IIC intron retroelement poised to undergo the first step of reverse splicing. Our findings have important implications for understanding mechanistic function of the spliceosome and non-LTR retrotransposons, which continue to remodel and impact the function of human genomes ( 12 , 13 ).

To investigate the mechanism of DNA insertion, we captured a group II intron retroelement prior to the first step of reverse-splicing into DNA ( Fig. 1A ). We first conducted in vitro splicing reactions of the IIC Eubacterium rectale (E.r.) ( 14 ) intron in complex with its encoded maturase (MarathonRT) ( 15 , 16 ) and purified the reaction mixture to obtain a branched lariat-maturase complex ( fig. S1, A to C ). Purity and stability of this RNP complex were assessed using biophysical methods: sedimentation velocity analytical ultracentrifugation and size exclusion chromatography coupled to multi-angle light scattering indicated that the sedimentation coefficient and molecular mass of the RNP were larger compared to the those of the individual lariat or maturase components, suggesting complex formation ( fig S1 , D to F ). To visualize the retroelement in action, we introduced a desthiobiotin-tagged DNA substrate to the intron-maturase RNP and isolated ternary complexes by affinity purification on an avidin column ( fig S2 ). The purified elution fraction was vitrified on grids and the holoenzyme molecules appeared as monodisperse particles on cryoEM micrographs, thereby allowing structure determination ( fig. S2 , B to D and fig. S3 ).

Initial data analysis suggested preferred orientation of the sample, so a tilted data collection strategy was required to obtain additional projection views ( fig. S3 ). After further classification and focused refinement, we obtained a 2.8Å resolution cryoEM structure of the E.r . group IIC intron in complex with its specific IEP and DNA target ( Fig. 1 , B and C , and fig. S4 and S5 ), thereby revealing the state immediately prior to the first step of reverse splicing ( Fig. 1A ). The overall high-resolution 3D reconstruction was of sufficient quality to permit modelling of individual nucleotides ( movie S1 ) and metal ions. The catalytic core formed by D5, the lariat branchpoint, EBS-IBS (exon binding site-intron binding site) sequences and the protein thumb and DNA binding domain (DBD) were resolved to < 3Å.

The overall structure reveals a compact assembly of intron RNA and maturase protein that is closely associated with the DNA substrate through a network of interactions ( movie S2 ). The intron core adopts a similar fold to that of intron structures derived from truncated and modified constructs ( 17 , 18 ). Tertiary interactions identified in previous group II introns are present, along with several additional novel interactions that are observed in this full-length intron construct that contains all six intron domains ( Fig. 1D ). The fold of the maturase resembles that of previously studied IIC proteins ( 15 , 19 ), although the thumb and DNA binding domains are now clearly resolved ( Fig. 1C and fig. S5 ). The bound DNA contains a short spacer, the intron insertion site and a 5’ stem-loop motif unique to group IIC introns ( 20 , 21 ) ( Fig. 1D ).

Despite extensive efforts, a complete group II intron holoenzyme active site had not yet been visualized. In this work, we capture the complete ribozyme core architecture, which includes hallmark elements identified in earlier biochemical and structural studies ( 8 , 22 ). For example, we see that the 2’−5’ lariat linkage, between the first intron nucleotide (G1) and the branchpoint A (A632), is a crucial structural motif for organizing the ribozyme core. The branch-site actively engages the 3’ end of the intron (G1-A637 pairing), helping to position the terminal nucleotide (U638) for nucleophilic attack on DNA ( Fig. 2 , A and B ) ( 23 , 24 ). Facilitating this process, U638 base-pairs with A327 to form the γ-γ’ interaction ( Fig. 2 , E and F ) ( 23 , 24 ). The adjacent G328 and C329 nucleotides of the J2/3 linker form major-groove base triples with C562 and G563 ( fig. S6A ), giving rise to the catalytic triplex common to all group II introns and the spliceosome ( 25 , 26 ). The 2-nt bulge (A580, C581) and catalytic triad (C562, G563, C564) in D5, along with U638, all serve to coordinate catalytic magnesium ion M1, placing it between the nucleophilic 3’ OH and scissile phosphate, in an arrangement poised for the first step of reverse splicing ( Fig 2 , A , B and E ) ( 17 ). A second magnesium ion, M2, is located 3.9Å away from M1, consistent with the two-metal ion catalysis mechanism ( Fig. 2 , A , B and E ) ( 17 , 27 ). We identified two additional, unambiguous densities at positions previously assigned to monovalent ions K1 and K2 in studies that employed anomalous scattering to establish sites of stable K + binding ( 26 , 28 ). In that case, as in this instance, NH 4 + can functionally substitute for K + at these same positions ( Fig. 2 , A , B and E ). The specific coordination and placement of these monovalent ions is essential for positioning the catalytic divalent metal ions, forming a reactive, heteronuclear metal ion cluster. Several tertiary interactions stabilize the periphery of the catalytic core, with D3 and a novel A-stacking interaction bracing the backside of the D5 helix (μ-μ’) ( fig. S6 , B to C ). D2 contacts D6 (π-π’) to hold the lariat in place ( 23 , 29 ) ( fig. S6D ). Although many of these active site elements have been observed independently, in linear introns or in introns of other classes, they have not been simultaneously captured in a single structure until now, thereby demonstrating that these active site elements function in concert and are conserved. The E.r. holoenzyme structure provides a detailed view of a complete, reactive intron catalytic core ( movie S3 ).

Close inspection of the active site reveals structural interdependence between the intron and its encoded maturase. Within the active site, the intron RNA forms short base pairings with its target DNA via the EBS-IBS interactions (EBS1-IBS1 and EBS3-IBS3) ( Fig. 2 , A , B , E and F ). These otherwise unstable short pairing interactions are buttressed and positioned by the maturase, which presses the middle α-helices of the DBD and the third α-helix of the thumb domain against the EBS1 and EBS3 recognition loops respectively ( Fig. 1B and 2C ), rigidifying them and helping to form a central cavity for engagement with DNA ( Fig. 2 , C and D ). These findings establish that the retroelement core does not consist solely of RNA, rather it is a collaborative, ribonucleoprotein active site. The new roles we observe for the maturase thumb and DBD help to explain the strong maturase dependence for both RNA splicing and intron integration, particularly in vivo , and they highlight the symbiotic relationship between the intron RNA and its protein cofactor, which are known to have co-evolved ( 30 , 31 ).

A striking feature of the retroelement holoenzyme is the expansive D4 arm, which extends far from the core and then curves around to cradle the maturase ( Fig. 3A ). D4a, the high affinity maturase-binding subdomain ( 15 , 32 ), forms two anchor points with basic protein surfaces ( Fig. 3 , A and B ) ( 33 ). At the first anchor point, residues extending from the protein (R58, D152, T156, and R160) interact with RNA phosphate and ribose oxygens, securing the insertion helix within the finger domain (IFD) of the IEP against the minor groove interface in the middle of the long D4a hairpin ( Fig. 3 , B and C ). A sharp turn places the distal portion of the D4a subdomain between α-helices 9 and 10 of the protein, where largely basic residues (R217, S234, S237, R240, R243, N244 and R247) approach the RNA backbone from either side, fastening the palm to the D4a arm ( Fig. 3 , B and D ). In contrast with other group II RNPs, the surface of the finger domain (RT0) is not utilized for RNA recognition ( 9 , 10 , 15 ) ( fig. S7 ).

The distinct intron-maturase recognition strategy places the maturase thumb and DBD next to the intron core, allowing the protein to participate in catalysis by rigidifying the active-site ( Fig. 3 , A and E ). The thumb and DBD grasp the EBS1 and EBS3 loops, directly coordinating substrate recognition elements within the retroelement active site ( Fig. 3E ). One approach of this strategy involves locking EBS nucleotides into a conformation conducive for substrate binding (i.e. K388 with G187O6 of EBS1 and K358 with A231N7 of EBS3) ( Fig. 3 , E to G ). A secondary tactic includes immobilizing the EBS3 phosphate backbone through interactions with a multitude of basic residues on the protein thumb (K300, K303, S309, R347 and K358) ( Fig. 3G ). A third strategy consists of DBD amino acids (Y350, R389, N395 and main chain amines of I390 and A391), stabilizing the turn in EBS1 and enabling the formation of δ-δ’, thereby reinforcing this single base pair interaction (C183 with G158) that bridges the EBS loops. ( Fig. 3F ). Interestingly, R308 of the protein thumb provides additional stabilization by simultaneously coordinating the phosphate backbone of EBS1 and 3 (through C183 and A230) ( Fig. 3H ). These interactions demonstrate a specific mechanistic role for the maturase protein during catalysis, showing that it promotes proper formation of multiple active site components ( 34 ). These findings reveal the inextricable, functional coordination of intron and protein during the mechanism of splicing and retrotransposition.

Some of the most remarkable features of this structure involve the DNA target and the unusual strategies for molecular recognition by the holoenzyme. Here we show that the DNA is recognized through a combination of shape-selectivity and base-specific interactions ( movie S4 ), only a few of which involve canonical WC pairing. The DNA itself has distinct structural features that support this recognition strategy. Most prominent is an unusual, structurally conserved, DNA stem, which is composed of a short helix [9 base pairs (bp)] that is capped by an undertwisted duplex comprised of two noncanonical G-A DNA base-pairs and a G-C base pair. Together, these extend the DNA stem to 12 bp, which approximates the consensus stem length for IIC insertion targets. The terminal DNA loop serves as a stacking platform for long-range interactions. Adjacent to the DNA stem is a short spacer, which is followed by IBS1 nucleotides and the IBS3 nucleotide that flanks the DNA insertion site ( Fig. 4A and B ).

The DNA stem lies in a cleft that is formed by regions of both the protein (DBD and thumb) and the intron RNA (D1d and D4a). Two clusters of amino acids along the third α-helix of the protein thumb domain anchor the DNA stem by making contacts at both ends of the DNA helix, at positions separated by approximately one helical turn. The first cluster (S346, R347, R349, R353, N395, and N405) secures the base of the stem through contacts with dG1 and dA2 ( Fig. 4C ). The second group (S336, M337, K338, and T339) appears to locally deform the top base pairs of the stem at dC20 and dT21 ( Fig. 4C ). This is the result of a striking DNA-protein interaction network that involves insertion of a prolyl-aromatic loop into the distorted, widened minor groove at the tip of the DNA stem. The complementary fit of this peptide loop is mediated by interactions between largely buried side chains (Y278, F279 and P281) and the methylene edges of DNA sugar moieties ( Fig. 4D ). These protein-DNA interactions are supported by contacts between the DNA and RNA backbone residues (dA4O3’ and dG5OP1 with G163 2’OH), reminiscent of ribose-zipper interactions observed within folded RNA molecules ( Fig. 4E ) ( 17 ). Collectively, these interactions enable the holoenzyme to coordinate and selectively identify the shape of a DNA helix.

This shape-selective recognition strategy of the DNA stem is complemented by sequence-specific interactions between the holoenzyme and single-stranded regions of the DNA target. Phylogenetically covarying base-pairs are formed between substrate-recognition regions of the intron and single-stranded DNA nucleobases downstream of the DNA stem ( 35 ). In the holoenzyme, we not only identify these critical WC pairings, but we also observe an unexpectedly complex network of interactions mediated by the spacer DNA that connects the stem with the IBS sequences. This sequential network of DNA IBS elements and the adjacent spacer interactions begins with the nucleotide located immediately downstream of the insertion site (dT36), which forms a single-base-pair interaction (EBS3-IBS3) with a nucleotide extending from the D1d coordination loop within the intron (A231) ( Fig. 4F ). Stacked atop this pair is a short helix formed via base-pairings between the subsequent stretch of DNA nucleotides (IBS1: dT35, dT34, dT33 and dC32) and a second substrate recognition loop that projects from the terminus of intron D1d (EBS1: A184, A185, A186 and G187) ( Fig. 4F ). Like the short codon-anticodon helix in the ribosome ( 36 ), the EBS-IBS1 duplex is further stabilized via formation of an A-minor motif between A75 and the dC32-G187 base-pair ( Fig. 4G ). Intriguingly, the structure reveals that EBS1-IBS1 is not limited to four contiguous base-pairs, rather, it is extended by an additional base-pair that is formed between the next consecutive nucleotide (A188) in the EBS1 loop and a discontinuous nucleotide from the DNA spacer region (dT30). Indeed, the intervening DNA nucleotide (dT31) is extrahelical and stabilized by interactions with protein residues (vide infra) ( Fig. 4H ). Through these sequential stacking networks, supported by contacts with the protein (i.e., dT36O4 with K361), the intron achieves stable, base-pairing specificity with the DNA target.

Nucleotides within the DNA spacer region participate in binding the RNP, adopting an ordered structure that engages in specific interactions with the holoenzyme. Rather than forming a helical stack, the spacer nucleotides (dA28, dT29, dT30 and dT31) form an unusual motif in which the nucleotides splay in alternating directions on either side of the central phosphate spine (Pauling-like DNA), thereby exposing a large interaction interface to the adjacent DBD ( Fig. 4 , F and H ). Amino acids from the DBD intercalate between the DNA spacer nucleotides while forming an abundance of interactions with both the bases and the phosphate backbone ( Fig. 4H ). For example, N3 of dT31 interacts with amide oxygens of N378 while its adjacent phosphate oxygens interact with proximal arginine residues (R381 and R382). Together, these interactions stabilize an unusual backbone conformation that enables the dT30-A188 pair to form atop the EBS-IBS1 helix. In turn, these interactions with the DBD pull the DNA into place, positioning the specialized barb-like structure formed by the α-helical bundle within the DBD at the base of the DNA stem ( Fig. 4 , B and H ).

To better understand molecular rearrangements that might occur when the intron retroelement binds to DNA substrate, we solved the structure of the apo-RNP, visualizing the free intron-maturase complex at a resolution of 3.6Å ( Fig. 5A and fig. S9 ). We were surprised to observe that the apo-RNP has an architecture that is almost identical to that of the complex bound to DNA, and that substrate binding induces only minor changes in the structure. Most remarkably, the RNP active site remains completely intact ( Fig. 5 , A and B ) ( 9 – 11 ). The maturase does not change its orientation in the absence of DNA, remaining coordinated at two anchor points along the D4a arm, with the thumb and DBD inserted into the active site to participate in catalysis ( Fig. 5A ). In this configuration, the binding interface for the target DNA is maintained, enabling the RNP to readily recognize an incoming DNA target and rapidly engage in retrotransposition ( Fig. 5A ). Upon recognition of the DNA stem-loop, the RNP (palm, fingers and D4a) appears to become more rigid, as we observe a concomitant increase in local resolution at these positions ( fig. S3B and S9B and movie S5 and S6 ). This is reminiscent of many protein enzymes, whereby docking of ligand into the active site freezes out local motions and locks the substrate in place. In previous ligand-free intron structures, EBS nucleotides were found to be disordered or rearranged ( 23 , 24 , 26 ). Here, we observe that the positions of the EBS nucleotides are unchanged, likely due to the presence of the maturase. These findings reinforce the mechanistic role of the protein as a stabilizing catalytic component ( Fig. 5C ). Further evidence of a pre-formed catalytic core includes the persistence of the heteronuclear metal ion cluster, which remains organized around the lariat, although M2 is not visible in this case ( Fig. 5D ).

The structures presented here reveal how components of the holoenzyme help promote activity of the ribozyme core. The protein buttresses the catalytic residues responsible for specifically positioning the DNA substrate, providing a missing link in understanding how maturases unlock the full catalytic potential of group II intron ribozymes ( Fig. 2 ). Interactions with protein residues stabilize the intron substrate recognition loops and precisely arrange nucleotides for DNA binding. These interactions contribute to proper orientation of reaction components throughout ribozyme catalysis. Our findings provide a direct mechanistic role for the protein cofactor, and they help explain the lowered salt and magnesium requirements in its presence ( 38 ).

Prior studies, due to resolution limitations or construct design, were unable to identify a specific function for the maturase protein, except in transient D6 stabilization ( 9 ). By contrast, we can now show that not only are the protein thumb and DBD proximal to D1 catalytic residues, but also that they have critical roles in stabilizing substrate binding. Given its analogous spatial placement, it is possible that Prp8 may play a similar role during spliceosomal catalysis ( 39 ) ( fig. S10 ).

The high-resolution cryoEM structures we provide here offer an unprecedented glimpse into RNP strategies for recognizing DNA ( Fig. 1B ). The holoenzyme structure reveals a stem-loop DNA nestled within the retroelement, bound to RNA and protein. Within this cleft, the protein assists in positioning the insertion site and aligning the DNA stem for steric fit against the complementary maturase surface ( Fig. 3 ). Additional aspects of the unusual recognition strategy include splayed Pauling-like DNA, a stabilizing A-minor motif, and intermolecular stacking moieties involving both RNA and protein ( Fig. 4 ). These interactions highlight the symbiotic nature of RNA and protein and underscore the multiplicity of strategies available to RNPs for achieving selective substrate recognition. Proteins have long been known to recognize DNA structures, but here we show that RNPs, with their expanded repertoire of DNA molecular recognition determinants, have this ability too ( 40 ).

The DNA stem loop motif is exclusive to IIC introns, which contain an abbreviated D1 scaffold and short exon recognition sequences ( 7 ). Intriguingly, in the more highly evolved IIA and IIB introns, the RNP binding motif that we find occupied by the DNA stem in IIC introns is instead replaced by intron insertion motif D1d2, an RNA subdomain that includes EBS2, which is absent in the IIC class ( 7 ). Comparison of this region across intron classes suggests that EBS2 evolved to imitate the target DNA stem ( fig. S11 ). Indeed, the DNA stem motif structurally resembles the EBS2-IBS2 interactions typical of IIA and IIB introns and it functionally emulates EBS2 by anchoring the DNA substrate to the RNP. This mimicry suggests that initial recognition of a structured DNA motif by the more primitive IIC introns was replaced by novel RNA domains within the intron itself, resulting in longer target recognition sequences that provided greater base-pairing specificity for the retroelement.

A surprising feature of our structures is the way that the protein is positioned within the holoenzyme. Encircled by RNA, the exterior surfaces of the protein are occupied, but the concave interior of the protein, adjacent to the catalytic core, is conspicuously solvent accessible, which has functional implications. During reverse splicing, the D6 helix undergoes a conformational change that places the lariat linkage into the active site ( 9 ). To accomplish this, D6 disengages from D2 and swings 90° upward, contacting D1c and a basic patch on the protein thumb. Our structures do not preclude D6 helix dynamics, as there is ample space for a similar movement and the regions that D6 contacts are accessible. The open architecture we observe provides a direct route for DNA to approach the RT active site, as it remains unobstructed by other intron domains and can readily accommodate an entire hybrid duplex for reverse transcription ( 41 ). This suggests that initiation of RT activity, within the current holoenzyme assembly, may be possible without significant conformational rearrangement.

Group II intron retroelements are proliferative, invasive agents and our structures explain why. The apo-retroelement is completely poised to react and does not require any reorganization of structure upon target DNA binding. The arrangement of the active site, from substrate recognition nucleotides to the heteronuclear metal ion cluster to the DNA binding interface, is preserved despite the absence of DNA substrate ( Fig. 5 ). This prearranged organization is consistent with the biological role of group II introns as parasitic genetic elements ( 42 ). Use of the same catalytic core from splicing to integration eschews the need for major rearrangements or host cofactors and allows complete autonomy, which is highly advantageous for a genetic parasite.

Total integration of the RNP requires faithful and accurate reverse transcription of the intron sequence, including the long ORF that encodes the protein, after insertion. This is accomplished using the RT activity of the multifunctional IEP. MarathonRT, the protein within the holoenzyme visualized here, is a well characterized, robust, accurate and ultraprocessive RT enzyme capable of copying through long, structurally complex templates ( 43 ). The intimate association of the parent intron with this protein allows access to its exceptional reverse transcriptase properties and ensures that the intron sequence, which is pivotal to its tertiary architecture, is preserved, allowing the retroelement to continually propagate.

Study of group II intron complexes provides a window into our understanding of non-LTR retrotransposons, such as the L1 RNP, an active mobile element that continues to disperse in human genomes ( 12 , 13 ). Computationally predicted structures of ORF2p, the mobility factor of L1, show that its RT and thumb domain resemble that of the maturase, MarathonRT ( fig. S12 ) ( 44 ). ORF2p contains an additional N-terminal endonuclease and a C-terminal extension, but these domains do not block the exterior basic surfaces of the RT and thumb. MarathonRT and ORF2p are evolutionarily related, and they are implicated in similar mobility mechanisms, so it is possible that the same surfaces are used for anchoring and substrate recognition ( 45 ). Given the lack of structural information on L1 and the strong parallels between systems, our work provides a starting point for imagining how a similar retroelement like L1 might assemble.

In conclusion, we present high-resolution cryoEM structures that reveal the detailed molecular architecture of an intron retroelement complex, thereby shedding light on the mechanism of maturase-facilitated ribozyme catalysis and retrotransposition. The structures reveal novel strategies for RNP interaction with DNA structural motifs and they explain the proliferative nature of group II intron retrotransposons, with implications for understanding the spliceosome and evolutionarily related retroelements. This study underscores the multiplicity of molecular interactions and strategies that are employed as diverse biomolecules carry out the reactions central to genomic stability and plasticity.

articles.title: Maternal trans-vaccenic acid shapes neonatal T cell development and early-life immune imprinting.
articles.authors: Fan H, Zheng Z, Oliphant K, Li J, Mack R, Ju CW, Trandai B, Tu J, Zhang FQ, Zhang R, Xie Z, Yin C, Cai C, Kennedy MS, McNeely T, Cham C, Shah H, Dong L, Su R, Martin CR, Layden BT, Hamanaka RB, Mutlu GM, Chang EB, Zhang J, Chi H, Claud EC, He C, Chen J.
articles.abstract: How maternal nutrition influences neonatal immune development and imprinting through breastfeeding remains largely unclear. We report that maternal supplementation with trans-vaccenic acid (TVA), the predominant naturally occurring trans-fatty acid in human breast milk (HBM), promoted neonatal T cell development in mice. Neonates fed by mothers on a TVA-enriched diet showed an expanded naïve CD4 + T cell population and enhanced adaptive immunity against infection. TVA reprogrammed neonatal naïve CD4 + T cells through a G protein-coupled receptor (GPR43)-CCCTC-binding factor axis and promoted Th1-skewing by cooperating with the transcription factor TBX21. Early-life exposure to maternal TVA via breastfeeding supported long-lasting antiviral immunity in adulthood. Our findings establish the multifaceted benefits of maternal nutrition and breastfeeding via TVA in promoting infant immune homeostasis and protective immunity.
paragraphs: How maternal nutrition influences neonatal immune development and imprinting through breastfeeding remains largely unclear. We report that maternal supplementation with trans-vaccenic acid (TVA), the predominant naturally occurring trans-fatty acid in human breast milk (HBM), promoted neonatal T cell development in mice. Neonates fed by mothers on a TVA-enriched diet showed an expanded naïve CD4 + T cell population and enhanced adaptive immunity against infection. TVA reprogrammed neonatal naïve CD4 + T cells through a G protein-coupled receptor (GPR43)-CCCTC-binding factor axis and promoted Th1-skewing by cooperating with the transcription factor TBX21. Early-life exposure to maternal TVA via breastfeeding supported long-lasting antiviral immunity in adulthood. Our findings establish the multifaceted benefits of maternal nutrition and breastfeeding via TVA in promoting infant immune homeostasis and protective immunity.

Early-life nutritional exposures can shape physiology and disease risk across the lifespan, yet the mechanisms by which maternal diet influences neonatal immune development remain poorly understood. Maternal nutrition is a critical determinant of human breast milk (HBM) composition, which is pivotal for breastfeeding to help build the infant’s immune system and lower the risk of infections and dysfunctional organ development ( 1 – 4 ). HBM contains nutritional components such as fatty acids, carbohydrates, and vitamins, as well as immunomodulatory substances, including infection-protecting antibodies, anti-inflammatory cytokines, and bacteria for the establishment of healthy microbial gut colonization for effective immunological responses against infection and inflammation in newborns( 1 , 5 – 8 ). Therefore, the benefits of breastfeeding are generally attributed to the combined action of multiple components, raising the question of whether a single dietary molecule in breast milk can directly shape neonatal immune development and long-term immune imprinting.

Maternal intake of dietary fatty acids directly impacts the composition and levels of fatty acids in HBM, which can be critical for immune development in infants by playing a nutritional role and influencing the gut microbiome( 9 , 10 ). However, it remains unclear whether a single diet-derived fatty acid delivered through breastfeeding can independently instruct immune development in newborns. TVA is the predominant naturally occurring trans-fatty acid in HBM and is derived exclusively from maternal diet because the human body cannot produce TVA( 11 – 13 ). TVA in humans is mainly from ruminant-derived food, including beef, lamb, milk, and butter, but naturally less than 20% of dietary TVA is metabolized by the human body( 12 – 15 ). We recently reported that the circulating TVA enhances adult CD8 + effector T cell function and anti-tumor immunity( 16 ). TVA can function as an immunomodulator and inactivate CD8 + T cell-surface receptor GPR43, an immunomodulatory G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), triggering activation of the cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP)-protein kinase A (PKA)-cAMP-response element-binding protein (CREB) axis to reprogram adult CD8 + T cells. We thus asked whether maternal TVA as a single HBM nutrient via breastfeeding could shape neonatal immune development and immunity.

We found that TVA levels in HBM samples from mothers correlated to serum TVA levels from their preterm infants ( Fig. 1A ). To test the effects of maternal dietary TVA on neonatal immune development, lactating mouse dams were fed diets supplemented with 0.1% or 1% TVA starting in pregnancy ( Fig. 1B ). Both TVA-supplemented groups produced milk with comparable TVA levels, whereas no TVA was detected in milk from dams on a control diet ( Fig. 1C ). Pups fed TVA-milk showed time-dependent serum accumulation of TVA until weaning (3 weeks post-birth; on TVA-enriched diet afterwards), whereas control pups had no detectable serum TVA ( Fig. 1D ). Pups on TVA-milk (TVA-pups) or control milk had comparable body weights (BWs) ( fig. S1A ), suggesting that TVA in milk did not affect neonatal growth.

Spleen size was increased in TVA-pups compared to controls at 2-3 weeks but became comparable by 5 weeks ( Fig. 1E ). At 2 weeks, TVA-pups had elevated numbers of total splenocytes, CD4 + and CD8 + T cells, B cells, neutrophils, dendritic cells (DCs), and monocytes in spleens ( fig. S1B ), with only increased frequency of CD4 + T cells ( fig. S1C ). In contrast, by 5 weeks, total splenocytes and most immune cell numbers were comparable ( fig. S1D ), with increased CD8 + T cell frequency and reduced percentages of B cells and DCs ( fig. S1E ). Further analysis at 2 weeks revealed increased CD4 + and CD8 + T cell numbers ( fig. S1F – G ) and elevated naïve CD4 + T cell frequency ( fig. S1H ) in spleens of TVA-pups, whereas other T cell subsets were unchanged ( fig. S1H – K ) except for increased expression levels of the T cell activation marker, CD69, on CD8 + T cells ( fig. S1K ).

TVA-pups (2 weeks) also had increased thymus weights ( fig. S1L ), with reduced frequency of CD4/CD8 double-negative (DN) precursors but increased frequency of later stage CD4/CD8 double-positive (DP) thymocytes, whereas thymotic percentages of both CD4 + (4SP) and CD8 + (8SP) cells were comparable between TVA-pups and controls ( fig. S1M ). We did not observe differences between TVA-pups and controls (2 weeks) in the frequencies of CD4 + and CD8 + T cells, regulatory T cells, naïve T cells, or CD69 + T cells within the lung immune microenvironment ( Fig. S1N – Q ).

We performed single-nuclei (sn) multi-omics, including sn-RNA-seq and sn-ATAC-seq, to characterize transcriptional profiles and chromatin accessibility of splenic cells of TVA-pups and controls (2 weeks; Fig. 1F , Data S1 – 2 ). We identified 20 distinct clustered populations ( Fig. 1F , S2A , Data S3 ). TVA-pups exhibited increased frequencies of T cell subsets, including multiple CD4 + and CD8 + populations that mapped to distinct differentiation states. Naïve CD4 + (cluster C3) and naïve CD8 + (C4) cells expressed lymphoid-homing and quiescence-associated genes ( Sell, Ccr7, Tcf7, Lef1 , and Il7r ) without a cytotoxic module. CD4 effector cells (C9) upregulated a Th1-like activation module, including the type 1 cytokine Ifng , the Th1 lineage factor Tbx21 , the trafficking receptor Cxcr3 , and the effector molecule Gzmk , together with low levels of exhaustion-associated genes ( Pdcd1/Tox/Lag3 ), consistent with recently activated Th1-skewed cells. CD8 clusters further resolved into Bcl11b + naïve-like/precursor state poised for differentiation cells (C6), ICOS + early-activated/progenitor-exhausted cells (C10; Icos, Pdcd1, Tox, Lag3 , minimal Gzmb ), and terminal effector cells (C15; Gzmb, Prf1, Zeb2, Cx3cr1, Ifng, Tbx21 ). The naïve CD4 + subset (C3) represented the most expanded T cell population in the TVA group. Moreover, γδ T cells (C20), together with mature follicular B cells (C5) and classical dendritic cells (C18), all critical for T cell–dependent adaptive immunity, were also expanded compared with controls ( Fig. 1G ).

In splenic T cells isolated from TVA-pups compared to controls, we identified increased promoter accessibility scores (promoter sums), reflecting greater chromatin accessibility at the promoters of representative genes related to T cell maturation and function (e.g. Il2rb , Tnfrsf9 , Ifng , Gzmb , and Icos ), proliferation and survival (e.g. Bcl2 , Bcl11b , and Cd28 ), and migration and trafficking (e.g. Ccl5 , Cxcr6 , and Ccr8 ) ( Fig. 1H ). The promoter sums of Gpr43 ( Ffar2 ), which was identified as a TVA target in adult CD8 + effector T cells( 16 ), were increased in clusters of T cells that are expanded in TVA-pups compared to controls, including naïve CD4 + T cells (C3), naïve CD8 + T cells (C4), CD4 + effector T cells (C9), CD8 + T cells (C10), and CD8 + effector T cells (C15) ( Fig. 1I ). Transcription factor (TF) motifs of CREB and TBX21 (T-bet) were increased in TVA-expanded neonatal naïve CD4 + T cells (C3) ( fig. S2B – C ). We concluded that TVA-milk primarily promoted neonatal T cell development, especially in the naïve CD4 + T cell compartment.

To determine the role of the cell-surface receptor GPR43( 16 ), we examined the effects of TVA on neonatal mice which had naïve CD4 + T cells that were deficient in Gpr43 ( Gpr43 −/− ) ( Fig. 2A , left ). CD4 + T cells isolated from neonatal mice fed on TVA-milk showed increased Th1 polarization ex vivo (assessed by %T-bet + IFN-γ + in CD4 + T cells), activation (assessed by CD69 expression), and cell expansion ( Fig. 2A right , S2D ) but had minimal effects on Th2 and Th17 polarization ( fig. S2E – F ). CD4 + T cells from Gpr43 −/− pups on control milk showed elevated Th1 polarization, activation, and cell expansion compared to cells from control pups ( Fig. 2A right, S2D ). This suggested that GPR43 might have an immunosuppressive role in neonatal CD4 + T cells. In contrast, TVA-milk had minimal effects on neonatal CD4 + T cells in Gpr43 −/− pups ( Fig. 2A right , S2D ).

In addition, we compared the effects of the three most abundant unsaturated fatty acids in milk: oleic acid, linoleic acid, and palmitoleic acid; and the three most abundant trans fatty acids: TVA, elaidic acid, and conjugated linoleic acid. Only TVA increased the frequency of T-bet + IFN-γ + CD4 + T cells ( Fig. S3A ). This effect was completely absent in cells from Gpr43 −/− pups ( Fig. S3B ). Consistent with our previous finding that TVA inactivates GPR43 to increase cAMP production and PKA activity( 16 ), treatment with cell permeable 8-Bmoro-cAMP and PKA inhibitor resulted in increased and decreased Th1 polarization of neonatal naïve CD4 + T cells, respectively, and both abolished the effects of TVA ( fig. S3C ). However, treatment with CREB inhibitor had minimal effects on Th1 polarization of neonatal naïve CD4 + T cells, nor did it affect TVA-enhanced Th1 polarization ( fig. S3C ). These data suggested that TVA reprogrammed neonatal naïve CD4 + T cells through the GPR43-cAMP-PKA axis, which, however, was CREB-independent.

To identify the TFs responsible for the effects of TVA on neonatal naïve CD4 + T cells, we focused on 4 subclusters with distinct TVA-dependent patterns of TF activity in the splenic neonatal naïve CD4 + T cell population ( Fig. 2B – C ). CTCF in subcluster 1 represented the only TF with increased activity ( Fig. 2D , fig. S3D ), whereas minimal changes of CREB were detected ( fig. S3E ). CTCF (CCCTC-binding factor) is a zinc finger TF that regulates three-dimensional genome organization and prevents improper interactions between enhancers and promoters( 17 ). CTCF cooperates with TBX21 (T-bet), which is critical for Th1 polarization to ensure proper gene expression in Th1 cells, including Ifng ( 18 ). The promoters of Tbx21 and Ifng showed higher accessibility in subcluster 1 compared with the other subclusters ( fig. S3F ). We found that knockdown of Ctcf , but not Creb1 ( fig. S3G ), abolished Th1 polarization and TBX21 (T-bet) activation enhanced by either TVA or 8-Bmoro-cAMP in neonatal naïve CD4 + T cells ( Fig. 2E ). Moreover, treatment with TVA enhanced CTCF TF activity assessed by increased DNA binding ability in neonatal naïve CD4 + T cells, which was not further enhanced by 8-Bmoro-cAMP and could be abolished by treatment with a PKA inhibitor ( Fig. 2F , fig. S3H ). Since the promoter sums of Ctcf were not altered in subclusters of naïve CD4 + T cells ( fig. S3I ), we concluded that TVA reprogrammed neonatal naïve CD4 + T cells through a GPR43-cAMP-PKA-CTCF axis, likely by enhancing CTCF TF activity but not its expression.

To determine whether maternal TVA broadly changed immunologically relevant milk components, we measured representative milk immune factors. The levels of IgA, lactoferrin, and cytokines, including IL-1b and IL-7, in milk from dams on the TVA diet were comparable to those in milk from control dams ( fig. S4A – D ). Comprehensive lipid (fatty acids) profiling analysis of milk from the TVA and CON groups revealed that TVA was the only fatty acid that differed between the two groups ( fig. S4E , Data S4 ). In addition, the diversity and patterns of microbial distribution in mouse milk varied widely without a clear trend among samples from different mice in the same group of dams, suggesting that feeding TVA-enriched diet to mouse dams did not alter the milk microbiome substantially ( fig. S4F – I ). Analysis of the fecal microbiome in 2-week-old pups by 16S rRNA sequencing revealed no substantial differences in microbial diversity between TVA and CON groups. Instead, litter (cage effect) was the dominant source of microbiome variation, with no clear separation between cohorts ( Fig. S5A – C ). We performed Low-input Multiple Methylation Sequencing (LIME-seq) on 2-week-old pups’ fecal RNA to assess microbial abundance and methylation signatures( 19 ). Consistent with the 16S data, LIME-seq showed highly similar microbial compositions between groups ( Fig. S5D – E ), and differential analysis of microbiome-associated methylation ratios, reflecting microbial metabolic activity, did not identify robust group-specific differences ( Fig. S5F ). These results were consistent with the early-life gut microbiome being unaffected by dietary TVA, and that observed variability was primarily driven by litter-associated effects rather than diet.

To determine the functional effect of maternal TVA on neonatal immunity, we used a neonatal mouse model of lung infection with the H1N1 influenza A virus A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 (PR8)( 20 ) via intranasal administration ( Fig. 3A ). Although TVA- and control pups at 10 days showed comparable BWs ( fig. S6A ), TVA-pups had enhanced survival ( Fig. 3B ) and reduced clinical score ( fig. S6B – C ) following influenza A infection. Moreover, pathologic analysis of lung tissues from control pups showed that influenza A virus caused lung epithelial damage ( fig. S6D , upper , quantitative results shown in Fig. 3C , left ) with reduced normal epithelium ( fig. S6D , lower , quantitative results shown in Fig. 3C , right ), compared to pups without viral treatment. TVA-pups showed reduced lung damage and increased normal epithelium, compared to controls with viral infection ( fig. S6D , quantitative results shown in Fig. 3C ).

Further analysis of lung tissues revealed that, compared to controls, TVA-pups had reduced viral loads in lungs as early as Day 7 and Day 10 post-infection ( Fig. 3D ). Although the frequency of lung-infiltrating CD4 + T cells (gating strategies in fig. S7A ) was not altered in TVA-pups ( fig. S7B ), these cells had elevated CD69 and CD44 levels ( Fig. 3E , left , fig. S7C ) on Day 7 post-infection. In addition, the frequency of influenza-specific CD4 + T cells accessed as CD11a + /CD49d + - ( fig. S7D ) and NP 331-325 + (epitope of viral N protein)-specific cells ( Fig. 3E right , S7E ) were also elevated in TVA-pups on Day 7 but reduced on Day 10 post-infection, whereas these populations peaked on Day 10 post-infection in controls. Similar results were obtained for lung-infiltrating CD8 + T cells ( fig. S7F , Fig. 3F , left ). The frequency of influenza-specific (PA 224-233 + ) CD8 + T cells was elevated on Day 7 but reduced in TVA-pups on Day 10 post-infection, compared to this population in controls that was increased only on Day 10 post-infection ( Fig. 3F right , S7G ). Ex vivo activation of lung CD4 + and CD8 + T cells following viral infection revealed that, compared with controls, TVA-pups exhibited an increased expression of IFN-γ, T-bet + , and TNF-α by CD4 + T-cell subsets. The frequencies of IFN-γ + and TNF-α + cells were also markedly increased within the CD8 + T-cell compartment ( Fig. S8A ). T reg cells in the lung and spleen following influenza A virus infection showed no differences between TVA-pups and controls ( Fig. S8B ).

Most of the populations of lung-infiltrating B cells, NK cells, macrophages, DCs, neutrophils, and monocytes ( fig. S8C – H ) were not altered in TVA-pups compared to controls. Only populations of lung-infiltrating B cells and NK cells were increased or reduced in TVA-pups on Day 10 post-infection, respectively. TVA-pups showed reduced inflammation assessed by decreased IL-1b in lungs ( Fig. 3G ) and TNF-a levels in lungs and serum ( fig. S8I – J ). When TVA exposure was restricted to first-generation pups ( Fig. S9A ), the spleen development ( Fig. S9B ) and influenza A virus response results of pups ( Fig. S9C ) remained consistent with our previous findings.

We concluded that TVA-milk enhanced the readiness of neonatal T cells, leading to an early but more effective response to viral infection and inflammation in lungs to improve the survival of virus-infected pups.

We performed snMulti-Omics analysis of lung tissue cells of pups that were sacrificed on Day 7 post-viral infection ( fig. S10A , Data S5 – 6 ). Results of snRNA-seq identified 20 distinct clusters ( Fig. 3H , S10B , Data S7 ). Upon viral infection, pups on TVA-milk had increased lung-infiltrating populations of diverse T cell subsets including CD8 + effector T cells and Th1-like T cells, but reduced lung-infiltrating Th2-like T cells compared to controls ( Fig. 3I ). These results suggested that maternal TVA through breastfeeding implemented a shift from Th2-biased neonatal immunity to Th1-skewing, which enhanced recruitment of lung infiltrating Th1 cell subset to help clear viral loads more effectively in infected lungs.

Lung-infiltrating cell clusters with increased populations had higher Gpr43 transcript levels ( fig. S10C – D ). In addition, snATAC-seq analysis revealed a total of 15 clusters ( fig. S10E ), of which 4 clusters had increased cell populations in lung tissues from TVA-pups with viral infection. These clusters were identified as Th1 cells (C1) and CD8 + effector T cells (C4, C7, and C9 ( fig. S10F ), and which had indications of increased TF activity of TBX21 (T-bet) ( fig. S10G ). The activity of CREB was increased in lung-infiltrating CD8 + effector T cell populations, but not Th1 cells, of TVA-pups compared to controls ( fig. S10H ), consistent with our finding that TVA-milk functioned through GPR43-dependent activation of CTCF.

To examine the role of TBX21 and Th1-skewing shift in effects of maternal TVA on neonatal immunity, we used Tbx21 knockout ( Tbx21 −/− ) mice that cannot effectively develop Th1 cells ( Fig. 3J ). Tbx21 gene deficiency abolished anti-viral effects of TVA-milk, leading to comparable survival and clinical score between TVA-pups and controls ( Fig. 3K , fig. S11A – B ). Similar results were obtained using TCR-α knockout (KO) mice deficient of αβ T cells ( fig. S11C – E ), and CD4 KO mice ( fig. S11F – H ). To assess the role of GPR43, we used Gpr43 whole-body KO ( Gpr43 −/− ) and T cell-specific Gpr43 KO ( Gpr43 fl/fl CD4 Cre ) mice. TVA treatment improved clinical scores and survival in littermate controls but not in Gpr43 −/− ( fig. S11I – K ) or Gpr43 fl/fl CD4 Cre pups ( Fig. 3L , S11L ). These results were consistent with GPR43 expression on CD4 + T cells mediating the antiviral protective effects of TVA in neonates.

We employed an adoptive transfer approach ( fig. 4A left , S12A ) to compare CD4 + T cells from TVA-pups and controls. Endogenous CD4 + T cells were depleted in CD45.2 recipients using an anti-CD4 antibody. Neonatal naïve CD4 + T cells from 2-week-old pups were co-transferred at a 1:1 ratio: CD45.1 cells from controls and CD45.1/2 cells from TVA-pups (ratio confirmed by flow cytometry, fig. S12B ). Recipient CD45.2 mice, maintained on a control diet, were challenged with influenza A virus. Seven days post-infection, CD45.1/2 CD4 + T cells (derived from TVA-pups) outcompeted CD45.1 CD4 + T cells (from controls) in the spleen ( fig. 4A right , S12C upper ). This advantage was even more pronounced among lung-infiltrating Th1 cells ( fig. 4A middle , S12C lower ), where the CD45.1/2:CD45.1 ratio was higher in the lung than in the spleen ( fig. S12D ). These data indicated that TVA-programmed neonatal naïve CD4 + T cells possessed a cell-intrinsic advantage in survival, expansion, and Th1 differentiation upon viral challenge.

We established a Th1-dependent infection model using Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium ( S. Typhimurium ), in which bacterial burden is assessed in the spleen, liver, and lung. Breeders were fed CON or TVA diets, and their 2-week-old pups were challenged with S. Typhimurium ( Fig. 4B left ). By day 3 post-challenge, infection disrupted normal body-weight gain in CON pups, whereas TVA mitigated this effect ( fig. S13A ). TVA-pups showed reduced bacterial colonization in spleen and liver ( Fig. 4B middle ). Overall CD4 + frequencies among CD45 + leukocytes were comparable between groups ( fig. S13B left ), but TVA enhanced Th1 polarization, increasing T-bet + CD4 + ( Fig. 4B right ) and IFN-γ + CD4 + T cells ( fig. S13B right ), and IFN-γ + CD8 + T cells ( fig. S13C ). Other splenic immune populations were unchanged, apart from neutrophils, which were reduced in TVA-pups, consistent with decreased bacterial burden ( fig. S13D ).

We examined the relationship between TVA level and cytokine profile in the blood of mouse pups and human infants. Serum TVA levels of TVA-pups (2 weeks) positively correlated with IL-2, IL-22, and CXCL9 levels, all of which are related to T cell functions, but inversely correlated with IL-4 ( fig. S14A , Data S8 ). Similar results were obtained using blood spot samples from preterm infants ( Fig. 4C , Data S9 ). Infant blood TVA levels correlated positively with IL-2, negatively with IL-4, and with an increased IFN-γ/IL-4 ratio ( Fig. 4C , left , middle , and right ). Given that IL-2 is important for naïve T cell expansion and the IFN-γ/IL-4 ratio is a widely used readout of Th1/Th2 balance( 21 ), this finding was consistent with TVA-milk preferentially promoting T cell expansion and a shift toward Th1 neonatal immunity. Moreover, to directly test the effect of TVA on human neonatal naïve CD4 + T cells, we isolated naïve CD4 + T cells from human umbilical cord blood and treated them with TVA in vitro . Consistent with our mouse data, TVA treatment enhanced Th1 polarization in all three independent cord blood samples ( Fig. 4D , S14B – C ).

Preterm infants have enfeebled Th1 immune responses and thus are vulnerable to infections, which may cause chronic inflammation, leading to disrupted organ development with an increased risk of diseases such as bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), which is strongly associated with lung inflammation( 22 – 24 ). We used a mass spectrometry-based fatty acid profiling approach to examine the link between human milk fatty acids and preterm-associated inflammatory BPD ( Fig. 4E , left ). We found that TVA levels in HBM samples from mothers as the first in rank, inversely correlated with the incidence of BPD for their preterm infants ( Fig. 4E , right , Data S10 – 11 ). Moreover, TVA levels in the blood spot samples from a group of preterm infants inversely correlated with BPD incidence ( Fig. 4F , Data S12 ). These results together suggested a link between TVA in breastmilk and neonatal T cell function lowering risk of preterm inflammatory BPD.

To distinguish prenatal and postnatal TVA exposure via breastfeeding, we used a mouse-fostering strategy( 25 ) in which pups born to C57BL/6 mothers on TVA-enriched or control diet were nursed by FVB/NJ foster mothers on either diet ( Fig. 5A ). Serum TVA was detected only in pups with postnatal exposure (TVA-to-TVA and CON-to-TVA) groups, but not in control pups (CON-to-CON), nor in pups with prenatal exposure alone (TVA-to-CON) ( fig. S15A ). Compared to controls, pups exposed to TVA postnatally (TVA-to-TVA and CON-to-TVA) showed enhanced survival ( Fig. 5B ) with reduced clinical score in response to influenza viral exposure ( fig. S15B – C ). These pups also exhibited reduced viral load in lungs ( fig. S15D ) with increased population and activation states of lung-infiltrating CD4 + and CD8 + T cells, whereas other immune cell populations were unchanged ( Fig. 5C , S15E – H ). In contrast, prenatal TVA exposure alone (TVA-to-CON) had no effects. These results together showed that postnatal exposure of TVA via breastfeeding was the predominant driver of neonatal T cell reprogramming.

Early-life immune imprinting describes how exposures to environmental cues such as dietary factors during infancy and early childhood impact immune development and have long-lasting effects on immune responsiveness and disease susceptibility( 26 ). Neonatal CD4 + naïve T cells contribute to the foundation of adaptive immunity and play a crucial role in early-life immune imprinting shaping lifelong immunity( 27 ). To examine whether postnatal TVA exposure through breastfeeding had an immune imprinting effect, we fed control diet to both TVA-pups and controls after weaning at three weeks (TVA-CON and CON-CON, respectively) and performed the mouse model of lung infection with influenza A virus treatment when the mice reached adulthood at 6–10 weeks ( Fig. 5D , upper ). TVA-pups (3 weeks) accumulated serum TVA, which became undetectable at adulthood after being fed on control diet post-weaning ( Fig. 5E ). However, following influenza A infection, mice in the group of TVA-CON showed enhanced survival ( Fig. 5F ) with reduced clinical score upon viral infection ( fig. S16A – B ). We examined the adult naïve CD4 + T cells from mice in both groups ( Fig. 5D , lower ) and found increased CTCF activity ( Fig. 5G , fig. S16C ) and enhanced Th1 polarization ( Fig. 5H ) in cells from mice in the TVA-CON group, compared to CON-CON mice. Similarly, TVA exposure via breastmilk during postnatal weeks 0–3 improved clinical scores and survival of 8–12-week-old adult mice following influenza A virus challenge ( fig. S16D – F ).

To determine whether TVA exposure must occur within a defined developmental window to imprint adult immunity, we shifted TVA exposure to weeks 5–8 after birth, and assessed antiviral responses at 10–12 weeks ( Fig. 5I ). TVA feeding during weeks 5–8 led to detectable serum levels at 8 weeks, which returned to baseline by weeks 10–12 after switching to the control diet at 8 weeks ( Fig. 5J ). However, this TVA exposure did not enhance resistance to influenza A virus infection ( Fig. 5K , S16G – H ). Naïve CD4 + T cells isolated from these adult mice failed to exhibit the Th1 polarization advantage observed following neonatal TVA exposure ( Fig. 5L ). Ex vivo analyses showed that TVA increased Th1 polarization in neonatal, but not adult naïve CD4 + T cells ( Fig. S16I – J ). We concluded that TVA-mediated immune imprinting was restricted to a critical neonatal window, and that exposure during adulthood was insufficient to reprogram naïve CD4 + T cell fate or confer long-term antiviral protection ( fig S17 ).

Our findings identify maternal trans-vaccenic acid as a systemic signal linking maternal diet to neonatal immune development in mice. Although breast milk is widely viewed as a complex system whose benefits arise from the interaction of many components, our study shows that a single dietary molecule can be sufficient to program neonatal T cell development, immunity, and long-term immune imprinting. These results reveal a direct molecular pathway through which maternal nutrition shapes infant immune trajectories. However, our current human dataset does not clarify whether the association between milk TVA and immune outcomes differs between term and preterm infants. Future studies incorporating term infants and explicitly testing gestational-age–dependent effects are therefore warranted.

Compared to adult T cells, neonatal T cells show slower responses to influenza infection with defective migration into infected lungs( 28 ). We found that TVA promoted a shift to neonatal Th1 polarization and reduced neonatal mortality rate upon viral infection. Given that immune polarization in human neonates is influenced by multiple factors, including tissue environment, developmental stage, and postnatal exposures, rather than merely reflecting the uniform Th2 bias observed in mouse neonates, our work addresses this gap by integrating mechanistic insights from murine studies with analyses of human preterm infant samples, offering translational insight into how maternal nutrition shapes early immune trajectories. We also identified cell type-specific functional and regulatory differences between neonatal naïve and effector T cells. Future studies are warranted to define how GPR43 selectively signals through CTCF in neonatal naïve CD4 + T cells.

Our study suggests breastfeeding as a critical developmental window during which neonatal immune cells can be reprogrammed to yield durable imprinting effects that shape immunity in adulthood. We propose that TVA acts selectively on neonatal naïve CD4 + T cells, the foundation of adaptive immunity, thereby providing a mechanistic link between maternal milk nutrients and early-life immune programming. Notably, the benefit is temporally restricted to the breastfeeding period in mice (0–3 weeks of age): TVA exposure confined to this window enhances adult immune responses, whereas delayed exposure failed to elicit comparable effects. These observations suggest that TVA-dependent imprinting is gated by a narrow developmental timeframe. Whether earlier withdrawal of TVA, or discrete sub-windows within 0–3 weeks, is sufficient to establish durable programming remains unresolved and will require future investigation.

Our findings hint that a diet including foods with high TVA levels, or dietary supplementation of TVA, might be beneficial during pregnancy and lactation. This possibility should be interpreted cautiously, given the well-established adverse health effects of industrial trans fats. However, industrial trans fats such as elaidic acid differ from naturally occurring ruminant trans fats such as TVA in source and composition and may therefore have distinct biological effects. In mice, an elaidic acid–rich diet promotes atherosclerotic lesion development, whereas a TVA-rich butter diet doesn’t increase plaque burden and is less atherogenic under hypercholesterolemic conditions( 29 ). Consistent with this distinction, prospective meta-analyses generally report no association between typical ruminant trans-fat intake and coronary heart disease risk( 30 ). Epidemiological studies further suggest that circulating TVA is associated with lower adiposity, reduced diabetes risk, and lower systemic inflammation, and in rodent models of dyslipidemia, a TVA-enriched diet lowers circulating triglycerides( 31 – 33 ). Furthermore, it is possible that TVA-supplemented infant formula, an ingredient not currently included, may enhance immune system maturation, strengthen early-life immune responses, and promote durable immune imprinting.

Mouse neonatal or adult naïve T cells were isolated from the spleen and peripheral lymph nodes (PLN) of 10-14 days old or 8-12 weeks old C57BL/6 mice by magnetic bead purification using Easy Sep ™ Mouse Naïve T Cell Isolation Kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Stem Cell Technologies). Cells were cultured in Click’s media at 37° and 5% CO 2 incubator for further experiments.

Animal experiments were conducted and designed according to protocols approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of The University of Chicago. Mice were housed and bred at the University of Chicago Animal Resource Center in specific pathogen-free conditions. Mice were on 12-hour light/dark cycles that coincided with daylight in Chicago, IL, USA. The housing facility was maintained at 20-25°C and 30-70% humidity. Mice were euthanized by carbon dioxide inhalation followed by a secondary physical method to ensure death. C57BL/6J (The Jackson Laboratory, JAX:000664; RRID: IMSR_JAX:000664), TCRα Knock-out (B6.129S2-Tcratm1Mom/J) (The Jackson Laboratory, JAX:002116; RRID: IMSR_JAX:002116), FVB/NJ (The Jackson Laboratory, JAX: 001800; RRID: IMSR_JAX:001800), Tbx21 −/− (B6.129S6-Tbx21 tm1Glm /J) (The Jackson Laboratory, JAX: 004648; RRID: IMSR_JAX:004648), CD4 KO (B6.129S2-Cd4 tm1Mak /J) (The Jackson Laboratory, JAX: 002663; RRID: IMSR_JAX:002663), CD4Cre (B6.Cg-Tg(Cd4-cre)1Cwi/BfluJ) (The Jackson Laboratory, JAX: 022071; RRID: IMSR_JAX:022071), B6 CD45.1 (B6.SJL-Ptprc a Pepc b /BoyJ) (The Jackson Laboratory, JAX: 002014; RRID: IMSR_JAX:002014) mice were purchased from The Jackson Laboratory. Blood spot cards of preterm infants and paired milk samples from their moms or donors were provided by Dr. Erika C. Claud from the Microbiome In Neonatal Development (MIND) study. For the preterm infants, breastmilk intake did not differ between infants with and without PBD, gestational age was comparable between these groups, and the amount of TVA in donor milk was similar to that in mothers’ own breastmilk. The MIND study recruits preterm infants (infants born < 37 weeks postmenstrual age) from the University of Chicago Comer Children’s Hospital after retrieving written informed consent from a parent. Exclusion criteria included the presence of genetic syndromes, severe congenital anomalies, or nonviability. All sample collection and study procedures were approved by the University of Chicago Institutional Review Board (IRB16-1431), which abides by the Declaration of Helsinki.
