The blood spot cards of the preterm infants were used for TVA level detection. 3.2-mm (1/8-inch) diameter disks (11-24 disks) were punched from dried infant blood-spots in a 20 mL glass vial and spike 10 μL of 13 C 5 -trans vaccenic acid and extracted with the modified Matyash et al method( 34 ). In brief, the disks were extracted with 800 μL of ice-cold methanol (containing 0.1 mg/mL butylated hydroxytoluene-BHT) and sonicated for 15 minutes, followed by the addition of 2400 μL of methyl-tert-butyl ether and sonicated for 45 minutes at room temperature and centrifuged at 18,000g for 15 minutes. The upper 2 mL of the organic layer was dried using Genevac 2.4 EZ-elite evaporator and stored at −20°C until analysis. On the day of the LC-MS analysis, samples were re-suspended in 80 μL of 3/2/1 isopropanol/acetonitrile/water, sonicated for 2 minutes, thermomixer for 10 minutes at 15 °C. The supernatant was transferred to the LC-MS vial after spinning it down at 18,000g for 20 minutes at 15°C. Chromatography separation was performed using the Cortecs T3 (2.1x100mm, 1.6micron, part # 186008499 Waters Corporation) column connected to a Vanquish Horizon UHPLC system and IQ-X tribrid mass spectrometers. The column temperature, injection volume, and flow rate were 40°C, 5 μL, and 0.3 mL/minute, respectively. The mobile phase A (MPA) was 60/40 acetonitrile/water, 10 mM ammonium formate+0.1% formic acid, and MPB was 89.1/9.9/0.99 isopropanol/acetonitrile/water, 10 mM ammonium formate +0.1% formic acid. The chromatographic gradient was 0 minute: 5%B, 1.2 minute: 5%B, 5 minutes: 50%B, 9.00 minute: 50%B, 13.00 minute: 70%B, 15.5 minute: 70%B, 17.00 minute: 100%B, 20.00 minute: 100%B, 20.2 minute: 5%B, 28.00 minute: 5%B. MS1 parameters were as follows: spray voltage: 2800 V negative, sheath gas: 40, auxiliary gas: 10, sweep gas: 1, ion transfer tube temperature: 300°C, vaporizer temperature: 350°C, orbitrap resolution: 60K, scan range(m/z): 120-500, RF lens (%): 60, automatic gain control (AGC) target: 100%, and a maxIT of 118 milliseconds (ms). The TVA levels were normalized to an added stable isotope standard- 13 C 5 trans vaccenic acid, and calculated for the 10 disks.

Establishing TVA-feeding mouse lines: For each mouse line, we start to feed 8-week-old C57BL/6J males and females with the TVA-enriched diet or control diet for two weeks before pairing them for breeding. Their offspring were kept on the TVA-enriched diet or control diet and inbred to continue this line. After the control diet and TVA diet mouse lines stabilized (2-3 generations), the breeders and neonatal pups of each group were used for further analysis. To avoid potential transgenerational effects, we also had acute TVA exposure paradigms that restricted parental dietary exposure to the first generation. Specifically, we used 8-week-old male and female C57BL/6J mice and established breeders under two new dietary timing regimens:1. Diet switch at breeder setup (TVA or control diet initiated on the day breeders were paired); 2. Late-gestation switch (diet changed 3 days prior to delivery, E17). In these experiments, pups remained with their biological mothers in both the CON and TVA diet groups. For each condition, we used more than five breeder cages, and pups were collected from multiple independent cages. To ensure robustness and minimize cage-specific effects, we performed three to five independent experiments, each including five or more mice per group. These experimental designs reduce potential cage effects and ensure the reliability of the statistical analyses.

For mouse milk collection, breeders were separated from their 1- or 2-week-old pups for 1 hour. Following this, each breeder received a 1 IU intraperitoneal (IP) injection of oxytocin. Fifteen minutes later, milk samples were collected from the breeders. Blood samples were also collected from pups aged 1 to 5 weeks from each group. Additionally, BW, spleen weight, and thymus weight were monitored. Spleen, thymus, and lung tissues were further analyzed for immune cell profiling. Spleen samples from 2-week-old pups in each group were also used for single-nuclei multi-omics analysis, including snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq (samples from 5 mice/group pooled).
Diets for mouse experiments were obtained from Research Diet Inc. Control diet (D12450J), 0.1% TVA diet (D23031402), 1% TVA diet (D19110701).

Mouse spleens were disrupted with a syringe plunger in 1 mL PBS in a 40 μm strainer, and cells were filtered to a 15 mL tube, then the cells were washed with PBS, and centrifuged at 300×g for 5 minutes. The resulting cell pellets were re-suspended with 2 mL red cell lysis buffer (Invitrogen), then the cells were incubated at room temperature for 10 minutes and centrifuged at 300×g for 5 minutes after adding 13 mL PBS. The resulting cell pellets were designated splenocytes and used for the following experiments.

Peripheral lymph nodes were disrupted with a syringe plunger in 1 mL PBS in a 40 μm strainer, and cells were filtered to a 15 mL tube, then the cells were washed with PBS, and centrifuged at 300×g for 5 minutes. The resulting cell pellets were designated lymph node cells and used for the following experiments.

Mouse thymuses were disrupted with a syringe plunger in 1 mL PBS in a 40 μm strainer, and cells were filtered to a 15 mL tube, then the cells were washed with PBS, and centrifuged at 300×g for 5 minutes. The resulting cell pellets were re-suspended with 2 mL red cell lysis buffer (Invitrogen), incubated at room temperature for 10 minutes, and centrifuged at 300×g for 5 minutes after adding 13 mL PBS. The resulting cell pellets were designated thymus cells and used for the following experiments.

Mouse primary naïve CD8 + or CD4 + T cells were isolated from the spleen and peripheral lymph nodes (PLN) of C57BL/6 mice by magnetic bead purification using EasySep ™ Mouse naïve CD8 + or CD4 + T Cell Isolation Kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Stemcell Technologies). Isolated primary CD8 + or CD4 + T cells were activated in vitro for 18 hours with plate-bound anti-CD3 (1 μg/mL; Biolegend) and anti-CD28 (0.5 μg/mL; Biolegend) antibodies in Click’s media at 37° and 5% CO 2 incubator. Activated CD8 + or CD4 + T cells were ready for further experiments. A naïve T cell control was maintained in Click’s media containing 10 ng/mL IL-7 (BioLegend).

After collecting milk samples from each group (five samples per group), 10 μL of each sample was used for IgA level detection by Mouse IgA ELISA Kit (Invitrogen, 88-50450-88), 10 μL of each sample was used for lactoferrin level detection by Mouse LTF/Lactoferrin ELISA Kit (Invitrogen, EEL103), 10 μL of each sample was used for IL-7 level detection by Mouse IL-7 ELISA Kit (Invitrogen, EMIL7), and 10 μL of each sample was used for IL-1β level detection by Mouse IL-1 beta ELISA Kit (Invitrogen, BMS6002), according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

TVA diet-fed and CON diet-fed C57BL/6J and Gpr43 −/− mouse lines were generated as described above. Neonatal offspring were harvested at postnatal day 10, and naïve CD4 + T cells were isolated for the following assays: Th polarization: Cells were seeded on plates precoated with anti-CD3 (1 μg/mL) and anti-CD28 (0.5 μg/mL) and incubated for 12 hours. Thereafter, Th1, Th2, or Th17 differentiation cocktails were added, and cells were cultured for 48 hours. The frequency of polarized Th subsets was determined by flow cytometry: T-bet + IFNγ + CD4 + as Th1, GATA3 + IL-4 + CD4 + as Th2, RORγ + IL17 + CD4 + as Th17. Early activation (CD69) assay: Naïve CD4 + T cells were stimulated on anti-CD3/CD28-coated plates (same coating concentrations) for 6 hours, then stained for CD69 and analyzed by flow cytometry. Proliferation assay: Following a 12-hour activation on anti-CD3/CD28-coated plates, cells were transferred to fresh medium containing 5 IU/mL human IL-2, 1 ng/mL mouse IL-7, and 5 ng/mL mouse IL-15, and cultured for an additional 48 hours. Cell expansion was assessed by counting or proliferation dye dilution.

Naïve CD4 + T cells were isolated from neonatal (10–14 days old) or adult (8–12 weeks old) C57BL/6J mice. Cells were treated with 10 ng/mL mouse IL-7 in the presence of either DMSO, 20 μM TVA, oleic acid, linoleic acid, palmitoleic acid, elaidic acid, or conjugated linoleic acid (cis-9, trans-11-octadecadienoic acid) for 24 hours. Following treatment, cells were stimulated on anti-CD3/CD28-coated plates for 12 hours. Subsequently, Th1 differentiation cocktails were added, and cells were cultured for an additional 48 hours. The frequency of Th1-polarized cells was then assessed by flow cytometry.

Similarly, naïve CD4 + T cells were isolated from neonatal (10–14 days old) Gpr43 −/− mice and treated with 10 ng/mL mouse IL-7 along with DMSO or 20 μM TVA for 24 hours, followed by anti-CD3/CD28 stimulation for 12 hours. Th1 differentiation cocktails were then applied, and cells were cultured for 48 hours. Th1 polarization was analyzed by flow cytometry.

To examine the role of cAMP-PKA signaling, naïve CD4 + T cells from neonatal (10–14 days old) C57BL/6J mice were treated with 10 ng/mL IL-7 and either DMSO, 20 μM TVA, 200 nM PKA inhibitor H-89 dihydrochloride, or 1 μM 8-Bromo-cAMP for 24 hours. Cells were then stimulated with anti-CD3/CD28 for 12 hours, followed by Th1 polarization for 48 hours. Th1 cell frequency was assessed by flow cytometry.

To investigate transcriptional regulation, naïve CD4 + T cells from neonatal (10–14 days old) C57BL/6J mice were treated with Accell si Ctcf (Horizon, E-044693-00-0020), Accell si Creb1 (Horizon, E-040959-00-0020), or Accell control siRNA (Horizon, D-001910-10-05) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. After confirming knockdown efficiency, cells were treated with DMSO or 20 μM TVA for 24 hours, followed by 12-hour anti-CD3/CD28 stimulation and 48-hour Th1 differentiation. The frequency of Th1 cells was analyzed by flow cytometry.

CTCF DNA-binding activity was assessed using the Pierce ™ LightShift ™ Chemiluminescent EMSA Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, cat# 20148) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. A biotin-labeled double-stranded DNA oligonucleotide probe containing a known CTCF-binding motif was synthesized (Integrated DNA Technologies) with the following sequence:5′-gtagtgacccCGgagccaCGtggagccaccttcagacccagagctgaagcaggagggtgacCGg-3′ (biotin-dT at the 5′ end of the reverse strand). For in vitro treatment assays, naïve CD4 + T cells were isolated from five 10-day-old C57BL/6J mice per sample. Cells were treated with 10 ng/mL recombinant mouse IL-7 in the presence of DMSO (vehicle), 20 μM TVA, 200 nM PKA inhibitor H-89 dihydrochloride, or 1 μM 8-Bromo-cAMP for 24 hours. Nuclear proteins were then extracted using the NE-PER ™ Nuclear and Cytoplasmic Extraction Reagents (Thermo Fisher Scientific, cat# 78833). For imprinting experiments in adult mice, naïve CD4 + T cells were isolated from TVA-to-CON and CON-to-CON adult mice (five mice per group). Nuclear extracts were prepared as described above. Equal amounts of nuclear protein (quantified by BCA assay) were incubated with the biotin-labeled DNA probe and subjected to non-denaturing polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis. DNA-protein complexes were transferred to a nylon membrane, detected by chemiluminescence, and quantified by densitometry to evaluate the ratio of CTCF-DNA complex/ free probe to indicate CTCF activity.

C57BL/6J neonatal mice from the control or TVA groups were challenged with influenza A virus (H1N1; A/Puerto Rico/8/1934, PR8). Ten-day-old pups from either the TVA or control diet groups were infected intranasally with PR8 at 0.04 TCID50/g BW in 7 μL sterile saline. Pups were weighed and monitored daily for activity, respiratory rate, and maternal interaction. Neonates that were ignored by the dam, exhibited weight loss, or showed minimal spontaneous movement were removed from the cage per humane monitoring criteria. For survival studies, pups were followed for 14 days post-infection, and clinical scores were recorded daily using the following scale: 0, no signs of disease (active, well groomed, feeding normally; normal breathing); 1, mild disease (slightly ruffled fur; slight reduction in activity; subtle weight loss, 20% weight loss); 5, death.

For endpoint analyses, cohorts were euthanized on days 4, 7, or 10 post-infection to assess viral burden, lung pathology, and immune responses by flow cytometry. Flow panels included leukocyte lineage markers (CD45, CD3, CD4, CD8, TCRδ, NK1.1, CD11b, Ly6G, F4/80, Ly6C, MHC II, CD11c, B220, Foxp3) and T cell activation/virus-reactive markers (CD49d, CD11a, CD44, CD69) as well as influenza-specific CD8 + T cell tetramers (NP 331–339 and PA 224–233 ). For intracellular cytokine staining, lung single-cell suspensions were stimulated ex vivo with PMA in the presence of brefeldin A for 6 h, followed by detection of IFN-γ, T-bet, and TNF-α in CD4 + T cells and IFN-γ and TNF-α in CD8 + T cells. In addition, lungs were collected on day 7 post-infection for single-nucleus multi-omics (snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq), with samples from five mice per group pooled for each analysis.

Neonatal C57BL/6 mice challenged with Influenza A virus were euthanized, placed in a supine position, and secured with pins. The chest area was disinfected with 70% ethanol. Using sterile scissors, the thoracic cavity was carefully opened to expose the heart. A 23-G needle was inserted into the right ventricle, and 10–15 mL of ice-cold PBS was slowly perfused to flush out circulating blood. Lungs were carefully dissected, rinsed in PBS to remove residual blood, and transferred to a Petri dish containing 5 mL of RPMI-1640 supplemented with 2% fetal bovine serum (FBS). Lung tissues were minced into small fragments using sterile scissors and transferred to a 15 mL conical tube containing 5 mL of digestion buffer (RPMI-1640 supplemented with 1 mg/mL Collagenase D and 100 U/mL DNase I). The tissue suspension was incubated at 37°C for 30–40 minutes with gentle shaking every 5–10 minutes. Following digestion, the cell suspension was passed through a 70 μm cell strainer into a 50 mL conical tube to obtain a single-cell suspension. The strainer was subsequently washed with an additional 5 mL of RPMI-1640 containing 2% FBS. Red blood cells were lysed by incubating the suspension with RBC lysis buffer for 2–3 minutes at room temperature. The cells were then washed with RPMI-1640 and centrifuged at 300 × g for 5 minutes at 4 °C. The resulting cell pellet was designated as lung-infiltrating cells and used for subsequent experiments.

Lung tissues were collected from mice at 4, 7, and 10 days post influenza A virus challenge, and rinsed briefly in cold PBS to remove blood contaminants. Tissues were weighed and homogenized in ice-cold PBS supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche, Complete Mini) using a bead mill homogenizer. Homogenates were centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 15 minutes at 4°C, and the supernatants were collected for analysis. IL-1β and TNF-α levels in the lung homogenates were measured using a commercially available mouse IL-1β ELISA kit (Biolegend, 432601) and TNF-α ELISA kit (Biolegend, 430901) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Blood samples were collected from mice at 4, 7, and 10 days post influenza A virus challenge. Samples were centrifuged at 2,000 × g for 10 minutes at 4°C to isolate the serum. The supernatant (serum) was carefully collected and stored at −80°C until analysis. Serum TNF-α levels were quantified using a commercially available mouse TNF-α ELISA kit (Biolegend, 430901) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Single nuclei Multiome library preparation, sequencing, and analysis were conducted by Singulomics Corporation ( https://singulomics.com/ , Bronx, NY). Single nuclei gene expression libraries and single nuclei ATAC libraries were constructed from nuclei isolated from cryopreserved mouse spleen cells on the 10x Genomics Chromium System using the Chromium Next GEM Single Cell Multiome ATAC + Gene Expression Reagent Bundle. Cryopreserved, viable single cell suspensions were thawed, washed, resuspended in cell culture media with 0.04% BSA, and counted. The cells were lysed and permeabilized with Nonidet P40 Substitute, Digitonin, and Tween-20. The isolated nuclei were purified, centrifuged, and resuspended in Diluted Nuclei Buffer. The nuclei were then loaded into the Chromium Controller (10x Genomics, Pleasanton, CA) to encapsulate single nuclei into droplet emulsions following the manufacturer’s recommendations. 6,000 nuclei were targeted to be captured per sample. Library preparation was performed according to the Chromium Next GEM Single Cell Multiome ATAC + Gene Expression User Guide. Amplified cDNAs and the libraries were measured by Qubit dsDNA HS assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Wilmington, DE) and quality assessed by TapeStation (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA). Libraries were sequenced on a NovaSeq 6000 instrument (Illumina, San Diego, CA, United States), and reads were subsequently processed using 10x Genomics Cell Ranger ARC (v 2.0.2) analytical pipeline and mouse mm10 (2020-A) reference. Dataset aggregation was performed using the cellranger-arc aggr function, normalizing for the total number of confidently mapped reads across libraries.

Single nuclei Multiome library preparation, sequencing, and analysis were conducted by Singulomics Corporation ( https://singulomics.com/ , Bronx, NY). Single nuclei gene expression libraries and single nuclei ATAC libraries were constructed from nuclei isolated from flash-frozen mouse lung tissue samples on the 10x Genomics Chromium System using the Chromium Next GEM Single Cell Multiome ATAC + Gene Expression Reagent Bundle. Flash-frozen mouse lung tissue samples were homogenized, lysed, and permeabilized with Nonidet P40 Substitute, Digitonin, and Tween-20. The isolated nuclei were purified, centrifuged, and resuspended in Diluted Nuclei Buffer. The nuclei were then loaded into the Chromium Controller (10x Genomics, Pleasanton, CA) to encapsulate single nuclei into droplet emulsions following the manufacturer’s recommendations. 7,000 nuclei were targeted to be captured per sample. Library preparation was performed according to the Chromium Next GEM Single Cell Multiome ATAC + Gene Expression User Guide. Amplified cDNAs and the libraries were measured by Qubit dsDNA HS assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Wilmington, DE) and quality assessed by TapeStation (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA). Libraries were sequenced on a NovaSeq 6000 instrument (Illumina, San Diego, CA, United States), and reads were subsequently processed using 10x Genomics Cell Ranger ARC (v 2.0.2) analytical pipeline and mouse mm10 (2020-A) reference. Dataset aggregation was performed using the cell ranger-arc aggr function, normalizing for the total number of confidently mapped reads across libraries.

All data were generated using the 10x Chromium Single Cell Multiome platform. For each sample, the analysis input is the Cell Ranger ARC output, then we applied Seurat v5.1.0( 35 ) and Signac v 1.13.0( 36 ) to create a multi-omics Seurat object with paired gene expression and DNA accessibility profiles for each sample. The 10x multiome workflow encompasses quality control (QC), dimensionality reduction, clustering, and UMAP visualization across RNA, ATAC, and a joint neighbor graph. This graph represents both gene expression and DNA accessibility measurements via weighted nearest neighbor (WNN) methods( 37 ). The workflow also includes cell type annotations, gene activity assessment, peak calling using MACS2( 38 ), and the identification and visualization of condition-specific candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs), differentially active motifs, and key regulators. For each sample, we conducted QC, dimensionality reduction, clustering, and cell type annotations, followed by the integration of all samples for downstream analysis. For each gene and cell, promoter accessibility was quantified as the sum of Tn5-corrected ATAC fragments overlapping the promoter region, defined as transcription start site (TSS) ±2 kb (GENCODE vM25, mm10). Fragments were deduplicated, offset by +4/−5 bp to adjust for transposase integration, and filtered to exclude mitochondrial and ENCODE blacklist regions. Promoter sums were normalized either as counts per million (CPM) or by term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) prior to downstream analyses( 36 , 39 ). Cluster-level values represent the mean promoter sum across cells within each cluster. Then, TF “activity” was predicted based on the presence of binding motifs within DA chromatin regions using chromVAR( 40 ), and the positional weight matrix (PWM, refer to https://genome.ucsc.edu/goldenPath/help/hgRegMotifHelp.html ) was obtained from the JASPAR2020 database( 41 ). Paired data provides an opportunity to identify transcription factors (TFs) that satisfy multiple criteria, helping to narrow down the list of putative regulators to the most likely candidates. We aim to identify TFs whose expression is enriched in multiple cell types in the RNA measurements and with enriched accessibility for their motifs in the ATAC measurements. To do this, we use the “presto” package (detailed in https://immunogenomics.github.io/presto/articles/getting-started.html ) to perform fast differential expression in gene expression data and chromVAR motif accessibilities. presto calculates an “AUC” statistic, which reflects the power of each gene (or motif) to serve as a marker of cell type. A maximum AUC value of 1 indicates a perfect marker. Since the AUC statistic is on the same scale for both genes and motifs, we calculate the average of the AUC values from the two tests and use this to rank TFs for each cell type. Then, we visualize the TF expression (RNA level), gene activity (ATAC level), and motif activity (chromVAR) of the key regulators.
