The binding of NHE6s and NHE9 to PIPs was validated by in vitro binding experiments. Nano differential scanning fluorimetry (nanoDSF) measurements confirmed that PI(3,5)P2 stabilizes NHE6.1 (Δ T m of ~4 °C), while PI(4,5)P2 exerted an even stronger effect (Δ T m of ~7 °C) (Supplementary Fig. 8D ). NHE6.0 and NHE9 displayed a similar preference for doubly-phosphorylated phosphoinositides, although the thermostabilizing effects were less pronounced for NHE9 compared to NHE6 (Supplementary Fig. 8D ). This observation suggests that PIPs may bind to NHE9 at sites distinct from the identified NHE6-specific PIP2 site. Addition of PI(3)P to purified NHE6.1 did not result in significant thermostabilization, yet we observed modest effects for NHE6.0 and NHE9 (Supplementary Fig. 8D ). These findings indicate isoform-specific differences for PI(3)P binding. Taken together, the data suggest that variations in PIP and PIP2 levels may contribute to the partially overlapping yet non-redundant functional roles of NHE6 and NHE9 in different cellular compartments.

Our results provide further structural insights into human NHE9 and NHE6 transporters, demonstrating both share a highly conserved ion coordination site. Although all our structures were captured in the inward-facing state, they are consistent with the gating and transport mechanisms proposed for the mammalian NHE family 35 . Our cryo-EM structure of NHE9 (2.6 Å) and NHE6.1 (2.33 Å) achieves sufficient resolution to unambiguously resolve a bound sodium within the ion binding site of the transport domain in contrast to earlier studies that inferred ion binding sites from structural and chemical homology to the archaeal PaNhaP 46 . Our high-resolution structures reveal the inward tunnel is open and solvent accessible with water molecules filling the cavity and region around the ion-binding site. Consistent with previous MD simulations of horse NHE9 35 , the bound sodium ion is coordinated by conserved Asp244, Asn243, Ser240, and Thr214 residues in human NHE9, or homologous residues in NHE6. In the MD simulations, sodium was only able to bind NHE9 when the equivalent of Asp244 was unprotonated. This agrees with the expected protonation state of aspartate side chains at our experimental pH of 7.5, though Asp244’s exact pKa may be modulated by the local environment 47 and cannot be directly determined from our cryo-EM maps.

Based on our structural data and homologous sodium-proton exchangers, oligomerization of NHE6 and NHE9 to form homodimers is a prerequisite for their transport activity. Dimerization is facilitated through the scaffold domains of each protomer with interfaces involving TM helices. The luminal crown domain present in NHE6.1 and NHE9 makes additional contributions to their dimerization interface (Supplementary Fig. 6D ). Notably, in our structural and biochemical data, NHE6.0 exhibits markedly reduced thermostability relative to NHE6.1 despite high sequence similarity between the two isoforms (Supplementary Fig. 8B ). This suggests that the NHE6.1-specific crown domain’s additional 1848 Å 2 of buried surface area and specific contacts with the transport domain underlie this increase in protein stability (Supplementary Fig. 6D ). Western blot analysis of cell lysates revealed NHE6.1 is partially resistant to SDS, with monomer and dimer species, while NHE6.0 is primarily monomeric indicating it has a less stable dimeric configuration (Supplementary Fig. 8C ). Furthermore, we found that paralog-specific differences determine thermostability, as NHE9 is similar to NHE6.1 in architecture and surface area at the dimer interface, yet is more thermostable and the dimeric species is SDS resistant. As membrane protein thermostability and oligomer resistance to SDS can correlate with in vivo protein localization or activity 48 , 49 , these in vitro biochemical differences might indicate distinct functional roles. We also observed phospholipid-dependent differences in thermostability. Similar to bacterial NapA, whose dimer retention is stabilized by cardiolipin 50 , annular lipids like PIP2 have been proposed to stabilize organellar NHE dimers 23 , 35 . In our NHE6 and NHE9 structures, the hydrophobic pocket created at the dimer interface is occupied by DDM molecules and consistent with a hydrophobic cavity at the luminal dimer interface capable of accommodating phospholipids. The uniformity of four DDM molecules filling the luminal hydrophobic pocket in all our structures suggests that the observed thermostabilization of NHE6.1, NHE6.0 and NHE9 by lipids is due to binding at distinct sites.

Doubly or triply phosphorylated phosphoinositides are known to differentially regulate NHE1’s transport activity, mediated by positively charged regions in the protein’s CTD that form electrostatic bonds with negatively charged lipids 32 – 34 . PI(4,5)P2 binding increases NHE1 transport activity and is regulated by competition with the inhibitory PI(3,4,5)P3 and possibly PI(3,5)P2 32 . Consistent with these observations, our structure of NHE6 revealed a phosphoinositide binding pocket that is sufficiently large to accommodate these multiple phosphorylation states of the PIP. Parallel work by Feilen et al. reported a 3.4 Å structure of human NHE6.1 51 . Similar to our NHE6.0 structure without added PIP2, this NHE6.1 map contains non-protein density consistent with ordered lipid within the CTD pocket. Our high-resolution structure of NHE6.1 with supplemented PI(3,5)P2 provides direct evidence that this site can bind PIP2 and reveals the previously unseen phospholipid binding sites PL1 and PL2. Our thermostability data corroborate that both PI(3,5)P2 and PI(4,5)P2 are able to bind to NHE6.1. The differential stabilizing effects of the various phosphoinositides on NHE6.0, NHE6.1, and NHE9 suggest differentiated regulatory roles of these lipids on these endosomal NHEs. The central role of NHE6 in regulating pH in early and recycling endosomes as well as at the plasma membrane by stimuli-induced recruitment from intercellular stores further supports a dual regulatory role of lipids. This may explain why NHE6 interacts with both endosomally enriched PI(3,5)P2 and plasma membrane-dominant PI(4,5)P2. By analogy to NHE1 33 , NHE6 activity can be modulated by these regulatory lipids. Hence, in addition to previously proposed roles of lipids to stabilize and regulate sodium-proton antiporters at the dimer interface, our results reveal PIP2 and other lipids binding NHE6 and NHE9 at the cytoplasmic face of the transport domain. However, this regulation may be complex as the lipid composition will vary by organelle and signaling processes, and the effects of each lipid may differ across NHE genes and the differing species of origin used in experimental studies.

Similar to NHE1, it is likely that NHE6 requires tight positioning of the proximal CTD region involved in RACK1-binding with the inner surface of the plasma membrane for optimal transport configuration. Notably, a structural feature that differs between NHE6 and NHE9 is the TM13-CH1 connecting loop, which is eight residues longer in NHE9. We hypothesize that this additional length increases flexibility, effectively decoupling the proximal CTD from the transmembrane core. This mobility likely reduces local order and thereby diminishes resolvability in the cryo-EM map under our sample conditions. Moreover, three cysteine residues, including a predicted palmitoylation site, are localized in the CH3 region of NHE6’s proximal CTD, and their sidechains project towards the membrane. Palmitoylation is the post-translationally reversible attachment of a C16 fatty acid to primarily Cys residues, which is crucial for regulating a vast array of cellular signalling processes, including facilitating PIP2 binding to proteins, including SLCs 52 . We did not observe density compatible with confident modeling of a palmitoyl group in our NHE6 structures, though this is not surprising due to the detergent-solubilized condition and the limitations of cryo-EM for resolving flexible post-translational lipidations. Nevertheless, it is tempting to speculate that the challenges in resolving the RACK1-binding region in NHE9 may be linked to stability differences in CTD regions, whereas NHE6 adopts a more stable configuration, possibly aided by palmitoylation, and hence allowing structure resolution.

The aberrant activity of NHE9 linked to glioblastoma progression and NHE6’s central role in neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s disease, and more recently, in adipocyte biology 53 , highlight these transporters as promising therapeutic targets. However, so far it has proven challenging to develop subtype-specific inhibitors for these organellar NHEs 54 . Therefore, the identification of a PIP2-specific site in NHE6 is interesting as it may represent a potential modulatory site that could be selectively targeted 55 . Such targeting might be achieved either through small molecule binders or manipulating downstream effectors to alter cellular PIP2 levels, thereby offering new avenues for therapeutic intervention.

Stable cell-lines with doxycycline-inducible expression of human full-length NHE9 (645 aa), NHE6.1 (701 aa), and NHE6.0 (669 aa) were generated by the RESOLUTE Consortium as previously described 56 . Briefly, codon-optimized cDNAs were cloned into a modified pJTI R4 CMV-TO MCS pA vector (Thermo Fisher Scientific) that contained a C-terminal HA-Twin-Strep tag. Jump-In T-REx HEK293 cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were stably transfected with these constructs as recommended by the manufacturer’s protocol. Transgene expression was induced via doxycycline treatment at 1 µg/ml for 24 h or the duration indicated. Parental Jump-In T-REx HEK293 cells were authenticated by STR profiling (Microsynth). Before analysis, the adherent HEK293JI-SLCx-SH cell lines were selected in DMEM medium supplemented with 10% v/v FBS, 100 µg/ml Pen/Strep, 5 μg/ml Blasticidin, and 2 mg/ml Geneticin for 2–3 passages and then cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% v/v FBS and 100 µg/ml Pen/Strep at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 . Expression of the codon-optimised transgenes was verified by RNA sequencing, Western blotting, and immunofluorescence imaging. Plasmid constructs were verified by Sanger sequencing prior to cell line generation. No additional STR profiling or karyotyping was performed on the derived stable cell lines.

HEK293JI-SLCx-SH cells seeded (0.15 × 10 6 cell density) in cell culture imaging dishes with a 35 mm diameter and a coverslip bottom (Ibidi GmbH) were induced by doxycycline at 1 µg/ml for 24 h. For plasma membrane staining, live cells were labeled using 7.5 µg/ml wheat germ agglutinin (WGA) Alexa Fluor 647 conjugate diluted in Hank’s balanced salt solution according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Invitrogen). All cells were fixed with 4% formaldehyde in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for 15 min, then permeabilized and blocked in blocking buffer consisting of PBS supplemented with 2% w/v fish gelatin and 0.1% w/v saponin for 1 h. For plasma membrane or nuclei co-staining, the permeabilized cells were incubated with mouse monoclonal Alexa Fluor 488 anti-HA.11 Epitope Tag [16B12] (Biolegend #901509, 1:1000) for 2 h at room temperature or overnight at 4 °C. For nuclei co-staining, cells were counterstained with SYTOX Deep Red Nucleic Acid Stain (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. For co-immunolabelling, the permeabilized cells were incubated for 2 h at room temperature with the indicated primary antibody diluted in blocking buffer: HA (Biolegend #902301), 1:500; EEA1 (Proteintech #68065-1), 1:1000 and LAMP-1 (DSHB Cat# h4a3, RRID:AB_2296838), 1:200. The cells were then washed with PBS three times over 30 min and then incubated for 1 h with either Alexa Fluor 647-labeled goat anti-mouse IgG (Invitrogen #A-21236) or Alexa Fluor 488-labeled goat anti-rabbit IgG (Invitrogen #A-11034) antibodies diluted 1:800 in blocking buffer. Finally, cells were again washed with PBS three times over 30 min and then mounted with ProLong Glass Antifade Mountant (Invitrogen/Thermo Fisher Scientific). Imaging was performed on an LSM 710 laser-scanning confocal microscope system connected to a Zeiss AXIO Observer Z1 inverted microscope using an EC Plan-Neofluar 40/1.30 objective. Figures were prepared using FIJI (ImageJ v1.54p) to merge the pictures taken with different channels 57 .

Cells cultured in T-25 flasks were harvested at sub confluency following 24 h doxycycline (1 µg/ml) treatment, washed in PBS, and cell pellets were flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen until use. Cell pellets were then thawed and lysed in RIPA lysis and extraction buffer (Thermo Scientific) supplemented with Protease Inhibitor Cocktail III (EMD Millipore, 1:1000) and Benzonase Nuclease (EMD Millipore, 1:1000 dilution of ≥250 units/μl solution). Lysates were centrifuged at 14,000 × g for 15 min (4 °C), and the protein concentration in the supernatant was determined by the Pierce BCA Protein Assay (Thermo Scientific). Lysates (40 µg) were then subjected to standard SDS-PAGE and blotted onto nitrocellulose membranes. The membrane was blocked for 1 h in PBS and 0.1% (w/v) Tween 20 (PBS-T) containing 6% (w/v) skimmed milk. The membrane was washed with PBS-T containing 2% (w/v) skimmed milk, and then probed with primary antibodies comprising polyclonal rabbit anti-HA.11 epitope Tag (BioLegend #902301, 1:1000) and monoclonal mouse β-Actin antibody (Sigma-Aldrich #A5441, 1:500) in PBS-T containing 2% (w/v) skimmed milk. Detection was performed with fluorescently-conjugated Alexa Fluor 680 goat anti-rabbit IgG (H+L) (Invitrogen #A-21076, 2 mg/ml, 1:5000) and Alexa Fluor 790 goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) (Invitrogen #A11375, 2 mg/ml, 1:5000) using a LI-COR ODYSSEY CLx imager.

To produce recombinant NHE proteins, HEK293JI-SLCx-SH cells were first expanded adherently in T-175 flasks, then converted into suspension cell cultures by standard serum dilution in 2 l air-vented shaker flasks. Subsequently, cells were cultured at 37 °C, 175 rpm, 5% CO 2 in FreeStyle293 medium. Protein expression of human full-length NHE9, NHE6.1, or NHE6.0 was induced at a cell density of 2 × 10 6 cells/ml by addition of 1.5 µg/ml doxycycline to suspension-adapted HEK 293JI-SLCx-SH cell lines and cultured at 30 °C, 175 rpm, 5% CO 2 . After 72–96 h, the cells were harvested by centrifugation at 900 × g for 20 min, washed with PBS, and pelleted again prior to flash-freezing in liquid nitrogen, and then stored at −80 °C until use.

To purify overexpressed protein, the cell pellets were resuspended in Buffer A (50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 200 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol) and lysed by mechanical disruption with two passes through an Emulsiflex C5 homogenizer (Avestin). The NHE proteins were extracted from cell membranes by addition of a 10:1 mixture of n-dodecyl-β-D-maltopyranoside (DDM)/cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS) to a final concentration of 1% (w/v) for DDM and 0.1% for CHS. The cell suspension was incubated at 4 °C for 1 h on a rotator (10 rpm) before centrifugation at 32,000 × g for 1 h at 4 °C to remove insoluble cell debris. The supernatant was aspirated, added a slurry of Buffer A pre-equilibrated 50% v/v Strep-Tactin XT Sepharose chromatography resin (Cytiva) at 2 ml per l original culture volume, and incubated at 4 °C on a rotator (6 rpm) for 2 h. The resin was collected by centrifugation at 700 × g for 5 min, washed three times with 10 column volumes of Buffer A supplemented with 0.03% w/v DDM/0.003% CHS, and transferred to a gravity column. The resin-bound proteins were eluted with 0.1 M D-Biotin (Chem-Impex) dissolved in Buffer A after adjusting to pH 7.5 and supplementing with 0.03% DDM/0.003% w/v CHS. Protein-containing fractions were pooled and concentrated to <1 ml using a 100 kDa MWCO Vivaspin concentrator centrifugal concentrator (GE Life Sciences) and further purified by size exclusion chromatography (SEC) on a Superose 6 Increase 10/300 GL size exclusion column (GE Life Sciences) in SEC buffer (20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 200 mM NaCl, 0.015% DDM/ 0.0015% CHS).

For all thermostability measurements, proteins were diluted to a final concentration of 6 µM in SEC buffer. For reducing conditions, the proteins were incubated with 5 mM TCEP on ice for 1 h. To characterize phosphoinositide binding, stock solutions of the respective lipids, phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate diC16 (PI(3)P; Echelon Biosciences cat no. P-3016), phosphatidylinositol 3,5-bisphosphate diC16 (PI(3,5)P2; Echelon Biosciences cat no. P-3516) and phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate diC16 (PI(4,5)P2; Echelon Biosciences cat no. P-4516) were prepared with final concentration of 1 mg/ml in SEC buffer. The respective lipids were added to the purified proteins to a final concentration of 0.1 mg/ml and incubated for 1 h on ice. Subsequently, the protein samples were filled (10 µL) into Prometheus Standard Capillaries (NanoTemper). Melting curves were determined using Prometheus NT.48 NanoDifferential Scanning Fluorimetry (nanoDSF) by monitoring the intrinsic fluorescence at 350 nm relative to 330 nm during a temperature ramp with a rate of 1 °C/min from 20 to 95 °C. In vitro binding was conducted twice ( n = 2 independent measurements). The melting temperature was determined from four technical replicate measurements for all samples, and the results were plotted using Prism 11.0.0 (GraphPad).

Grids were prepared by plasma-treating Quantifoil R1.2/1.3 mesh 200 or 300 gold grids and applying 3 µl freshly prepared protein sample at 4–5 mg/ml, followed by blotting for 7–9 s with blot force −5 and 20–30 s wait times at 100% humidity at 4 °C. Grids were then vitrified in liquid ethane, using a Vitrobot Mark IV (Thermo Fisher Scientific). For the NHE9 data, purified protein was incubated with the NHE inhibitor BAY-5784 (SMILES: ClC1=C(C=CC=C1)N2CCC(C3=C2C=C(N4C[C@@](N)(C)CCC4)C(F)=C3)=O) at 0.2 mM for 3 h at 4 °C, prior to protein concentration and grid preparation. The grids used for collecting this NHE6.1 data were prepared after adding 0.25 mM BAY-5784 and 10:1 mol/mol ratio of PI(3,5)P2 diC16 to protein and incubated for 3 h at 4 °C prior to grid preparation. Grids for NHE6.0 were prepared without the addition of additional lipids or inhibitors.

EM grids were screened on a 200 kV Glacios microscope prior to high-resolution imaging on a Titan Krios G3i microscope operating at 300 kV. In all cases, data were recorded using a Falcon 4i direct electron detector equipped with a SelectrisX energy filter using EPU software (Thermo Fisher) with a defocus range of −0.8 to −2.4 µm, energy filter slit width of 10 eV and a total exposure dose of 50 e − /Å 2 . (See Supplementary Table 1 for magnification, pixel size, and other collection details for the various datasets).

Data processing workflows are shown in Supplementary Figs. 3 – 5 . The majority of the data processing was carried out in cryoSPARC (v3.3.1) 58 . Particles were exported to RELION (v4) using the PYEM Python package (v 0.5) 59 .

The collected 11504 EER movies were grouped so that each frame experienced a dose of 1 e − /Å 2 and motion-corrected in RELION with 5 × 5 patches. Corrected movies were imported into cryoSPARC for CTF correction (Supplementary Fig. 3 ). A subset of images was used for blob picking and 2D classification to generate templates to train a TOPAZ (v 0.2.4) picking model 60 . Subsequently, a total of 1,690,899 particles were identified from the full image set, extracted in a 384px box, and binned to a pixel size of 2.92 Å. The particle set was cleaned up using several rounds of 2D classification, resulting in a set of 773,749 particles which underwent 3D heterogenous refinement. The best set (557,760 particles) yielded an initial reconstruction with a GSFSC resolution of 3.29 Å. These particles were exported to RELION, re-extracted and binned to a pixel size of 1.09545 Å and subjected to static 3D classification ( K = 10, T = 4) using a protein only mask, followed by Bayesian polishing and CTF refinement. These particles were subjected to further 3D static classification after re-refinement in cryoSPARC ( K = 10, T = 8, protein mask). Particles from the best populated class (212,266 particles) were re-imported into cryoSPARC for final NU refinement, which generated a reconstruction with a GSFSC resolution of 2.83 Å with no symmetry imposed, and 2.72 Å with C2 symmetry applied. This C1 map was used for modeling and refining the full-length protein including the crown domain. The C1-refined particles also underwent further selection using CRYOSIEVE (v. 1.2.3) 61 . Each cycle of particle selection (“sieving”) was evaluated by reimporting particles from each CRYOSIEVE iteration back into cryoSPARC and monitoring final GSFSC resolution achieved after non-uniform (NU) refinement with C1 symmetry. Using this procedure, the “best” minimal subset of high-quality NHE9 particles (69556 particles) yielded a final cryo-EM map with a GSFSC resolution of 2.60 Å. This reconstruction was used to model the core TM region and more clearly highlighted the position of the sodium ion and some ordered solvent molecules.

The 9002 movies collected were patch motion and CTF corrected in cryoSPARC (Supplementary Fig. 4 ). A subset of images was blob picked to obtain good quality templates for training a TOPAZ picking model. A total of 1,090,375 particles were extracted in a 320-pixel box and downsampled to a pixel size of 3.728 Å. After 2D classification, the remaining 586,700 particles were re-extracted in a box size of 360px at 0.932 Å/px and used to generate an ab initio model, which, after NU refinement gave an initial reconstruction of 2.64 Å with C2 symmetry imposed. Particles were subsequently corrected for local motion, and CTF global and per particle corrections were applied. These polished particles yielded a 2.55 Å map with no symmetry applied. Particles were further triaged with CRYOSIEVE using the same procedure as processing NHE9 to yield a reduced set of 153,800 particles that gave a final reconstruction after non-uniform refinement with a GSFSC resolution of 2.33 Å.

The 6700 movies were motion-corrected using the eBIC on-the-fly auto processing pipeline in RELION with 5 × 5 patches (Supplementary Fig. 5 ). Patch CTF correction was applied in cryoSPARC. Particles picked using crYOLO (v1.9.6) 62 were 2D classified to select a representative set of particles and used to train TOPAZ within cryoSPARC. A total of 1,001,670 particles were initially selected and extracted in a 384px box, downsampled to 128px at a pixel size of 2.763 Å. After 2D classification, 100,000 particles were used to generate 3 representative ab initio volumes that were used to classify all particles. The best resolved subset of particles was refined to give an initial 3.8 Å map with C2 symmetry imposed. Particles were re-extracted in a 256px box at 1.3815 Å/px and subjected to Bayesian polishing, and global and per-particle CTF refinement in RELION. Following re-refinement in cryoSPARC, the aligned, polished particles underwent 3D classification in RELION without alignment (10 classes, T = 4) using a mask covering the protein. Particles in the best class were re-imported into cryoSPARC for final non-uniform refinement, yielding a GSFSC resolution of 3.44 Å with C2 symmetry imposed and 3.59 Å without symmetry. The C1-refined particles underwent further selection using CRYOSIEVE, resulting in a subset of 52,384 particles that gave a final GSFSC resolution of 3.2 Å.

In all cases, the initial model was fitted into the cryo-EM maps and manually adjusted with Coot (v. 0.9.8.93) 63 . The resulting model was then subjected to refinement with ISOLDE (v1.3) 64 followed by phenix.real_space_refine (Phenix v. 1.21.1-5286) using secondary structure and loose reference model restraints to the input model. Ligand restraints were generated using Grade2 (v1.6.0) 65 . No restraints were used for the sodium site.

An initial model derived from the AlphaFold database 66 was fitted into the final cryoSPARC reconstruction obtained after particle filtering using CRYOSIEVE. In this map, the core TMD domain was well resolved, but the crown domain (73–120) was poorly defined (Supplementary Fig. 3A ). Furthermore, the expected CTD region (495–645) was disordered. The model was adjusted manually in Coot and refined against the auto-sharpened map. The final NHE9 core model encompasses residues 15–494 excluding the crown domain, lipids PL1 and PL2, a sodium ion, 3 peripheral DDM molecules, and a handful of solvent molecules per monomer. Density at the dimer interface was modeled as four detergent DDM molecules based on the length of the acyl chains. In each case, the first glucose unit in the maltoside headgroup was reasonably well-resolved and has been included. While the PL1 and PL2 lipids were modeled as phosphatidylcholine (PC), their headgroup is not sufficiently resolved in the EM maps to categorically identify the precise lipid type. For the full-length model including the crown domain, the predicted NHE9 dimer was generated by AlphaFold2-multimer, and the crown domain of residues 69–123 was aligned within the cryo-EM map obtained prior to particle sieving based using the TMD helices TM2 and TM3 from the core TM model as anchor points. The cytoplasmic domain structure was then relaxed into the map, refined using ISOLDE, grafted onto the core TMD model, and further refined in Phenix using a map sharpened with a B-factor of −25 Å 2 . As the cryo-EM map for the crown was less well resolved, most sidechains for this region were truncated in the model. The interchain disulfide bridge between adjacent Cys83, predicted by AlphaFold, was preserved and appears compatible with the experimental map.

The trimmed AlphaFold NHE6.0 model was initially fitted into the final 3.2 Å cryo-EM map obtained after particle sieving. As with NHE9, the sieved map has well resolved density for the core TM helices but, in addition, the proximal cytoplasmic domain of residues 528–578 was also apparent. The remaining 91 residues (579–669) at the C-terminus were disordered and not modeled. Manual adjustments were carried out in Coot, followed by refinement with ISOLDE and Phenix. The refined model comprises the entire protein chain for residues 59–578, apart from the poorly resolved loops between TM2-TM3 (122–140) and TM13-CH1 (512–527). In addition to the protein, well resolved lipids PL1 and PL2, and 2 DDM molecules were modeled per monomer. The PL1/PL2 lipids were modeled as phosphatidylethanolamine based on the size and shape of the headgroup. At 3.2 Å, discrete density for the sodium ion is unresolved (Supplementary Fig. 7C ).

The refined dimer model for the NHE6.0 short isoform was fitted into the NHE6.1 map obtained after particle sieving. In addition to the PL1 and PL2 lipids, well-defined cryo-EM density was observed for the added PIP2 at the cytoplasmic face of the transporter. Manual adjustments of the local structure around the PIP2 binding site were carried out using Coot. Well-ordered solvent molecules were added, as well as a Na + ion in the Na site (Supplementary Fig. 7A ). The final model for the core transporter comprises protein residues 59–121, 170–543, and 559–612 as well as one sodium ion, the three ordered lipids PL1, PL2, and PIP2, two DDM molecules, and 21 solvent molecules per monomer. As with NHE6.0, the distal C-terminal residues (613–701) were disordered. Overall, the cryo-EM density map for the cytoplasmic crown domain in NHE6.1 was less defined than NHE9, and local resolution estimation indicated that this region has a resolution of around 6 Å. As with NHE9, a dimeric model of the full-length NHE6.1 transporter was initially predicted using AlphaFold3. The crown domain from this structure was initially aligned using the TM2 and TM3 helices and then relaxed into the NHE6.1 cryo-EM 2.55 Å map obtained from all polished particles (blurred with an applied B-factor of 40 Å 2 ) using ISOLDE. The crown domain region was then grafted onto the core TM model with most sidechains pruned to Cbeta and then refined in Phenix using Ramachandran and loose reference model restraints to the input coordinates.
Figures were prepared with ChimeraX v1.3 67 and PyMOL (2.2.0) 68 .

articles.title: The effects of intracrystalline chain diffusion on the non-linear mechanics of semicrystalline polymers.
articles.authors: Michell RM, Petzold A, Thurn-Albrecht T.
articles.abstract: Large deformability is a specific property of many semicrystalline polymers that is enabled by plastic flow going along with a restructuring of the semicrystalline morphology in combination with strain hardening caused by network forces. This ability has been linked with the intracrystalline chain diffusion (ICD), which allows chains to move within the crystals. However, the influence of ICD on the non-linear mechanics remains unclear. We here study the intrinsic non-linear mechanical properties of two model polymers, namely PEO with fast ICD and PCL without ICD by mechanical testing in plane strain compression in dependence of strain rates and temperature. For both polymers the stress could be decomposed in an elastoplastic contribution and a network contribution. Strong differences in the true stress-true strain curves became evident by comparing the rate dependence at larger deformation. The stress in PEO depends strongly on rate and temperature, indicating relaxation of the network contribution, while the stress in PCL is rate independent. Experiments for PEO with different molecular weights indicate that the relaxation affects entire chains as expected for ICD.
paragraphs: Large deformability is a specific property of many semicrystalline polymers that is enabled by plastic flow going along with a restructuring of the semicrystalline morphology in combination with strain hardening caused by network forces. This ability has been linked with the intracrystalline chain diffusion (ICD), which allows chains to move within the crystals. However, the influence of ICD on the non-linear mechanics remains unclear. We here study the intrinsic non-linear mechanical properties of two model polymers, namely PEO with fast ICD and PCL without ICD by mechanical testing in plane strain compression in dependence of strain rates and temperature. For both polymers the stress could be decomposed in an elastoplastic contribution and a network contribution. Strong differences in the true stress-true strain curves became evident by comparing the rate dependence at larger deformation. The stress in PEO depends strongly on rate and temperature, indicating relaxation of the network contribution, while the stress in PCL is rate independent. Experiments for PEO with different molecular weights indicate that the relaxation affects entire chains as expected for ICD.

Intracrystalline chain diffusion (ICD) allows chains to move within the crystals in semicrystalline polymers and has been linked to the deformability of such polymers but the influence of ICD on the non-linear mechanics remains unclear. Here the authors study the intrinsic non-linear mechanical properties of two model polymers with fast and without ICD.

Semicrystalline polymers exhibit distinctive mechanical properties, such as strength, flexibility, and toughness, that set them apart from other crystalline and amorphous materials, primarily due to their chain-like nature and their nanoscopic two-phase structure consisting of thin lamellar crystals separated by disordered amorphous layers that contain entanglements retained during crystallization 1 . More specifically, beyond the linear elastic region, upon yielding, plastic flow sets in, going along with a restructuring of the semicrystalline morphology, while at the same time, the stress-strain curves show strain hardening caused by network forces.

Starting from the 1970s, a lot of work deals with the question by which microscopic processes the semicrystalline morphology is transformed during tensile deformation from an initial isotropic spherulitic structure to a final oriented fibrillar structure. Two main processes were proposed: crystallographic slip and melting/recrystallization 2 – 4 . Subsequent work by the groups of Strobl 5 – 10 and later Bartczak 11 – 14 , as well as Schrauwen 15 extended the focus to the role of the amorphous regions and the entanglements contained therein. They used mechanical tests at constant true strain rates in tensile deformation and in compression in combination with structural investigations to analyze different stages of deformation. A recent review is given in reference 16 .

From all these studies, a qualitative explanation of the mechanical properties of semicrystalline polymers arises. In the linear range at small deformation, the stress is caused by a skeleton made up of small, relatively stiff crystals that are part of the spherulitic microstructure. At yield, this skeleton breaks up. The network forces showing up at larger deformation beyond the yield point are caused by the amorphous parts of the chains. However, the crystals play an important role here. Whereas in a polymer melt, the entanglements can only act as transient junction points and therefore form only a transient network, crystallization leads to the formation of a permanent network. Crystals, even if fragmented during deformation, can act as permanent junction points, on the one hand trapping the entanglements and making them permanent, on the other hand introducing new effective network strands like tie chains, entanglement loops or even more complex topological structures like entanglement links, all of them connecting different crystals (cf. Fig. 1a ). Fig. 1 Models describing mechanical properties of semicrystalline polymers and underlying microscopic structure. a Sketch of the mechanically relevant nanostructural elements of semicrystalline polymers. Thin lamellar crystals with a typical thickness of the order of 10 nm (black) separated by amorphous layers are mechanically connected by tie-chains (red), entanglement loops (blue) or entanglement links (magenta). b – d Physical-based models describing the mechanical properties of semicrystalline polymers following different authors: b Haward and Thackray 19 , c Boyce et al. 21 , and d Strobl et al. 10 .

a Sketch of the mechanically relevant nanostructural elements of semicrystalline polymers. Thin lamellar crystals with a typical thickness of the order of 10 nm (black) separated by amorphous layers are mechanically connected by tie-chains (red), entanglement loops (blue) or entanglement links (magenta). b – d Physical-based models describing the mechanical properties of semicrystalline polymers following different authors: b Haward and Thackray 19 , c Boyce et al. 21 , and d Strobl et al. 10 .

Closely related to the structural studies, numerous attempts have been made to model the stress-strain relationship of semicrystalline polymers during deformation. Two main approaches have been used, the so-called phenomenological models and physics-based models 17 , 18 . The former describes the data without necessarily connecting it to the microscopic polymer structure or molecular mechanism of stress generation. In contrast, the physical-based approach seeks to base the models exactly on this connection.

The latter kind of models are mostly inspired by the early model of Haward and Thackray 19 that was initially developed for glassy polymers, but was later also applied to semicrystalline ones 20 . This model comprises three elements (cf. Fig. 1b ): a linear Hookean spring, a Langevin spring, and an Eyring dashpot. The linear spring is related to the initial linear elastic part of the mechanical response. The Langevin spring is used to describe the elastic amorphous network, while the dashpot represents the plastic deformation of the crystalline skeleton. If used for the analysis of network forces at intermediate or larger strains, the strain of the Hookean elastic spring is typically neglected, leading to results that are equivalent to the model by Boyce et al. discussed next 21 . They interpreted the response of semicrystalline polymers as resulting from two parallel components; one represents the intermolecular resistance to deformation, which describes the elastoplastic contributions of the crystalline skeleton, whereas the second is due to the orientation and stretching of the molecular network, which causes rubber-like forces under large deformation. (cf. Fig. 1c ). Based on this approach, many modifications have been developed; Fig. 1c shows the simplest version without relaxing elements in the network branch 18 . The stress resulting from this parallel arrangement of the elements is described by a differential equation that can be solved analytically for simple deformations 22 .

Based on a detailed analysis of the elastic and plastic contributions to deformation, in which they found deviations from ideal elastoplastic behavior, Strobl and co-workers introduced a further modification, cf. Fig. 1d 10 . This model incorporates an empirical element describing the “finite plasticity” of the crystalline skeleton, a network element and a relaxation branch. The latter is taken to describe in a combined way relaxations occurring in the crystalline as well as the amorphous parts of the sample, whereby the network itself is assumed to remain intact during deformation.

A key characteristic of semicrystalline polymers is the existence of a crystalline relaxation process, the so-called α c –relaxation. This process is caused by mobile conformational defects in the crystalline phase and leads to intracrystalline chain diffusion (ICD) 23 , 24 . Within certain limits, the time scale of the fundamental conformational dynamics as well as that of the resulting transport of chains between crystalline and amorphous phases can be measured by solid-state NMR. It typically shows an Arrhenius-type temperature dependence and varies greatly between different polymers. Recent studies showed that this process is very important for the formation of the semicrystalline morphology, as the interplay of lateral crystal growth and crystal thickening enabled by ICD determines the crystal thickness and the crystallinity to a large extent 25 , 26 . Furthermore, there are strong indications that part of the entanglements existing in the melt prior to crystallization are dissolved during crystallization in so-called crystal-mobile polymers, i.e., semicrystalline polymers with fast ICD 27 , 28 . In other materials, the process is so slow or even non-existing, that it plays no role during primary crystallization. These are the so-called crystal-fixed polymers.

In addition, this relaxation process couples also to the linear mechanical properties and shows up, e.g., in the dynamic shear modulus 23 , 24 , 29 . The storage modulus of linear PE, e.g., at frequencies below and above the α c –relaxation, differs by about an order of magnitude 30 , 31 . However, studies on the effect of ICD on the non-linear mechanical properties are scarce. Hu and Schmidt-Rohr reviewed the presence of this relaxation in different semicrystalline polymers and showed that it is a requirement for ultradrawability, i.e., large tensile deformability of semicrystalline polymers with reduced entanglement concentration 23 . Temperature-dependent differences in structural changes during deformation in polypropylene and polyethylene have been observed and linked to the α c -relaxation 32 , 33 . The latter reference also reports mechanical measurements, but without closer analysis, it focuses on the analysis of cavitation phenomena at large strain. Also, the poor creep properties of UHMWPE fibers are a consequence of the intracrystalline mobility and ICD 34 , 35 . Finally, chain diffusion in the crystal, the required forces and energy dissipation have also been measured on a microscopic scale by single-molecule force spectroscopy in the AFM 36 .

Despite these observations, quantitative investigations and a comprehensive analysis connecting deformation, ICD, and the different stress contributions are missing. Furthermore, the majority of experiments are based on the most common semicrystalline polymers, polyethylene and polypropylene, which are both crystal-mobile. To identify the effects of ICD has therefore been difficult.

In this study, we therefore investigate the intrinsic mechanical properties of two model polymers: poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), which serves as an example of a polymer with slow ICD, and poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO), which exemplifies a polymer with fast ICD 25 . Using plane strain compression geometry, we measured true strain and true stress under deformation with a constant true strain rate. We focus on the region of larger deformation beyond the yield point, where the amorphous network dominates the mechanical response, as the effects are largest in this region, as shown below. In this way, we could identify fundamental differences in the properties of PEO and PCL that are related to the ICD, offering new insights into the understanding of the mechanical performance of semicrystalline polymers in general.

To measure the intrinsic mechanical properties of the polymers under study, we performed nonlinear mechanical tests in plane strain compression geometry. Supplementary Fig. 1 shows a schematic of the custom-made sample holder employed for the experiments in a testing machine. During compression, one direction is constrained, and deformation occurs only in two directions; this geometry leads to a pure shear deformation 37 . One significant advantage of this setup is that the force is applied over a constant area, which allows a direct determination of the true stress. Moreover, the compression geometry minimizes the formation of cavities and suppresses necking. In this way, it is therefore feasible to study the behavior of semicrystalline polymers with reduced influence from the instabilities common in tension 38 , 39 .

A first series of measurements with different true strain rates was performed at a temperature of 30 °C on two samples of moderate molecular weight, PCL and PEO100, with molecular weights of 80 kg/mol and 100 kg/mol, respectively. Qualitatively, this discussion reveals that the observed strain hardening is very weak. A rubber whose initial network modulus G n and length of network strands N has the same values as the plateau modulus \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$${G}_{n}^{m}$$\end{document} G n m and the length of the entanglement strands N e as a PCL melt would exhibit a much stronger strain hardening, as illustrated in Fig. 7 . This comparison indicates that the network that causes the stress in semicrystalline polymers is not fixed, it evolves during deformation. It is well known that the semicrystalline morphology transforms during deformation from an originally isotropic spherulitic structure to an oriented fibrillar structure. Crystallites act as junction points of an effective network, and of course, the deformation-induced breakup and reorganization of the semicrystalline morphology happens in such a way that the strands of this network release stress. As a result, the strain hardening becomes weaker than expected from an extrapolation of the former parts of the stress-strain curve. The fit parameters G n and N should therefore only be considered as effective parameters that describe the stress-strain curve, rather than a real network that would remain unchanged during deformation. Nevertheless, the interpretation of G n as the modulus of the initial network still seems reasonable. Note also that the discussed changes of the network structure are obviously rate-independent, at least for the range covered in our experiments.

In summary, the stress-strain curves of the semicrystalline polymers under study could be consistently decomposed into two contributions: the elastoplastic contribution that dominates the first part of the curve until yielding, after which this contribution remains constant, and a second one, caused by network stresses. Using this approach, we found fundamental differences in the intrinsic mechanical properties of semicrystalline polymers between a so-called crystal-fixed and a crystal-mobile polymer, that depend on the existence and/or time-scale of the α c -relaxation and the related ICD, and that strongly affect the network stresses. We expect these differences to be of general validity.

The network stress of PCL, a semicrystalline polymer with very slow ICD, can be described using the neo-Hookean model plus some rather weak additional strain-hardening at larger deformation. It does not show evidence of relaxation in the investigated parameter range. In contrast, the network stress for PEO is temperature- and rate-dependent, due to a relaxation that involves the entire chain across the entanglements and crystals. While these effects are strongest at large deformation, the presence or absence of an α c -relaxation also affects the initial network modulus or strain-hardening modulus. Entanglements as well as small crystal fragments can act as junction points of the network, whereby an active α c -relaxation reduces the role of the crystals. As a consequence, the crystal-fixed polymer under investigation, namely PCL, displays a significantly larger initial network modulus G n than PEO, for which its value depends on temperature, molecular weight and deformation rate. Obviously, all these properties are highly relevant at large global or local deformation and on the other hand, for processing in the solid state, for example, in cold drawing. Qualitatively, ICD enables large deformations at considerably lower stresses at small deformation rates. Understanding the criteria for terminal failure, on the other hand, requires further work and is out of scope for this publication.

Future research should further check the extent to which the observed effects of ICD are indeed of general validity beyond the model polymers used. In this context, it is important to realize that polyethylene, one of the most heavily used commercial polymers, also belongs to the class of crystal mobile polymers. Furthermore, the nature of the observed relaxation after nonlinear deformation should be further clarified. A possible next step would consist of stress relaxation experiments to determine the shape, amplitude and time/temperature dependence of the relaxation. Such experiments would hopefully also provide further evidence that can be used to refine the mechanical models used for semicrystalline polymers as they are depicted in Fig. 1 . It is obvious that to describe the properties of PEO, the simple version of the Boyce model shown in Fig. 1c lacks an element leading to relaxation in the network branch. On the other hand, introducing a relaxing branch in parallel, as suggested by Strobl, does also not allow a relaxation of the network as detected in our work. Furthermore, in this work, we focused on the impact of the α c -relaxation﻿ and ICD on the network properties, while we neglected their effects on the elastoplastic stress contribution. As mentioned above, these turned out to be weaker, but they exist as suggested before 15 .

We hope that in the long-term experiments and analyses as shown here, will provide a more fundamental understanding of material properties that are usually investigated only under special conditions of standard material testing and add in this way criteria for the suitability of different semicrystalline polymers for different applications.

articles.title: Molecular basis of nick ligation in the nucleosome by DNA Ligase IIIα.
articles.authors: Boesch DJ, Martin NI, Kontor CA, Nguyen AG, Tomkinson AE, Van Houten B, Gillet N, Bignon E, Whitaker AM, Weaver TM.
articles.abstract: Abstract Genomic DNA is packaged into chromatin through a fundamental repeating unit known as the nucleosome core particle. Chromatinized genomic DNA is constantly exposed to endogenous and exogenous stresses that result in DNA damage, which must be repaired to maintain genome stability. Single-strand breaks (SSBs) are a prevalent form of DNA damage that arise via the oxidation-induced disintegration of the sugar-phosphate backbone or as repair intermediates during base excision repair. DNA ligase IIIα (LigIIIα) is one of the primary enzymes responsible for repairing ligatable SSBs during the terminal step of single-strand break repair (SSBR) and base excision repair (BER). To date, a mechanistic description of how LigIIIα processes nicks within chromatin remains elusive. Here, we use a combination of biochemical assays, molecular dynamics simulations, and cryogenic electron microscopy to define the molecular basis of nick ligation in the nucleosome by LigIIIα, providing foundational insight into the terminal step of chromatin-based SSBR/BER. Subject terms: Cryoelectron microscopy, DNA repair enzymes, Single-strand DNA breaks
paragraphs: Genomic DNA is packaged into chromatin through a fundamental repeating unit known as the nucleosome core particle. Chromatinized genomic DNA is constantly exposed to endogenous and exogenous stresses that result in DNA damage, which must be repaired to maintain genome stability. Single-strand breaks (SSBs) are a prevalent form of DNA damage that arise via the oxidation-induced disintegration of the sugar-phosphate backbone or as repair intermediates during base excision repair. DNA ligase IIIα (LigIIIα) is one of the primary enzymes responsible for repairing ligatable SSBs during the terminal step of single-strand break repair (SSBR) and base excision repair (BER). To date, a mechanistic description of how LigIIIα processes nicks within chromatin remains elusive. Here, we use a combination of biochemical assays, molecular dynamics simulations, and cryogenic electron microscopy to define the molecular basis of nick ligation in the nucleosome by LigIIIα, providing foundational insight into the terminal step of chromatin-based SSBR/BER.
Subject terms: Cryoelectron microscopy, DNA repair enzymes, Single-strand DNA breaks

DNA Ligase IIIα is responsible for sealing single-strand breaks during single-strand break repair and base excision repair. Here, the authors define how DNA Ligase IIIα seals single-strand breaks within the nucleosome, improving the understanding of chromatin-based single-strand break repair and base excision repair.

Genomic DNA is organized into chromatin by a fundamental repeating structural unit known as the nucleosome core particle (NCP). The NCP is a protein-nucleic acid complex composed of an octameric assembly containing two copies each of histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4, wrapped by ~147 bp of nucleosomal DNA 1 , 2 , which functions as a structural scaffold and a regulatory barrier that controls access to genomic DNA. Chromatinized genomic DNA is continuously exposed to a variety of endogenous and exogenous stressors that generate DNA damage. This DNA damage occurs ubiquitously throughout chromatinized and non-chromatinized regions of genomic DNA 3 – 14 and must be faithfully repaired to maintain genome stability. How DNA repair enzymes overcome the nucleosome barrier to repair DNA damage and maintain genome stability remains poorly understood.

Single-strand breaks (SSBs) are among the most prevalent forms of genomic DNA damage 15 , 16 , and unrepaired SSBs result in mutagenesis, genome instability, and/or cell death 16 – 19 . SSBs arise from multiple independent mechanisms and are repaired via distinct pathways 16 . One common mechanism for generating SSBs is through oxidation-induced disintegration of the sugar-phosphate backbone, and these SSBs are repaired via the single-strand break repair (SSBR) pathway. During SSBR, the ends of the SSB are initially processed by one or more end processing enzymes (e.g., APE1, PNKP, TDP1, TDP2, APTX, and FEN1) that generate a ligatable SSB containing an intact 5′-phosphate and 3′-OH (nick) 19 – 21 . In addition, SSBs can also arise indirectly as intermediates during the base excision repair (BER) of oxidative and alkylative DNA base damage through the combined actions of a DNA glycosylase, APE1, and DNA Polymerase β, which also generates a ligatable nick containing an intact 5′-phosphate and 3′-OH 22 – 24 . Though the upstream processing steps differ between SSBR and BER, repair is ultimately completed through a common terminal step where the nick intermediate containing a 5′-phosphate and 3′-OH is ligated by DNA Ligase I or a heterodimeric complex of X-ray repair cross-complementing protein 1 (XRCC1) and DNA Ligase IIIα (LigIIIα) 25 .

LigIIIα is one of the primary enzymes responsible for sealing the nick intermediate containing a 5′-phosphate and 3′-OH to complete BER and SSBR 25 , 26 . Similar to the other human DNA ligases 27 , 28 , LigIIIα possesses a catalytic core made up of three domains, including a DNA-binding domain (DBD), a nucleotidyl transferase (NTase) domain, and an oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide-fold binding domain (OBD) that facilitate nick recognition and ligation 25 , 29 . In addition, LigIIIα uniquely contains an N-terminal zinc finger (ZnF) motif that contributes to DNA binding 29 – 34 , as well as a C-terminal BRCT domain that mediates complex formation with XRCC1 35 – 37 . Over the past several decades, mechanistic insight into how LigIIIα binds and ligates nicks within non-chromatinized DNA has come from robust structural and biochemical studies that identified a multi-step mechanism for nick ligation (Fig. 1a ) 28 , 29 , 33 , 38 . LigIIIα initially catalyzes the transfer of AMP from ATP to an active-site side chain (K421) in a Mg 2+ -dependent reaction, generating an adenylylated LigIIIα intermediate. The adenylylated LigIIIα then engages the Nick-DNA substrate, which is mediated by encircling of the duplex DNA by the DBD, NTase, and OBD of the catalytic core. Following engagement of the Nick-DNA substrate, LigIIIα catalyzes the transfer of AMP to the 5′-phosphate of the nick in a Mg 2+ -dependent reaction, generating an adenylylated DNA intermediate. In the final step, the 3′-OH of the nick performs nucleophilic attack on the adenylylated 5′-phosphate, resulting in phosphodiester bond formation and release of AMP. Though these prior studies have provided comprehensive molecular insight into how LigIIIα catalyzes nick ligation within non-chromatinized DNA, how LigIIIα catalyzes nick ligation within chromatin remains poorly understood. Prior in vitro studies established that LigIIIα activity is partially inhibited by nucleosome structure 39 – 43 , suggesting that nick ligation may represent the rate-limiting enzymatic step of chromatin-based SSBR/BER 39 , 43 . Despite these initial observations, the molecular mechanism underlying the reduced ligation efficiency of LigIIIα in the nucleosome remains unknown. Here, we use a combination of biochemical assays, molecular dynamics simulations, and cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to define the molecular basis of nick ligation in the nucleosome by LigIIIα.

Ligation rates were not determined (ND) for Nick-NCP−2 and Nick-NCP0 due to minimal product formation (<10%) during the kinetic time course. The data points represent the mean ± standard error of the mean from three independent replicate experiments. See Supplementary Fig. 2 for associated data. e Apparent binding affinities ( K d, app ) for the interaction of LigIIIα with Nick-NCP−6, Nick-NCP−4, Nick-NCP−2, and Nick-NCP0 obtained from the EMSA analysis. The data points represent the mean ± standard deviation from three independent replicate experiments. See Supplementary Fig. 3 for associated data. All source data in this figure are provided as a Source data file.

To explore the molecular basis of nick ligation in the nucleosome by LigIIIα, we initially designed four 601 strong positioning DNA sequences containing a single ligatable nick with a 5′-phosphate and 3′-OH 44 . Each nick is located in a solvent-exposed rotational orientation at superhelical locations SHL−6, SHL−4, SHL−2, and SHL0 (Fig. 1b, c ), herein referred to as Nick-NCP−6, Nick-NCP−4, Nick-NCP−2, and Nick-NCP0, respectively. These nick positions were chosen as solvent-exposed locations in the nucleosome are more prone to direct single-strand breaks 45 , 46 . In addition, nicks arising as BER intermediates also have a strong propensity to form at solvent-exposed positions in the nucleosome, as upstream BER enzymes (i.e., DNA glycosylases, APE1, and DNA Polymerase β) have robust preferences for processing solvent-exposed nucleosomal DNA damage 46 – 50 . Each Nick-NCP was then reconstituted using recombinant human histones (Supplementary Fig. 1a, b ), and the nucleosome substrates used to dissect the molecular basis of nick recognition and ligation in the nucleosome by LigIIIα.

To determine the ligation kinetics of LigIIIα in the nucleosome, we utilized single-turnover (pre-steady-state) conditions to monitor the ability of LigIIIα to convert a nicked nucleosome substrate to a ligated nucleosome product with an intact phosphate backbone. Under these conditions, the concentration of LigIIIα is in vast excess of the concentration of each Nick-NCP, ensuring the kinetic time course represents a single catalytic turnover. The resulting kinetic time course is fit to an exponential to determine the rate constant k obs , which represents the apparent rate-limiting step(s) of the reaction up to and including catalysis. Of note, the positioning of the 6-fluorescein label on the nucleosomal DNA precludes the ability to distinguish the adenylyl transfer from the nick sealing step of the ligation reaction 38 . Therefore, the k obs reported here reflects the overall ligation rate within the nucleosome. To determine how the nucleosome impacts the ligation kinetics of LigIIIα, we performed the single-turnover kinetic analysis on the Nick-NCP−6, Nick-NCP−4, Nick-NCP−2, and Nick-NCP0 substrates, and compared the ligation rates to those obtained with a 50 bp Nick-DNA substrate (Fig. 1d , Supplementary Fig. 2a,b , and Supplementary Table 1 ). The single-turnover kinetic analysis on the 50 bp Nick-DNA substrate revealed biphasic kinetics, consistent with two observable LigIIIα ligation phases with k obs values of 0.21 ± 0.027 s −1 (fast phase) and 6.1 × 10 −3 ± 2.0 × 10 −3 s −1 (slow phase). Importantly, the ligation rate of the fast phase is almost identical to the ligation rate previously determined for LigIIIα and a 28 bp Nick-DNA substrate under similar buffer conditions 38 . Similar to the 50 bp Nick-DNA substrate, biphasic behavior was also observed for Nick-NCP−6 and Nick-NCP−4, consistent with two observable LigIIIα ligation phases at both positions in the nucleosomal DNA (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Fig. 2a,b ). The ligation rates ( k obs ) of LigIIIα for Nick-NCP−6 were 0.061 ± 5.6 × 10 −3 s −1 (fast phase) and 2.4×10 −3 ± 1.3 × 10 −3 s −1 (slow phase), which represent a 3.4-fold and 2.5-fold decrease in ligation rate compared to the 50 bp Nick-DNA control, respectively. The ligation rates ( k obs ) of LigIIIα for Nick-NCP−4 were 6.8 × 10 −3 ± 1.0 × 10 −3 s −1 (fast phase) and 8.1 × 10 −4 ± 2.2 × 10 −4 s −1 (slow phase), which represent a 31-fold and 7.5-fold decrease in ligation rate compared to the 50 bp Nick-DNA control, respectively. In contrast to Nick-NCP−6 and Nick-NCP−4, we observed minimal product formation during the kinetic time course for Nick-NCP−2 and Nick-NCP0 (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Fig. 2a,b ), indicating that LigIIIα exhibits severely impaired ligation kinetics for solvent-exposed nicks at translational positions in proximity to the nucleosome dyad. The inability of LigIIIα to catalyze nick ligation at SHL−2 and SHL0 is not a consequence of using the 601 strong positioning sequence, as we observed similar impaired LigIIIα ligation kinetics for nicks at SHL−2 and SHL0 in nucleosomes reconstituted with a 5S rDNA sequence from Xenopus borealis (Supplementary Fig. 2c, d ). Together, these results demonstrate that LigIIIα preferentially ligates nicks at the nucleosome entry/exit site 43 , albeit at reduced rates compared to non-nucleosomal DNA.

To exclude the possibility that the position-dependent LigIIIα ligation rates are the result of a differential ability to engage nicks at the unique translational positions in the nucleosome, we performed electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSAs) to determine the apparent binding affinity ( K d,app ) of LigIIIα for the four Nick-NCPs (Fig. 1e , Supplementary Fig. 3 , and Supplementary Table 1 ). Importantly, the EMSAs were performed in the absence of Mg 2+ to prevent adenylyl transfer and ligation. The EMSA analysis revealed LigIIIα binds Nick-NCP−6 with a K d,app of 120 ± 5 nM, Nick-NCP−4 with a K d,app of 135 ± 8 nM, Nick-NCP−2 with a K d,app of 106 ± 11 nM, and Nick-NCP0 with a K d,app of 134 ± 2 nM, indicating that LigIIIα has a similar apparent binding affinity for each Nick-NCP. Notably, we observed apparent cooperativity for the interaction of LigIIIα with each Nick-NCP, with Hill coefficients ranging from 1.5 to 3 (Supplementary Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table 1 ). Although the precise mechanism underlying this cooperativity is unclear, it may result from the ability of LigIIIα to simultaneously engage the blunt DNA ends of the nucleosomal DNA 33 , 51 and/or due to the ability of LigIIIα to cooperatively engage nicks using the ZnF and the catalytic core 33 . Ultimately, the similar apparent binding affinities for LigIIIα and the four Nick-NCPs strongly suggest that the position-dependent differences in ligation kinetics are not attributable to differences in substrate binding affinity.

One plausible explanation for the position-dependent ligation kinetics of LigIIIα in the nucleosome is that the unique translational position of each nick may differentially impact nucleosome stability, structure, and/or dynamics 52 , 53 . To evaluate if the unique translational position of each nick differentially impacts nucleosome stability, we performed nucleosome stability assays on each Nick-NCP by monitoring the conversion of intact nucleosome to free DNA following incubation at 37 °C for 24 hours (Fig. 2a,b and Supplementary Fig. 12a ) 54 . After the 24 hour-incubation, we observed 87 ± 3%, 82 ± 3%, 87 ± 3%, and 78 ± 6% of intact nucleosomes remaining for Nick-NCP−6, Nick-NCP−4, Nick-NCP−2, and Nick-NCP0, respectively, which is similar to the 85 ± 4% of intact nucleosomes remaining for a non-damaged NCP (ND-NCP). This data indicates that the solvent-exposed nicks at each unique translational position in the nucleosomal DNA have minimal impact on overall nucleosome stability.

To determine if the unique translational position of each nick differentially impacts nucleosome structure, we obtained cryo-EM reconstructions of the ND-NCP, Nick-NCP−6, Nick-NCP−4, Nick-NCP−2, and Nick-NCP0 at overall resolutions of 2.6 Å, 2.8 Å, 2.7 Å, 2.9 Å, and 2.8 Å, respectively (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Figs. 4 - 11 ). Structural comparison of each Nick-NCP to the ND-NCP structure revealed an overall RMSD of 0.15 Å for Nick-NCP−6, 0.15 Å for Nick-NCP−4, 0.16 Å for Nick-NCP−2, and 0.10 Å for Nick-NCP0 (Supplementary Fig. 12b ), indicating that nicks do not substantially alter the conformation of the core histone octamer or the nucleosomal DNA. Of note, we did observe subtle changes within the nucleosomal DNA at each nick site (Supplementary Fig. 12c ), consistent with localized fraying around the nick site. However, these localized changes at the nick site were observed at all four translational positions, suggesting that localized DNA fraying cannot explain the position-dependent ligation kinetics of LigIIIα in the nucleosome. Together, this structural analysis indicates that solvent-exposed nicks at unique translational positions in the nucleosomal DNA do not substantially alter nucleosome structure.

To probe whether the unique translational position of each nick differentially impacts nucleosome dynamics, we performed 1 µs MD simulations on the ND-NCP, Nick-NCP−6, Nick-NCP−4, Nick-NCP−2, and Nick-NCP0. These simulations provide direct insight into dynamics of damaged nucleosomes on the microsecond timescale (e.g., DNA fraying) 52 , 55 , 56 , but the relatively short timescale of the MD simulations precludes the ability to probe how DNA lesions impact nucleosome dynamics that occur on longer timescales (e.g., unwrapping of the nucleosomal DNA at the entry/exit site) 57 – 59 . Initial inspection of the MD simulations confirmed the overall stability of the nucleosome containing nicks at each unique translation position throughout the trajectories, as only subtle differences in the overall conformation of the histone octamer and the nucleosomal DNA were observed (Supplementary Fig. 13a ). However, these subtle differences include elevated DNA dynamics at the nick sites for Nick-NCP−6, Nick-NCP−4, and Nick-NCP−2 (Fig. 2d ), which correspond to localized fraying events that separate the 5′-phosphate and 3′-OH (Supplementary Fig. 13b ). Of note, these elevated DNA dynamics at the nick site were not observed for Nick-NCP0 (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. 13b ), consistent with the enhanced stability of the nucleosomal DNA adjacent to the nucleosome dyad. Despite these observations, the elevated DNA dynamics at the nick site for Nick-NCP−6, Nick-NCP−4, and Nick-NCP−2 do not correlate with the position-dependent differences in LigIIIα ligation kinetics in the nucleosome (Fig. 1d ). The MD simulations indicate that nicks have minimal impact on overall nucleosome structure, and only a subtle impact on microsecond-timescale nucleosome dynamics at the nick site (i.e., nick fraying). Collectively, these data indicate that the unique translational position of each nick has minimal impact on nucleosome stability, structure, and fast timescale dynamics, and therefore cannot fully account for the position-dependent ligation kinetics of LigIIIα in the nucleosome.

To further probe the mechanistic basis for the position-dependent LigIIIα ligation kinetics in the nucleosome, we obtained cryo-EM reconstructions of LigIIIα bound to the four NCPs containing a nick at SHL−6, SHL−4, SHL−2, and SHL0 (Fig. 3 ). This was accomplished by generating complexes of adenylylated LigIIIα bound to Nick-NCP−6, Nick-NCP−4, Nick-NCP−2, and Nick-NCP0 that were stabilized via glutaraldehyde crosslinking. Of note, these complexes were formed in the absence of Mg 2+ to ensure a pre-catalytic conformation was captured prior to adenylyl transfer and ligation. The complexes were then subjected to single particle analysis, which resulted in cryo-EM reconstructions of the LigIIIα-Nick-NCP−6, LigIIIα-Nick-NCP−4, LigIIIα-Nick-NCP−2, and LigIIIα-Nick-NCP0 complexes at overall resolutions of 2.8 Å, 2.9 Å, 3.0 Å, and 2.5 Å, respectively (Supplementary Figs. 5 - 8 , 14 - 17 and Supplementary Tables 2 - 4 ). The local resolution of LigIIIα in the LigIIIα-Nick-NCP−6 and LigIIIα-Nick-NCP0 reconstructions were of sufficient quality to dock a previously determined X-ray crystal structure of LigIIIα bound to non-nucleosomal Nick-DNA 29 and manually build most amino acid side chains throughout the LigIIIα DNA binding interface and active site (Supplementary Fig. 14 , 17 ). In contrast, the local resolution of LigIIIα in the LigIIIα-Nick-NCP−4 and LigIIIα-Nick-NCP−2 reconstructions was not sufficient to observe amino acid side chains throughout most of the LigIIIα DNA binding interface and active site (Supplementary Fig. 15 , 16 ). Therefore, the LigIIIα side chain residues within these structures generally reflect their position within the higher-resolution LigIIIα-Nick-NCP0 structure.

The LigIIIα NTase domain (orange) was resolved in the cryo-EM reconstructions, whereas the remaining LigIIIα domains (light orange) were unable to be resolved. b Composite cryo-EM map and model of the LigIIIα-Nick-NCP−6 complex. c Composite cryo-EM map and model of the LigIIIα-Nick-NCP−4 complex. d Composite cryo-EM map and model of the LigIIIα-Nick-NCP−2 complex. e Cryo-EM map and model of the LigIIIα-Nick-NCP0 complex.

Prior structural studies of LigIIIα bound to non-nucleosomal Nick-DNA identified that nick recognition is mediated by the coordinated action of the DNA-binding domain (DBD), nucleotidyltransferase domain (NTase), and oligosaccharide-fold binding domain (OBD), which completely encircle the DNA to engage the nick 29 , 33 . Interestingly, of the three domains that contribute to nick recognition in non-nucleosomal DNA (DBD, NTase, and OBD), we only observed clear density for the LigIIIα NTase domain in the reconstructions of LigIIIα bound to a nick in the nucleosome at SHL−6, SHL−4, SHL−2, and SHL0 (Fig. 3 ). Closer inspection of each reconstruction after applying a low-pass filter (8 Å) revealed additional density adjacent to the LigIIIα NTase (Supplementary Fig. 18 ), though the substantial structural heterogeneity precludes the ability to assign this density to other domains within the catalytic core (i.e., the DBD or OBD), the ZnF, or the BRCT domain.

The structures of LigIIIα bound to nicks in the nucleosome at SHL−6, SHL−4, SHL−2, and SHL0 provide molecular insight into nick recognition in the nucleosome. In all four structures, the LigIIIα NTase engages the nucleosomal DNA with an ~6 bp footprint that encompasses the nick site (Fig. 4 ). Importantly, LigIIIα only interacts with the nucleosomal DNA and does not make discernible contacts with the histone octamer core. The interaction between the LigIIIα and the nucleosome is primarily driven by non-specific electrostatic interactions with the phosphate backbone of the damaged nucleosomal DNA strand (Fig. 4 ). On the 3′ side, Lys444, His449, and Lys450 coordinate the phosphate backbone of 4 bp of nucleosomal DNA. On the 5′ side of the nick, Arg441, Arg584, and Lys588 make direct contacts with the 5′-phosphate. Notably, structural comparison of the LigIIIα DNA-binding interfaces at SHL−6, SHL−4, SHL−2, and SHL0 reveals a consistent mode of DNA binding at each unique translational position (Supplementary Fig. 19 ), indicating that LigIIIα recognizes nicks at different translational positions in the nucleosome using a similar general mechanism.

Prior structural studies of LigIIIα bound to non-nucleosomal Nick-DNA established the structural basis of nick ligation 29 , 33 . To catalyze nick ligation in non-nucleosomal Nick-DNA, the LigIIIα NTase, DBD, and OBD completely encircle the DNA duplex and introduce a sharp kink at the nick site (Supplementary Fig. 20a ). This ultimately transitions the DNA on the 3′ end of the nick from B-form to A-form and shifts the 3′ nucleotide from a C2′-endo conformation to a C3′-endo conformation, which properly organizes the nick within the active site for catalysis (Supplementary Fig. 20a ). Importantly, our inability to resolve the DBD and OBD in the reconstructions of LigIIIα bound to nicks at SHL−6, SHL−4, SHL−2, and SHL0 indicates that these domains are unable to encircle the nucleosomal DNA in a stable manner (Fig. 3 ), suggesting that these structures may represent a conformation of LigIIIα that is incompatible with nick ligation. To further explore this possibility, we compared the structures of LigIIIα bound to nicks in the nucleosome at SHL−6, SHL−4, SHL−2, and SHL0 to the apo Nick-NCP structures (Supplementary Fig. 20b–e ). This structural comparison revealed that LigIIIα induces subtle rearrangements in the nucleosomal DNA upon nick recognition at each of the four translational positions, which are largely localized to the 5′-phosphate and involve a modest ~5 Å to ~7 Å movement of the 5′-phosphate toward the active site (Supplementary Fig. 20b–e ). Despite clear stabilization of the 5′-phosphate within the NTase domain, the nucleosomal DNA on the 3′ end of the nick remains in B-form and the 3′ nucleotide remains in the C2′-endo conformation (Fig. 5a–d and Supplementary Fig. 20f–i ). The inability of LigIIIα to encircle the nucleosomal DNA, transition the nucleosomal DNA on the 3′ end of the nick to A-form, and shift the 3′ nucleotide into a C3′-endo conformation indicate these structures represent LigIIIα in a conformation that is incompatible with nick ligation. Importantly, these observations provide a structural rationale for the severely reduced ligation kinetics at SHL0 and SHL−2 and the moderate ligation kinetics observed at SHL−4 and SHL−6 (Fig. 1d ). At all four nick locations in the nucleosome, encircling and kinking the nucleosomal DNA for ligation would generate substantial clashes between the LigIIIα OBD/DBD and the core histone octamer (Fig. 5e-h ). However, the nucleosomal DNA at the entry/exit site is prone to spontaneous unwrapping from the histone octamer 58 – 60 , which could provide an opportunity for LigIIIα to encircle and deform the nucleosomal DNA for ligation at SHL−6 and SHL−4 without steric conflict with the histone octamer (see discussion). Together, this structural analysis indicates that LigIIIα is readily able to engage nicks at multiple translational positions within the nucleosomal DNA but is unable to efficiently encircle and deform the nucleosomal DNA to properly organize the active site for nick ligation when the nucleosomal DNA remains engaged with the histone octamer.

LigIIIα forms a heterodimer with the scaffolding protein XRCC1 61 – 64 , which is important for LigIIIα stability 62 , 65 – 67 and recruitment of LigIIIα to sites of DNA damage in cellular chromatin 68 , 69 . We reasoned that XRCC1 may stimulate the ability of LigIIIα to bind and/or ligate nicks in the nucleosome. To test this possibility, we generated an XRCC1-LigIIIα complex from recombinant XRCC1 and adenylylated LigIIIα purified from E. coli (Supplementary Fig. 1e ). We then performed single-turnover kinetic analysis with the XRCC1-LigIIIα complex and a 50 bp Nick-DNA, Nick-NCP−6, Nick-NCP−4, Nick-NCP−2, and Nick-NCP0 substrates to determine whether XRCC1 could stimulate LigIIIα nick ligation in the nucleosome (Fig. 6b , Supplementary Fig. 21 , and Supplementary Table 1 ). Similar to the analysis with LigIIIα alone, the single-turnover kinetics of the XRCC1-LigIIIα complex on Nick-NCP−6 and Nick-NCP−4 revealed biphasic behavior indicating two kinetic phases of ligation at both positions in the nucleosomal DNA (Fig. 6b ). The ligation rates ( k obs ) of XRCC1-LigIIIα on Nick-NCP−6 were 0.034 ± 1.9 × 10 −3 s −1 (fast phase) and 2.2 × 10 −3 ± 1.1 × 10 −3 s −1 (slow phase), and the ligation rates ( k obs ) of XRCC1-LigIIIα on Nick-NCP−4 were 7.5 × 10 −3 ± 0.8 × 10 −3 s −1 (fast phase) and 6.9 × 10 −4 ± 2.1 × 10 −4 s −1 (slow phase). These ligation rates for the XRCC1-LigIIIα complex on Nick-NCP−6 and Nick-NCP−4 are strikingly similar to those determined for LigIIIα alone (compare Fig. 1d and Fig. 6b ), indicating that XRCC1 does not substantially enhance LigIIIα nick ligation at translational positions near the nucleosome entry/exit site. Notably, we also observed minimal product formation during the XRCC1-LigIIIα kinetic time course on Nick-NCP−2 and Nick-NCP0 (Fig. 6b and Supplementary Fig. 21 ), consistent with the observations for LigIIIα alone (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Fig. 2 ), indicating that XRCC1 does not substantially enhance LigIIIα nick ligation at translational positions in proximity to the nucleosome dyad.
