To define whether XRCC1 enhances the ability of LigIIIα to recognize nicks in the nucleosome, we performed EMSAs to determine the apparent binding affinity ( K d,app ) of the XRCC1-LigIIIα complex for Nick-NCP−6, Nick-NCP−4, Nick-NCP−2, and Nick-NCP0 (Fig. 6c , Supplementary Fig. 22 , and Supplementary Table 1 ). The EMSA analysis revealed XRCC1-LigIIIα binds Nick-NCP−6 with a K d,app of 99 ± 3 nM, Nick-NCP−4 with a K d,app of 106 ± 14 nM, Nick-NCP−2 with a K d,app of 100 ± 5 nM, and Nick-NCP0 with a K d,app of 125 ± 15 nM. Notably, the apparent binding affinities of the XRCC1-LigIIIα complex for the Nick-NCPs are strikingly similar to those observed for LigIIIα alone (Compare Fig. 1e and Fig. 6c ), indicating that XRCC1 does not substantially enhance LigIIIα nick binding within the nucleosome.

To determine if XRCC1 alters the structural mechanism used by LigIIIα to engage nicks in the nucleosome, we obtained a cryo-EM reconstruction of the XRCC1-LigIIIα complex bound to a NCP containing a nick at SHL−6 (Fig. 6d ). This was accomplished by generating a complex of adenylylated XRCC1-LigIIIα bound to Nick-NCP−6 that was stabilized via glutaraldehyde crosslinking. The complex was then subjected to single-particle analysis, which resulted in a 2.9 Å reconstruction of the XRCC1-LigIIIα-Nick-NCP−6 complex (Fig. 6d , Supplementary Fig. 23 , 24 , and Supplementary Table 5 ). Similar to the LigIIIα-Nick-NCP−6 reconstruction, we only observed clear density for the LigIIIα NTase domain in the XRCC1-LigIIIα-Nick-NCP−6 reconstruction (Fig. 6d ), and the remaining catalytic core of LigIIIα (OBD and DBD), the ZnF, and the BRCT domain were unresolved. We were also unable to resolve XRCC1 in the reconstruction, including the known interaction interface between the BRCT domain of LigIIIα and the BRCT2 domain of XRCC1 35 – 37 , 64 , 70 . Closer inspection of the XRCC1-LigIIIα-Nick-NCP−6 structure revealed several striking similarities to the LigIIIα-Nick-NCP−6 structure (Fig. 6e ). In the XRCC1-LigIIIα-Nick-NCP−6 structure, the LigIIIα NTase engages the nucleosomal DNA with an ~6 bp footprint and directly coordinates the nick using the same general mechanism observed for LigIIIα alone (Fig. 6f,g ). Importantly, LigIIIα remains unable to encircle the nucleosomal DNA, transition the nucleosomal DNA on the 3′ end of the nick to A-form, nor shift the 3′ nucleotide into a C3′-endo conformation (Fig. 6h ), indicating that the presence of XRCC1 does not enable LigIIIα to adopt a ligation-competent conformation on the Nick-NCP. Collectively, these biochemical and structural observations suggest that XRCC1 does not play a substantial role in facilitating the ability of LigIIIα to perform nick ligation in the nucleosome.

Our work has established the molecular basis of nick ligation in the nucleosome by LigIIIα, providing fundamental insight into the terminal step of SSBR/BER in chromatin. Our kinetic analysis revealed that the ligation kinetics of LigIIIα in the nucleosome are highly dependent on the nick position within the nucleosomal DNA. Nicks near the nucleosome entry/exit site are ligated by LigIIIα with moderate ligation rates, whereas nicks near the nucleosome dyad are refractory to ligation. Despite this strong positional preference for ligation, our nucleosome binding assays demonstrate that LigIIIα robustly binds nicks at both the nucleosome entry/exit site and the nucleosome dyad, indicating that the position-dependent differences in ligation kinetics are not the result of large differences in substrate binding affinity. Our cryo-EM structures of LigIIIα bound to solvent-exposed nicks at four distinct translational positions provide a structural rationale for these observations. These structures reveal the LigIIIα NTase domain readily engages solvent-exposed nicks at all four translational positions in the nucleosome. However, the inability of the DBD and OBD to encircle and kink the nucleosomal nick prevents LigIIIα from adopting a catalytic conformation compatible with nick ligation. While these structures reveal why LigIIIα is generally unable to efficiently ligate nicks at translational positions adjacent to the nucleosome dyad, they do not directly explain how LigIIIα catalyzes nick ligation near the nucleosome entry/exit site. We hypothesize that spontaneous unwrapping of the nucleosomal DNA at the entry/exit site 58 – 60 may transiently relieve the steric constraints imposed by the histone octamer, providing an opportunity for LigIIIα to encircle and kink the nucleosomal DNA to facilitate nick ligation. Though we were unable to capture a structure of LigIIIα bound to the nucleosome in this configuration, the ligation rates determined for LigIIIα near the nucleosome entry/exit site (Supplementary Table 1 ) are less than the rate constant determined for spontaneous unwrapping of the nucleosomal DNA from the histone octamer at the entry/exit site 58 , 59 . This suggests that intrinsic nucleosome dynamics at the entry/exit site may represent the rate-limiting step of LigIIIα nick ligation in the nucleosome at these locations.

Over the past several years, structural studies have defined how the SSBR/BER enzymes that act upstream of LigIIIα, including multiple DNA glycosylases 5 , 71 , 72 , APE1 73 , and DNA Polymerase β 74 , recognize and process DNA lesions in the nucleosome. These structural studies demonstrated that SSBR/BER enzymes use localized or global DNA sculpting mechanisms (i.e., enzyme-induced deformations in the nucleosomal DNA) to reposition their cognate DNA lesions into the active site for catalysis 47 . In contrast to the upstream SSBR/BER enzymes, our structures reveal that LigIIIα is unable to perform the nucleosomal DNA sculpting required for catalysis, which includes encircling the DNA and introducing a sharp kink at the nick site to properly position the nick into the active site. Instead, LigIIIα likely relies on intrinsic nucleosome dynamics to transiently expose the nick to facilitate ligation. This fundamental difference between LigIIIα and upstream SSBR/BER enzymes likely explains why nick ligation represents the rate-limiting enzymatic step of BER at most positions in the nucleosome 39 , 43 . Of note, it is interesting to speculate whether the nucleosome barrier to ligation may be partially overcome through substrate channeling 75 – 79 , the process where sequential BER enzymes act in a coordinated fashion to prevent the accumulation of toxic repair intermediates 80 – 82 . Given the requirement that LigIIIα encircle and sharply kink the nucleosomal DNA for catalysis 29 , it is possible that the stepwise DNA sculpting induced by upstream SSBR/BER enzymes progressively displaces the nucleosomal DNA from the histone octamer to facilitate LigIIIα binding in a catalytically competent conformation 47 . While recent work has begun to probe substrate channeling between BER enzymes in the nucleosome 43 , 83 , future work will be needed to unambiguously determine whether substrate channeling can occur in the nucleosome and decipher the impact this coordination has on the ability of LigIIIα to catalyze nick ligation in the nucleosome.

XRCC1 is a central scaffold in the BER and SSBR pathways that forms a heterodimer with LigIIIα 61 – 63 , which is important for LigIIIα stability 62 , 65 – 67 and recruitment of LigIIIα to sites of DNA damage in cellular chromatin 68 , 69 . Prior work identified that XRCC1 modestly stimulates the ability of LigIIIα to catalyze nick ligation in the nucleosome 40 by partially disrupting nucleosome structure 39 , 40 , suggesting that XRCC1 may help LigIIIα partially overcome the nucleosome barrier to repair. In contrast to these prior observations, our biochemical assays demonstrate that XRCC1 does not substantially impact LigIIIα nick recognition or nick ligation in the nucleosome. Consistent with our biochemical observations, our structural analysis of nick recognition in the nucleosome by the XRCC1-LigIIIα complex revealed that XRCC1 does not directly engage the nucleosome, does not disrupt overall nucleosome structure, and does not promote a LigIIIα conformation compatible with catalysis. The basis of these conflicting results is unclear, though one notable difference is that the prior work utilized XRCC1 purified from insect cells 40 , whereas our study used XRCC1 purified from E. coli cells. It is possible that the XRCC1 purified from insect cells carries post-translational modifications 84 – 89 that enable XRCC1 to modulate nucleosome structure and/or stimulate LigIIIα nick ligation in the nucleosome, which are not present in XRCC1 purified from E. coli cells. Nevertheless, our data support the idea that the primary role of XRCC1 in chromatin-based SSBR/BER is to recruit LigIIIα to sites of DNA damage 68 , 69 and/or to coordinate substrate channeling between upstream SSBR/BER enzymes and LigIIIα within chromatin 68 , 90 – 92 , rather than directly facilitating the ability of LigIIIα to catalyze nick ligation in the nucleosome.

Our work, in conjunction with prior biochemical studies, strongly suggests that LigIIIα is incapable of efficiently catalyzing nick ligation in the nucleosome at nick positions outside of the nucleosome entry/exit site 39 , 40 , 43 . This raises the important question of how LigIIIα overcomes the nucleosome barrier to ligation at these positions in order to successfully complete chromatin-based SSBR/BER. We hypothesize that the nucleosome barrier to ligation is overcome through a combination of stochastic and DNA damage-dependent chromatin remodeling, both of which could generate a chromatin environment permissive for LigIIIα to catalyze nick ligation. Stochastic changes in chromatin structure (i.e., chromatin remodeling) that arise during nuclear processes such as transcription and DNA replication may randomly reposition nicks to more accessible locations in the nucleosome, displace nicks into linker DNA regions, or completely disassemble the nucleosome, all of which would enhance LigIIIα nick ligation. In addition to stochastic chromatin remodeling, DNA damage-dependent chromatin remodeling may also play a key role in facilitating nick ligation in the nucleosome. For example, the chromatin signaling cascade involving Poly-(ADP-ribose) Polymerase 1 and 2 (PARP1 and PARP2), Histone PARylation Factor 1, and downstream ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling enzymes has been implicated in facilitating BER and SSBR within cellular chromatin 93 – 110 . Consistent with this idea, the recruitment of XRCC1-LigIIIα to sites of DNA damage is dependent on ADP-ribosylation 69 , 94 , 98 , 110 , 111 , and recent work identified that histone ADP-ribosylation enhances XRCC1-LigIIIα nick ligation in the nucleosome by altering nucleosome dynamics 42 . In addition, the multiple ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling enzymes (e.g., Amplified in Liver Cancer 1) recruited downstream of PARP1/2 may function to reposition nicks to more accessible locations in the nucleosome (e.g., the nucleosome entry/exit site) and/or displace nicks into linker DNA regions that would also promote productive LigIIIα nick ligation. Our structural observation that LigIIIα can engage nicks in the nucleosome without adopting a ligation-competent conformation raises the intriguing possibility that this non-productive binding, or alternative modes of nucleosome binding mediated by the LigIIIα ZnF 112 , may tether LigIIIα at the nucleosomal nick until stochastic or DNA damage-dependent chromatin remodeling occurs. However, future work will be needed to further dissect the impact of stochastic and DNA damage-dependent chromatin remodeling on LigIIIα function during chromatin-based SSBR/BER.

All oligonucleotides used to generate recombinant nucleosomes containing nicks were synthesized by Integrated DNA Technologies (Coralville, IA). A complete list of the oligonucleotides used for generating recombinant nucleosomes containing nicks can be found in Supplementary Tables 6 and 7 . The oligonucleotides were resuspended to a final concentration of 100 µM in a buffer containing 10 mM Tris (pH 7.5) and 1 mM EDTA. Equimolar amounts of complementary oligonucleotides (see Supplementary Table 6 and 7 ) were mixed and diluted with a buffer containing 10 mM Tris (pH 7.5) and 1 mM EDTA to a final concentration of 10 µM. The complementary oligonucleotides were then annealed by heating to 95 °C for 2 minutes and cooling to 10 °C at a rate of −5 °C/min. The annealed oligonucleotides were stored short-term at 4 °C prior to nucleosome reconstitution.

Recombinant H. sapiens histone H2A (UniProt identifier: P0C0S8 ), histone H2B (UniProt identifier: P62807 ), histone H3 C110A (UniProt identifier Q71DI3 ), and histone H4 (UniProt identifier: P62805 ) proteins were generated from a tagless pET3a expression vector. The plasmids containing histone H2A, H3, and H4 were transformed and expressed in T7 Express lysY/I q competent E. coli cells (New England BioLabs). The plasmid containing histone H2B was transformed and expressed in BL21-CodonPlus (DE3)-RIPL E. coli cells (Agilent). The cells were grown in M9 minimal media at 37 °C to an OD 600 of 0.4 and histone expression was induced with 0.4 mM IPTG (histone H2A, H2B, and H3) or 0.3 mM IPTG (histone H4) for 3 hours (histone H3 and H4) or 4 hours (histone H2A and H2B) at 37 °C. The cells were harvested via centrifugation and cell pellets were stored long-term at −80 °C. The purification of each individual histone was carried out using well-established methods 113 – 115 . In brief, the cell pellets were lysed via sonication in a buffer containing 50 mM Tris (pH 7.5), 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM benzamidine, 1 mM DTT, and 1 mM EDTA, and the cell lysate was clarified via centrifugation. The resulting pellet was washed two times with a buffer containing 50 mM Tris (pH 7.5), 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM benzamidine, 1 mM DTT, 1 mM EDTA, and 1% Triton X-100, and further washed one time with a buffer containing 50 mM Tris (pH 7.5), 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM benzamidine, 1 mM DTT, and 1 mM EDTA. The histones were then extracted from inclusion bodies under denaturing conditions using 6 M Guanidinium-HCl. The extracted histones were then purified under gravity flow using a combination of anion-exchange and cation-exchange chromatography. The purified histones were dialyzed against H 2 O, lyophilized, and stored long term at −20 °C.

H2A/H2B dimers and H3/H4 tetramers were prepared prior to nucleosome reconstitution using established methods 113 – 115 . To generate H2A/H2B dimers, lyophilized histone H2A and H2B were resuspended in a buffer containing 20 mM Tris (pH 7.5), 6 M Guanidinium-HCl, and 10 mM DTT. The resuspended histone H2A and H2B were then mixed in a 1:1 molar ratio and dialyzed three times against a buffer containing 20 mM Tris (pH 7.5), 2 M NaCl, and 1 mM EDTA at 4 °C. To generate H3/H4 tetramers, lyophilized histone H3 and H4 were resuspended in a buffer containing 20 mM Tris (pH 7.5), 6 M Guanidinium-HCl, and 10 mM DTT. The resuspended histone H3 and H4 proteins were then mixed in a 1:1 molar ratio and dialyzed three times against a buffer containing 20 mM Tris (pH 7.5), 2 M NaCl, and 1 mM EDTA at 4 °C. The refolded H2A/H2B dimers and H3/H4 tetramers were then purified using a HiPrep Sephacryl S-200 16/60 HR gel filtration column (Cytiva) in a buffer containing 20 mM Tris (pH 7.5), 2 M NaCl, and 1 mM EDTA. Fractions containing pure H2A/H2B dimers and H3/H4 tetramers were combined and stored long-term at −20 °C in 50% glycerol.

All nucleosomes were prepared using an established salt-dialysis method 113 – 115 . H2A/H2B dimers, H3/H4 tetramers, and annealed Nick-DNA were mixed at a 2.2:1:1 molar ratio, respectively. Nucleosomes were reconstituted by sequentially decreasing the concentration of NaCl from 2 M NaCl to 1.5 M NaCl, to 1.0 M NaCl, to 0.75 M NaCl, to 0.5 M NaCl, to 0.25 M NaCl, and to 0 M NaCl over 24 hours. The reconstituted nucleosomes were then purified by sucrose gradient ultracentrifugation (10–40% gradient). Final nucleosome purity and homogeneity was assessed via native PAGE (5%, 59:1 acrylamide:bis-acrylamide ratio), and the nucleosomes were stored in a buffer containing 10 mM Tris (pH 7.5) and 1 mM EDTA at 4 °C. Native PAGE gels of the final nucleosomes can be found in Supplementary Fig. 1a-c .

Nucleosome stability assays were performed by incubating each NCP (200 nM) in a reaction buffer containing 20 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM MgCl 2 , 0.1 mM TCEP, and 0.2 mg/ml BSA. Samples were taken immediately after resuspension (0′ time point) and after incubation for 24 hours at 37 °C. Nucleosomes were mixed with 2x sucrose loading dye (10% sucrose, 0.025% bromophenol blue, 0.1 mg/ml BSA, 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), and 1 mM EDTA), and nucleosome integrity was assessed by native polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (5%, 59:1 acrylamide:bis-acrylamide). The gels were stained with SYBR Gold (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and the bands corresponding to nucleosome and free DNA were quantified using ImageJ 116 .

The codon-optimized DNA for H. sapiens LigIIIα was cloned into a pET24a bacterial expression vector containing a C-terminal His-tag by GenScript. LigIIIα was expressed and purified using a previously established method 38 with minor modifications. The pET24a-LigIIIα plasmid was transformed and expressed in BL21 (DE3) E. coli cells (Agilent). The transformed cells were grown at 37 °C to an OD 600 of 1.0, and LigIIIα expression was induced with 0.5 mM IPTG for 16 h–18 h at 25 °C. The resulting cells were lysed via sonication in a buffer containing 25 mM HEPES (pH 8.0), 300 mM NaCl, 0.25 mM TCEP, 10 mM imidazole, and a cocktail of protease inhibitors (AEBSF, leupeptin, benzamidine, pepstatin A). The lysate was clarified via centrifugation and loaded onto a HisTrap HP column (Cytiva) equilibrated with 25 mM HEPES (pH 8.0), 300 mM NaCl, 0.25 mM TCEP, 10 mM imidazole, and eluted in a buffer containing 25 mM HEPES (pH 8.0), 300 mM NaCl, 0.25 mM TCEP, 400 mM imidazole (0–100% gradient). The LigIIIα protein was then loaded onto a HiTrap Heparin HP column (Cytiva) equilibrated with 25 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 200 mM NaCl, and 0.1 mM TCEP, and eluted in a buffer containing 25 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 1000 mM NaCl, and 0.1 mM TCEP (0 – 100% gradient). The LigIIIα protein was further purified using a HiPrep SP HP column (Cytiva) equilibrated with 25 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 200 mM NaCl, and 0.1 mM TCEP, and eluted in a buffer containing 25 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 1000 mM NaCl, and 0.1 mM TCEP (0–100% gradient). LigIIIα was then adenylylated by incubation with 20 mM MgCl 2 and 2 mM ATP for 60 minutes at 4 °C. The LigIIIα protein was then polished via size-exclusion chromatography using a HiPrep Sephacryl S-200 26/60 HR (Cytiva) equilibrated in a buffer containing 20 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, and 0.1 mM TCEP. The purity of LigIIIα was confirmed by denaturing SDS-PAGE, and the purified LigIIIα was stored long-term at −80 °C. An SDS-PAGE gel of the purified LigIIIα protein can be found in Supplementary Fig. 1d .

The codon-optimized DNA for H. sapiens XRCC1 was cloned into a pET-His-GFP bacterial expression vector using GenScript. The pET-His-GFP-XRCC1 plasmid was transformed and expressed in BL21 (DE3)-RIPL E. coli cells (Agilent). The transformed cells were grown at 37 °C to an OD 600 of 1.0, and XRCC1 expression was induced with 0.5 mM IPTG for 16 h–18 hours at 18 °C. The resulting cells were lysed via sonication in a buffer containing 25 mM HEPES (pH 8.0), 500 mM NaCl, 0.25 mM TCEP, 10 mM imidazole, and a cocktail of protease inhibitors (AEBSF, leupeptin, benzamidine, pepstatin A). The lysate was clarified via centrifugation and loaded onto a gravity flow column containing HisPur Ni-NTA Resin (Thermo Fisher Scientific) equilibrated with 25 mM HEPES (pH 8.0), 500 mM NaCl, 0.25 mM TCEP, 10 mM imidazole, and eluted in a buffer containing 25 mM HEPES (pH 8.0), 300 mM NaCl, 0.25 mM TCEP, 400 mM imidazole. The XRCC1 protein was then liberated from the His-GFP tag via incubation with PreScission Protease, loaded onto a HiTrap Heparin HP column (Cytiva) equilibrated with 25 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 200 mM NaCl, and 0.1 mM TCEP, and eluted in a buffer containing 25 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 1000 mM NaCl, and 0.1 mM TCEP (0 – 100% gradient). The XRCC1 protein was further purified using a HiPrep SP HP column (Cytiva) equilibrated with 25 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 200 mM NaCl, and 0.1 mM TCEP, and eluted in a buffer containing 25 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 1000 mM NaCl, and 0.1 mM TCEP (0 – 100% gradient). The XRCC1 protein was then polished via size-exclusion chromatography using a HiPrep Sephacryl S-200 26/60 HR (Cytiva) equilibrated in a buffer containing 20 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 100 mM NaCl, and 0.1 mM TCEP. The purity of XRCC1 was confirmed by denaturing SDS-PAGE, and the purified XRCC1 was stored long-term at −80 °C. An SDS-PAGE gel of the purified XRCC1 protein can be found in Supplementary Fig. 1d .

The XRCC1-LigIIIα complex was generated by mixing purified recombinant XRCC1 and adenylylated LigIIIα at a 1:1 molar ratio in a buffer containing 25 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 100 mM NaCl, and 0.1 mM TCEP. The reactions were incubated on ice for 2 hours, and the XRCC1-LigIIIα complex was purified via size-exclusion chromatography using a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL (Cytiva) equilibrated in a buffer containing 25 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 100 mM NaCl, and 0.1 mM TCEP. The purity of the XRCC1-LigIIIα complex was confirmed by denaturing SDS-PAGE, and the purified XRCC1-LigIIIα complex stored long-term at −80 °C. An SDS-PAGE gel of the purified XRCC1-LigIIIα complex can be found in Supplementary Fig. 1e .

Single-turnover kinetic reactions were carried out by mixing LigIIIα (2 µM) or XRCC1-LigIIIα (2 µM) with each respective Nick-NCP (100 nM) or Nick-DNA (100 nM) in a buffer containing 50 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP, and 0.1 mg/ml bovine serum albumin. The reactions were incubated for 10 minutes at 37 °C, ligation was initiated through the addition of Mg 2+ -ATP (2 mM Mg 2+ , 1 mM ATP), and the ligation reactions were quenched at various time points with a solution containing 100 mM EDTA, 80% deionized formamide, 0.25 mg/ml bromophenol blue, and 0.25 mg/ml xylene cyanol. For Nick-NCP0, Nick-NCP−2, Nick-NCP−4, the reaction time points were 10 sec, 20 sec, 30 sec, 60 sec, 120 sec, 240 sec, 600 sec, 1200 sec, 1800 sec, 3600 sec, 7200 sec, and 14400 sec. For Nick-DNA and Nick-NCP−6, the reaction time points were 5 sec, 10 sec, 15 sec, 20 sec, 30 sec, 60 sec, 120 sec, 240 sec, 600 sec, 1200 sec, 1800 sec, and 3600 sec. For 5S -Nick-NCP0 and 5S -Nick-NCP−2, the reaction time points were 10 sec, 20 sec, 30 sec, 60 sec, 120 sec, 240 sec, 600 sec, 1200 sec, 1800 sec, 3600 sec, 7200 sec. The quenched reactions were incubated at 95 °C for 5 min and substrate and product bands were separated by 8% (Nick-NCP0, Nick-NCP−2, Nick-NCP−4, 5S -Nick-NCP0 and 5S -Nick-NCP−2) or 12% (Nick-DNA and Nick-NCP−6) denaturing urea polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (29:1 acrylamide:bis-acrylamide). All data collection parameters can be found in Supplementary Tables 2 – 5 . The cryo-EM data were processed with cryoSPARC 117 using similar data processing workflows. Each individual data processing workflow can be found in Supplementary Figs. 4 - 8 and 23 . In brief, the micrographs for each dataset were initially imported into cryoSPARC and subjected to pre-processing using patch motion correction and patch CTF-estimation. An initial cycle of blob particle picking was performed to generate a training set for Topaz, and Topaz 118 used to generate the final particle stack. Ab initio models were then generated using the final particle stacks, and heterogeneous refinement(s) and/or 3D classifications (with mask for LigIIIα and the adjacent nucleosomal DNA) were performed to separate the free Nick-NCPs and LigIIIα-containing Nick-NCP complexes. A composite map was then generated by combining the consensus and local refinement maps using PHENIX combine focus maps. The local resolution estimation for each composite map was generated using cryoSPARC local resolution estimation after combining the half maps from the consensus and local refinements in PHENIX.

All simulations were performed with the AMBER20 suite of programs 123 . The starting models of the ND-NCP, Nick-NCP0, Nick-NCP−2, Nick-NCP−4, and Nick-NCP−6 used in the MD simulations were computationally generated using a previously determined cryo-EM structure of a nucleosome containing a 1-nt gap (PDB: 9DWF) 74 . The ff19SB 124 and OL21 125 force fields were used for protein and DNA. Each system was solvated in a truncated octahedron box of OPC water 126 with a buffer of 12 Å around the solute. Sodium and chloride ions were added to reach a final salt concentration of 0.15 M, resulting in final systems of approximately 250,000 atoms. Each system was subjected to a 10,000-step minimization, followed by a 10 ps NVT thermalization with 10 kcal/mol restraints on the solute atoms. Two 4 ns NPT equilibration steps with decreasing restraints on the solute backbone atoms were then carried out, followed by a final 40 ns equilibration and a 1 μs unrestrained production run. Three replicates were performed with random starting velocities for the ND-NCP, Nick-NCP0, Nick-NCP−2, Nick-NCP−4, and Nick-NCP−6 systems. The Particle Mesh Ewald approach was used with an 8 Å cutoff for electrostatic contributions, and a 4 fs timestep enabled by the use of Hydrogen Mass Repartitioning 127 . The Langevin thermostat and Berendsen barostat were used to maintain the temperature and pressure at 300 K and 1 bar, respectively. The per-nucleotide contribution to the DNA flexibility was quantified using a PCA-based analysis 128 previously used on similar systems 129 , 130 . Contact maps were generated with the cpptraj tool of AMBER20 using default parameters.

articles.title: Largest eigenvalue statistics of wavefront shaping in complex scattering media.
articles.authors: Schehr G, Yılmaz H.
articles.abstract: In wavefront shaping, light, sound, and other waves are focused through complex scattering media onto one or more target positions, and the resulting intensity enhancement is quantified by the enhancement factor. While reproducible enhancement is crucial in experiments, the fluctuations of the enhancement factor remain largely unexplored. Here, we combine experiments, numerical simulations, and exact random-matrix theory to determine its full distribution for multi-target focusing. Exact finite-size random-matrix predictions accurately describe both the mean enhancement factor and its fluctuations beyond the asymptotic Marčenko-Pastur regime, whenever long-range mesoscopic correlations are negligible (e.g., in weakly scattering media or when only a limited number of input channels is controlled). In contrast, strongly scattering media exhibit giant enhancement-factor fluctuations that increasingly exceed these parameter-free predictions as the number of controlled input channels increases. These findings establish the enhancement factor not only as a measure of focusing performance, but also as a sensitive statistical observable that provides a simple and experimentally accessible probe of long-range mesoscopic correlations.
paragraphs: In wavefront shaping, light, sound, and other waves are focused through complex scattering media onto one or more target positions, and the resulting intensity enhancement is quantified by the enhancement factor. While reproducible enhancement is crucial in experiments, the fluctuations of the enhancement factor remain largely unexplored. Here, we combine experiments, numerical simulations, and exact random-matrix theory to determine its full distribution for multi-target focusing. Exact finite-size random-matrix predictions accurately describe both the mean enhancement factor and its fluctuations beyond the asymptotic Marčenko-Pastur regime, whenever long-range mesoscopic correlations are negligible (e.g., in weakly scattering media or when only a limited number of input channels is controlled). In contrast, strongly scattering media exhibit giant enhancement-factor fluctuations that increasingly exceed these parameter-free predictions as the number of controlled input channels increases. These findings establish the enhancement factor not only as a measure of focusing performance, but also as a sensitive statistical observable that provides a simple and experimentally accessible probe of long-range mesoscopic correlations.

Wavefront shaping enables waves to focus through complex scattering media. Here, authors show that focusing enhancement exhibits giant fluctuations that reveal long-range mesoscopic correlations, establishing the enhancement factor as a sensitive statistical probe of mesoscopic wave transport.

Wavefront shaping stands as a paradigm-shifting framework for the coherent control of light, sound, and other waves in complex scattering media, such as biological tissue and disordered materials 1 – 8 . Experimental demonstrations have shown that by precisely tailoring the incident wavefront, the total transmission of microwaves, acoustic, elastic, or optical waves can be dramatically enhanced—or waves can even be tightly focused—through strongly scattering media 1 , 9 – 19 . In optics, this level of precise coherent control over light holds profound implications for imaging 11 , 20 – 23 , quantum secure optical authentication 24 , high-dimensional quantum optics 25 – 27 , optical manipulation 28 , photothermal therapy 3 , 29 , microsurgery 30 , and optogenetics in complex scattering environments 31 – 33 , including biological tissue, ensembles of micro- and nanoparticles, and other seemingly opaque media.

The measurement of the transmission matrix—encoding the input-output field relationship of a medium—is essential for controlling the output field via input wavefront shaping 34 . Once known, the transmission matrix enables focusing light to single or multiple target positions 1 , 11 , 17 , 20 – 28 , 31 – 42 , or transmitting images through scattering media 43 . In particular, simultaneous focusing on multiple positions has important applications in optical metrology 37 , optical trapping of microparticles 28 , programmable multiport optical circuits 25 – 27 , and focusing on extended guide stars 32 , 33 , 36 , 44 . A key metric for evaluating the efficacy of wavefront shaping in these contexts is the enhancement factor, which quantifies the intensity enhancement achieved at the target positions 1 , 4 , 36 . It is defined as \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\eta={\sum }_{m=1}^{{M}_{2}}| \mathop{\sum }_{n=1}^{{M}_{1}}{A}_{mn}{E}_{n}^{{{\rm{opt}}}}{| }^{2}/\overline{\mathop{\sum }_{m=1}^{{M}_{2}}| \mathop{\sum }_{n=1}^{{M}_{1}}{A}_{mn}{E}_{n}}{| }^{2}$$\end{document} η = ∑ m = 1 M 2 ∣ ∑ n = 1 M 1 A m n E n opt ∣ 2 / ∑ m = 1 M 2 ∣ ∑ n = 1 M 1 A m n E n ¯ ∣ 2 , where A is the M 2 × M 1 sub-transmission matrix of the medium, with n labeling the incident Fourier components at the input and m the position of the targets at the output. Here, M 1 denotes the number of degrees of freedom at the input, while M 2 denotes the number of target (focusing) points, see Fig. 1 . The vector E opt is the input wavefront that maximizes the total intensity over these M 2 targets. The denominator in the definition of η is the same total intensity, but averaged over statistically equivalent disorder realizations (i.e., over different sub-transmission matrices A ) or, equivalently, over independent unit-power input wavefronts E whose complex field components are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) circularly symmetric complex Gaussian entries. Fig. 1 The wavefront-shaping concept to focus light through a scattering medium onto multiple target points is shown. (a) A sketch of the speckle pattern in transmission when an unshaped wavefront is incident onto a scattering medium is demonstrated. (b) The incident wavefront is shaped by a spatial light modulator with M 1 degrees of freedom at the input, focusing light onto two selected target points (output channels) M 2 = 2.

(a) A sketch of the speckle pattern in transmission when an unshaped wavefront is incident onto a scattering medium is demonstrated. (b) The incident wavefront is shaped by a spatial light modulator with M 1 degrees of freedom at the input, focusing light onto two selected target points (output channels) M 2 = 2.

One typically employs an optimization algorithm to determine the optimal input wavefront E opt that maximizes the intensity at the target locations 4 , 45 . For a single target ( M 2 = 1), digital optical phase conjugation attains the global maximum of the enhancement factor η 4 . For multiple targets ( M 2 > 1), the global maximum of η equals the largest eigenvalue \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$${\lambda }_{\max }$$\end{document} λ max of the focusing operator A † A , where A denotes an M 2 × M 1 sub-transmission matrix of the disordered medium, with t the normalized transmission matrix obeying Var( t m n ) = 1/ M 2 (see e.g. 17 ).

In practical wavefront-shaping focusing experiments, one typically operates in the regime M 1 ≫ M 2 . The dependence of the mean enhancement \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\langle {\lambda }_{\max }\rangle$$\end{document} ⟨ λ max ⟩ on the number of controlled degrees of freedom M 1 and output targets M 2 has been observed experimentally and is widely recognized in the wavefront shaping community to exhibit the scaling \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\langle {\lambda }_{\max }\rangle \sim {M}_{1}/{M}_{2}$$\end{document} ⟨ λ max ⟩ ~ M 1 / M 2 4 , 32 , 36 , 44 . On the other hand, if one assumes that the entries of A are independent complex Gaussian numbers, then the focusing operator is an (anti)-Laguerre-Wishart (LW) random matrix 46 . In this case, for large M 1 and M 2 with fixed ratio M 1 / M 2 , the mean largest eigenvalue \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\langle {\lambda }_{\max }\rangle$$\end{document} ⟨ λ max ⟩ coincides with the upper edge of the Marčenko–Pastur (MP) spectrum 47 – 49 : 1 \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\langle {\lambda }_{\max }\rangle \,={\left(\sqrt{\frac{{M}_{1}}{{M}_{2}}}+1\right)}^{2}.$$\end{document} ⟨ λ max ⟩ = M 1 M 2 + 1 2 .

While the MP law predicts \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\langle {\lambda }_{\max }\rangle \sim {M}_{1}/{M}_{2}$$\end{document} ⟨ λ max ⟩ ~ M 1 / M 2 in the limit M 1 ≫ M 2 , the applicability of this formula ( 1 ) in experimental situations where M 1 and M 2 are finite remains questionable.

Furthermore, predicting the sample-to-sample and target-to-target fluctuations of the enhancement factor, i.e., \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\Delta {\lambda }_{\max }\equiv \sqrt{\langle {\lambda }_{\max }^{2}\rangle -{\langle {\lambda }_{\max }\rangle }^{2}}$$\end{document} Δ λ max ≡ ⟨ λ max 2 ⟩ − ⟨ λ max ⟩ 2 , is key to establishing the fundamental limits of experimental reproducibility. Yet, its full statistical distribution and fluctuations remain largely unexplored, apart from the simpler case of single-point focusing ( M 2 = 1), which can be analysed rather straightforwardly 50 .

In this work, we employ a random matrix framework to describe the full distribution of the enhancement factor for focusing light onto multiple target locations ( M 2 > 1) through diffusive media. Under standard assumptions, the focusing operators can be described by random matrices belonging to the so-called Laguerre–Wishart ensemble 46 . This framework accurately predicts both the mean enhancement factor and its fluctuations at finite M 1 and M 2 , extending beyond the asymptotic Marčenko–Pastur limit and providing a parameter-free baseline for identifying excess fluctuations arising from long-range mesoscopic correlations. It is known that while long-range mesoscopic correlations do not affect the mean enhancement factor for small values of M 2 , they increase the background intensity, with this effect becoming experimentally observable for large values of M 1 10 , 17 , 51 – 53 . These long-range mesoscopic correlations originate from coherent interference among multiple scattering paths and constitute one of the defining signatures of mesoscopic wave transport in disordered media 6 , 46 , 54 – 62 . They manifest themselves through connected four-field correlation functions and underlie several hallmark mesoscopic phenomena, including universal conductance fluctuations 63 , 64 , the emergence of open transmission channels with near-unity transmittance 6 , 8 , 18 , 19 , 46 , 65 , 66 , and Anderson localization 56 , 67 , 68 . They also play a fundamental role in wavefront shaping by limiting and modifying the coherent control of waves in complex scattering media 13 , 15 , 17 , 18 , 52 , 65 , 66 . An outstanding question is whether long-range mesoscopic correlations influence the second-order statistics of the enhancement factor.

Our experiments and numerical simulations address this question by revealing correlation-induced giant fluctuations that exceed the predictions of the Laguerre–Wishart (LW) random-matrix model, thereby identifying correlation-driven deviations from the LW baseline. From a fundamental perspective, our results demonstrate that the enhancement factor is not merely a measure of focusing performance, but also a statistical observable whose fluctuations encode long-range mesoscopic correlations in wavefront-shaping experiments. This establishes enhancement-factor fluctuations as a simple and experimentally accessible probe of long-range mesoscopic correlations. From an applied perspective, the finite-size LW framework provides accurate parameter-free predictions for the enhancement factor and its fluctuations when the influence of long-range mesoscopic correlations is negligible, while providing a correlation-free baseline for identifying excess fluctuations when such correlations become significant. This framework, therefore, enables more reliable performance estimates for applications in biomedical imaging, optical metrology, optical trapping, and optical communications through scattering media.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In the Results section, we first present the experimental enhancement-factor statistics and compare them with the exact finite-size Laguerre–Wishart predictions. We then introduce the random-matrix framework based on the Laguerre–Wishart ensemble and provide exact predictions for the enhancement-factor statistics. Next, we investigate the role of long-range mesoscopic correlations by combining numerical simulations, analytical predictions, and experimental measurements, demonstrating that these correlations give rise to giant fluctuations in the enhancement factor beyond the Laguerre–Wishart baseline. In the Discussion section, we place our findings in a broader context and summarize the main results. Finally, the “Methods” section provides details of the experimental transmission-matrix measurements and wave-propagation simulations.

The transmission matrix of a scattering medium provides the information required to modulate the incident wavefront with a spatial light modulator (SLM) and focus light onto single or multiple target points, as illustrated in Fig. 1 : an unmodulated beam produces a random speckle pattern [Fig. 1 a], whereas a shaped input beam enables simultaneous focusing at multiple target points [Fig. 1 b].

Experimentally, we measure the transmission matrix t of a scattering sample using phase-shifting interferometry 69 , see Supplementary Note 3 for a sketch of the experimental setup. The scattering sample consists of a densely packed zinc oxide (ZnO) nanoparticle layer on a cover slip, with a thickness of approximately 10 μm, much larger than the transport mean free path l t = 1μm, ensuring that light transport within the ZnO layer is diffusive. In our measured t m n , the input channel n corresponds to a 9 × 9 SLM segment (≈one Fourier component on the front surface). The output channel m corresponds to a position on the back surface, i.e., t m n maps the SLM field to the outgoing field at the back surface.

Starting from the experimental transmission matrix t m n , we generate an ensemble of focusing operators A † A , with A denoting a randomly chosen sub-transmission matrix of size M 2 × M 1 . We work in the regime M 1 ≫ M 2 , with \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$${M}_{1}\in [100,1000]\cap {\mathbb{Z}}$$\end{document} M 1 ∈ [ 100 , 1000 ] ∩ Z and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$${M}_{2}\in [1,5]\cap {\mathbb{Z}}$$\end{document} M 2 ∈ [ 1 , 5 ] ∩ Z . Having presented the experimental results for the mean enhancement factor and its probability distributions, together with their comparison to the analytical predictions, we now detail the random-matrix framework from which these predictions are derived. Our approach is based on an analytic treatment of the spectral properties of the focusing operator within a random-matrix framework. To this end, we model the entries of the M 2 × M 1 sub-transmission matrix A as independent complex Gaussian variables. This is the standard statistical description of open scattering systems that support a large number of channels, in which the coherent superposition of many scattering paths gives rise to fully developed speckle and approximately Gaussian field statistics 71 – 74 . The resulting Gaussian model provides the simplest parameter-free description of enhancement-factor statistics in the absence of long-range mesoscopic correlations, serving as a quantitative reference for identifying correlation-induced excess fluctuations. Under this assumption, the focusing operator A † A belongs to the complex anti–LW ensemble 46 , where “anti” indicates that the underlying matrix A is rectangular with more columns than rows ( M 1 > M 2 ) 75 – 77 . The LW-based framework is built on correlation-free random matrices. In contrast, it is well established that the transmission matrix of a disordered medium exhibits long-range mesoscopic correlations 54 – 62 . The systematic excess of the experimental fluctuations over the LW prediction in Fig. 4 a, b, therefore naturally raises the question of whether the observed fluctuations of the largest eigenvalue (i.e., the enhancement factor) in wavefront-shaping focusing experiments originate from such long-range correlations.

In contrast, we show here that long-range correlations can be detected from much smaller datasets—using submatrices with only M 1 ≲200 and even a single output channel ( M 2 = 1)—and through samples as thin as ≈10 l t . This is possible because the LW-based analytical framework provides exact predictions in the absence of correlations, allowing systematic excess fluctuations beyond the correlation-free baseline to serve as a sensitive signature of long-range mesoscopic correlations.

In conclusion, our work establishes the statistical foundations of the enhancement factor, a key measure of coherent control of light transport through complex scattering media with implications for biomedical imaging, optical metrology, secure communications, optical trapping, and quantum photonics. By combining experiments, numerical simulations, and exact random-matrix results, we determine the full probability distribution of the enhancement factor for multi-point focusing. For finite numbers of input and output channels, and within the Laguerre–Wishart (LW) random-matrix framework (i.e., in the absence of long-range mesoscopic correlations), the theory quantitatively captures both the mean and the fluctuations, going beyond the Marčenko–Pastur prediction for the mean and the Tracy–Widom law for fluctuations in the asymptotic large-channel limit. These results provide, for the first time, a comprehensive statistical description directly relevant to experimentally accessible finite-channel regimes.

Beyond applying the Laguerre–Wishart framework to enhancement-factor statistics in wavefront shaping, we demonstrate that strongly scattering media exhibit giant fluctuations arising from long-range mesoscopic correlations. While probing long-range mesoscopic correlations through the mean largest eigenvalue would normally require nearly complete transmission matrices containing 10 4 –10 6 channels 13 , 15 , 17 , 70 , 91 , our results show that enhancement-factor fluctuations already provide a sensitive probe when only M 1 ≲ 200 input and M 2 = 1 output channels are controlled. This establishes a direct connection between wavefront-shaping experiments and mesoscopic wave transport, revealing the limitations of correlation-free random-matrix predictions in the presence of long-range mesoscopic correlations.

A natural question is whether these correlation-induced deviations can instead be described within the framework of correlated Wishart ensembles 92 – 95 . Consequently, these physical correlations cannot, in general, be represented solely through a prescribed covariance matrix for Gaussian transmission coefficients. Existing theories either explicitly incorporate long-range mesoscopic correlations into random-matrix models while describing only the global eigenvalue density 70 , or accurately reproduce the global spectrum without explicitly encoding these correlations, as in radiant-field theory 96 , 97 . Establishing a predictive mapping between mesoscopic multiple-scattering theory and correlated random-matrix theory—and ultimately an accurate theory for the extreme eigenvalue statistics in the presence of long-range mesoscopic correlations—therefore remains an important open problem.

Although demonstrated here for optical wavefront shaping, the underlying mechanism relies only on multiple scattering and finite-size statistics, suggesting that the fluctuation physics uncovered in this work should extend naturally to acoustic, elastic, microwave, and matter-wave systems. More broadly, our results establish the enhancement factor not merely as a measure of focusing performance, but as a statistical observable that provides a simple and experimentally accessible probe of long-range mesoscopic correlations in complex scattering media.

articles.title: Listeria promotes systemic infection by targeting the host deubiquitinase CYLD.
articles.authors: Ammendolia DA, Ellison CJ, Zheng Y, Coyaud E, Laurent EMN, Yan BR, Manning B, Waldmann AK, Tan JMJ, Frendo-Cumbo S, Lyons C, Youn JY, Raught B, Ireton K, Higgins DE, Elliott PR, Brumell JH.
articles.abstract: Abstract Listeria monocytogenes ( Lm ) is an intracellular pathogen that can cause life-threatening systemic infections. Internalin C (InlC) is a secreted factor required for full Lm virulence in systemic models of infection by mechanisms that remain unclear. Here, we show that InlC binds to CYLD, a host deubiquitinase and regulator of innate immunity. Structurally, we reveal the LRR domain of InlC binds the CAP-Gly2 domain of CYLD, independently of InlC’s binding site for other host target proteins. Lm strains harboring amino acid substitutions in InlC that selectively disrupt binding to CYLD were examined. We demonstrate that after Lm accesses the host cytosol, InlC recruits CYLD to ubiquitin-positive bacteria. Recruitment of CYLD was dependent on the host E3 ligase RNF213, a major initiator of ubiquitin-mediated defenses. Furthermore, InlC-CYLD binding contributed to Lm virulence in mice. Together, these findings reveal how a secreted bacterial factor promotes the recruitment of a host deubiquitinase to cytosolic bacteria in response to ubiquitin-mediated defenses. Subject terms: Bacterial pathogenesis, Pathogens, Bacterial infection, Cellular microbiology

Subject terms: Bacterial pathogenesis, Pathogens, Bacterial infection, Cellular microbiology

Secretion of protein InlC into the host cytosol is important for virulence of the intracellular pathogen Listeria monocytogenes . Here, Ammendolia et al. show that InlC recruits a host deubiquitinase to cytosolic bacteria in response to ubiquitin-mediated defenses.

Ubiquitin-mediated defenses are critical for the detection and control of intracellular pathogens, leading to outcomes such as immune signaling and autophagic clearance 1 . The host E3 ligase RNF213 is a key initiator of this process, capable of ubiquitinating a diverse set of pathogens from bacteria to parasites 2 . Bacterial countermeasures against RNF213 activity are best understood in the context of gram-negative bacteria upon ubiquitination of lipopolysaccharide 3 – 5 , whereas little is known about the response of gram-positive species.

Listeria monocytogenes ( Lm ) is a gram-positive, facultative intracellular bacterium that causes listeriosis, a systemic form of disease with a high mortality rate (20%–30%) amongst foodborne pathogens 6 . The ability of Lm to grow within the cytosol of host cells and to spread directly from cell to cell contributes to its virulence 7 . After uptake by host cells, Lm employs a pore-forming toxin and phospholipase C enzymes to facilitate vacuolar escape. Upon entering the cytosol, Lm undergoes actin-based motility through the expression of ActA, a bacterial surface protein 8 . Through binding to host actin regulatory factors, ActA promotes intracellular motility in the cytosol and the formation of cell surface protrusions, leading to eventual uptake by adjacent cells. ActA is also known to have other functions 9 , including evasion of host ubiquitin-mediated defenses 2 , 10 , 11 . Indeed, RNF213 has been shown to promote ubiquitination events at the surface of Lm that are greatly enhanced in non-motile (Δ actA ) bacteria 2 , 11 . Whether additional virulence factors act cooperatively with ActA to mediate evasion of ubiquitin-mediated defenses remains unclear.

Internalin C (InlC) is a secreted Lm virulence factor that is highly expressed when bacteria access the cytosol of host cells 12 – 14 . While InlC is not required for Lm growth in the cytosol of various cell lines in vitro 12 , it has been linked to cellular phenotypes relevant to in vivo infection. Specifically, InlC binds the host actin regulator TUBA to promote cell-to-cell spread 14 , 15 and also interacts with the IκB kinase (IKK) complex to dampen innate immune signaling 16 . These versatile roles led us to speculate that InlC has additional binding partners in the host cell cytosol that enable Lm to cause systemic infection.

Here, we identify the host deubiquitinase CYLD as a target of InlC. We reveal that InlC binds directly to the CAP-Gly2 domain of CYLD, independently of its known protein-protein interactions with other host binding partners. InlC binding does not impair CYLD’s deubiquitinase activity, but instead promotes CYLD recruitment to ubiquitinated bacteria in a manner dependent on RNF213 activity. We further demonstrate that InlC-CYLD binding contributes to Lm virulence in vivo by promoting bacterial dissemination in the liver. Collectively, our results reveal how a secreted bacterial factor promotes the recruitment of a host deubiquitinase in response to host ubiquitin defenses.

To identify host protein interactors of InlC, we performed proximity-dependent biotin identification (BioID) 17 , 18 in HEK293 cells by expressing the secreted portion of InlC fused to an abortive mutant of the Escherichia coli -derived biotin ligase BirA (R118G, termed BirA*) 19 (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. 1a, b ). Relative to the BirA* control, we identified CYLD and its binding partner SPATA2 as high-confidence proximity interactors of InlC (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Data 1 ). A previous high-throughput screen identified CYLD as a potential interactor of InlC 20 . Two members of the IκB kinase (IKK) complex, IKK-α and IKK-γ, were also detected, consistent with prior observations 21 . Through co-immunoprecipitation using eGFP-InlC as bait, we validated the binding of InlC to CYLD, SPATA2, and IKK-α/-γ (Fig. 1c ). As it remains unknown how Lm counteracts host ubiquitin defenses, we sought to further characterize the interaction of InlC with CYLD.

CYLD consists of three cytoskeleton-associated protein glycine-rich protein (CAP-Gly) domains and a C-terminal ubiquitin-specific peptidase (USP) domain (Fig. 1d ). Established protein-protein interactions for these domains include IKK-γ (CAP-Gly3) and SPATA2 (USP) (Fig. 1d ) 22 , 23 . To determine which region of CYLD mediates binding to InlC, we performed co-immunoprecipitation of eGFP-InlC in CYLD KO HEK293T cells complemented with individual domains of HA-CYLD (Fig. 1d, e ). We observed that eGFP-InlC bound the N-terminal half of HA-CYLD (CAP-Gly1-3). Binding to the CAP-Gly2 domain was deemed both sufficient (Fig. 1e ) and necessary (Fig. 1f ) for binding to InlC.

As a complementary approach, we used isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) to measure direct binding between recombinant InlC and CAP-Gly2 (Fig. 1g ). InlC bound with high affinity to the CAP-Gly2 domain of CYLD with a Kd of 185 ± 29.5 nM. In contrast, InlC did not bind to either the CAP-Gly1 or CAP-Gly3 domains. These data demonstrate that InlC directly binds to CYLD via its CAP-Gly2 domain.

The secreted form of InlC comprises an α-helical-cap, a leucine-rich repeat (LRR) domain, and an IgG-like domain 24 . To define the molecular interaction between InlC and CYLD CAP-Gly2, we determined the structure of the complex to 1.8 Å resolution by X-ray crystallography (Fig. 2a , Supplementary Fig. 2 , and Supplementary Table 1 ). Dissection of this interaction highlighted two key interfaces employing different modes of action. First, a hydrophobic interface clustered around InlC residues Ile159 and Phe182 stabilizes a hydrophobic patch in CYLD including residues Leu261, Phe264 and Phe280. The second interface is driven by hydrogen bond interactions from InlC residues Asn198 and Lys236 to CYLD backbone carbonyl groups of Gly274 and Glu292, respectively (Fig. 2a ).

Notably, Gly274 lies within the “GKNDG” motif signature of CAP-Gly domains 25 . Sequence alignment revealed that this motif is highly conserved amongst species where listeriosis has been reported 6 (Fig. 2b ), suggesting an important role in pathogenesis. Mutagenesis of the motif in its entirety or single residues (G274A, W276A, G278A) was found to block or greatly reduce CYLD binding to InlC as determined by co-immunoprecipitation (Fig. 2c ). ITC analysis additionally confirmed that mutation of G274A prevented recombinant InlC binding, whereas mutation of CYLD Asn275 to introduce steric hinderance (N275Q) or a repulsive charge (N275E) only reduced the affinity for InlC (Fig. 2d ).

The CAP-Gly2 domain can bind ubiquitin to regulate the deubiquitinase activity of CYLD 26 . However, mutation of Phe288 (F288A) within CAP-Gly2, a critical residue for binding ubiquitin, did not impact InlC binding to CYLD as determined by co-immunoprecipitation (Supplementary Fig. 3a, b ). Furthermore, using a cell-free system with full-length recombinant CYLD, we did not observe any impact of InlC on CYLD deubiquitinase activity against either Lys63- or Met1-linkages (Supplementary Fig. 3c ). Thus, InlC binds the CAP-Gly2 domain of CYLD, independently of CAP-Gly2-ubiquitin binding, and does not impact the deubiquitinase activity of CYLD.

Next, we examined critical residues of InlC that mediate binding to the CAP-Gly2 domain of CYLD (Fig. 2e ). Mutation of bulky hydrophobic residues I159A or F182A within InlC reduced binding affinity to CAP-Gly2 (4-fold and 166-fold, respectively), whereas introduction of a negative charge abolished (I159D) or severely reduced (F182E, 2568-fold) binding. Also of note, the disruption of hydrogen bonds from InlC Lys236 reduced binding affinity to CAP-Gly2 by 264-fold. Previous work revealed that host-mediated ubiquitination of InlC impacts its interaction with host proteins during Lm infection 20 . This led us to question whether modification of other InlC lysine residues, potential targets of ubiquitination 20 , influenced binding to CYLD in a cellular context. However, mutagenesis of all other lysine residues of InlC did not affect CYLD binding (Supplementary Fig. 3d, e ). Furthermore, using recombinant proteins, a GST pulldown assay confirmed that InlC K236A blocked binding to CAP-Gly2 (Supplementary Fig. 3f ). We conclude that Ile159 and Lys236 of InlC play critical roles in binding to the CAP-Gly2 domain of CYLD.

During the cytosolic phase of Lm infection, secreted InlC binds the cortical actin regulator TUBA to promote Lm protrusion formation 14 , 15 . The LRR domain of InlC mediates binding to the sixth Src Homology 3 domain (SH3-6) present in TUBA, and InlC Phe146 was identified as a critical residue at this binding interface 14 . Overlay of the InlC-CAP-Gly2 structure with a previously determined structure of InlC bound to the SH3-6 domain of TUBA (PDB: 4CC4) revealed independent binding sites on opposing faces of InlC (Supplementary Fig. 4a ). This finding was experimentally validated through ITC as both WT and K236A InlC bound the purified SH3-6 domain of TUBA (Supplementary Fig. 4b ). In contrast, mutation of InlC Phe146 to alanine (F146A) abrogated binding to TUBA, consistent with prior observations 14 (Supplementary Fig. 4b ).

InlC can also bind IKK-α, and this interaction is suggested to dampen immune signaling during infection 21 . Using a co-immunoprecipitation assay with eGFP-InlC as bait, we found that the InlC F146A mutation also blocked binding to IKK-α/-β/-γ (Supplementary Fig. 4c ). In contrast, InlC mutants that perturb CYLD binding (I159D and K236A) did not impact the interaction of InlC with the IKK complex. We conclude that the LRR domain of InlC employs two different binding sites for its host protein targets.

To understand the role of InlC-CYLD binding during infection, we complemented ∆ inlC strains with InlC mutants defective in CYLD binding (Fig. 2f ). Using tools previously described 27 , FLAG epitope-tagged mutants of inlC were stably integrated into the tRNA Arg locus of the Lm chromosome. These strains were then used for infection of bone marrow-derived macrophages, major contributors of host defense amidst listeriosis 28 . Following 6.5 h post-infection, immunoprecipitation of InlC-FLAG recovered endogenous CYLD, whereas this interaction was ablated in strains harboring InlC I159D or K236A (Fig. 2g ). As expected, CYLD-binding defective mutants of InlC retained binding to IKK-α. In contrast, the F146A mutant retained binding to CYLD but was defective in binding IKK-α. These interactions were also observed in Lm -infected HeLa cells (Supplementary Fig. 4d ), indicating they are not specific to macrophages.

We then visualized transiently expressed HA-CYLD during Lm infection of RAW264.7 macrophages. In WT Lm -infected cells at 4 h post-infection, HA-CYLD was recruited to a subset of bacteria (17%), where it co-localized with ubiquitinated proteins detected by the FK2 monoclonal antibody (Fig. 3a, b ). Recruitment of HA-CYLD to bacteria was not observed in ∆ inlC or a triple mutant strain (∆ hly ∆ plcA ∆ plcB ) that is unable to escape the phagosome. Prior studies demonstrated that the non-motile strain (Δ actA ) is heavily ubiquitinated in the cytosol of host cells 2 , 10 . Consistent with this, we observed a significant increase in HA-CYLD recruitment to Δ actA mutant bacteria (81%) (Fig. 3b ). A time course experiment revealed that InlC accumulation in host cells coincided with the emergence of HA-CYLD-positive Δ actA bacteria at 3–4 h post-infection (Supplementary Fig. 5a–c ). In both the case of WT and Δ actA infection, all HA-CYLD-positive bacteria were found to be positive for ubiquitin (Supplementary Fig. 5d ).

Given that HA-CYLD recruitment to ubiquitin-positive Lm coincided with InlC accumulation, we hypothesized that InlC promotes CYLD recruitment to a cytosolic population of bacteria upon recognition by the host ubiquitin system. To test this, we utilized the Δ actA mutant to exploit the prevalence of HA-CYLD recruitment during infection. A double knockout strain (∆ actA ∆ inlC ) revealed the essential role of InlC in recruiting CYLD to ubiquitinated bacteria (Fig. 3c, d ). Complementation of the ∆ actA ∆ inlC strain with either wild-type inlC or the F146A mutant restored HA-CYLD recruitment to bacteria; however, CYLD-binding defective (I159D, K236A) mutants of InlC could not complement this recruitment. Using an antibody to detect endogenous CYLD, we confirmed its recruitment to the bacterial surface in an InlC-dependent manner (Supplementary Fig. 6 ). Consistent with our structural observations, mutation of the CAP-Gly2 domain was also sufficient to disrupt HA-CYLD recruitment to Δ actA mutant Lm (Supplementary Fig. 7a ). InlC-dependent HA-CYLD recruitment was also observed in mouse embryonic fibroblasts, a cell type previously used to study host ubiquitin defenses against Lm 2 (Supplementary Fig. 7b ). Thus, InlC promotes CYLD recruitment to ubiquitinated Lm in the cytosol of host cells.

Next, we asked if InlC also accumulates at the surface of ubiquitin-positive bacteria. For this, we infected cells with Lm expressing pLOV- inlC -FLAG for complementation of Δ inlC Lm with either wildtype inlC or single-point mutants defective in binding to CYLD (I159D, K236A). At 4 h post infection, cells were fixed and stained for the FLAG epitope to visualize the localization of InlC-FLAG. In accordance with previous studies 13 , 21 , we observed a diffuse, cytosolic signal for InlC that was above the background of the FLAG epitope antibody observed in cells infected with Lm transformed with an empty vector (i.e., no FLAG-tag expressed) (Supplementary Fig. 8a ). However, we did not observe enrichment of InlC at ubiquitin-positive bacteria, including non-motile Lm (Δ actA Δ inlC ). Similar cytosolic staining was observed in Lm strains expressing either WT InlC or CYLD-defective binding mutants, suggesting that InlC localization in the cytosol is unaltered by CYLD binding. Accordingly, we did not detect co-enrichment of InlC alongside HA-CYLD at ubiquitin-positive bacteria using both motile and non-motile Lm (Supplementary Fig. 8b ). Taken together, these results suggest that InlC does not accumulate at the surface of ubiquitin-positive Lm alongside CYLD.

The absence of InlC enrichment at CYLD-positive bacteria led us to question how CYLD is recruited to cytosolic Lm . We postulated that beyond InlC binding, there may be intrinsic factors of CYLD required for successful delivery and/or retention at the bacterial surface. Within CYLD’s USP domain lies a zinc-binding B-box module (Supplementary Fig. 9a ) that permits intermolecular interactions and partially regulates CYLD localization 23 , 29 . In uninfected RAW264.7 macrophages, HA-CYLD retained cytosolic localization upon deletion of this module (Supplementary Fig. 9b). While deletion of this module did not impair InlC-CYLD binding (Supplementary Fig. 9c ), we observed impaired recruitment of HA-CYLD ΔB-box to ubiquitin-positive Δ actA bacteria (Supplementary Fig. 9d ). A lack of recruitment was also observed with truncated versions of HA-CYLD lacking either its USP or CAP-Gly domains, despite the former retaining InlC-CAP-Gly2 binding (Supplementary Fig. 9c, d ). These findings suggest a co-requirement of InlC-CAP-Gly2 binding and the presence of CYLD’s B-box module for InlC-dependent CYLD recruitment to the bacterial surface.

Previous studies highlighted the critical role of ActA in evading host-ubiquitin defenses 10 , 30 , 31 . As Δ actA bacteria are vulnerable to detection by host ubiquitin defenses, we questioned the motility status of CYLD-positive WT Lm . Co-staining of HA-CYLD alongside filamentous actin (F-actin) revealed that the majority of CYLD-positive WT Lm were surrounded by non-polarized actin (referred to as actin clouds) (87%), indicating that the bacteria were not yet motile (Supplementary Fig. 10a, b ). Only a small fraction of CYLD-positive Lm was devoid of polymerized actin (11%), and in rare instances, displayed a comet tail (<2%). In agreement with these observations, we found that actin clouds were present at most ubiquitin-positive WT and Δ inlC bacteria (Supplementary Fig. 10c, d ). Notably, amongst motile strains we observed a modest yet significant increase (12%) in the frequency of ubiquitin-positive bacteria upon loss of InlC (Supplementary Fig. 10e ). These observations led us to speculate that the InlC-dependent recruitment of CYLD to the bacterial surface serves to accelerate ubiquitin clearance prior to actin-based motility.

To determine the functional impact of CYLD recruitment to ubiquitinated bacteria, we performed CRISPR-mediated knockout of Cyld in RAW264.7 cells (Supplementary Fig. 11a ) and complemented these cells by expression of either wildtype (Supplementary Fig. 11b , upper panels) or catalytically inactive HA-CYLD (C601A) (Supplementary Fig. 11b , lower panels). Macrophages were then infected with Δ actA bacteria, fixed and stained for total ubiquitinated proteins (FK2 + ), Lys63-linked ubiquitin, and Met1-linked ubiquitin as indicated (Supplementary Fig. 11b ). While both forms of HA-CYLD were recruited to bacteria at a similar frequency (Supplementary Fig. 11c ), we measured a significant decrease of Lys63-linked ubiquitin staining in wildtype HA-CYLD-transfected cells compared to catalytically inactive HA-CYLD (Supplementary Fig. 11d ). In contrast, total ubiquitinated proteins or Met1-linked ubiquitin were unaffected by wildtype HA-CYLD recruitment to bacteria. These findings suggest that CYLD recruited to the bacterial surface is catalytically active, with a preference towards deubiquitinating Lys63-linkages.

The E3 ligase RNF213 plays a major role in ubiquitin-dependent cellular defenses against cytosolic pathogens and is known to promote ubiquitination events on the surface of Lm 2 , 11 . Given that HA-CYLD was recruited to ubiquitin-positive Lm , we hypothesized that RNF213 may be required. To test this possibility, we performed CRISPR-mediated knockout of Rnf213 in RAW264.7 cells (Supplementary Fig. 12a ) and found these cells were unable to accumulate ubiquitin on the surface of Δ actA mutant bacteria (Supplementary Fig. 12b, c ), consistent with previous findings 2 . In Rnf213 KO RAW264.7 cells, we also did not observe HA-CYLD recruitment to either WT or Δ actA bacteria (Fig. 3e, f ). Thus, RNF213 is required for the InlC-dependent recruitment of CYLD to cytosolic Lm .

In agreement with original findings in macrophages 12 , we observed that loss of InlC did not affect the growth of motile or non-motile Lm strains in RAW264.7 cells (Supplementary Fig. 13a, b ). While RNF213-mediated defenses can be augmented upon interferon stimulation 32 , we similarly did not observe an InlC-dependent impact on bacterial growth in IFN-γ-primed cells (Supplementary Fig. 13a, b ). We also observed that loss of InlC did not affect Lm cell-to-cell spread in either RAW264.7 cells (Supplementary Fig. 13c, d ) or MEFs (Supplementary Fig. 13e, f ), including untreated or IFN-γ-primed cells. These findings led us to speculate that InlC-CYLD binding may counteract host defenses encountered in vivo.

Prior studies established that Rnf213 knockout mice are more susceptible to Lm infection 11 , indicating an important role for host ubiquitin defenses during systemic disease. In addition, optimal Lm virulence in mice was found to require InlC 12 , 33 . Building on this knowledge, we sought to determine the contribution of InlC-CYLD binding to Lm virulence using a murine model of systemic listeriosis.

Animals were infected by tail vein injection with WT or ∆ inlC strains complemented with either wildtype inlC or the K236A mutant. Animal weight was monitored over the course of infection (Fig. 4a ). Three days post-infection, we observed significant weight loss in mice infected with WT (11.66%) or ∆ inlC + inlC bacteria (10.42%) compared to groups infected with ∆ inlC (2.84%) or ∆ inlC + K236A (4.28%) (Fig. 4b ). Higher bacterial burdens (~1 log) were also observed in the spleen and liver of animals infected with wildtype inlC -expressing strains (Fig. 4c, d ). We then visualized the distribution of infection within the liver (Fig. 4e ), a major site of Lm growth 6 . In accordance with animal weight loss and higher bacterial burden, we found that strains expressing wild-type inlC displayed a greater number of infection foci throughout the liver compared to Δ inlC or InlC K236A-expressing strains (Fig. 4f ). Thus, we conclude that InlC-CYLD binding promotes optimal Lm virulence during systemic infection in mice.

Initial findings by Perrin et al. demonstrated the importance of ActA-mediated evasion from the host ubiquitin system 10 . Here, we reveal a cooperative role for InlC in the Lm strategy to counteract ubiquitin-mediated host defenses by promoting recruitment of the host deubiquitinase CYLD to the bacterial surface following recognition by the ubiquitin E3 ligase, RNF213 (Fig. 5 ). Despite the protection conferred by ActA, we postulate the need for a complementary evasion mechanism during the stage of infection following phagosome escape and prior to actin-based motility.

Upon internalization by a host cell, Listeria monocytogenes ( Lm ) undergoes phagosome escape through expression of a pore-forming toxin and phospholipase C enzymes. Entry into the cytosol permits RNF213-mediated ubiquitination of cytosolic bacteria. However, Lm can overcome this defense through secretion of InlC, which interacts with the CAP-Gly2 region of CYLD. InlC targets CYLD to the surface of ubiquitinated bacteria, where it can remove Lys63-linked ubiquitin. At the bacterial surface, ActA production also contributes to evasion of ubiquitin-mediated defenses. During systemic disease, InlC-CYLD binding promotes bacterial growth in the liver and spleen of mice.

Our findings reveal that the LRR domain of InlC has two binding sites for its host protein targets. We propose that InlC acts through these host binding partners to execute different functions over the course of infection. Upon phagosome escape, bacteria are exposed to the cytosol and susceptible to innate detection such as RNF213-mediated ubiquitination 11 . To counter this, InlC binds CYLD to indirectly promote deubiquitinase recruitment to the bacterial surface. At later stages of infection, bacteria undergo actin-based motility to evade further recognition by the ubiquitin system. InlC then serves a second function, targeting TUBA through its SH3-6 domain to promote protrusion formation 14 . In this manner, InlC may serve as a protein scaffold, analogous to viral proteins such as Tax (HTLV-1) 34 and Nsp1α (PRRSV) 35 , which control different aspects of the virus lifecycle.

How does InlC promote recruitment of CYLD to the bacterial surface? The lack of InlC enrichment at the surface of ubiquitin-positive bacteria suggests several possible mechanisms. First, InlC may traffic CYLD to the bacterial surface and then become rapidly displaced upon the association of CYLD with target substrates. Such a dynamic interaction of InlC with the bacterial surface would likely be undetected with the immunofluorescence microscopy approach applied in this study. Second, InlC-CYLD binding may operate through a displacement model, analogous to InlC-TUBA binding, which involves the displacement of N-WASP 14 . In this scenario, InlC binding to the CAP-Gly2 domain would displace CYLD from preexisting locations, such as microtubules and immune receptors 25 , 26 . In support of this mechanism, recent evidence highlights the peptide-binding abilities of CYLD’s CAP-Gly domains, which serve as auxiliary regions to regulate deubiquitinase localization 36 . A major limitation in our ability to assess this displacement model arises from the use of CYLD overexpression. Live-cell imaging of endogenously tagged CYLD may elucidate whether InlC promotes the recruitment of distinct populations of CYLD. Third, it remains possible that another host or bacterial factor is required to translocate CYLD to the bacterial surface. The inability of InlC to promote the recruitment of a truncated form of CYLD comprising only CAP-Gly1-3, despite proper binding, revealed a requirement for CYLD’s C-terminus for successful recruitment. In the context of immune signaling, the B-box-dependent dimerization of CYLD permits binding to SPATA2, an adapter protein that facilitates CYLD recruitment to immune receptors 23 . Our identification of the B-box as a necessary determinant for CYLD translocation suggests a similar role for CYLD dimerization and additional host factors to mediate CYLD delivery.

Here, we identify RNF213 as a critical host determinant for the ubiquitination of Lm in macrophages. While RNF213 possesses a RING domain, coating of Lm has been demonstrated to occur non-canonically through an RZ finger domain 2 . In the case of gram-negative bacteria, RNF213-mediated ubiquitination leads to the recruitment of additional E3 ligases such as the linear ubiquitin chain assembly complex (LUBAC) 3 . Recent evidence suggests that ubiquitination by RNF213 is the predominant cue for CYLD recruitment to Lm rather than ensuing E3 ligases such as LUBAC 37 . The ability of RNF213 to interact with, and even ubiquitinate CYLD 38 , 39 raises the possibility of interplay between these two proteins at the bacterial surface. Whether RNF213 has scaffolding functions at the bacterial surface independent of its E3 ligase activity remains an area of future exploration.

Other intracellular pathogens can disrupt ubiquitin-mediated cellular defenses through secreted virulence proteins. For example, Chlamydia trachomatis secretes a deubiquitinase (Cdu1) 40 that acts cooperatively with GarD 32 to protect pathogen-containing inclusions from RNF213-mediated ubiquitination. Shigella flexneri translocates a member of the IpaH family of bacterial E3 ubiquitin ligases into host cells to selectively target RNF213 for degradation 4 . During Burkholderia pseudomallei infection, a secreted deubiquitinase (TssM) reverses RNF213-dependent ubiquitination 5 . The host and bacterial factors subject to ubiquitination/deubiquitination reactions during Lm infection remain unknown. RNF213 is known to ubiquitinate lipopolysaccharide on the surface of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium 3 , a target lacking on gram-positive bacteria. It remains plausible that an abundant lipid species of the Listeria cell wall, such as teichoic acids, is a substrate of RNF213 activity. Our findings indicate that during Lm infection, CYLD acts to selectively reverse RNF213-dependent ubiquitination events with a preference for Lys63-linkages, akin to CYLD’s role at innate receptors 23 . Whether CYLD catalyzes the removal of Lys63-linked ubiquitin attributed to RNF213 activity 41 or ensuing E3 ligases remains to be elucidated. InlC-CYLD binding may also have additional roles beyond the bacterial surface.

Cyld −/− mice are known to be protected from systemic Lm infection 42 . This protection is thought to be conferred by CYLD’s homeostatic role in the regulation of ubiquitin-dependent immune responses 43 . In support of this notion, Cyld −/− mice display enhanced inflammation, reduced cell apoptosis and impaired intracellular growth of Lm 42 , 44 , 45 . Here, using site-specific binding mutants of InlC, we show that InlC-CYLD binding is required for full virulence of Lm in mice. During listeriosis, immune cells express an isoform of CYLD lacking the CAP-Gly3 domain to augment immune signaling 46 , 47 . Our results suggest Lm exploits the conserved nature of the CAP-Gly2 domain to retain InlC-CYLD binding and bypass this host adaptation.

Lastly, our in vivo findings suggest InlC-CYLD binding contributes to Lm virulence. We propose that InlC-dependent CYLD recruitment promotes bacterial fitness against ubiquitin-mediated defenses encountered in vivo. We speculate that InlC promotes bacterial survival within primary-infected regions during the initial stages of infection, resulting in more dissemination events as infection proceeds. The importance of establishing multiple foci for virulence is reflected in clinical observations of listeriosis where increased focus number is associated with a poorer prognosis 48 . We conclude that CYLD is relevant to Lm infection for both its homeostatic role in immune regulation and as a specific target of a bacterial virulence factor. As such, our findings provide further insight into how intracellular pathogens modulate host ubiquitin defenses.
