Note that the KKKC/ATP system forms coacervates when oxidized electrochemically but not after reaction with NaBO 3 . [KKKC] = [ATP] = 1.34 mM, [pAA] = 4 mM (in monomer units) [NaCl] = 100 mM in the samples with pAA, 10 mM in the samples with ATP. The size of scale bars is 25 µm.

First, we explored the oxidation of KKKC and its effect on coacervate formation. Mixing KKKC with either pAA or ATP did not lead to coacervate formation in our experimental conditions. When KKKC was oxidized by the addition of NaBO 3 , the solution containing pAA became turbid, and we could observe the formation of coacervates by optical microscopy (Fig. 2b ). On the other hand, the sample containing ATP did not form coacervates even after oxidation, indicating that complexation is less favorable in this case due to the lower multivalency of ATP. Oxidation with H 2 O 2 also led to coacervate formation, while reduction with TCEP led to coacervate dissolution, confirming the redox-responsiveness of these coacervates (Fig. S1 ). Having confirmed that coacervation can be triggered by chemical oxidation, we studied if the same could be achieved electrochemically. For this, we prepared an undivided cell by introducing flat silver electrodes in a solution containing KKKC and pAA, and applied an external potential with a commercial power supply. The solution was not degassed, and therefore oxygen could act as a sacrificial electron acceptor as a counter-reaction to the oxydation of KKKC 45 . Note that, in the final system, the oxydation of MV is the counter-reaction (see below). As soon as the potential was applied, we observed the formation of coacervate droplets close to the surface of the anode (Fig. 2c ). No droplets were observed in absence of either pAA or KKKC, confirming that these droplets were indeed the result of complex coacervation (Fig. S2 ). We used Ellman’s test (Fig. S3 ) and 1 H-NMR spectroscopy (Fig. S4 ) to characterize their chemical composition, revealing that electrochemical oxidation also results in thiol oxidation and the formation of a disulfide dimer. Previous reports have shown that cysteine derivatives are difficult to oxidize on the surface of solid electrodes 46 – 48 . Particularly, Guan and coworkers did not observe the formation of disulfides on a glassy carbon electrode (GCE), only detecting irreversible oxidation at high potentials 49 . This was also the case for KKKC, for which we could not detect any electrochemical response by cyclic voltammetry (CV) or coacervate formation when using a GCE as a working electrode (Figs. S5 and S6 ). On the other hand, when the working electrode was changed to silver, we detected a broad anodic peak corresponding to the oxidation of thiols to disulfides at 160 mV (Fig. S7 ), consistent with our observations in the undivided cell. The reverse reaction could also be observed, as a broad reduction peak between −0.3 and −0.1 V. We ascribe the difference between the two electrodes to the high affinity of thiols for silver 50 – 52 .

Surprisingly, the KKKC/ATP system also formed coacervates upon electrochemical oxidation (Fig. 2c ), even if it did not when oxidized with NaBO 3 . We initially hypothesized that this difference was due to the ionic by-products resulting from the chemical oxidation: the reaction between NaBO 3 and KKKC produces borate salts, which increase the ionic strength of the solution, potentially preventing coacervate formation. However, adding an excess of different borate salts to electrochemically-formed coacervates did not result in coacervate dissolution (Fig. S8a ). Increasing the pH of chemically-oxidized samples did not lead to coacervate formation either, which excludes the possibility of the pKa of ATP changing in the electric field (Fig. S8b ) 53 . Preparing (KKKC) 2 by electrochemical oxidation and mixing it with ATP once that the potential had been removed also led to coacervates, further excluding any possible effects due to the electric field (Fig. S8c ). Finally, we examined the possibility that Ag + ions, coming from the electrode surface, could be facilitating coacervate formation. To our surprise, adding small amounts of AgNO 3 to (KKKC) 2 /ATP mixtures formed by chemical oxidation resulted in the formation of complex coacervates (Fig. S8d ). In order to characterize this effect, we determined the salt resistance (SR) of (KKKC) 2 /ATP and (KKKC) 2 /pAA coacervates in presence and in absence of AgNO 3 (Figs. S9 and S10 ). In all of the cases, the addition of Ag + to the medium led to an increase in the SR of the coacervates, indicating an increase in their stability. We hypothesize that this stabilization is due to the formation of a complex between Ag + and KKKC 2 , which links multiple peptides together, increasing their multivalency. The formation of complexes between Ag + and disulphides has been previously described, markedly between multiple silver ions and disulphide-containing molecules 54 . Similar complexes formed between Ag + and (KKKC) 2 should be highly charged, and therefore much more prone to coacervation. Additionally, the Ag + ions could act as reversible crosslinks, stabilizing the coacervate phase. The stabilizing effect of silver was more pronounced for coacervates with an excess of positive charges, confirming the binding between Ag + and peptides. However, adding too large of an excess of either peptide or ATP/pAA quickly resulted in coacervate dissolution, indicating that the crosslinking due to Ag + was weak compared to electrostatic repulsion. Importantly, when the same titrations were performed in presence of an excess of TCEP, no phase separation could be detected for any of the systems, even in presence of Ag + and with no added NaCl. It is important to note that all the subsequent experiments in this work that involve coacervate formation and destruction were performed with KKKC:pAA and a salt concentration of 100 mM, conditions in which the electrochemistry-mediated formation of coacervates is independent of Ag + .

Coacervate droplets can move in electric fields by electrophoresis 42 , 43 . Both the direction and the velocity of this movement depend on the ζ-potential of the droplets, and thus on the ratio between positive and negative charges in their composition. Determining the ζ-potential for coacervates cannot be done with conventional methods 42 , and requires an in-depth characterization of their viscosity, which we could not do in the current systems due to the large volumes of coacervate required. For this reason, we did not calculate the ζ-potential of these coacervates, and instead relied on electrophoretic speed as an indication of their relative surface charge. To determine the speed of (KKKC) 2 -containing coacervates and optimize their movement for a complete electrochemical cycle, we tracked the position of individual droplets over time, after the application of an electric field. (Fig. 3 , Supplementary Video 1 ). When KKKC and pAA were mixed in a stoichiometric charge ratio (1:1) and an electric field of 0.95 V/cm was applied (0.7 V, 0.74 cm), the coacervates moved towards the cathode with a constant speed of ~1 µm/s, indicating that their overall charge was slightly positive but close to neutral. When KKKC was added in excess (2.5:1 charge ratio), their speed increased to 12.5 µm/s, and the droplets reached the cathode in ca. 10 min. This confirmed that the movement of the coacervates was mainly driven by electrophoresis, and that the non-stoichiometric mixing ratio between precursors was translated to a charge imbalance in the composition of the coacervates. For the systems containing ATP as the oligoanion, a 1:1 mixing ratio resulted in negatively-charged droplets (Fig. S11 ), consistent with other ATP-containing coacervates 42 . These droplets initially moved away from the anode due to droplet-droplet repulsion, but after an initial displacement they started moving back towards it. This resulted in a fixed front of coacervates that remained ~30 µm away from the electrode surface. Increasing the amount of KKKC in this system resulted in positively-charged coacervates that moved towards the cathode, but still at a slower speed than in the system containing pAA. These results show that there is a direct relationship between the composition of coacervates and their movement speed. Therefore, the mixing ratio between polycation and polyanion can be used to control the lifetime of the droplets: since coacervate destruction only takes place in the proximity of the cathode (see below), slower coacervates will have a longer lifetime and vice-versa.

Keeping a constant electric potential for longer than 10 min led to a continuous flow of coacervate droplets reaching the cathode. Even though we could not monitor the behavior of these droplets on the surface of the electrode (due to the latter blocking the light in our setup), we could detect their coalescence by the formation of a continuous coacervate phase in the bottom of the cell (Fig. S13 ). While some droplets sink to the bottom of the cell through its entire length, the coalesced phase was distinctly propagating from the cathode, indicating that coacervates were accumulating in that area instead of reacting. In other words, the rate at which coacervates were dissolved by the electrochemical reduction of (KKKC) 2 was significantly slower than the rate at which they formed and reached the cathode. We hypothesize that this accumulation is caused by a difference in reaction rates between oxidation and reduction: while KKKC is soluble and its thiol group is easily accessible, most of the (KKKC) 2 that reaches the cathode is in the form of coacervates, which potentially shield the disulfides from reaching the surface of the electrode. We confirmed this hypothesis by CV (Fig. S14 ): while the peak corresponding to the oxidation of KKKC was practically identical in presence or in absence of pAA, the current corresponding to disulfide reduction was significantly smaller when pAA was added. This indicates that a significant fraction of disulfides is unavailable for reaction after the coacervates are formed.

In order to facilitate the reduction of (KKKC) 2 and the dissolution of coacervates, we used methyl viologen (MV) as an electrocatalyst. Methyl viologen is an organic divalent cation that can be reduced to the radical cation MV ·+ , which in turn reacts with disulfides, reducing them chemically 37 . Since MV ·+ is small and relatively stable, it can diffuse in and out of the coacervates, reacting with (KKKC) 2 and regenerating MV and KKKC (Fig. 4a ). We tested this reaction by CV (Figs. 4b , S15 and S16 ). In presence of coacervates, a new cathodic peak appeared for MV at −594 mV, a slightly lower potential than its reduction in water (−682 mV). We attribute this peak to the reduction of the MV molecules that are compartmentalized into the coacervates. Since the coacervate phase is relatively hydrophobic, the coacervate droplets can sequester MV from the solution, acting as a new solvent and changing the ΔG of the reduction 19 . The intensity of the peak increases with each cycle of oxidation and reduction, consistent with the formation of more coacervates on the surface of the electrode. While the reduction of free MV in water is reversible, the cathodic peak at −594 mV appears to be irreversible. This is consistent with a chemical reaction consuming MV ·+ as soon as it is formed 37 – in this case, the reduction of (KKKC) 2 . Next, we confirmed that the MV-mediated reduction of (KKKC) 2 led to the dissolution of coacervates. For that, we prepared a sample containing KKKC, pAA, and MV, and generated coacervates by using a constant electric potential of 0.7 V. This potential already generates enough MV ·+ to reduce (KKKC) 2 and enable the recirculation of material (as shown below), but to clearly visualize the effect, we waited until some coacervate droplets had settled on the bottom of the cell next to the cathode and applied a higher potential (1.5 V). As soon as this potential was applied, we observed a blue color next to the cathode, characteristic of the MV ·+ radical cation (Fig. 4c ). The intensity of the color was significantly stronger within the coacervates than in the surrounding solution, indicating that the diffusion of MV ·+ into the coacervate phase is a favorable process. Furthermore, the size of the coacervates decreased quickly after the application of the potential, confirming the MV-mediated reduction leads to the dissolution of the coacervates (Fig. 4d ). Finally, we studied the chemical reduction and oxidation of (KKKC) 2 /pAA coacervates in presence of MV (Fig. S17 ), showing that the compartmentalization of MV in the coacervates does not affect their redox-responsiveness.

When the coacervates are dissolved, free KKKC and pAA can return to the anode (by diffusion or by convective flows generated by the movement of coacervates) and participate in oxidation and coacervate formation again. In this way, the system can be driven into a sustained formation-movement-destruction regime. We characterized this regime in two systems containing KKKC and pAA. Only one of the systems contained MV, enabling the regeneration and recirculation of coacervate precursors, while the other one was taken as a control with only the “forward” part of the cycle (Figs. 5 , S18 , Supplementary Video 2 , Supplementary Video 3 ). For each system, we prepared two samples and studied them for a long period of time during the application of an electric potential, in one case monitoring the proximity of the anode and in the other one monitoring the proximity of the cathode. In an initial stage, both systems were almost identical, and we could observe the formation of coacervates next to the anode followed by their migration towards the cathode (Figs. 5a , S19 ). The number of droplets forming next to the anode increased for the first hour before starting to decrease as KKKC and pAA were depleted. As expected, the same trend was observed on the cathode, albeit with a short delay due to the movement along the cell. Additionally, the droplet density was slightly lower at the cathode than at the anode, as some of the coacervates sank to the bottom of the cell along the way, leading to a loss of material.

After this initial period, the number of coacervates continued to drop quickly in the system without MV, until no more droplets could be observed after 5 h at the anode (Fig. 5b ) or 8.5 h at the cathode (Fig. 5c ). We took this point as the moment in which the concentration of KKKC next to the anode was too low for oxidation, and the reaction could not continue without the recirculation of material. In the case of the system containing MV, the number of coacervates also decreased initially, but it never stopped completely. On the contrary, the system reached a steady state after 6 h, with a constant number of coacervates being produced and destroyed at the two respective electrodes. This steady state could be maintained for at least another 10 h without any significant changes, for a total of more than 16 h of simultaneous formation, movement and destruction. In order to confirm the role of MV in this cycle, we repeated the electrochemically-driven experiments in two samples without MV, waiting until the proximity of the anode was depleted of droplets in both of them (Fig. S20 , Supplementary Video 4 ). We then added a solution of MV to one of the samples, and the same volume of water to the other. In the sample to which MV was added, we observed a quick increase in the density of droplets next to the anode, followed by a steady state similar to that reached in Fig. 5 . On the other hand, no significant changes were observed in the sample where water was added, confirming that the formation of new droplets was mediated by MV and not simply an effect of mixing.

In order to quantify the regeneration of thiols by the reaction between MV and (KKKC) 2 , we prepared six coacervate samples by oxidation of KKKC in presence of pAA. We then applied an electric potential and added MV to three of them, while the other three were used as controls to which water was added. Immediately after the addition of MV, the concentration of thiols doubled, confirming the ability of MV to reduce the disulfides inside of the coacervates and regenerate KKKC (Fig. S21 ). As an additional characterization of the electrochemical reactions involved in this system, we performed chronoamperometric measurements, comparing the amount of total charge to the conversion of KKKC to calculate the Faradaic efficiency of the electrochemical cell (Fig. S22 ). In absence of MV, the Faradaic efficiency was very low (15 ± 10%), indicating multiple competing side-reactions and a low efficiency for thiol oxidation. On the other hand, when the same experiment was repeated in samples containing MV, the apparent Faradaic efficiency of the system was significantly higher for the first two min of the reaction (up to 30 ± 10%), due to a higher conversion of thiols to disulfides. It is worth remarking that, when MV is present in the system, the disulfides that are produced in the anode can react with the MV ·+ produced in the cathode and convert back to thiols, decreasing the apparent conversion. Therefore, the reported 30 ± 10% value for the sample containing MV is an underestimation of the real Faradaic efficiency. This experiment showed that the presence of MV contributes to the sustained operation of this system in two ways: by reducing (KKKC) 2 and replenishing the thiols in the anode, but also by providing a suitable counter-reaction to thiol oxidation and increasing the Faradaic efficiency of the cell.

To evaluate the effect of oxygen in this system, we repeated the experiment of Fig. 5 using a degassed solution and sealing the experimental setup to prevent exchange with air (Fig. S23 , Supplementary Video 5 ). This degassed sample behaved in a similar way to those shown in Fig. 5 , reaching a steady state after approximately 6 h. However, this steady state contained a significantly higher number of droplets, confirming that oxygen hampers the sustained formation of coacervates in this system. We hypothesize two different reasons for this: first, the reduction of O 2 in the surface of the cathode can compete with the reduction of MV, preventing the regeneration of thiols. Second, oxygen can accelerate the passivation of the electrodes due to the formation of silver oxide. Nonetheless, the steady state still stopped after 18 h in the degassed experiment, a comparable time to the experiments in which oxygen was not removed. This confirms that other factors are responsible for the eventual collapse of the steady state, such as the degradation of the electrodes.

In order to characterize the changes happening in the system during the electrochemical cycle, we monitored the pH and conductivity of the reaction crude over a 21 h experiment (Fig. S24 ), as well as its composition using 1 H-NMR. Our results show that the conductivity of the system does not significantly change over the course of the experiment—therefore, the build-up of ions is negligible. The pH increases by ~1.0, likely due to the reduction of O 2 to OH - as a competing reaction taking place in the cathode. It is important to note that this difference in pH is well within the range of values in which KKKC 2 and pAA are charged, and the corresponding coacervates remain stable and redox-responsive in this window (Fig. S25 ). Finally, we could not observe significant changes in the 1 H-NMR spectrum of the mixture (Fig. S26 ), besides the oxidation of KKKC to its disulphide and a shift of the KKKC peaks, likely due to the change in pH. Over the course of the experiment, the coacervates themselves remained as spherical droplets, with a slight increase in their size—from 5 to 10 µm in diameter over 10 h of experiment. (Fig. S27 ) We attribute this change in size to a drift in the solution composition in the proximity of the anode, as KKKC and pAA should not diffuse back from the cathode at the same speed.

These results show that, while the current electrochemical setup is not completely innocent, the secondary processes that take place in the electrodes (e.g. silver leaching, oxygen reduction) do not have a major impact in coacervate formation or stability. Furthermore, none of these processes are directly connected to the reaction cycle that controls coacervate formation and dissolution. Therefore, these secondary processes can be minimized by optimizing the reaction conditions (e.g. electrode composition, cell geometry), without changing the coacervate components or the overall design. This represents a fundamental difference between electrically-fuelled and chemically-fuelled systems: this system eventually stops working due to practical constraints, but not to anything intrinsic to the system.

As described above, the transient formation and movement of coacervate droplets are particularly appealing because of their ability to compartmentalize and transport solutes. In order to test if the electrochemically-formed coacervates described in this work can be used as compartments, we incubated different fluorescent dyes in presence of electrochemically-generated (KKKC) 2 /pAA and (KKKC) 2 /ATP coacervates, and studied their partition by fluorescence microscopy (Figs. S28 – S31 ). Interestingly, the partition of the different dyes between solution and coacervate depends strongly on the chemical nature of the polyanion and the dyes, as well as the charge ratio and the salt concentration: depending on these parameters, some dyes were concentrated inside of the coacervates while others were excluded almost completely. It is worth remarking that these partition coefficients were determined after the overnight incubation of the dyes in presence of the coacervates, and therefore they represent equilibrated concentrations. In systems driven out-of-equilibrium, the gradients in concentration that are generated when the electric potential is applied might lead to further changes in the partition. The dye-containing coacervates still merged and coalesced, (Figs. S32 and S33 ) and the addition of TCEP resulted in their dissolution (Figs. S34 and S35 )—confirming that they still were liquid and redox-responsive. Additionally, we could observe the electrochemically-driven cycle of coacervate formation, movement, and destruction in presence of one of these dyes (Brooker’s merocyanine), including a decrease in the rate of coacervate formation when MV was absent and a recovery of activity when it was added to the solution (Fig. S20 ). Taken together, these results open the door for using these coacervates as selective transporters, with a preference for compartmentalizing and moving some cargo molecules over others.

To summarize, here we have designed a waste-free, electricity-driven system for the transient formation of complex coacervates. By applying a potential between two electrodes in an undivided cell, we were able to drive simultaneous coacervate formation and coacervate dissolution (mediated by an electrocatalyst) in different regions of the cell. Furthermore, the electrochemically-formed coacervates move by electrophoresis in the direction of the electric field, effectively going from the point where they are formed to the point where they are destroyed. Each coacervate moves over a distance of 7.4 mm, over three orders of magnitude larger than their size; and while the lifetime of individual droplets is ~10 min, the regime of coacervate formation, movement and destruction can be maintained for more than 16 h. Sustaining this regime for such a long period of time would have been practically impossible in a chemically-driven system, as the accumulation of ionic side-products in the solution would destabilize the coacervate phase.

The system described here can be used as a starting point to build artificial systems that exhibit coacervate-based active transport. We have shown different molecules to be more soluble inside of the coacervate phase than in the surrounding supernatant, spontaneously being sequestered inside of the droplets. By combining this spontaneous compartmentalization with an electric potential, one can envision coacervate droplets that form in the anode, sequester cargo from their surroundings, and transport it to the cathode, releasing it upon reduction of the coacervate. As long as the coacervate-mediated transport is faster than the diffusion of free solute back to the starting point, this would lead to electrically-driven transport using coacervates as transient carriers, and to the formation of a chemical gradient. Our preliminary data show that this transport can be selective, and this selectivity could be further enhanced by including specific binding motifs in the sequence of the coacervate-forming peptides.

The system shown here was kept as simple as possible, only including two flat electrodes with a constant electric field between them. However, by combining multiple electrodes in different geometries, more complex systems can be designed, with multiple sources and sinks of coacervate droplets, and complex flows between them.

articles.title: Heritable transgenic schistosomes as a living platform for SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing antibody secretion.
articles.authors: Ittiprasert W, Smout MJ, Mann VH, Moyle M, Kinahan SM, Ackerman DN, Rivera DN, Santarpia JL, Carnes EC, Mentink-Kane MM, Costa MR, Hokke CH, Roestenberg M, Bottazzi ME, Bracken BK, Rosa BA, Djuranovic S, Pickering DA, Giacomin PR, Watterson D, Modhiran N, Moescheid MF, Grevelding CG, Mitreva M, Loukas A, Brindley PJ.
articles.abstract: Abstract We report the generation and propagation of not only the first heritable transgenic schistosome line but also a line that secretes a functional therapeutic protein in vivo. Using multiplexed CRISPR/Cas-mediated homology-directed knock-in targeted to a predicted genomic safe-harbor, we inserted a VHH–IgG1 Fc (termed C5-Fc) transgene into Schistosoma mansoni eggs. Single-miracidium infections of Biomphalaria glabrata yielded parental P0 lines; serial passage through snail and mouse hosts produced an F2 cohort in which all parasites carried the C5-Fc transgene and secreted C5-Fc into the murine venous circulation. Molecular assays confirmed chromosomal insertion, germline transmission and systemic secretion. Sera from mice harboring C5-Fc transgenic worms neutralized SARS-CoV-2 in vitro with potent activity consistent with the expected ACE2-binding blockade by the C5 variable domain of heavy-chain-only antibody (VHH). These results demonstrate (i) stable, heritable transgenesis of a platyhelminth, (ii) delivery of a biologically active antibody fragment by a live helminth in a mammalian host, and (iii) feasibility of using transgenic schistosomes as sustained, single-dose protein delivery platforms. This technology and delivery system enable new experimental approaches for schistosome biology and motivate exploration of living-foundry therapeutics. Subject terms: Parasite genetics, Parasitic infection, CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, Mutagenesis, Immunization

A heritable CRISPR knock-in in Schistosoma mansoni generated a transgenic line that secreted a functional anti–SARS-CoV-2 antibody into mouse circulation. Virus neutralization by infected mouse sera demonstrated a worm-based living biofoundry for sustained, in vivo biologic delivery.

To date, heritably transgenic lines of schistosomes, or of any parasitic platyhelminth – clade Neodermata within phylum Platyhelminthes, have not been described. If such lines were available, progress in deciphering the biology and pathophysiology of these major neglected tropical disease (NTD) pathogens would be hastened, for example on fundamental questions such as what controls host range and specificity of the schistosome species, how do schistosomes locate their predilection site within the human host, which factors are decisive for bidirectional female-male interaction, and which genes encode target proteins of therapeutic value. As with other species, the ability to manipulate the schistosome would represent a step-change for the field and enable deep investigation of the (patho)biological nature of this pathogen. Transgenic lines of schistosomes also would be useful for investigating the value of helminth therapy for autoimmune and metabolic diseases 1 – 3 . The recent development of human challenge models of single-sex schistosome infections 4 , 5 paves the way for clinical assessment of transgenic schistosomes as living foundries for synthetic biology applications 6 . Pertinent also are recent reports that exposure to lung-migrating helminths, including schistosomes, protect against Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection through macrophage-dependent T cell activation and remodeling of the lung environment 7 , 8 . Tractable, routine derivation of transgenic lines of schistosomes, and indeed other helminths that are used therapeutically in human challenge models 9 , would be unarguably welcome.

Deploying Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats/CRISPR-associated (proteins) (CRISPR/Cas)-driven functional genomics including programmed knock out (KO) and knock-in (KI) mutagenesis for schistosomes was first reported in 2019, in research from our laboratory 10 . However, heritable transgenesis via insertion of a transgene into the germ line had not been achieved, reflecting multiple obstacles: a complex life cycle that cannot be completed in vitro, difficulties with transfection in a multicellular organism, limited germ-line access, lack of chromosomal safe-harbor sites, diploidy and dioecy, and sparse knowledge of secretion. We now report this advance, enabled by a combined suite of technical and conceptual innovations: 1) targeting transgene insertion to a predicted genome safe harbor site 11 , 12 ; 2) deploying several overlapping guide RNAs to enhance the likelihood of RNA-guided chromosomal double stranded break (DSB) and homology directed repair (HDR) by transgene insertion 13 – 15 ; and 3) by transfecting the immature egg stage of the schistosome 16 . Our goal was vertical transgene transmission via natural infection of the snail by the (transgenic) miracidium larval stage, and propagation of the transgenic schistosome line.

Derivation of a heritably transgenic line of S. mansoni represents transformative progress in tropical medicine. The line was established using CRISPR-based knock-in of an antibody-encoding transgene into the genome of the egg stage of S. mansoni . A parental female P0 and a parental male P0 generation were established by single miracidium exposure of the intermediate host, the aquatic gastropod Biomphalaria glabrata . Mice were infected with these P0 generation female and male line cercariae. Eggs subsequently recovered from the mice represented the F1 generation of the transgenic line, which we termed the “C5-Fc line”. In turn, snails were infected with miracidia hatched from the eggs. In this way, the C5-Fc line was propagated through to the F2 generation (Fig. 1 ). The transgene encodes an IgG1 Fc-fusion of C5, a variable domain of heavy-chain-only antibody (VHH) 17 , which targets the angiotensin converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor binding site of the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 18 . The C5-Fc line of schistosomes secreted the VHH into the blood of mice infected with these worms, and sera from these mice potently neutralized the SARS-CoV-2 virion.

a Life cycle highlighting human infection. Cercariae, released from Biomphalaria snails, penetrate skin and transform into schistosomula. These migrate via circulation and lungs to the hepatic portal system, where the adult female and male schistosomes pair and females deposit eggs. Eggs traverse the gut for fecal excretion or lodge in tissues, causing hepato-intestinal disease. Eggs hatch in water to release miracidia, which infect snails and develop asexually into sporocysts that produce cercariae. b Transgenesis workflow in the laboratory, using the mouse as a surrogate for the human definitive host 47 . Immature eggs (containing the schistosome zygote) were transfected with CRISPR components and transgenes 12 , 16 . Single-miracidium infections of B. glabrata (NMRI strain) 40 , 87 yield clonal, single-sex cercariae which infect mice, pair, and propagate transgenic lines. Transgenic schistosomes delivering a therapeutic encoded by the transgene represents a major goal of this endeavor 88 . Panel 1b created in BioRender. Smout, M. (2026) https://BioRender.com/2e178ah .

Amino acid sequences of three VHHs targeting the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein were obtained from the literature – VHH-C5 18 and VHH-E and VHH-V 19 along with a variant of VHH-C5 that was fused to the human IgG1 Fc domain, which we termed VHH-C5-Fc (Supplementary Fig. 1 ). All four VHHs expressed at high concentrations in HEK293F cells and were isolated in recombinant forms to >95% purity with single step, immobilized metal ion affinity chromatography (IMAC) (Supplementary Fig. 2a ). Recombinant VHHs were assayed for virus neutralizing capacity using two independent assays: 1) an immunofluorescence-visualized pseudotyped lentiviral plaque assay 20 , and 2) by the SARS-CoV-2 plaque reduction neutralization test (PRNT) 21 . For the pseudotyped lentiviral plaque assay, neutralization was benchmarked against the Human SARS-CoV-2 Convalescent Serology Standard from the National Institute for Biological Standards and Control (NIBSC), NIBSC 20/130 22 . All VHHs neutralized pseudotyped lentivirus in the low microgram (VHH-E, VHH-V) to nanogram per milliliter ranges (VHH-C5, VHH-C5-Fc) VHH-C5-Fc was more potent than VHH-C5 with IC 50 values of 5 ng/ml and 273 ng/ml, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 2b ).

After confirming the neutralizing activity of the VHHs against pseudotyped lentivirus (an assay surrogate for SARS-CoV-2), we tested their neutralizing capacity directly against an isolate, SARS-CoV-2 USA-WA1/2020 23 , by the PRNT 21 . Neutralization of SARS-CoV-2 in this assay was benchmarked against the Human SARS-CoV-2 Serology Standard from the Frederick National Laboratory for Cancer Research ( https://frederick.cancer.gov/resources/universal-standards-reference-materials/human-sars-cov-2-serology-standard ) 22 , 24 ; referred to here as FNLCR serum. Dose-dependent neutralization was obtained with all VHHs (Fig. 2a ) and as also seen in the pseudotyped lentivirus assay, VHH-C5 and VHH-C5-Fc were the more potent of these VHHs, with IC 50 values of 791 ng/ml and 24 ng/ml, respectively (Fig. 2b ).

a Dose-dependent neutralization measured by plaque reduction neutralization test. Percent reduction in plaque counts (relative to virus-only control), with each data point the mean of 3 technical replicates ± SEM bars, plotted against VHH concentration. b IC₅₀ values calculated from panel A using log (inhibitor) vs normalized response with variable Hill slope; bars represent best-fit values for IC₅₀ with 95% confidence interval error bars. Source data are provided as a Source Data file.

Based on the IC 50 values for HEK293F-expressed VHHs for neutralization of SARS-CoV-2, we selected the VHH-IgG1 Fc fusion, C5-Fc, as the transgene to insert into the configurable expression chassis for RNA-programmed CRISPR/Cas9 delivery into the germline of S. mansoni . Figure 3 diagrammatically depicts the transgene, its components and expression product, the CRISPR knock-in strategy, including orientation of the promoter, signal peptide, C5-Fc coding region and amino acid sequence, dimerization of the VHH endowed by the IgG1 Fc fusion partner, and terminator motif (Fig. 3a–d ), along with potential knock out as well as knock in alleles following transfection of the schistosome egg with the donor transgene and RNPs (Fig. 3e, f ). Supplementary Fig. 3 provides the donor transgene sequence, while Supplementary Table 1 lists the nucleotide sequences of the guide RNAs and oligonucleotide primers deployed in the study.

For insertion into the S. mansoni genome, we targeted a site in Genome Safe Harbor 1 (GSH1) on chromosome 3 of S. mansoni 12 and deployed three overlapping guide RNAs for programmed CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in, a target site and tactics that we had previously shown to be both not apparently harmful to the targeted schistosome egg and effective for insertion of a reporter gene into S. mansoni genome 12 . To prepare a synthetic transgene construct encoding the C5-Fc anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibody, we included short (50 nt each) left and right side homology arms, and the promoter and terminator of an endogenous ubiquitin gene of S. mansoni , Gene ID, Smp_335990, UBB protein (WormBase Parasite, version WBPS19) 25 – 27 to drive expression of the transgene (Fig. 3a, b ). The rationale for using this promoter was that using an endogenous, ubiquitously expressed gene promoter (like ubiquitin) has advantages, especially in non-model organisms 28 , 29 , including broad, constitutive expression in tissues, cells and developmental stages 30 . Indeed, based on transcriptomics data for this schistosome, the Smp_335990 gene is strongly, ubiquitously, and stage-independently expressed 31 , 32 . We anticipated its compatibility with native transcription machinery since an endogenous promoter would be likely to be recognized and accurately regulated by the helminth’s own transcription machinery (transcription factors, chromatin context) and this could be expected to reduce the risk of failure or silencing. Non-endogenous – viral or foreign – promoters can trigger epigenetic silencing, especially over time or in specific tissues 33 . The promoter and terminator sequences of Smp_335990 represent tractable and not overly large regulatory elements for donor constructs 12 , 26 and, indeed, we had previously used the ubiquitin promoter and its terminator in transgene constructs for knock-in experiments, with Cas9 and Cas12a, encoding a GFP reporter, inserted at the same GSH1 site 26 .

The secretory signal peptide from the hookworm protein, ASP2, known to actively drive secretion of diverse helminth proteins in mammalian cell lines 34 , served to direct the nanobody fusion protein into the schistosome’s secretory pathway. Translation initiation is a major rate limiting step in protein synthesis and given the positive impact of translation of the amino acids encoded by codons 3 to 5 35 , we preemptively inserted two extra residues, Lys-Leu, at amino acid positions 3 and 4 of the signal peptide, MV KL VLVPLLALLAVSVH, aiming to improve protein synthesis of the transgene-encoded nanobody and, in turn, secretion of the recombinant C5-Fc fusion protein (Fig. 3c, d ).

Our experimental approach had two strategic components. First, using S. mansoni as a biological foundry exploited the male schistosome’s long-term survival to enable continuous in situ production of the therapeutic transgene product. Second, fusing the C5 VHH to the Fc region of human IgG1 induced dimerization, yielding a bivalent antibody with two identical antigen-binding sites to enhance SARS-CoV-2 neutralization (Fig. 3d ). We leveraged Fc-induced bivalency to amplify the potency of the parental VHH through the avidity effect. – a key advantage for targeting viruses with repeating surface antigens like the SARS-CoV-2 36 . Indeed, recombinant C5-Fc expressed in HEK293F cells was >30-fold more potent than C5 alone in the same system (Fig. 2 ). Additionally, the Fc domain promotes neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn)-mediated recycling, extending serum half-life and improving tissue distribution 37 . Finally, the Fc domain confers effector functions, including antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and phagocytosis that could aid in the detection and clearance of virus-infected cells 38 , 39 .

Figure 4a schematically displays the technical steps used to derive the C5-Fc line of transgenic S. mansoni . In vitro laid (immature) schistosome eggs (IVLEs) were transfected by electroporation with three overlapping RNPs targeting GSH1 on chromosome 3 of S. mansoni 12 along with a 5′-modified-double stranded DNA donor encoding C5-Fc. A polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based screen using transgene specific primers of a sample of the hatching population of these eggs and miracidia confirmed the presence of the C5-Fc transgene (302 bp amplicon; Figs. 4 b, c and 4004 bp amplicon; Supplementary Fig. 4e ). Forty-eight Biomphalaria glabrata snails were each exposed to a single miracidium hatched from this cohort (monomiracidial infection 40 ). By 12 weeks later, C5-Fc-positive cercariae had been shed from three of the 48 snails (6.3%), whereas 16 snails shed wild type cercariae. Male cercariae shed from one of those three transgene positive snails, female cercariae from a second, and the third died before yielding enough cercariae for mouse infections (Supplementary Fig. 4b ).

The sex of cercariae shed from each snail was determined using a competitive PCR 41 ; a 404 bp amplicon specific for the rpS4 gene, located only on the Z chromosome – confirming the sex of the cercariae as male, and a 195 bp amplicon of W6 repetitive element for the W chromosome, confirming the sex of the cercariae as female. In this PCR, a higher Z-specific gene: a W-localized repetitive element copy ratio results in the presence of both 404 and 195 bp amplicons and indicates male DNA, whereas the presence of only the 195 bp amplicon indicates female DNA. Figure 4b shows representative PCR results including the demonstration of both P0 transgenic and WT cercariae from the monomiracidial infection of the snails.

Each of six mice was exposed first to ~90 male cercariae and then a few weeks later (when the female cercariae became available) to ~100 female transgene (TG)-positive cercariae, aiming to establish a sexually reproducing population of P0 generation transgenic schistosomes within each mouse. About eight weeks after the infection with the female cercariae, the mice were euthanized, and adult schistosomes perfused from the portal circulation. Among the perfused worms, we observed up to five paired adult schistosomes among the ~20 worms obtained from each mouse. These adult schistosomes represented the foundation P0 generation of the C5-Fc line. Concurrently, we also recovered the schistosome eggs from the livers of the mice, the eggs representing the F1 generation. Samples of the adult P0 female and male worms were positive for the C5-Fc transgene (Fig. 4b ) as were samples of the F1 generation eggs (Supplemental Fig. 4. b-e ).

Eggs of this F1 cohort, isolated under aseptic conditions by collagenase digestion of all six mouse livers 42 , pooled into a single digest, were induced to hatch. Again, 48 snails were individually exposed to miracidia hatched from this transgene positive cohort of F1 generation eggs. In turn, shedding of cercariae was periodically induced from the snails from five weeks after exposure. By 12 weeks, C5-Fc-positive cercariae had been shed from seven of the 48 snails (14.6%); five of these snails shed female cercariae and two shed male cercariae. Over several weeks from the first appearance of transgenic F1 generation cercariae onwards, and as sufficient numbers of cercariae became available, six mice were each infected with ~100 female and ~100 male cercariae of the F1 generation of the nascent C5-Fc line. In turn, eggs were recovered from the livers of these mice, which also were C5-Fc positive, and thus represented the F2 generation.

The F2 generation was similarly propagated, with miracidia hatched from F2 eggs. PCR of F2 cercariae from individual snails infected by these F2 generation miracidia showed a 97% transgenic rate – 33 of 34 snails shed transgenic F2 cercariae (Fig. 4c , lower gel). Figure 4c (upper gel) shows PCR screening of a representative batch of cercariae from nine of these 33 snails; four snails produced male and five produced female cercariae (Fig. 4c , lower gel). Amplicons of Z and/or W chromosome- localized markers provided a DNA integrity control.

C5‑Fc produced by transgenic S. mansoni was detected in both excretory/secretory products (ESP) and sera of infected mice and mediated potent neutralization of the SARS‑CoV‑2 virus. Figure 5a provides a schematic overview of our assessment approach. Specifically, a quantitative capture ELISA revealed the presence of C5-Fc in ESP from pools of adult, mixed sex schistosomes, confirming secretion of C5‑Fc by the schistosomes at a concentration of 54.9 ± 4 ng/ml culture medium (Fig. 5b ). The ELISA detected much lower C5‑Fc levels in the ESP of two negative-control worm groups: worms transfected with donor transgene but without RNPs, or mock‑transfected worms (Fig. 5b ). Thereafter, we examined whether ESP containing the secreted C5-Fc could neutralize SARS-CoV-2 virus, as described for C5-Fc in the original report for recombinant C5-Fc 18 . We assessed neutralization of SARS-CoV-2 virus using the PRNT assay, in which the FNLCR was included as the positive control (Fig. 5c, d ). ESP and FNLCR were diluted up to 31,250-fold, and neutralization levels plotted alongside the negative control ESP groups. ESP from the transgenic schistosomes diluted 1/108 completely ( ~ 100%) neutralized SARS-CoV-2, with an IC 50 of 1,443 dilution factor (DF), a neutralization capacity only modestly lower than that of FNLCR (4,345 DF). By contrast, the ESPs from each of three negative control schistosome groups including the donor transgene only (no RNPs) exhibited significantly less virus neutralization power and markedly lower IC 50 values (Fig. 5c, d ). However, among the negative controls, ESP from the donor transgene only did exhibit some anti-viral neutralization (IC 50 value of 11 DF), which may have resulted from low level expression of episomal (non CRISPR integrated) transgene DNA.
