articles.title: Cell-derived lactate triggers local hydrogelation and phenotype remodelling.
articles.authors: Braun MG, Schneider TC, Koynov K, Gieß S, Driehaus-Ortiz L, Förch L, Schuler M, Wagner M, Synatschke CV, Régnier-Vigouroux A, De Laporte L, Ng DYW, Weil T.
articles.abstract: Abstract Many tumours release lactate as a major metabolic product and signalling molecule. Here we use lactate flux as an endogenous trigger for covalent hydrogel formation. Phenol-functionalised alginate remains soluble until cell-derived lactate is oxidised by lactate oxidase; the generated hydrogen peroxide is used by horseradish peroxidase to crosslink phenols and form a matrix at metabolically active sites. Hydrogels form within minutes and reach storage moduli from approximately 10 Pa to 5 kPa. In tumour-spheroid models, including a patient-derived glioblastoma spheroid model, local lactate production generates spatially confined gelation that extended up to around 1 mm from the spheroid surface. Nanoindentation and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy reveal radial stiffness and polymer-density gradients, while proteome profiling and imaging indicate reduced proliferative signalling and increased markers associated with migration and matrix remodelling. These findings establish metabolite-gated hydrogelation as a strategy to couple cellular metabolism to covalent matrix assembly, mechanics and transport, providing a bio-synthetic platform for modelling cell–matrix reciprocity and tumour confinement. Subject terms: Biomaterials, Cancer microenvironment, Gels and hydrogels, Biopolymers

Synthetic hydrogels are widely used to mimic key extracellular matrix functions, but their biochemical and mechanical properties are typically predefined, requiring cells to adapt to a fixed environment. Here, the authors introduce a phenol-functionalized alginate hydrogel that undergoes in situ crosslinking in response to lactate secreted by cells. By coupling material formation to cellular metabolism, this system generates local mechanical gradients around metabolically active cells and spheroids, enabling dynamic, self-regulated matrix remodelling driven by metabolic fluxes.

The extracellular matrix (ECM) orchestrates cellular behaviour by integrating structural, biochemical, and mechanical cues 1 . While synthetic hydrogels emulate key ECM functions and are foundational to three-dimensional culture models 2 , most synthetic systems communicate with cells in a single direction; their chemistry and mechanics are preset, and cells must adapt to these imposed conditions. What remains missing is adaptive reciprocity, where materials sense endogenous changes in cellular activity and reconfigure their own state accordingly 3 .

Fluctuations in cellular metabolism provide a direct and quantitative readout of cell state 4 . In tumours, elevated glycolytic flux drives lactate accumulation, acidification, and lactate-dependent signalling that can reprogramme immunity and extracellular remodelling 5 . Compared with exogenous triggers such as pH, temperature, or light 6 – 8 , cell-derived metabolites provide an intrinsic, spatiotemporally-resolved handle to regulate covalent crosslinking reactions in adaptive matrix materials. In such systems, metabolites are not only biochemical readouts, but can also act as local chemical fuels that couple cell state to material formation. This insight frames our concept: cellular metabolism sets crosslinking kinetics; crosslinking defines matrix mechanics and transport; and mechanical states feed back to modulate cell phenotype 9 – 12 .

Here, we introduce a mode of cell-material communication that utilises a phenol-functionalised alginate, which crosslinks in situ in response to lactate secreted by cells (Fig. 1 ). Embedding lactate oxidase (LOx) and horseradish peroxidase (HRP) establishes a cascade that converts lactate to hydrogen peroxide, which oxidatively couples pendant phenols to form covalent network junctions in both two- and three-dimensional cultures. Because hydrogen peroxide is generated from lactate and consumed during phenol coupling, the cascade links redox flux to local matrix formation rather than relying on uniform external peroxide addition. Unlike HRP/H 2 O 2 -crosslinkable hydrogels that require exogenous peroxide 13 or glucose-oxidase fuelling 14 , gelation here is gated by endogenous lactate, connecting material formation directly to cellular metabolism and building mechanical gradients around metabolically active cells and spheroids. These gradients in turn trigger cellular adaptation, with phenotypic changes at the proteome and morphological levels that are consistent with reduced proliferative signalling and increased migration- and matrix-remodelling-associated programmes. In contrast to enzyme-instructed supramolecular assemblies 15 , the resulting network is covalent, mechanically tuneable, and stable, yet remains cell-instructed through metabolic flux.

Phenol and catechol chemistries are central motifs in bioinspired polymer design and living materials. Their robust oxidative coupling under biological conditions, exemplified by mussel adhesion, cuticle hardening and melanin formation 16 – 18 , has motivated their integration into covalently crosslinkable hydrogels 13 . To translate this chemistry into a metabolism-responsive matrix material, we designed and synthesised a phenol-functionalised alginate (AlgTA) by carbodiimide-mediated conjugation of tyramine to sodium alginate (1-ethyl-3-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)carbodiimide/N-hydroxysuccinimide, EDC/NHS chemistry; modified from Schulz et al. 13 ), introducing pendant phenols along the polysaccharide backbone (Fig. 2a ). The product was purified by extensive dialysis to remove residual reagents and soluble side-products and isolated in >95% yield across three independent syntheses. The degree of substitution (DS) averaged ~2.5 mol%, with narrow batch-to-batch variation, as determined by ¹H NMR spectroscopy (2.3–2.6 mol%). This low but reproducible modification density preserves polymer solubility while providing pendant phenols for enzymatic oxidative coupling.

¹H NMR spectroscopy confirmed successful tyramine conjugation (Fig. 2b ). Aromatic resonances at 7.10–7.60 ppm integrated relative to the guluronic-acid anomeric signal at 5.35 ppm yielded a DS of ~2.5 mol% tyramine per uronate unit. (Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2 , Supplementary Equations 1 and 2; further discussion of alginate characterisation and functionalisation is provided in the Supporting Information) 19 . ¹H diffusion-ordered NMR (DOSY) further supported polymer-bound tyramine by showing that the aromatic signals diffuse with the alginate backbone (D ≈ 10 −10.5 m 2 s −1 ; Supplementary Fig. 3 ). Minor resonances at 3.40–3.30, 2.10, and 1.27 ppm were assigned to residual EDC-derived N-acylurea side-products, as reported 20 . Importantly, the purified AlgTA material used in subsequent experiments, including these residual signals, retained HRP-mediated crosslinkability and showed no detectable reduction in cell viability under the tested material-exposure conditions (Supplementary Figs. 4 – 7 ).

Size-exclusion chromatography (SEC/GPC) further supported polymer-bound tyramine: co-elution of the alginate refractive index and UV (270 nm) signals indicated that the aromatic signal was associated with the polymer fraction, with a small shift in apparent molar mass from 68.8 ± 2.9 kg mol −1 (alginate) to 60.0 ± 0.9 kg mol −1 (AlgTA), consistent with the low degree of substitution (Fig. 2c , Supplementary Table 1 ). In the presence of hydrogen peroxide and horseradish peroxidase, pendant phenols undergo oxidative coupling to form covalent network junctions (Fig. 2d ). Using defined H 2 O 2 concentrations first decoupled the crosslinking reaction from cellular metabolism and established the accessible mechanical and transport-response window of AlgTA gels before introducing lactate-producing cells. This reaction therefore provides the chemical basis for metabolite-gated gel formation, in which cell-derived lactate is enzymatically converted to H 2 O 2 to initiate polymer crosslinking.

Peroxide-mediated crosslinking defines the mechanical window for lactate-gated gelation. To translate metabolic activity into material formation, we first examined peroxide-mediated crosslinking of AlgTA (~2.5 mol% tyramine per uronate unit) at 3 wt%. AlgTA and horseradish peroxidase (HRP, 10 U mL −1 ) were mixed and exposed to 0.5–3 mM hydrogen peroxide to yield covalently crosslinked hydrogels within 30 min (Supplementary Fig. 8 ). Gelation kinetics and mechanics were monitored by oscillatory shear rheology. Strain-sweep experiments defined the linear viscoelastic region, frequency sweeps characterised the final network response across different timescales and time sweeps monitored gel formation at 1% strain and 1 Hz (Supplementary Figs. 9 and 10 ). The linear viscoelastic region extended to at least 10% strain, and the gels showed a predominantly frequency-independent storage modulus ( G ′), consistent with formation of an elastic covalent network. At 0.75 mM H 2 O 2 , G ′ remained frequency-independent up to 2 Hz, whereas this response extended to 10 Hz at full crosslinking (3 mM). The plateau storage modulus extracted from time sweeps (1% strain, 1 Hz) revealed a pronounced H 2 O 2 dose response (Fig. 2e ). Control experiments lacking either HRP or H 2 O 2 remained at G ′ ≈ 10 Pa, comparable to unmodified 3 wt% alginate, demonstrating that both enzymatic oxidation and peroxide fuel are required for covalent network formation. Based on ~3.5 mM phenol groups per 3 wt% AlgTA, complete phenol pairing would correspond to a maximum junction concentration of ~1.75 mM H 2 O 2 (two phenols per covalent junction). Consistent with this stoichiometric estimate and reproducible across batches, gels stiffened sharply between 0.5 mM and 1.5 mM H 2 O 2 : G ′ increased from 30 ± 10 Pa to 4.8 ± 0.5 kPa, approaching a plateau at ~5 kPa (Fig. 2e ).

To benchmark the rheological behaviour under cell-culture conditions, gelation was performed in DMEM (Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium) supplemented with 10% foetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin. Detectable elastic gels formed at H 2 O 2 concentrations ≥0.75 mM, reaching G ′ = 70 ± 20 Pa at 0.75 mM and 2.8 ± 0.5 kPa at 3 mM. The attenuated stiffening in medium is consistent with phenolic competitors and peroxide scavenging: DMEM contains ~0.4 mM tyrosine, and FBS proteins contribute additional phenolic residues that can compete for HRP-mediated oxidation and consume peroxide-derived oxidants. Despite these interferences, the resulting stiffness range from sub-kPa to several kPa spans mechanical regimes relevant to lung and fibrotic tissues 21 – 23 . The hydrogels remained stable under cell-culture conditions and showed no detectable degradation upon incubation with cell lysate over 12 days (Supplementary Figs. 11 and 12 ).

To implement the full metabolite-responsive cascade, AlgTA was combined with HRP (10 U mL −1 ) and lactate oxidase (LOx, 1 U mL −1 ). Upon addition of sodium lactate (10 mM), rheology revealed gelation after a short induction period (Supplementary Fig. 13 ). The low initial modulus before the rise in G ′ is consistent with a physically entangled AlgTA solution, whereas the subsequent increase in G ′ reflects accumulation of covalent phenol junctions. Because LOx produces H 2 O 2 enzymatically upstream of HRP-mediated phenol coupling, gelation proceeded more slowly than with direct H 2 O 2 addition but reached comparable plateau moduli for equivalent oxidant yield (Supplementary Fig. 8 ). The low LOx loading was selected to limit extracellular peroxide accumulation while preserving mechanical tunability for subsequent cell experiments.

While classical oscillatory rheology reports bulk behaviour, it cannot resolve local heterogeneities under culture conditions. We therefore employed fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) as a local probe of network density and transport restriction 24 – 26 . FCS quantifies fluorescent tracer diffusion within a confocal sub-femtolitre volume, providing a sensitive readout of mesh size and molecular transport (Fig. 2f ) 24 , 25 , 27 . Alexa Fluor 488–labelled bovine serum albumin (BSA, hydrodynamic radius ≈3.5 nm) served as tracer. Gels were equilibrated for 24 h in PBS containing the tracer prior to measurement. Autocorrelation curves (Supplementary Fig. 14 ) were fitted (Eq. 1 ) to extract diffusion times ( τ ), and diffusion slowdown was expressed as τ gel / τ buffer . Diffusion was hindered progressively with increasing crosslinking: τ gel / τ buffer = 1.6 ± 0.1 for G ′ = 90 ± 35 Pa, 1.9 ± 0.1 at 520 ± 70 Pa, and 2.6 ± 0.25 at 4.8 ± 0.5 kPa (Fig. 2e ). Thus, tracer diffusion slowdown increased monotonically with storage modulus, establishing FCS as a calibrated, spatially resolved readout for local network density in AlgTA hydrogels (Fig. 2f ). This calibration provided the basis for mapping cell-driven gelation around metabolically active spheroids.

To test whether cell metabolism alone can initiate material formation, we assessed endogenous lactate-driven gelation using A549 lung adenocarcinoma cells, a highly glycolytic model with elevated lactate production under aerobic glycolysis 28 . Glucose-deprived cultures served as negative controls, as lactate production depends on glucose metabolism 29 . To physically separate gel formation from the cell layer and initially exclude direct mechanobiological feedback from an adjacent gel, AlgTA, LOx, and HRP were confined to a Transwell insert, while cells were cultured in the lower chamber (25,000 cells per well; 80–90% confluence by day 4) (Fig. 3a ). Lactate quantification confirmed continuous accumulation in glucose-fed cultures, but not in glucose-free controls (Fig. 3f ; Supplementary Fig. 15 ). In the presence of AlgTA/LOx/HRP, lactate was progressively depleted, by 45 ± 25% at 24 h, 58 ± 12% at 48 h, and 93 ± 9% at 72 h, relative to matched cell-only controls, consistent with enzymatic conversion to hydrogen peroxide and pyruvate. Correspondingly, extracellular H 2 O 2 concentrations increased up to threefold (Fig. 3g ; Supplementary Fig. 16 ), supporting the conclusion that the metabolic flux powered the oxidative cascade.

In glucose-containing medium, AlgTA precursors in the Transwell insert gradually transitioned from viscous fluids to self-supporting gels over 1–3 days: weak, viscous networks formed by day 1 ( E = 50 ± 40 Pa, nanoindentation) matured to stable gels by day 2 ( E = 1.5 ± 0.7 kPa) and to well-defined hydrogels by day 3 ( E = 2.9 ± 1.3 kPa) (Fig. 3b, e ). Increasing yellow colouration was consistent with progressive phenol oxidation 30 . FCS corroborated this mechanical maturation, with tracer diffusion slowing from τ gel / τ buffer = 1.58 ± 0.13 (day 1) to 2.36 ± 0.05 (day 2) and subsequently 2.75 ± 0.05 (day 3) (Fig. 3e ; Supplementary Fig. 17 ). In glucose-free conditions, no gel formed, consistent with absent lactate and lack of fuel for the enzymatic crosslinking cascade.

As lactate is processed by the AlgTA/LOx/HRP cascade, extracellular H 2 O 2 accumulates to micromolar concentrations (Fig. 3g ), overlapping with the ranges typical of epithelial lining fluids and vascular lumens 31 . Whereas exogenous H 2 O 2 at ≥100 µM typically induces overt cytotoxicity in A549 epithelial cells 32 , 33 , the extracellular H 2 O 2 levels generated here remain within the lower ~1–50 µM range associated with redox signalling and adaptive responses in epithelial cells 34 . Nevertheless, cumulative exposure may lead to cytotoxic effects: metabolic activity (resazurin assay) and relative calcein positive cells decreased progressively under AlgTA/LOx/HRP conditions over 3 days, indicating progressive metabolic suppression and loss of viable cell fraction during prolonged exposure (Fig. 3c , Supplementary Fig. 18 ). At day 2, relative proteome profiling revealed marked increases in insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 1 (IGFBP-1) and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), accompanied by decreased insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 3 (IGFBP-3) relative to the control. IGFBP-1 upregulation has been linked to activation of mitochondrial superoxide dismutase (SOD2), enhancing oxidative-stress tolerance 35 ; loss of IGFBP-3 can remove a growth-inhibitory brake 36 , while elevated VEGF promotes angiogenic signalling to maintain nutrient supply 35 , 37 , 38 . Together, these proteomic changes are consistent with reactive oxygen species (ROS)-associated signalling in response to lactate-fuelled, spatially decoupled oxidative crosslinking (Fig. 3d , Supplementary Figs. 19 and 20 , Supplementary Table 2 ).

The 2D cell cultures, together with the remote gelation setup, allow spatially separated analysis of how hydrogel formation and cell-derived signals communicate across space. However, 2D cell monolayers lack the mature extracellular matrix and cell-cell interactions that define tumour architecture. A 3D tumour model is therefore required to assess how lactate-gated gelation shapes the mechanobiological landscape in the immediate vicinity of metabolically active cell aggregates.

Unlike in 2D cell cultures, where lactate dissipates into the bulk medium, 3D tumour spheroids generate steep gradients that radiate from the surface of these densely packed cell clusters. When embedded in DMEM containing AlgTA, LOx, and HRP, spheroids locally converted lactate to hydrogen peroxide, initiating oxidative coupling of AlgTA phenols and forming a covalently crosslinked pericellular gel within one day. As lactate accumulated and was enzymatically consumed, gelation progressed outward, yielding stable, self-supporting gel–spheroid composites (Fig. 4a ). After two days, the mean gel–spheroid composite diameter reached 2100 ± 100 µm (Supplementary Fig. 21 ).

To convert diffusion slowdown into a lactate-dependent crosslinking readout, ( τ gel / τ buffer ) was calibrated using preformed gels generated with defined lactate concentrations under matched LOx/HRP conditions. We therefore report an apparent lactate-equivalent concentration ( c lac,eq ), rather than a true time-integrated concentration (Fig. 4c ). Diffusion slowdown ( τ gel / τ buffer ) served as a local proxy for network density. Within 100–400 µm from the spheroid surface, τ gel / τ buffer = 2.2 ± 0.1 indicated a densely crosslinked network with a lactate-equivalent concentration c lac,eq ≥ 5 mM (Fig. 4d ). The ratio gradually decreased to 1.8 ± 0.1 and to 3.8 ± 0.3 mM c lac,eq at 500 µm reaching 1.00 ± 0.01 corresponding to c lac,eq ≤ 0.5 mM at 1000 µm, marking the outer gel boundary. Spheroid-derived lactate thus spatially instructs covalent crosslinking and defines the hydrogel architecture within its microenvironment.

The proteomic response under lactate-gated 3D encapsulation differed markedly from that observed in the separated 2D Transwell experiments. In 2D, cells were exposed to diffusible H 2 O 2 generated by the AlgTA/LOx/HRP cascade, leading to a pronounced redox-signalling signature. In 3D spheroids, however, locally produced H 2 O 2 can be rapidly consumed during phenol coupling at the spheroid surface, which limits peroxide accumulation and shifts the dominant cue toward pericellular network formation, transport restriction and mechanical confinement. Consistent with this, relative-abundance proteomics revealed a distinct expression profile during 3D encapsulation (Fig. 4e , Supplementary Figs. 20 and 23 , Supplementary Table 2 ): IL-8 (Interleukin-8) increased strongly, whereas IGFBP-1, IGFBP-3, and PAI-1 (plasminogen activator inhibitor-1) showed moderate upregulation. VEGF remained essentially unchanged, while tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases-1 (TIMP-1) and basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF) decreased significantly. Functionally, elevated IL-8 and PAI-1 are associated with a pro-inflammatory and pro-migratory programme, and reduced TIMP-1 may relieve metalloproteinase inhibition to promote matrix remodelling 37 , 39 , 40 . The stable VEGF levels, in contrast to the strong VEGF induction in 2D, support the interpretation that soluble ROS-mediated signalling is attenuated in 3D, where peroxide is locally consumed by the crosslinking reaction rather than accumulating in the bulk medium (Fig. 4f ) 41 .

Morphologically, phalloidin staining revealed actin-rich protrusions and invasive extensions from spheroid edges only in the presence of AlgTA/LOx/HRP, consistent with a shift from growth-dominated behaviour toward migration- and matrix-remodelling-associated phenotypes in response to the pericellular gel network 42 . Notably, the protrusions were absent in softer gels (1 or 2 wt% AlgTA; 35 ± 9 or 600 ± 100 Pa), suggesting that a threshold of mechanical stiffness is required to trigger these morphogenetic changes (Supplementary Figs. 24 and 25 ) 43 – 45 .

To isolate the chemical contribution of H 2 O 2 to this encapsulation response, HRP was replaced with catalase (Cat), which decomposes H 2 O 2 into water and oxygen and thereby prevents phenol coupling. Eliminating oxidative crosslinking abolished gel formation and yielded proteomic profiles closely resembling untreated controls (Supplementary Figs. 20 , 26 and 27 , Supplementary Table 2 ).

Encapsulation within the AlgTA/LOx/HRP matrix halted spheroid expansion and reduced metabolic activity. In gel-free controls, spheroids grew from 474 ± 18 µm to 507 ± 17 µm over two days ( P < 0.001), whereas encapsulated spheroids maintained a constant size (468 ± 22 µm to 472 ± 19 µm, P = 0.546; Fig. 4g ). The proportion of dead cells, marked by propidium iodide, increased substantially and comprised a major fraction of the spheroid (see Fig. 5a ). Consistently, ATP and NADH levels measured by CellTiter-Glo® 3D and resazurin assays were reduced to 51 ± 14% ( P < 0.001) and 75 ± 15% ( P < 0.001), respectively, compared to gel-free controls at day 2 (Fig. 4h ), reflecting suppressed proliferation and diminished metabolic activity under gel confinement.

To evaluate whether lactate-gated gelation extends beyond A549 cells, we applied the AlgTA/LOx/HRP system to 4T1 murine mammary carcinoma spheroids, a highly glycolytic tumour model that also secretes substantial lactate 46 . Under identical conditions (3 wt% AlgTA, 1 U mL −1 LOx, 10 U mL −1 HRP), stable pericellular gels formed at the spheroid interface, similar to the behaviour observed for A549 spheroids (Supplementary Fig. 28 ). Unlike A549, however, 4T1 spheroids did not develop actin-rich protrusions or invasive extensions into the surrounding matrix, indicating a tumour-model-specific morphological response to confinement (Supplementary Fig. 29 ). Growth was similarly suppressed: treated 4T1 spheroids decreased in diameter from 361 ± 9 µm to 306 ± 7 µm over two days ( P < 0.001; Supplementary Fig. 30 ). Propidium iodide staining revealed markedly enlarged necrotic cores in both A549 and 4T1 spheroids following encapsulation (Fig. 5a, b ; Supplementary Figs. 31 and 32 ), and calcein staining confirmed reduced viable cell fractions relative to untreated controls.

To further explore the translational relevance of this concept, we evaluated the system using patient-derived heterogeneous glioblastoma spheroids generated from surgically resected tumour material under institutional ethical approval and informed consent (Fig. 5c ). Over a culture period of seven days, the material promoted encapsulation of the spheroids and significantly reduced the invasive area compared to the AlgTA-free control (Fig. 5d, e ; Supplementary Fig. 33 ).
These results indicate that lactate-gated crosslinking is not restricted to a single cancer model and can impose growth- or invasion-limiting confinement across distinct tumour-spheroid systems.

Together, the 3D results establish a mechanistic link between cellular metabolism and material state and, ultimately, cell phenotype. Endogenous lactate released by the spheroids is enzymatically oxidised by lactate oxidase to hydrogen peroxide, which fuels the horseradish peroxidase–mediated oxidative coupling of AlgTA phenols. The resulting covalent crosslinking defines the stiffness and local transport properties of the hydrogel, and these evolving material states feed back onto cellular signalling and behaviour. Under lactate-gated encapsulation, A549 spheroids shift from expansion-dominated growth toward a migration- and matrix-remodelling-associated phenotype, while the surrounding network simultaneously constrains bulk expansion (Fig. 4b, g ). The proteomic signatures are consistent with the material readouts: as crosslink density increases and molecular diffusion decreases (FCS; Figs. 2 f, 3 e and 4d ), cells upregulate programmes associated with matrix remodelling, proteolysis, and invasion. Although the findings arise from an in vitro model, they demonstrate that metabolic flux can be transduced into covalent material assembly that, in turn, reshapes cell state. This feedback loop, in which metabolism directs crosslinking, crosslinking establishes mechanics and transport, and the resulting matrix state modulates phenotype, recapitulates a core principle of extracellular-matrix reciprocity in a bio-synthetic system.

This work establishes a materials design principle in which cellular metabolism sets covalent crosslinking kinetics, crosslinking defines matrix mechanics and transport, and these material states feed back to modulate cell phenotype. Leveraging lactate, a hallmark of the tumour microenvironment, enables cell-state-specific, spatially patterned gelation that couples material formation directly to metabolic activity. In spatially separated 2D cultures and 3D tumour spheroids, endogenous lactate generated by A549 cells is oxidised by the LOx–HRP cascade to hydrogen peroxide, which oxidatively couples AlgTA phenols to form a covalent hydrogel. Mechanics and transport evolve in tandem: the storage modulus is tuneable from ~10 Pa to ~5 kPa, gelation propagates approximately 1 mm from spheroid surfaces, and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy maps diffusion gradients that reflect local network density and apparent lactate-equivalent concentration, linking metabolic flux semi-quantitatively to matrix architecture and molecular transport.

Relative to HRP/H 2 O 2 hydrogels dependent on exogenous oxidants or glucose-oxidase fuelling, lactate-gated gelation places endogenous metabolism upstream of material formation, conferring both spatial selectivity and temporal synchrony with metabolic activity. Compared with enzyme-instructed supramolecular assemblies, this approach yields covalent networks with mechanically stable properties that nevertheless remain responsive to cell-derived fluxes. In 3D, relative proteome profiling and morphological readouts indicate that lactate-gated encapsulation suppresses spheroid expansion while inducing features associated with migration and matrix remodelling, including altered abundance of remodelling-associated proteins and actin-rich protrusions. The data also reveal compartment-dependent signalling. In the Transwell geometry, diffusible H 2 O 2 generated by the AlgTA/LOx/HRP cascade produces a redox-associated stress and adaptation signature. In spheroids, by contrast, locally generated H 2 O 2 is consumed during phenol coupling near the spheroid surface, shifting the dominant feedback from soluble redox signalling toward pericellular network formation, transport restriction and mechanical confinement. Because prolonged exposure reduced metabolic activity and viable cell fraction, the system should not be described as intrinsically non-cytotoxic; rather, it provides a material response that is compatible with cells over the early gelation window, followed by exposure- and confinement-associated metabolic suppression in tumour models.

Because gelation is gated by a disease-linked metabolite, this bio-synthetic chemistry suggests the possibility of autonomous, state-selective barriers that form preferentially in lactate-rich tumour niches while remaining inactive below a defined metabolic threshold. The AlgTA/LOx/HRP precursors produce a covalently crosslinked matrix that forms preferentially where local lactate exceeds a tuneable threshold, thereby constraining spheroid expansion and invasion in vitro. Such behaviour could inform strategies to limit local tumour-cell dissemination while modulating the transport of cytokines, nutrients and therapeutic agents. Selectivity could be refined by adjusting enzyme loadings to set a lactate threshold, multiplexing triggers such as lactate and hypoxia for Boolean gating, or co-encapsulating scavengers (for example, catalase) to quench excess reactive oxygen species during gelation. In a potential clinical scenario, such as the resection cavity following surgical removal of malignant glioblastoma tumours, the platform could be developed as a feedback-controlled mechanical containment barrier. Unlike conventional static hydrogels or cavity-filling materials, the system strengthens its network in response to elevated local lactate concentrations associated with highly glycolytic tumour regions. In this context, metabolic activity acts as a trigger for structural adaptation, enabling local matrix formation that may restrict the migration of residual infiltrative cells and therefore motivates evaluation as a locoregional strategy to reduce recurrence risk. We therefore envision this platform as a complementary locoregional strategy that could, in future, be combined with established surgical, chemotherapeutic or immunotherapeutic treatments rather than replacing them.

Translation toward therapeutic settings will require substantial further development. Key requirements include biodegradable or reversibly cleavable linkers for controlled matrix removal, pharmacokinetic and biodistribution studies to assess off-target gelation, evaluation in healthy and tumour-bearing tissue models, mitigation of enzyme immunogenicity, and operation under hypoxic conditions given the oxygen dependence of LOx. Patient-derived glioblastoma experiments support translational relevance, but larger donor cohorts, in vivo validation, immune-competent models and orthogonal validation of proteomic markers will be needed before therapeutic conclusions can be drawn.

Beyond containment, the matrix could be engineered as a metabolite-activated sense-and-respond depot in which gelation controls the retention or release of drugs, cytokines or signalling molecules. Linking metabolic flux to programmable materials behaviour opens routes toward materials that sense biochemical fluxes and respond through changes in network architecture. Near-term extensions include substituting other oxidases to gate gelation by diverse disease-associated metabolites, integrating enzyme cascades for Boolean logic over multiple biochemical inputs, and introducing reversible chemistries to incorporate relaxation and repair. Potential applications span tumour modelling, where mechanical properties are written directly from metabolism, morphogenesis, immuno-engineering in which activated immune cells provide the metabolic cue, and biofabrication processes where on-demand stiffening enhances structural fidelity. More broadly, the ability to translate endogenous biochemical fluxes into covalent network architecture establishes a blueprint for metabolism-addressable living materials that probe, pattern, and steer complex cell–matrix interactions.

Phenol-functionalised alginate (AlgTA, 3 wt%) was dissolved in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) or Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM), as indicated for each experiment. Horseradish peroxidase (HRP, stock 100 U mL −1 ) was added to a final concentration of 10 U mL −1 and gently mixed to avoid bubble formation. For peroxide-triggered gelation, hydrogen peroxide was added immediately before casting to final concentrations of 0–3 mM (stock 0–30 mM H 2 O 2 ). For lactate-triggered gelation, lactate oxidase (LOx, stock 10 U mL −1 ) was additionally included at 1 U mL −1 , and gelation was initiated by addition of sodium lactate at the indicated concentration. Unless stated otherwise, hydrogels were prepared with final concentrations of 3 wt% AlgTA, 10 U mL −1 HRP and either 0–3 mM H 2 O 2 or 1 U mL −1 LOx plus sodium lactate. Peroxide-triggered gels formed within minutes, whereas lactate-triggered gels formed over several hours, reflecting enzymatic H 2 O 2 generation upstream of HRP-mediated phenol coupling.

The rheological characterisation was performed using a DHR3 rheometer (TA Instruments; TRIOS software 4.0.2.30774), which was equipped with a temperature controller and a solvent trap to minimise hydrogel dehydration. The experiments were conducted using an 8 mm parallel-plate geometry, with hydrogel samples of 35 µL volume, resulting in a gap size ranging from 0.6 to 0.7 mm. The mechanical properties of the hydrogels were characterised at 25 °C.
Measurements were performed in triplicate from one batch, and data are reported as mean ± s.d. Several experimental procedures were conducted:
Strain Sweep: Oscillatory strain sweeps ranging from 0.01% to 100% strain were performed at a fixed frequency of 1 Hz at 25 °C.
Frequency Sweep: Frequency sweeps spanning from 0.1 Hz to 10 Hz were executed at a fixed strain of 1% at 25 °C.
Time Sweep: The linear viscoelastic region extended to at least 10% strain at 1 Hz. Oscillatory time sweeps were therefore performed at 1% strain and 1 Hz at 25 °C.

GPC measurements were performed on a 1260 Infinity instrument (Polymer Standard Service, Mainz; WinGPC UniChrom V8.40) with UV/Vis (270 nm) and refractive-index detection at 25 °C. The system was operated with 0.07 M Na 2 HPO 4 at a flow rate of 1 mL/min. Samples were dissolved at a concentration of 1 mg/mL and washed through a PTFE syringe filter (0.45 μm). Each sample injection volume was 200 μL. Suprema columns (Polymer Standard Service, Mainz) with a particle size of 5 μm were used. The GPC system was calibrated using pullulan standards supplied by Polymer Standard Service. The data was processed using WinGPC UniChrom V8.40, and graphs were generated using GraphPad Prism 10.2.2.

Fluorescence, absorbance & luminescence spectra were recorded on a SPARK 20 M microplate reader (Tecan Group Ltd; Sparkcontrol V.2.3). Fluorescence measurements were performed in Greiner 384 flat black well plates (Greiner Bio-One, 781906), luminescence measurements in Greiner white half-area well plates (Greiner Bio-One, 675075) and the absorbance measurements in a 384 UV-STAR® well plate (Greiner Bio-One, 781801). Data processing was done using Microsoft Excel and GraphPad Prism 10.2.2.

FCS experiments were performed using a commercial confocal microscope (LSM 880, Carl Zeiss, ConfoCor3 3.0, Jena, Germany). Alexa Fluor 488–labelled bovine serum albumin (Alexa488-BSA; hydrodynamic radius ≈3.5 nm) was excited with the 488 nm line of an argon laser, fibre-coupled to the microscope and focused into the sample using a C-Apochromat 40×/1.2 W water-immersion objective (Carl Zeiss, Jena, Germany). Emission light was collected through the same objective and, after passing through a confocal pinhole, directed to a spectral detection unit (Quasar, Carl Zeiss), with the detection window set to 500–550 nm. Ibidi µ-Slide 15 Well 3D Glass Bottom were used as sample chambers for both solutions and gels. In the case of spheroid-formed gels, the position of the spheroid was first visualised using confocal laser scanning mode. The FCS observation volume was then positioned at defined locations either within or outside the gel. At each location, five FCS measurements were recorded, with a total acquisition time of 150 s per position. Fluorescence intensity fluctuations, δI(t) , were recorded over time and analysed via the autocorrelation function: G(τ) = 1 + δI(t) · δI(t + τ) >/ 2 . The resulting experimental autocorrelation curves were fitted using a standard analytical model function 4 :

Here, N is the average number of diffusing fluorescence species in the observation volume, f T and τ T are the fraction and the decay time of the triplet state, f i and τ Di are, respectively, the fraction and the diffusion time of the i-th diffusion component. S = z 0 / r 0 is the so-called structure parameter, where z 0 and r 0 represent the axial and radial dimensions of the confocal volume, respectively. The fits yielded the corresponding diffusion times τ Di and through D = r 0 2 4 τ D the diffusion coefficients of the fluorescent species. As the value of r 0 depends on the specific characteristics of the optical setup, calibration experiments were performed using a fluorescent tracer with a known diffusion coefficient, i.e., Alexa 488 in water.

While most experimental autocorrelation curves were well described by a single-component diffusion model, a two-component fit (Eq. 1 , m = −2) was required in some cases - particularly for measurements conducted in stiffer gels. The second component represented a minor fraction (a few per cent) and was characterised by a significantly slower diffusion time, likely reflecting transient immobilisation of a subset of Alexa488-BSA tracers within the gel matrix 47 . Data processing was done using Microsoft Excel and GraphPad Prism 10.2.2.

Hydrogels of 10 µL per well were prepared in Ibidi µ-Slide 15 Well 3D glass-bottom chambers using 3 wt% AlgTA, 10 U mL −1 HRP and 1 U mL −1 LOx in DMEM supplemented with FBS. Sodium lactate was added at defined final concentrations of 0–10 mM (stock 0–100 mM). After 6 h, 30 µL of Alexa488-BSA (50 µM) in PBS was added on top of the gels and samples were incubated overnight to allow tracer equilibration. The next day, the diffusion-time ratio of Alexa488-BSA ( τ gel / τ buffer ) was measured by FCS at 3 positions in the gel. The calibration curve between 0.5 and 5 mM lactate followed the linear equation y = 0.245× + 0.869 with R ² = 0.9625. This calibration was used to estimate an apparent lactate-equivalent concentration, c lac,eq , in spheroid-derived gels.

Formed hydrogels were removed from the well plate inserts by carefully cutting the membrane along its curvature. The hydrogel was then detached from the cut-out membrane and placed on a poly-L-lysine (Poly-L-lysine, P4707, Sigma) coated 12-well plate (LABSOLUTE, 7696791, Th. Geyer GmbH & Co. KG). The poly-L-lysine coating was prepared one day in advance by pipetting 500 µL into the centre of each well and allowing the solution to evaporate overnight at room temperature in a fume hood. The hydrogel was allowed to sit on the coated well plate for 2 min. Afterwards, the well plate was filled with PBS, and measurements were conducted using a Pavone Nanoindenter with a spherical probe (radius = 47 µm, spring constant = 0.4 N m −1 ) (both Optics11). Samples were measured at room temperature, with an approach speed of 10 μm s −1 . Young’s moduli were derived by fitting the obtained force-indentation curves to a Hertz model up to an indentation depth of 5 µm. The contact point was determined at 20% of the maximum force measured. The Poisson ratio was assumed to be that of an incompressible material ( ν = 0.5). Data analysis was performed using the software DataViewer (V 2.5.7, Optics11). Technical triplicates were prepared for each day of incubation, and each replicate was measured three times, resulting in a total of 9 measurements per day.
F = Force, E = Young’s Modulus, ν = Poisson’s Ratio, R = Tip Radius, δ = Indentation Depth.

For the 1 H NMR experiments and the diffusion measurements (DOSY) 48 , a 5 mm triple resonance QXI 1 H/ 13 C/ 15 N/ 19 F probe equipped with a z-gradient on the 700 MHz Bruker AVANCE NEO system was used. The spectra were measured at 50 °C for functionalisation degree determination and at 90 °C for G/M ratio calculation. The solvent signal of deuterated water was used as a reference (4.79 ppm).

Proton measurements were performed either with water suppression using gradient excitation sculpting or as a normal single-pulse experiment (zg30) with a relaxation delay of 5 s. The number of scans depended on the signal-to-noise ratio and ranged from 8 to 64 with a 90° pulse of 14 μs and a spectral width of 14,000 Hz (20 ppm). The proton and 2D DOSY ( 1 H) spectra were referenced to the residual HDO at 4.70 ppm (δ( 1 H)).
The spectroscopic widths of the homonuclear 2D-COSY (cosygpprqf) experiments with water presaturation were typically 16,000 Hz in both dimensions (f1 and f2), and the relaxation delay 2 s.

For the diffusion measurements, a 2D sequence (DOSY, dstebgp3s) 49 , 50 was used, with a 2D sequence for diffusion measurement using double stimulated echo for convection compensation and LED using bipolar gradient pulses for diffusion using 3 spoil gradients 49 , 50 . The temperature was kept at 323 K for all experiments and regulated by a standard 1 H methanol NMR sample using the TopSpin 4.50 software (Bruker) to ensure the correct temperature (chemical shift distance in ppm from OH and CH 3 is temperature dependent). The control of the temperature was realised with a VTU (variable temperature unit) with an accuracy of ±0.1 K.

In this work, the gradient strength was varied in 16 steps from 2% to 100%. The diffusion time was optimised at 60 ms and the gradient length at 1.4 ms. The gradient strength was calibrated by analysis of a sample of 2 H 2 O/ 1 H 2 O at a defined temperature and comparison with the theoretical diffusion coefficient of 2 H 2 O/ 1 H 2 O. Diffusion gradient amplitudes were varied linearly from 1 to 53 G/cm (10 to 470 mT/m) over a total of 16 experiments to achieve a strong diffusion weighting. Diffusion coefficients were then calculated for the integrated peak areas using an exponential decay fit function over the 16 spectra (gradients)
where the diffusion sensitivity factor b was calculated as given in the sequence description:
The data were processed with MestReNova 15.0.1 or Bruker TopSpin 3.6.1.

EDC/NHS model coupling solutions were analysed using an Advion CMS with an electrospray ionisation (ESI) source in positive mode. Measurements were performed under low-fragmentation conditions. Raw data were processed using Advion Data Express 4.0.13.8, and figures were generated in GraphPad Prism 10.2.2.

A549 human lung adenocarcinoma cells (DSMZ, ACC 107) and 4T1 murine mammary carcinoma cells (ATCC, CRL-2539) were cultured at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 in DMEM high glucose (Gibco 31053-028) supplemented with 10% dialysed foetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco A33820-01) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin. Cells were maintained in T75 flasks and passaged two to three times per week. STR analysis according to the global standard ANSI/ATCC ASN-0002.1-2021 resulted in an authentic STR profile in the reference STR database. Certified free of Mycoplasma contamination when bought. No further tests for Mycoplasma for 4T1. A549 Mycoplasma test performed after purchase. Passages used for experiments are between 3 and 15.

A549 spheroids were generated by seeding A549 (DSMZ, ACC 107) cells at a density of 5000 cells per well in 50 µL of Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM, high glucose, Gibco 31053-028) supplemented with 10% dialysed foetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco A33820-01) and 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin within ultra-low attachment 96-well plates (4520, Corning Inc., New York, USA). The plates were then centrifuged at 200 × g for 5 min, and the cells were incubated for one week to allow spheroid formation.

4T1 spheroids were generated by seeding 4T1 (ATCC, CRL-2539) cells at a density of 7000 cells per well in 50 µL of Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM, high glucose, Gibco 31053-028) supplemented with 10% dialysed foetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco A33820-01) and 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin within ultra-low attachment 96-well plates (4520, Corning Inc., New York, USA). The plates were then centrifuged at 200 × g for 5 min, and the cells were incubated for one day to allow spheroid formation.

Brain tumour specimens were collected during surgical removal of tumour tissue from patients diagnosed with a high-grade brain tumour. Only specimens with pathological confirmation of glioblastoma diagnosis were included in the study. Patient-derived spheroids were generated from 3 donor specimens according to the previously published protocol 51 . Glioblastoma specimens were dissociated into single-cell suspensions by combined mechanical and enzymatic processing using the Brain Tumor Dissociation Kit (Miltenyi Biotec) supplemented with collagenase II. Following filtration, erythrocyte lysis (0.1 mM EDTA, 10 mM KHCO₃, 0.155 M NH 4 Cl) and debris removal (debris removal solution, Miltenyi Biotec), cells were resuspended in GB-cDMEM (DMEM, 10% heat-inactivated FBS, 2 mM L-glutamine, 10 µg/mL gentamicin and 1 mM MgCl 2 ). 20,000 cells per well were seeded into ultra-low attachment BIOFLOAT™ 96-well plates (Sarstedt) and maintained at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 to allow spheroid formation.

25.000 A549 cells were seeded in a 24-well plate and cultured using 600 µL Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM, high glucose, Gibco 31053-028) supplemented with 10% dialysed foetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco A33820-01) and 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin for 24 h. The medium was exchanged, the gel precursor-filled Transwell (Greiner Bio-One 662641) was added, and the experiment started. The Transwells were removed at the selected time and stored in PBS. PBS was exchanged 3 times within 2 h to dilute remaining lactate and hydrogen peroxide. The medium was collected from the wells for analysis of lactate and ROS levels.

The medium of the A549 spheroids in the ultra-low attachment 96-well plates (4520, Corning Inc.) was replaced by AlgTA/LOx/HRP dissolved in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM, high glucose) supplemented with 10% dialysed foetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin. Control spheroids were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM, high glucose) supplemented with 10% dialysed FBS and 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin. The spheroids were cultured for 2 days and analysed.

Hydrogels (AlgTA, 3 wt%; H 2 O 2 , 3 mM; HRP, 10 U mL −1 ) were prepared directly in the rheometer geometry, and the storage modulus ( G ′) was measured by oscillatory rheometry at 1% strain and 1 Hz. A549 cells were lysed with M-PER™ (Thermo Scientific, 78503) for 5 min and centrifuged (~14,000 × g , 10 min) to remove debris. Hydrogels were incubated in the resulting cell lysate or in lysis buffer (control) for 1, 3, 7 or 12 days at 37 °C and re-measured or photos taken. G ′ values were normalised to the initial modulus and the corresponding lysate-free control ( G ′ Lysate / G ′ PBS ).

The calorimetric Lactate Assay Kit (Sigma-Aldrich, MAK329) was performed in a transparent 384-well plate. The samples were taken from the medium of the corresponding experiment and directly used. Following the assay, absorbance intensity was measured using a SPARK 20 M microplate reader (Tecan Group Ltd; Sparkcontrol V.2.3). A lactate calibration curve was obtained, and the data were processed using Microsoft Excel. Graphs were generated using GraphPad Prism 10.2.2.

The fluorometric hydrogen peroxide assay Kit (Sigma-Aldrich, MAK165) was performed in a black 384-well plate according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Fluorescence was recorded on a SPARK 20 M microplate reader (Tecan Group Ltd; Sparkcontrol V.2.3). Raw data were processed using Microsoft Excel, and graphs were generated in GraphPad Prism 10.2.2.

Cell viability was quantified using a resazurin-based assay (Sigma-Aldrich, TOX8) in black 96-well plates according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Cells were incubated with the resazurin solution for 4 h prior to measurement. Fluorescence was recorded on a SPARK 20 M microplate reader (Tecan Group Ltd; Sparkcontrol V.2.3) with an excitation wavelength of 560 nm and an emission wavelength of 590 nm. Raw data were processed using Microsoft Excel, and graphs were generated in GraphPad Prism 10.2.2.

Cell viability was quantified using Calcein AM (Thermo Fisher, C34852 ) and Propidium iodide (PI; Sigma-Aldrich, 537060). 25.000 A549 cells were seeded in a 24-well plate and cultured using 600 µL Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM, high glucose, Gibco 31053-028) supplemented with 10% dialysed foetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco A33820-01) and 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin for 24 h. The medium was exchanged, the gel precursor-filled Transwell (Greiner Bio-One 662641) was added, and the experiment started. The Transwells were removed at the selected time, and staining stock containing Calcein AM and Propidium iodide was added to the samples, leading to a final concentration of 2 µg/ml Calcein AM and 4 µg/ml PI. The samples were incubated for 20 min and subsequently imaged. Raw data were processed using ImageJ v1.54f and Microsoft Excel; graphs were generated in GraphPad Prism 10.2.2.

The spheroids were treated with 50 µL 2.5 U/mL alginate lyase (A1603, Sigma-Aldrich) in DMEM at 37 °C for 45 min to remove the gel. All samples, including controls, underwent the same enzymatic treatment. Then, the spheroids were washed with PBS (5×) to remove enzyme and dissolved gel. Cell viability was quantified using the CellTiter-Glo® 3D Luminescent Cell Viability Assay (Promega) in half-area, white 96-well plates according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Luminescence was recorded on a SPARK 20 M microplate reader (Tecan Group Ltd). Raw data were processed using Microsoft Excel, and graphs were generated in GraphPad Prism 10.2.2.

The spheroids were treated with 50 µL 2.5 U/mL alginate lyase (A1603, Sigma-Aldrich) in DMEM at 37 °C for 45 min to remove the gel. All samples, including controls, underwent the same enzymatic treatment. Then, the spheroids were washed with PBS (5×) to remove enzyme and dissolved gel. Cell viability was quantified using a resazurin-based assay (Sigma-Aldrich, TOX8) in black 96-well plates according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Spheroids were incubated with the resazurin solution for 4 h prior to measurement. Fluorescence was recorded on a SPARK 20 M microplate reader (Tecan Group Ltd; Sparkcontrol V.2.3) with an excitation wavelength of 560 nm and an emission wavelength of 590 nm. Raw data were processed using Microsoft Excel, and graphs were generated in GraphPad Prism 10.2.2.

Proteome Analysis was performed with A549 2D culture and A549 spheroids after 2 days of incubation. Array data were interpreted as relative, semi-quantitative protein-abundance changes. For 2D cultures, three biological replicates were analysed with two on-membrane technical replicates. For 3D spheroids, three biological replicates were analysed, each consisting of 12 pooled spheroids, with two on-membrane technical replicates. For the 3D spheroid control experiment with AlgTA/LOx/Cat, two biological replicates with two on-membrane technical replicates were performed. Because the array was used for targeted exploratory profiling rather than unbiased quantitative proteomics, protein changes were interpreted together with orthogonal morphological and viability readouts.

Cells from 10 wells of a 24-well plate were used for each condition and washed with PBS (2×). The cells were lysed with RIPA buffer (100 µL per well; 39244.01, SERVA Electrophoresis) at 4 °C for 1 h and centrifuged at 4 °C for 15 min (10,000 × g ).

The spheroids ( n = 12) were transferred to an Eppendorf tube, washed with PBS (2×) and treated with 200 µL of 2.5 U/mL alginate lyase (A1603, Sigma-Aldrich) in DMEM at 37 °C for 45 min to remove the gel. All samples, including controls, underwent the same enzymatic treatment. Then, the spheroids were washed with PBS (5×) to remove enzyme and dissolved gel. The spheroids were lysed with RIPA buffer (100 µL per spheroid; 39244.01, SERVA Electrophoresis) at 4 °C for 1 h and centrifuged at 4 °C for 15 min (10,000 × g ).

The resulting supernatants were analysed using the Human Angiogenesis Array (R&D Systems, ARY007) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, samples were diluted and incubated with biotinylated detection antibodies before application to the nitrocellulose membranes. After washing, Streptavidin-HRP and chemiluminescent reagents were added. Signal intensity was captured via chemiluminescence (ChemiDoc Imaging System, Bio-Rad, Image Lab Touch Software V. 3.0.1.14), and quantified by calculating the background-subtracted mean pixel density of duplicate spots (“Gels” plugin of ImageJ V.1.54f). The mapping of the array coordinates and the corresponding targets is provided in Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 20 . Data were normalised to the untreated control cultured in regular medium without AlgTA/LOx/HRP. The data were processed with Microsoft Excel, and graphs were generated using GraphPad Prism 10.2.2.

Images of the cells were taken using a Keyence BZ-X800 microscope (BZ-X800 Viewer V. 1.3.0.1) using a 10× objective (BZ-PA10, NA 0.45, WD 4.0 mm), 20× objective (BZ-PF20LP, NA 0.45, WD 8.8–7.5 mm) and 40× objective (BZ-PF40LP, NA 0.60 WD 3.3–2.2 mm). Cells and spheroids were stained using NucBlue® Live ReadyProbes® reagent, Calcein AM, Alexa Fluor™ 488 phalloidin and/or propidium iodide, as indicated for each experiment. The fluorescence was imaged with 360/40 nm excitation and 460/50 nm emission filter for NucBlue® Live ReadyProbes® Reagent, 470/40 nm excitation and 525/50 nm emission filter for Calcein AM/Alexa Fluor™ 488 phalloidin and 545/25 nm excitation and 605/70 nm emission filter for propidium iodide. Cells in 2D culture were stained in 600 µL FBS supplemented medium containing 2 µg/ml Calcein AM, 4 µg/ml propidium iodide and 2 drops of NucBlue® Live ReadyProbes® reagent for 20 min. 3D spheroids were stained in 100 µL FBS supplemented medium containing 2 µg/ml Calcein AM, 4 µg/ml propidium iodide and 2 drops/mL of NucBlue® Live ReadyProbes® reagent for 1 h. Alexa Fluor™ 488 phalloidin staining was performed according to the manufacturer's protocol for 1 h after NucBlue® Live ReadyProbes® staining and fixation with pre-warmed paraformaldehyde in PBS (4% Roti-Histofix, Carl Roth) for 60 min.

Spheroid size was quantified from brightfield images using ImageJ v1.54f. For each spheroid, four diameters were measured along the horizontal, vertical and two diagonal axes at day 0 and after 48 h of incubation. The mean of the four measurements was used as the spheroid diameter, following previous literature 15 . Images were analysed using identical scale calibration and measurement settings for all conditions. The scale bar is 200 µm.

Primary glioblastoma spheroids were embedded into a collagen-based extracellular matrix to evaluate invasive growth. All matrix preparation steps were performed on ice. For each well of a 48-well plate, 200 µL collagen solution consisting of MEM supplemented with 0.02 M NaOH and 2.2 mg/mL bovine collagen was added and pre-incubated at 37 °C for 2 min to initiate matrix formation. Spheroids were subsequently placed centrally onto the semi-polymerised matrix. Following complete polymerisation for 2 h at 37 °C, 200 µL cDMEM (DMEM, 10% heat-inactivated FBS, 10 µg mL −1 gentamicin) was added to each well. For lactate-gated gelation, cDMEM contained 3 wt% AlgTA, 1 U mL −1 LOx and 10 U mL −1 HRP. Control wells received cDMEM only. Invasive outgrowth was monitored by brightfield microscopy using a Leica DM IL LED Fluo microscope equipped with a 5× objective.

Quantitative image analysis was conducted in CellProfiler using a standardised workflow for all samples. Images were subjected to grayscale conversion, illumination correction and intensity inversion prior to object identification. Spheroid cores and invading cells were identified using the IdentifyPrimaryObjects module with Otsu-based thresholding following logarithmic intensity transformation. The total occupied area of spheroid and invasive regions was quantified while excluding background signals. Accuracy was verified by overlaying detected object outlines onto the original images, and all measurements were normalised to the corresponding spheroid area at day 0.

Data are presented as mean ± s.d. unless stated otherwise. Statistical analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism 10.2.2 or Microsoft Excel. Comparisons between two groups were performed using unpaired two-tailed Welch’s t -tests unless stated otherwise. Exact P -values are reported where practical; P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Sample sizes, replicate definitions and numbers of independent experiments are stated in the corresponding figure legends and the “Methods” section. For cell-based assays, biological replicates refer to independent wells, spheroids, gels or independently repeated experiments as indicated; technical replicates refer to repeated measurements within the same biological sample. No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. No data were excluded unless exclusion criteria are explicitly stated. Experiments were not randomised unless stated otherwise. Image analysis of patient-derived glioblastoma invasion was performed using a standardised CellProfiler pipeline applied identically to all images. Proteome-array data were treated as relative, semi-quantitative measurements and interpreted together with orthogonal viability, morphology and material-characterisation readouts.

articles.title: SpaCEy links spatial tissue patterns to clinical outcomes using explainable graph neural networks.
articles.authors: Rifaioglu AS, Ervin EH, Sarigun A, Germen D, Bodenmiller B, Tanevski J, Saez-Rodriguez J.
articles.abstract: Tissues are complex ecosystems organised in space, and alterations in this organisation underpin multiple diseases. Spatial omics enables molecular profiling of tissue organisation, but linking these patterns to clinical outcomes remains challenging. We present SpaCEy ( Spa tial C linical E xplainabilit y ), an explainable graph neural network that identifies tissue patterns predictive of clinical outcomes in spatial proteomics datasets. SpaCEy models tissues as spatial graphs from molecular marker expression, without using predefined cell-type labels or anatomical regions as model inputs. Its embeddings capture intercellular relationships and molecular dependencies for predicting overall survival and disease progression. An integrated explainer identifies recurring spatial patterns and coordinated marker expression relevant to model predictions. Applied to a spatial proteomic lung cancer cohort, SpaCEy identifies spatial and protein-expression patterns associated with disease progression. Across multiple breast cancer proteomic datasets, it stratifies patients by overall survival, both across and within established clinical subtypes, and highlights protein markers underlying this stratification.
paragraphs: Tissues are complex ecosystems organised in space, and alterations in this organisation underpin multiple diseases. Spatial omics enables molecular profiling of tissue organisation, but linking these patterns to clinical outcomes remains challenging. We present SpaCEy ( Spa tial C linical E xplainabilit y ), an explainable graph neural network that identifies tissue patterns predictive of clinical outcomes in spatial proteomics datasets. SpaCEy models tissues as spatial graphs from molecular marker expression, without using predefined cell-type labels or anatomical regions as model inputs. Its embeddings capture intercellular relationships and molecular dependencies for predicting overall survival and disease progression. An integrated explainer identifies recurring spatial patterns and coordinated marker expression relevant to model predictions. Applied to a spatial proteomic lung cancer cohort, SpaCEy identifies spatial and protein-expression patterns associated with disease progression. Across multiple breast cancer proteomic datasets, it stratifies patients by overall survival, both across and within established clinical subtypes, and highlights protein markers underlying this stratification.

SpaCEy uses explainable graph neural networks to link spatial tissue organisation with clinical outcomes, identifying spatial and molecular patterns associated with cancer progression and patient survival.

Cells often organize into specific arrangements in space within tissues and the relationship between the spatial organisation of tissues and function, both in health and disease, is widely acknowledged 1 , 2 . The amount of spatially resolved molecular data at the single-cell level has been rapidly increasing with technological improvements 3 . In particular, advancements in multiplex imaging enable precise mapping of cell populations and their diverse states within their tissue environment at the single-cell level, exploration of the organisation and interaction of cells in the tumour microenvironment, communication patterns, and novel disease mechanisms 3 , 4 . Spatial omics also offers new translational opportunities by revealing similarities and differences in tissue organisation and function among patients assigned to the same treatment group 1 , 3 , 5 – 7 . This tissue organisation frequently shows characteristic changes in spatial arrangements of cells which are shared across patients in diseases like cancer and fibrosis. Identifying these changes is critical because they are often structured as spatially important regions, which are localised structural patterns of cells and molecules within the tissue 8 . The high resolution offered by spatial omics technologies now makes it possible to identify these spatial motifs, providing an opportunity to link this spatial variation directly to clinical outcomes.

Analysing complex, high-dimensional omics data requires advanced machine learning methods capable of integrating diverse datasets, modelling relationships within and across tissues, and extracting meaningful biological insights to support the prediction of clinical outcomes. Subsequently, such models allow for studying the link between the changes in these relationships in response to perturbations, such as disease or drug treatment. Some of these methods do not incorporate spatial information for clinical outcome prediction. For example, Fast Survival SVM applies a max-margin framework for time-to-event prediction for survivability prediction 9 , Random Survival Forests use ensemble tree models to capture nonlinear relationships between omics data and survival outcomes 10 , and Gradient Boosting Survival Analysis builds an ensemble of decision-tree models in a stage-wise manner to capture nonlinear predictors of time-to-event outcomes 11 . In contrast, spatially informed approaches have been developed to model tissue organisation directly, enabling the integration of spatial coordinates to solve complex tasks such as clinical outcome prediction and characterisation of tissue microenvironments. For instance, Wu et al. developed a graph neural network (GNN) to model tumour microenvironments using spatial protein profiles from tissue specimens 12 . This method leverages multiplexed immunofluorescence imaging to capture the complex interactions within the tumour microenvironment and predict patient outcomes based on local cell type compositions. Similarly, STELLAR combines spatial and molecular information to enhance cell-type annotation and discovery in spatially resolved single-cell datasets. Using geometric deep learning, it assigns cells to known types, identifies novel cell states, and captures higher-order tissue structures 13 . SPACE-GM models tumour microenvironments as cellular graphs with the aim of predicting cancer recurrence and patient survival based on cell-type compositions of neighbourhoods 12 . A recent study by Ali et al. applied GNNs to spatial proteomics data, showing their models capture meaningful spatial features by analysing the embeddings of the samples 14 . Graph-based neural approaches have also been developed extensively for spatial transcriptomics, including methods for spatial-domain detection, representation learning, integration, and deconvolution such as SpaGCN 15 , STAGATE 16 , GraphST 17 , DeepST 18 , SEDR 19 and SpaceFlow 20 . However, these methods have largely focused on characterising tissue organisation, while important limitations remain in connecting spatial patterns to clinical outcomes and translating model predictions into biologically interpretable tissue-level insights. Overall, spatially aware methods highlight the value of incorporating tissue architecture into single-cell analysis, enabling graph neural networks to uncover deeper insights into cellular function and tissue organisation.

Despite recent developments of spatially informed methods for analysing tissue organisation, major limitations remain in translating predictive power into biological or clinical insight. One of the key limitations, when applied to spatial tissue graphs, existing methods often rely on predefined cell-type labels or local clustering, which prevents the discovery of emergent organisational patterns directly from continuous molecular measurements. At the same time, the aforementioned machine learning models, despite their strong predictive performance, fall short in identifying contiguous, spatially coherent regions of importance and in effectively incorporating spatial information into their modelling frameworks 21 . They typically limit interpretability to analyses of model-derived latent representations or cell-level importance scores, thereby limiting their ability to uncover spatial motifs that are critical to clinical outcomes. Consequently, current methods lack the capacity to simultaneously revealing the spatially important regions and providing a concise set of molecular markers that collectively drive the observed clinical outcomes. Addressing these limitations is essential for improving confidence in model decisions, reliability, and the potential of obtaining novel biological insights 22 , and to ultimately deploy machine learning models in clinical practice.

We present SpaCEy, an explainable method for discovering spatially important regions on the tissues associated with clinical outcomes using GNNs. Unlike approaches that require predefined cell-type labels or clustering as model inputs, SpaCEy identifies shared contiguous spatial patterns directly from measured cell-specific marker abundances. By representing each tissue sample as a spatial graph and learning predictive embeddings, SpaCEy bridges the gap between tissue architecture and clinical stratification. To overcome limitations of current approaches, which often produce predictive embeddings without revealing the structural or molecular features driving their predictions, SpaCEy integrates an explainer model that highlights connected sets of spatially adjacent nodes and edges responsible for its outputs by identifying compact subgraphs 23 . This enables interpretable insights into tissue organisation and molecular determinants of disease. Furthermore, SpaCEy identifies a concise set of marker proteins that are most influential for predicting the corresponding clinical outcomes, providing molecular-level interpretability alongside spatial insights. This workflow is annotation-agnostic during model input, training, prediction, and explanation generation. Annotations are only used to assist post-hoc analysis to contextualise the interpretation to particular groups of samples of interest. By capturing emergent patterns across patients, SpaCEy links complex spatial structures to clinical outcomes. By offering a scalable, explainable and data-driven framework for analysing tissue organisation, SpaCEy paves the way for insights into the spatial determinants of disease and their impact on patient outcomes.

SpaCEy is an explainable method that detects spatial patterns in tissue samples which are linked to clinical outcomes. The model input consists of protein-abundance measurements at single-cell level represented as spatial graphs; clinical outcomes are used as supervised labels, while clinical annotations are only retained for descriptive and post hoc interpretation (Methods, Data preprocessing and Training settings) (Fig. 1 a). Cell-type and compartment annotations are not used as SpaCEy node features, but are retained as metadata for descriptive and post hoc biological interpretation. The spatially resolved samples are transformed into a spatial graph by Delaunay triangulation method 24 . This approach ensures that each cell is connected to its spatially nearest neighbours, preserving the tissue architecture in the graph structure. In these spatial graphs, each node represents a cell, and the features of each node represent the abundance of each measured protein marker in the corresponding spatial location. A GNN model is then trained on this spatial graph representation, leveraging the connectivity and spatial relationships between cells to learn meaningful latent representations of the input samples (Methods, Model architecture) (Fig. 1 a). To interpret the learned model, an explainer model generates feature and edge masks that highlight the most relevant components contributing to the GNN’s predictions for the clinical outcome of interest (Methods, Explainer model) (Fig. 1 b) 23 . The input to the explainer model consists of the trained model and constructed spatial graph, and its output is the learned edge masks (i.e., edge importance values) for the input graph. A key novelty of SpaCEy lies in its ability to generate interpretable spatially contiguous regions (i.e., connected subgraphs) that uncover spatially localised molecular drivers of clinical outcomes. Node importance values are computed by aggregating edge-mask values from k-hop neighbours of each node, enabling the identification of key spatially contiguous, compact subgraphs that mark important regions in the tissue (Methods, Node importance and important regions). Here, node and edge importance scores produced by the explainer quantify unsigned relevance magnitudes. Thus, they identify the graph components that are most influential for the model prediction, but they do not by themselves encode the direction of effect, i.e., whether a given node, edge, or spatial motif shifts the prediction toward or away from a clinical outcome of interest. Using these importance values together with the latent representations from the trained model, we perform unsupervised analysis of the latent space representations of samples, and perform differential analysis to extract biologically relevant insights (Fig. 1 c). Based on the identified molecular and spatial features, SpaCEy provides a data-driven framework for understanding the heterogeneity of structure and function in the tumour microenvironment and enables an improved patient stratification (Fig. 1 c). Fig. 1 SpaCEy model architecture and analysis workflow. a Samples from multiple cohorts were collected as the source of high-dimensional spatial data for this study. These samples were converted into spatial graphs using the Delaunay triangulation method, and a graph neural network (GNN) was trained on these graphs, integrating spatial information and clinical data to predict relevant clinical outcomes. b The trained GNN model is then analysed using the explainer model, which outputs learned edge masks. Node importance values are computed by aggregating edge-mask values within the k-hop neighbourhood of each node, enabling the identification of compact connected subgraphs that define important spatial regions in the tissue. c Latent representations of samples and identified important regions were then used for visualisation, differential analysis, and biological interpretation based on node importance values, ultimately enabling patient stratification and downstream analysis. We first applied SpaCEy to a recently published lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) imaging mass cytometry data by Sorin et al. 25 comprising samples from 416 patients. In the LUAD cohort, we modelled progression as a supervised binary classification task using the progression annotations provided with the dataset. Summary statistics and cohort characteristics of LUAD dataset is provided in Supplementary Table 1 . Fig. 2 a shows Kaplan–Meier estimates of overall survival stratified by progression status, with censoring marks indicated on each curve, revealing no significant difference in overall survival between the two progression groups (log-rank p = 0.0767). To investigate the relationship between the clinical outcomes and the latent representations generated by our model, we visualised the embeddings across all nodes for each sample in UMAP space (Fig. 2 b), with each point representing a sample and coloured by progression status. Together, these visualisations demonstrate that the learned embedding is associated with clinical progression. Analysis of marker abundance in the important nodes revealed distinct immune microenvironments and tumour-associated profiles between patients with and without progression Fig. 2 c. The T-cell labels follow the source annotations from Sorin et al. 25 : Th cells refers to CD4-enriched helper T cells, Tc refers to CD8a-enriched cytotoxic T cells, Treg refers to FOXP3-enriched regulatory T cells, and T other denotes T cells not assigned to these specific subsets. Here, important nodes refer to a group of cells selected by the explanation module as part of model-informative spatial regions. In contrast, non-progressing tumours exhibited areas with elevated numbers of Th cells, Tc cells, and B cells. Specifically, FOXP3, CD163, Histone H3, and DNA1 were enriched in the important nodes of progression group. FOXP3 is a canonical regulatory T-cell marker, and CD163 + macrophages form part of an immunosuppressive axis previously associated with aggressive LUAD architecture and poor outcomes 25 . In contrast, non-progressing patients exhibited areas with higher expression of HLA-DR and CD4, and a slight upregulation of epithelial cancer cell marker pan-cytokeratin. HLA-DR marks primarily antigen-presenting cells that are part of an active anti-tumour immune response 26 , 27 . In the original Sorin et al. study, Th and Tc populations showed stronger cancer-cell interactions in lower-grade tumours than in high-grade solid LUAD 25 . Therefore, SpaCEy specifically highlights these regions of cancer-immune cell interactions that are characteristic of tumours with better prognosis. Analysis of cell-type proportions revealed differences between progression and non-progression groups Fig. 2 d which shows cell-type enrichment among important nodes. Tumours from patients who progressed showed areas with significantly increased frequencies of macrophage populations, including CD163 + macrophages, as well as higher cancer and endothelial cell content. This is consistent with the original publication demonstrating that CD163 + tumour-associated macrophages, typically linked to immunosupression and tumour progression, are enriched in high-grade tumours and strongly co-occur with FOXP3 + regulatory T cells 25 . The increased co-localisation and interaction between cancer and endothelial cells observed in higher-grade histological patterns reflects their aggressive nature and high metastatic potential 25 . To provide an image-level example, we selected a representative progressor LUAD sample and visualised direct graph contacts between explainer-important cancer and endothelial cell nodes, highlighted with bold edges (Fig. 2 e). This example illustrates local cancer–endothelial adjacency within an explainer-highlighted tissue region. Interestingly, SpaCEy also identifies a previously not described enrichment of CD163 − macrophages in regions associated with progression. In contrast, non-progressing tumours exhibited areas with elevated numbers of Th cells, Tc cells and B cells. To assess whether this immune-cell signal was located in direct proximity to tumour cells, we defined tumour adjacency as a direct graph edge between an important immune cell and at least one cancer cell. Using this definition, 49.9% of pooled important Tc cells (3,019 of 6,053 cells) and 40.9% of pooled important Th cells (4,416 of 10,803 cells) in the no-progression group were cancer-adjacent, indicating that this no-progression-associated T-cell signal is partly tumour-localised. For comparison with the entire Tc and Th cell populations in the same no-progression group, 46.8% of all Tc cells (38,074 of 81,330 cells) and 38.6% of all Th cells (48,467 of 125,557 cells) in the no-progression group were cancer-adjacent. Thus, important Tc and Th cells were only modestly more tumour-adjacent than the corresponding global Tc/Th populations. CD4, CD8a, and FOXP3 are measured marker channels, whereas Th, Tc, Treg, and T other are source cell-type annotation labels shown in Fig. 2 d. Tc and Th cells play key roles in anti-tumour immunity, whereas B cells have previously been associated with improved overall survival in LUAD 25 . Overall, these patterns indicate that SpaCEy identifies clinically relevant regions predictive of tumour progression and also shows potential to reveal emergent spatial trends.

We evaluated SpaCEy against two state-of-the-art baselines, Ali et al. 14 and SPACE-GM 12 , using five-fold cross-validation across all performance metrics (accuracy, F1-score, and AUC) Fig. 2 f. We performed a random split stratified by disease status and fixed the splits to ensure a fair comparison and an equal distribution of disease status across folds. SpaCEy achieved the highest overall performance and the most stable behaviour across folds. In terms of accuracy, SpaCEy reached a mean of 0.68, outperforming both Ali et al. (0.61) and SPACE-GM (0.55). Similar trends were observed for F1-score, where SpaCEy got 0.68 on average, whereas the method from Ali et al. and SPACE-GM achieved 0.59 and 0.52, respectively. SpaCEy also demonstrated higher discriminative capability, yielding the highest mean AUC (0.62), compared with 0.57 for Ali et al. and 0.52 for SPACE-GM. Notably, SpaCEy consistently performed strongly across folds, including peak values of 0.77 accuracy, 0.75 F1-score, and 0.78 AUC.

The second dataset used to train SpaCEy was an imaging mass cytometry dataset comprising 720 samples from two patient cohorts at the University Hospital of Basel and the University Hospital of Zurich, which includes breast cancer samples across a range of clinical subtypes and cancer stages 28 . We refer to this dataset as the JacksonFischer dataset throughout the remainder of the text. Here, our objective was to model overall survival (hereafter referred to as survival) in a censoring-aware time-to-event setting. Summary statistics and cohort characteristics are provided in Supplementary Table 2 . For the JacksonFischer dataset, Kaplan–Meier curves (Fig. 3 a) stratified by clinical subtype (HR+HER2+, HR+HER2-, HR-HER2+, and TripleNeg) showed significant differences among clinical subtypes in overall survival (log-rank p = 0.012), where patients with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) exhibit the lowest survival rates due to the aggressive nature of the subtype, lack of targeted therapies, and higher likelihood of early metastasis 29 , 30 . The corresponding UMAP of the embeddings learned by the SpaCEy is shown in (Fig. 3 b). The embeddings revealed a structured distribution of samples, with similarity grouping associated primarily with survival.
