articles.title: Spatiotemporal invasion dynamics of SARS-CoV-2 lineage B.1.1.7 emergence.
articles.authors: Kraemer MUG, Hill V, Ruis C, Dellicour S, Bajaj S, McCrone JT, Baele G, Parag KV, Battle AL, Gutierrez B, Jackson B, Colquhoun R, O'Toole Á, Klein B, Vespignani A, COVID-19 Genomics UK (COG-UK) Consortium, Volz E, Faria NR, Faria NR, Aanensen DM, Loman NJ, du Plessis L, Cauchemez S, Rambaut A, Scarpino SV, Pybus OG.
articles.abstract: Fueling outbreaks The B.1.1.7 lineage of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) has caused fast-spreading outbreaks globally. Intrinsically, this variant has greater transmissibility than its predecessors, but this capacity has been amplified in some circumstances to tragic effect by a combination of human behavior and local immunity. What are the extrinsic factors that help or hinder the rapid dissemination of variants? Kraemer et al . explored the invasion dynamics of B.1.1.7. in fine detail, from its location of origin in Kent, UK, to its heterogenous spread around the country. A combination of mobile phone and virus data including more than 17,000 genomes shows how distinct phases of dispersal were related to intensity of mobility and the timing of lockdowns. As the local outbreaks grew, importation from the London source area became less important. Had B.1.1.7. emerged at a slightly different time of year, its impact might have been different. —CA
paragraphs: The B.1.1.7 lineage of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) has caused fast-spreading outbreaks globally. Intrinsically, this variant has greater transmissibility than its predecessors, but this capacity has been amplified in some circumstances to tragic effect by a combination of human behavior and local immunity. What are the extrinsic factors that help or hinder the rapid dissemination of variants? Kraemer et al . explored the invasion dynamics of B.1.1.7. in fine detail, from its location of origin in Kent, UK, to its heterogenous spread around the country. A combination of mobile phone and virus data including more than 17,000 genomes shows how distinct phases of dispersal were related to intensity of mobility and the timing of lockdowns. As the local outbreaks grew, importation from the London source area became less important. Had B.1.1.7. emerged at a slightly different time of year, its impact might have been different. —CA
Disentangling the factors that contribute to the rapid spread of virus variants is essential for understanding their epidemiological consequences.

Understanding the causes and consequences of the emergence of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) variants of concern is crucial to pandemic control yet difficult to achieve because they arise in the context of variable human behavior and immunity. We investigated the spatial invasion dynamics of lineage B.1.1.7 by jointly analyzing UK human mobility, virus genomes, and community-based polymerase chain reaction data. We identified a multistage spatial invasion process in which early B.1.1.7 growth rates were associated with mobility and asymmetric lineage export from a dominant source location, enhancing the effects of B.1.1.7’s increased intrinsic transmissibility. We further explored how B.1.1.7 spread was shaped by nonpharmaceutical interventions and spatial variation in previous attack rates. Our findings show that careful accounting of the behavioral and epidemiological context within which variants of concern emerge is necessary to interpret correctly their observed relative growth rates.

The severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) lineage B.1.1.7 expanded rapidly across the United Kingdom ( 1 , 2 ) in late 2020 and subsequently spread internationally ( 3 , 4 ). As of 19 January 2021 (date of the most recent sample in our dataset), B.1.1.7 had reached all but five counties of Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland, and England, with onward transmission in each. Restrictions on international travel were enacted to contain B.1.1.7’s spread; however, genomic surveillance has since detected the presence and growth of the lineage in many countries worldwide ( 4 , 5 ). Analyses of genomic, laboratory, secondary contact, and aggregated epidemiological data estimate higher transmissibility of B.1.1.7 compared with previous SARS-CoV-2 lineages ( 1 , 6 – 9 ) and potentially a greater risk of hospitalization ( 10 – 13 ). The spatial heterogeneity of SARS-CoV-2 transmission—and of emerging infectious diseases in general—can have profound effects on the local likelihood and intensity of transmission, final epidemic size, and immunity ( 14 – 22 ). More specifically, estimates of B.1.1.7’s increased relative transmissibility declined during its emergence in the UK ( 7 , 9 ); understanding why this occurred is necessary if we are to respond effectively to future SARS-CoV-2 variants. We reconstructed and quantified the spatial dynamics of B.1.1.7’s emergence and investigated how human mobility and heterogeneity in previous exposure contributed to B.1.1.7’s initial spread and evaluation of higher transmissibility.

B.1.1.7 can be first detected in COVID-19 Genomics UK Consortium (COG-UK) genome data in Kent on 20 September 2020 and spread quickly across the UK, with each week adding detections in approximately seven new upper-tier local authorities (UTLAs) ( Fig. 1, A and B , and table S2). B.1.1.7 was already reported in several UTLAs before the start of the second English lockdown (5 November 2020). By the end of that lockdown (2 December 2020), B.1.1.7 was widespread throughout the UK ( Fig. 1, A and B ).

( A ) Map at the UTLA level of arrival dates of lineage B.1.1.7. Darker colors indicate earlier dates, and lighter colors indicate later dates. Arrival time is defined as the earliest sampling date of a B.1.1.7 genomic sequence in each UTLA. ( B ) Cumulative number of UTLAs in which B.1.1.7 has been detected, in 7-day intervals. The blue shaded area indicates the period of the second lockdown in England. ( C ) Relationship between the arrival time of B.1.1.7 and estimated number of movements from Kent and London during February 2020 for each UTLA (Pearson’s r = –0.73; 95% CI: –0.61, –0.81; P < 0.001) (materials and methods). ( D ) Human mobility at the UK local authority district level (LAD) (table S2) during the epidemiological week 29 November to 5 December 2020. Thicker lines (edges) indicate more movements between regions. Nodes with larger absolute incoming movements are indicated with darker colors. Red lines indicate movements from Greater London. (Insets I, II, and III) Mobility within three UK metropolitan areas. ( E ) Trends in human mobility across the UK (indicating movements between but not within LADs). The blue shaded areas indicate the period of the first, second, and third lockdown in England. Dark red indicates the timing (20 December 2020) of the Tier 4 restrictions imposed in southeast England, including London ( 56 ).

The spatial expansion of SARS-CoV-2 lineages [for example, ( 16 , 23 )] can be tracked by using data from the UK’s national surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 genomes ( 24 ). By combining these data with aggregated mobile phone data, we examined the dissemination of B.1.1.7 through human mobility, from its likely location of emergence (Kent and Greater London) to other UK regions ( Fig. 1, D and E , and supplementary materials, materials and methods). Human mobility among UK regions increased at the end of the second English lockdown, from 55 million to 75 million weekly movements ( Fig. 1E ). Because of its centrality, Greater London exhibits an important connective role in the UK human movement network ( Fig. 1D ; red lines indicate the week the second lockdown was eased). Compared with that of previous weeks, movements out of Greater London were more frequent and reached more destinations (fig. S1). For each UTLA, we found that the date of first detection of B.1.1.7 is predicted well by human mobility from Kent and Greater London to that UTLA [Pearson’s correlation coefficient ( r ) = –0.73; 95% confidence interval (CI): –0.61, –0.81; Akaike information criteria (AIC) = 734] ( Fig. 1C ) and similarly well by using movements from Kent and Greater London separately (fig. S2). This correlation strengthens through time as new locations of B.1.1.7 detection are added (fig. S3) and is robust to changes in human mobility through time in among-region human movement (Pearson’s r = –0.44; 95% CI: –0.16, –0.65; P < 0.01; mobility data through 23 January 2021) (materials and methods). Geographic distance from Greater London correlates less strongly with B.1.1.7 arrival times (Pearson’s r = 0.60; 95% CI: 0.44 to 0.71; AIC = 763) (fig. S4).

To understand better the spatial dispersal of B.1.1.7 during its emergence, we reconstructed its spread across England using large-scale phylogeographic analysis ( 25 – 27 ). We analyzed 17,716 B.1.1.7 genomes collected between 20 September 2020 and 19 January 2021 ( Fig. 2 and fig. S5), collated from polymerase chain reaction (PCR)–positive community samples that represent a random selection of SARS-CoV-2–positive samples ( 28 ). These genomes represent ~4% of UK B.1.1.7 cases during the study period [ n = 460,510 estimated tests with PCR S-gene target failure (SGTF) between 20 September 2020 and 19 January 2021]. Samples per location (UTLA) and per week in the SGTF and whole-genome datasets are strongly correlated (Pearson’s r = 0.69; 95% CI: 0.63 – 0.73; P < 0.001) (fig. S6) ( 7 ), making it feasible to reconstruct B.1.1.7 expansion history by using phylogeographic approaches ( 29 ).

( A and B ) Continuous phylogeographic reconstruction with phylogeny nodes colored according to their time of occurrence and dispersal direction of phylogeny branches indicated by edge curvature (counterclockwise). From left to right, data to 5 November, 1 December, and 20 December 2020, respectively. (B) Map of the entire reconstruction, up to 19 January 2021. ( C ) Estimated number of weekly exports of lineage B.1.1.7 from the Greater London area, inferred from the continuous phylogeographic analysis (red), and estimated from mobility and prevalence survey data (black). ( D ) Estimated number of cumulative B.1.1.7 introductions inferred from phylogeographic analysis into each administrative area (UTLA) by 12 December 2020.

We identified distinct phases to the emergence of B.1.1.7. Initially, during the second English lockdown, most (71.2%) B.1.1.7 phylogenetic branch movements originated and ended in Greater London or Kent; long-distance dispersal events were relatively infrequent ( Figs. 2 and 3 ). After the lockdown ended, and new cases in London subsequently rose rapidly, observed virus lineage movements from southeast England to other regions increased, and other large cities started to exhibit local transmission ( Figs. 2 and 3 ). This phase of a growing number of exported B.1.1.7 cases from London and environs stabilized in mid-December and coincided with reduced mobility from Greater London (Tier 4 restrictions were announced on 20 December 2020 and entailed a “Stay at home” order, closure of nonessential shops and hospitality, and strict limitations on household mixing) ( Figs. 1E and 2C ). However, the total number of B.1.1.7 lineage exports did not immediately decline because the growing number of B.1.1.7 cases in southeast England offset the decline in outward travel ( Fig. 2C ) ( 30 ), indicating a limited effect of delayed action on B.1.1.7 spread from Greater London. Our analysis did not allow us to establish a causal link between nonpharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) and their impact on lineage exportations, so these results should be interpreted with caution.

( A ) Curved arrows and line thicknesses indicate the direction and intensity of B.1.1.7 lineage flows among regions. Red circles indicate, for a given location, the ratio of inferred local movements to inferred importations into that location. Four time periods are shown (left to right) and roughly correspond to (i) before second lockdown, (ii) second lockdown, (iii) after second lockdown, and (iv) implementation of Tier 4 restrictions in southeast England. ( B ) Distribution of the geographic distances of phylogenetic lineage movement events (>50 km). Those from Greater London are in red, and those from other locations are in gray.

By combining mobility and SGTF data with estimates of the proportion of the population testing SARS-CoV-2–positive (materials and methods), we can estimate the frequency of B.1.1.7 export from Greater London to other English regions ( Fig. 2C and fig. S7) and explore its role in accelerating the lineage’s emergence. Using these combined data sources, we estimate that the number of B.1.1.7 case exports from Greater London rose during November (including during lockdown) from 12,000 in early December ( Fig. 2C , gray curve), reflecting growth in B.1.1.7 infections in Greater London and an increase in human mobility among UK geographic regions across in late November ( Fig. 1E ). The estimated intensity of B.1.1.7 case exportation from Greater London remained high in December, peaking in mid-December at ~20,000 weekly exports, before declining in early January after the third national lockdown started on 5 January 2021. These estimates ( Fig. 2C , gray curve) closely match the trends in lineage B.1.1.7 movement inferred from phylogeographic analysis ( Fig. 2C , red curve), cross-validating both data sources (exports estimated by using each method are strongly correlated; Pearson’s r = 0.62; 95% CI: 0.61 to 0.64; P < 0.001) (fig. S8). Lineage exportation events estimated from genomic data are lower from late December onward, possibly owing to reporting lags in genomic data generation and/or delayed care-seeking because of the Christmas holidays ( 31 ). Our simple model assumes that nonsymptomatic infectious individuals are equally likely to travel ( Fig. 2C , gray line), which may bias our estimates of infectious travellers upward.

B.1.1.7 dispersal dynamics shifted in late December to more bidirectional exchange of phylogenetic lineages in and out of Greater London ( Fig. 3 ), coinciding with rapid growth in B.1.1.7 cases across England ( 9 ). Throughout, the weekly number of B.1.1.7 cases in a UTLA was positively associated with the number of B.1.1.7 lineage introductions into that UTLA during that week (Pearson’s r = 0.41, 0.76, 0.91, and 0.73, for October, November, December, and January, respectively; P 500 inferred importations, despite our genomic dataset representing <4% of reported B.1.1.7 cases during the study period ( Fig. 2D ).

Detailed mapping of the spatial dynamics of SARS-CoV-2 lineages is difficult without comprehensive, well-sampled epidemiological and genomic data ( 32 , 33 ). However, the COG-UK data enables us to study dissemination trends by comparing inferred B.1.1.7 importations with within-location movements. Greater London (and to some extent Kent) acted as the main exporter of B.1.1.7 lineages to other UTLAs until mid-December 2020 ( Fig. 3A ). The longest (>100 km) and shortest (<100 km) dispersal events consistently originated from Greater London throughout the study period ( Fig. 3B ), primarily because of its large epidemic. However, the relative percentage of lineage movements that originated from Greater London approximately halved between September 2020 and January 2021 (table S1).

Using SGTF PCR-positive tests as a proxy for B.1.1.7 infection ( 34 ), we next examined daily growth rates of SARS-CoV-2 cases at the UTLA level for SGTF and non-SGTF cases (excluding case data from 25 to 31 January to account for reporting and testing delays) (materials and methods) ( 35 ). Case growth rates immediately after the November 2020 lockdown were highest in regions of southeast England connected to Greater London and/or Kent (fig. S9). Acceleration in SGTF case growth rates in Greater London began in mid-November and preceded acceleration in other regions ( Fig. 4B ). At the UTLA level, growth rates of SGTF cases were higher than non-SGTF cases (fig. S9), a key observation used to support an increased transmissibility for B.1.1.7 ( 7 , 9 ).

( A ) Seven-day rolling average number of cases reported that had the SGTF (green) and cases reported with non-SGTF (red) for three selected LTLAs, Birmingham, Liverpool, and Manchester (table S2). The black line indicates the weekly number of independent introductions estimated from the phylogeographic analysis. The gray shaded area indicates the timing of the second (5 November to 1 December) and start of the third (5 January) English lockdown. ( B ) Rolling 7-day average growth rates of SGTF cases in Greater London (red line) and outside of Greater London (blue line). ( C ) Association between per-region (LTLA) difference between SGTF and non-SGTF case growth rates (corrected to account for differences through time in sampling intensity of SGTF cases) and number of B.1.1.7 importations into that region, as estimated from prevalence surveys and human mobility (gray dots) ( Fig. 2C and materials and methods). The gray area shows the time of the second English lockdown. Modeling results for SGTF growth rates are shown in fig. S9, and regression results under different assumptions about the frequency of SGTF are shown in fig. S10.

We added to those findings by quantifying the import of B.1.1.7 cases from London and investigating the association of importation trends with lineage-specific case growth rates (materials and methods). Using our phylogeographic analysis results ( Figs. 2 and 3 ), we found that growth in the rate of B.1.1.7 importation into a lower-tier local authority (LTLA) closely matches the early growth rate of SGTF cases in that LTLA (Birmingham, Liverpool, and Manchester are shown in Fig. 4A ). We further calculated the per-region difference between SGTF and non-SGTF case growth rates [the estimated raw additive increase in SGTF growth rate is 0.0715, and the median multiplicative advantage is 1.576, assuming a generation time of 6.5 days, which is qualitatively similar to those reported previously ( 7 , 9 ), with the caveat that generation times may differ between B.1.1.7 and other lineages ( 36 , 37 )] (fig. S11). The degree to which this difference is positively correlated with B.1.1.7 importation rate grew during the latter half of the November lockdown and remained very high [coefficient of determination ( R 2 ) > 0.75] until mid-December, before declining (the trend remains when accounting for uncertainty in the estimated number of infections across Greater London) ( Fig. 4C and fig. S12). This result is robust to the data and methods used to estimate per-location B.1.1.7 importation rates (figs. S9 and S10). Accounting for continued export of B.1.1.7 from Greater London and Kent can explain in part why estimates of the growth advantage of B.1.1.7 declined during the second half of December 2020, before the implementation of tighter control measures (Tier 4, 20 December) ( 7 , 9 ).

The epicenter of SARS-CoV-2 transmission in the UK shifted during the November 2020 lockdown: between 1 September and 1 December 2020, ~80% of reported cases were reported outside London and southeast England, whereas those regions accounted for ~40% of all cases during 1 to 7 December. We sought to understand how, in each location, post-lockdown growth rates related to previous attack rates as well as travel inflow to that location. We investigated predictors of the increase in the relative frequency of B.1.1.7 genomes compared with that of other SARS-CoV-2 lineages ( Fig. 5A ) ( 7 , 9 ). In a multivariate model, we found that about half of the variation in the increase in B.1.1.7 relative frequency between 2 and 16 December is associated with human mobility from Greater London and attack rates before the November lockdown ( Fig. 5, B and C ). UTLAs with lower previous attack rates tended to have faster-increasing B.1.1.7 frequencies. We repeated this analysis using SGTF case frequency data and obtained similar results ( R 2 = 0.57, P < 0.001) (fig. S13). However, neither human mobility nor pre-lockdown attack rate were significant predictors of later changes. Instead, change in the relative frequency of B.1.1.7 genomes after 17 December was best predicted simply by its frequency on that date ( R 2 = 0.13, P < 0.01) (fig. S14), although a model identified through exhaustive search by using Bayesian information criteria (BIC) includes the “frequency of B.1.1.7 on 17 December,” an interaction between arrival time and “frequency of B.1.1.7 on 17 December,” and an interaction between incidence before the November lockdown and mobility from London (BIC 178.467; R 2 = 0.68; P < 0.001) (fig. S14). Mobility from Greater London remains a significant predictor of B.1.1.7 growth after controlling for population size by means of both a multivariate regression and model-selection by using exhaustive search with both BIC and AIC.

( A ) Frequency of B.1.1.7 at the UTLA level at different sampling times. Pre-lockdown, dates before 5 November; lockdown, 5 to 30 November; post-lockdown, 1 to 15 December; Tier 4, 16 to 31 December; and the most recent sampling point, 1 to 12 January(materials and methods). ( B ) Increase in the frequency of B.1.1.7 sampled genomes between 2 and 16 December 2020 is associated with mobility from Greater London. ( C ) Increase in the frequency of B.1.1.7 sampled genomes at the UTLA level is associated with previous attack rates in each location. Results for equivalent analyses of SGTF data are similar and are provided in the supplementary materials.

We found that the emergence of B.1.1.7 throughout the UK was associated with a high export frequency from a major source location that was identified only retrospectively. This pattern recapitulates at a national scale the role that international mobility played in the early spread of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic ( 38 – 40 ). We conclude that the exceptionally rapid spatial spread and early growth rates of lineage B.1.1.7 likely reflect the combined effects of its higher intrinsic transmissibility ( 1 , 7 , 9 ) and the spatial structure of incidence and mobility before, during, and after the second lockdown in England ( 41 ).

Understanding what causes a new SARS-CoV-2 lineage to grow and replace preexisting lineages is a complex problem. In addition to virus genetic changes to relevant phenotypes (such as per-contact transmissibility, duration of infectiousness, and immune evasion), lineage replacement dynamics are likely affected by spatiotemporal heterogeneity in incidence, NPIs, prior infection, and among-region mobility ( 42 ). The role of the latter may be enhanced in the context of low or declining prevalence, as suggested by the frequency growth of lineage B.1.177 in the UK and Europe during summer 2020, which was associated with international travel ( 43 – 45 ). Evidence for the increased intrinsic transmissibility of B.1.1.7 is clear, but estimates have varied considerably [38 to 130% increase ( 7 , 9 )]. The growth potential of new SARS-CoV-2 variants will depend also on the average durations of their exposed and infectious phases, as well as their per-contact transmissibility ( 36 ). Our results indicate that exportations from a high-incidence epidemic source region raised early location-specific growth rate estimates across the UK ( Fig. 4B ), and that this effect declined through time. Similar trends have since been observed for lineage B.1.617.2 into the UK, after its importation from high-incidence regions onto a background of low incidence and lockdown easing. This conclusion is relevant for the interpretation of the current and future estimates of the increased transmissibility of B.1.1.7 (and other variants of concern) in other countries [such as the Untied States and Denmark ( 3 )]. Further epidemiological and experimental work is needed to discriminate transient demographic factors from the permanent contribution to increased transmissibility conferred by the mutations carried by B.1.1.7.

Although B.1.1.7 was first detected in Kent, UK, and is speculated to have accumulated its mutations during a chronic infection ( 2 ), because of the strong correlation between human mobility from those areas and date of B.1.1.7 detection elsewhere our results support the hypothesis that B.1.1.7 originated in Kent or Greater London. Further, our phylogeographic reconstruction shows early lineage dissemination from Kent and Greater London, indicating that B.1.1.7 spread through the UK from one dominant UK source region, as opposed to a large undetected epidemic elsewhere, which would likely have resulted in multiple introductions through international travel ( 16 ).

We demonstrate that large-scale and well-sampled genomic surveillance data can reveal the detailed spatial transmission dynamics of individual SARS-CoV-2 lineages and compensate for their comparatively low genetic diversity ( 46 ). To achieve a representative genomic sample, we used only samples from population-level testing rather than those from specific outbreak investigations. However, this approach does not fully mitigate reduced representation from populations less likely to seek testing ( 47 ), and there is some geographic variation in the proportion of cases sequenced (fig. S15). Greater London consistently has a higher sampling proportion than other regions throughout the study timeframe. Although sampling biases cannot be wholly eliminated, the selection procedure used here, and our cross-validation between independent data sources (human mobility and SGTF datasets), help to ensure that our conclusions are robust. As SARS-CoV-2 genome sequencing efforts are accelerated worldwide, careful consideration and communication of sampling frameworks are needed to facilitate downstream epidemiological analyses ( 48 ). Spatial heterogeneity at the within-city scale was not accounted for in our analysis, consideration of which may further refine our understanding of the mechanisms of lineage emergence and invasion.

Coordinated and unified systems of genomic surveillance are needed worldwide to identify, track, and mitigate the transmission of SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern, including mechanisms to pair virus genomic and contact tracing data. Continuing rises in global incidence will increase the rate generation of viral genetic variation, and the accrual of higher levels of population immunity will create new selective pressures ( 49 ), the effects of which on virus evolution are difficult to predict ( 50 – 52 ). It is therefore critical to rapidly and accurately disentangle the contributions of genetic and ecological factors to the emergence of new SARS-CoV-2 variants. Geographic variation in vaccine availability, uptake, and delivery is expected to further contribute to variability in COVID-19 burden and the differential risk of disease resurgence ( 17 , 53 , 54 ), which can be mitigated through increased global access to vaccination and continued transmission control measures ( 52 ). Importation of SARS-CoV-2 lineages and variants from areas of high incidence will continue to pose a risk to those regions that are reducing NPIs after having controlled infection.

articles.title: Paleogeographic controls on Phanerozoic weathering rates and implications for climate regulation.
articles.authors: Graham RJ, Cael BB, Fu M, Abbot DS.
articles.abstract: Earth’s climate has remained habitable for billions of years, a stability usually attributed to a negative feedback from silicate weathering – the chemical breakdown of silicate rocks on land, which consumes atmospheric carbon dioxide faster as climate warms. However, whether temperature or hydrology primarily drives this feedback remains uncertain. Here we show the two controls leave geographic fingerprints: in an ensemble of climate simulations with randomized continents, temperature-controlled weathering depends on tropical land fraction, whereas hydrology-controlled weathering depends on continental fragmentation. Stronger weathering removes more carbon dioxide, cooling the planet, so each regime predicts anti-correlation between temperature and its controlling geography. Reconstructed global temperatures spanning 480 million years are anti-correlated with tropical land fraction, except from roughly 295 to 200 million years ago – overlapping the supercontinent Pangea – when they anti-correlate with continental fragmentation. The mechanism stabilizing Earth’s climate may thus have evolved, with temperature control apparently dominant for most of this period.
paragraphs: Earth’s climate has remained habitable for billions of years, a stability usually attributed to a negative feedback from silicate weathering – the chemical breakdown of silicate rocks on land, which consumes atmospheric carbon dioxide faster as climate warms. However, whether temperature or hydrology primarily drives this feedback remains uncertain. Here we show the two controls leave geographic fingerprints: in an ensemble of climate simulations with randomized continents, temperature-controlled weathering depends on tropical land fraction, whereas hydrology-controlled weathering depends on continental fragmentation. Stronger weathering removes more carbon dioxide, cooling the planet, so each regime predicts anti-correlation between temperature and its controlling geography. Reconstructed global temperatures spanning 480 million years are anti-correlated with tropical land fraction, except from roughly 295 to 200 million years ago – overlapping the supercontinent Pangea – when they anti-correlate with continental fragmentation. The mechanism stabilizing Earth’s climate may thus have evolved, with temperature control apparently dominant for most of this period.

Simulations with randomized continents show that temperature- and hydrology-controlled weathering results in climates that track different features of continental geometry. The Earth’s record suggests the control may have shifted over 480 million years.

Earth’s climate is regulated on long (10 5 to 10 6 year) timescales by stabilizing negative feedbacks within the carbonate-silicate cycle 1 , 2 . Silicate weathering reactions on Earth’s surface and seafloor release solutes that enter the ocean and react with oceanic carbon that is in chemical equilibrium with CO 2 in Earth’s atmosphere to form carbonate minerals. This process is the primary inorganic sink of CO 2 outgassed from Earth’s interior, and a combination of theoretical arguments, laboratory experiments, and observational evidence[e.g., refs. 1 , 3 – 5 ] suggest that weathering reactions accelerate under warmer conditions, providing a feedback mechanism to regulate Earth’s climate: When the planet warms, silicate weathering speeds up, accelerating the removal of CO 2 from the atmosphere. This carbon cycle response leads to CO 2 drawdown and climatic cooling, which in turn slows the silicate weathering rate until CO 2 is being removed from the atmosphere at the same pace that CO 2 is added by volcanic outgassing. The same process happens in reverse in response to climatic cooling. Although transient imbalances between CO 2 inputs and outputs due to organic carbon interactions 6 or limitations in silicate mineral supply 7 may have played important roles in Earth’s climate evolution, weathering-based coupling between atmospheric CO 2 removal and background climate appears to play a key role in maintaining the quasi-equilibrium in the carbon cycle necessary to avoid frequent excursions to extremely high or low surface temperatures that would have threatened the existence of complex life on Earth during the Phanerozoic 8 , 9 .

However, despite a general agreement among researchers about the importance of negative feedback within the carbonate-silicate cycle in sustaining Earth’s habitability, the details of the mechanism(s) mediating this stabilization through Earth's history remain highly uncertain. In this study, we examine a fundamental open question regarding the silicate weathering feedback on land [e.g., refs. 10 – 16 ]: Is its coupling to the climate mediated primarily by temperature in the weathering zone, or does hydrology play a stronger role? Many attempts to model Earth’s silicate weathering feedback have based their estimates of the temperature-dependence of Earth’s weathering rate on direct laboratory measurements of the kinetics of silicate dissolution[e.g., ref. 17 ]. But some recent modeling and theoretical studies have argued that the apparent global temperature-dependence of silicate weathering is significantly weaker than would be expected from laboratory measurements[e.g. 4 , 5 , 18 ]. One potential explanation for this discrepancy is that the feedback between climate and weathering may not be rooted directly in the kinetics of silicate dissolution, but is instead a result of the climate-dependence of the flux of water through the weathering zone 12 , 19 . Calculations of weathering rates that account for physicochemical interactions between water, dissolving silicates, and the secondary minerals (clays and silica) that precipitate during silicate weathering suggest that, depending on the local lithology, silicate weathering reactions can reach a chemical equilibrium where solutes in runoff are saturated, preventing further net silicate dissolution until unsaturated water flows through–a regime sometimes referred to as “chemostatic” or “runoff-limited” weathering 12 , 20 – 22 . In this regime, climate influences weathering through its influence on hydrologic intensity, with greater fluxes of water leading to proportional increases in silicate weathering, largely independent of local temperature. Since global runoff has a much weaker dependence on temperature than the kinetic temperature dependence of silicate weathering, hydrologically regulated weathering leads to a weaker apparent temperature-dependence and a significantly less effective thermostat compared to silicate weathering based on laboratory measurements of silicate dissolution 19 .

Although the behavior of silicate weathering and its interaction with the climate is still subject to debate, a substantial volume of work attempts to connect changes in paleogeography during the Phanerozoic Eon to changes in climate and CO 2 through the weathering feedback using models of widely varying complexity [e.g., refs. 23 – 32 ]. Early models, such as refs. 23 , 24 assumed a strong temperature control on weathering with no direct runoff-dependence and used bulk estimates of land area and average landmass latitude to predict climate as a function of paleogeography. The GEOCARB and GEOCARBSULF lineage of global-mean box models 26 used relationships derived from GCM studies like that of 33 to represent the impact of paleogeography on global-mean runoff and temperature, allowing for an effect on climate through a global weathering relationship based on both an assumed strong temperature sensitivity and a moderate runoff sensitivity. The GEOCLIM lineage of models[e.g., refs. 29 , 30 ] and successors like SCION 31 couple weathering parameterizations with strong temperature-dependence and strong (linear) runoff-dependence to output from GCM simulations in order to calculate spatially resolved weathering fluxes, allowing for investigations of climate and CO 2 evolution that directly account for paleogeographic changes in Earth history[e.g., refs. 27 , 28 , 34 – 39 ]. However, these models all take their chosen weathering feedback strengths for temperature and runoff as given (modulo occasional sensitivity tests), introducing a major source of uncertainty into their results and reconstructions.

Here, to assist in differentiating between signatures of hydrology-controlled and temperature-controlled weathering in Earth history, we analyze a large ensemble of GCM simulations that are identical except for their randomized continental configurations and post-process their runoff and temperature fields to estimate global weathering rates from them. This allows us to demonstrate that these alternative weathering controls lead to alternative predictions for Earth’s climate response to changes in aspects of bulk planetary continental geometry. Then, we statistically compare proxy-based reconstructions of Earth’s climate and land configuration to assess whether the geologic record supports one hypothesis over the other. Ultimately, our calculations are consistent with the hypothesis that Earth’s weathering control mechanism shifted twice in the last 480 Ma, from a temperature-based to a hydrology-based configuration ≈ 300 Ma and then back to a temperature-based configuration ≈ 200 Ma, though this relies on assumptions like weakly varying outgassing, a tight relationship between CO 2 and surface temperature, and the accuracy of uncertain paleogeographic reconstructions. Still, the results provide useful new insight into the structure of the carbon cycle which may lead to improved understanding of the evolution of Earth’s climate over the Phanerozoic.

In this section, we present an analysis of the correlations between continental geometry and global weathering rates in an ensemble of idealized GCM simulations that suggests a relationship between planetary processes that might be observable in the geologic record. The key point is that the carbon cycle responds very differently to variations in TLF (defined as the land fraction between 15 ∘ N/S for consistency with 40 , with results insensitive to variations in latitude range) and continental fragmentation (defined as continental perimeter divided by continental area) depending on whether the weathering feedback is mediated primarily by hydrology (see Fig. 1 ), temperature (see Fig. 2 ), or both (see Fig. 3 ). Figures 1 , 2 both display weathering rates for the same nine land configurations, with the two figures differing only in that weathering varies linearly with hydrology with no direct temperature dependence in Fig. 1 , while it varies exponentially with temperature and lacks hydrology dependence in Fig. 2 . In both figures, each row of plots displays increasing continental fragmentation moving left to right, and TLF increasing moving downward. From Fig. 1 , it is clear that hydrologically controlled weathering increases with increasing continental fragmentation (moving left to right) and is not strongly affected by TLF. On the other hand, temperature-controlled weathering (see Fig. 2 ) strongly increases with increasing TLF, while the effect of continental fragmentation is minimal or, in the case of the largest TLF cases, may even lead to a weathering increase with decreasing fragmentation (i.e., bottom row, Fig. 2 ). We note for clarity that these weathering values are all calculated with the same background CO 2 and global temperature and might therefore be better thought of as values of bulk “global weatherability,” since Earth’s climate would in reality adjust to bring the global weathering rate into balance with the background CO 2 outgassing rate if a change to continental geometry were to cause a large transient shift in weathering. In other words, these calculations are not intended to imply that the equilibrium global weathering rate has varied by this magnitude over Earth history (since the equilibrium global rate of weathering is set by outgassing), but instead to illustrate the degree to which changes in continental geometry can act as carbon cycle forcings under different assumptions about global weathering controls 41 . Several studies have identified changing “weatherability” as a potential major driver behind climate changes during the Phanerozoic Eon due to its influence on the equilibrium point of the carbon cycle and climate system 42 – 46 .

To quantify the apparent relationships between weathering and continental geometry, we calculated coefficients of determination between the global weathering rate and TLF and continental fragmentation for our GCM ensemble over a wide range of values for k (temperature-dependence of weathering; see eqn. ( 2 ) in Methods) and α (runoff-dependence of weathering; see eqn. ( 2 )), with results shown in Fig. 3 . When the weathering feedback is dominated by hydrology instead of temperature (large α , small k ), the coefficient of determination between the total global weathering rate ( W tot ) and the fragmentation index, R 2 ( W tot , fragmentation index), can exceed 50% (bottom right corner of top panel in Fig. 3 ), while R 2 ( W tot , TLF) falls to nearly zero (bottom right corner of bottom panel in Fig. 3 ). Conversely, when temperature regulation dominates over hydrology (small α , large k ), R 2 ( W tot , fragmentation index) falls to near zero, while R 2 ( W tot , TLF) climbs to more than 75%.

The reason for this divergence in response to continental geometry is straightforward. Within the GCM ensemble, global runoff is uncorrelated with TLF (R 2 = 0%) but strongly correlated with continental fragmentation (R 2 = 54%; see Fig. 4a, b ). The lack of correlation between TLF and runoff is due to an increase in land evaporation in high-TLF simulations that compensates for increased land precipitation, similar to an effect observed by ref. 33 . This occurs because tropical land intercepts more solar energy, allowing for more efficient recycling of water despite increased overall delivery to the land via precipitation in the wet tropics. Increasing fragmentation does not increase the ease of delivery of solar energy to land, but it does increase delivery of water, so runoff tends to increase as continents break up. So, when weathering is dominated by hydrology, changes to TLF have a minimal effect due to small changes in runoff, but more fragmented configurations produce more runoff, accelerating weathering. Fig. 4 Scatter plots of average values of different variables from the global climate model (GCM) ensemble. a shows the lack of correlation between runoff and tropical land fraction (TLF); b shows a relatively strong correlation between runoff and fragmentation; c shows a weak correlation between global-mean surface temperature and TLF; d shows no correlation between global-mean surface temperature and fragmentation; e shows a strong correlation between global-mean land temperature and TLF; and f shows a lack of correlation between global-mean land temperature and fragmentation.

a shows the lack of correlation between runoff and tropical land fraction (TLF); b shows a relatively strong correlation between runoff and fragmentation; c shows a weak correlation between global-mean surface temperature and TLF; d shows no correlation between global-mean surface temperature and fragmentation; e shows a strong correlation between global-mean land temperature and TLF; and f shows a lack of correlation between global-mean land temperature and fragmentation.

Conversely, although global-mean surface temperature is weakly correlated with TLF (R 2 = 16%) and uncorrelated with continental fragmentation (R 2 = 0%; see Fig. 4c, d ), global-mean land temperature is strongly correlated with TLF (R 2 = 71%), while remaining uncorrelated with fragmentation (R 2 = 1%; see Fig. 4e, f ). So, when temperature is the main driver of weathering, changes to TLF can change the weathering rate by altering the amount of land that experiences higher temperatures near the equator. The small positive relationship between global-mean surface temperature and TLF visible in Fig. 4c is due to an increase in high-albedo land snow in low-TLF simulations where land is colder and closer to the poles, since snow on land has higher albedo than sea ice in these simulations. Warmer global conditions moderate this effect: a smaller ensemble of simulations with 30 of the 120 paleogeographies from this paper and 40 with doubled CO 2 (2000 ppm) showed a TLF-global temperature correlation with an even weaker R 2 of 2% (see Supplementary Fig. 4 in Supplementary Information Section A.4 ) due to the reduced latitudinal extent of freezing temperatures while preserving a strong TLF-land temperature correlation. In general, the 30 warmer simulations showed the same basic behavior and relationships as the simulations seen in Fig. 4 , as did a set of 30 colder simulations (500 ppm CO 2 ) with the same subset of paleogeographies as the warmer simulations (see Supplementary Fig. 4 in Supplementary Information Section A.4 ).

These distinctive differences in the response of the weathering feedback to continental geometry naturally lead to a hypothesis: If Earth’s carbonate-silicate thermostat is dominated by surface weathering that is primarily sensitive to surface temperatures, then, for a given global outgassing rate, we should observe an anticorrelation between TLF and surface temperature through time, because an increase in TLF would be expected to increase the weathering rate and cause CO 2 drawdown and cooling. Similarly, a reduction in TLF would slow weathering and allow CO 2 to accumulate, leading to warming. Furthermore, we should not expect there to be a strong correlation between climate and continental fragmentation in this regime. Alternatively, if the silicate weathering response is dominated by Earth’s hydrological response to changes in climate, for a given outgassing rate and with all else being equal, we should expect an anticorrelation between continental fragmentation and climate and little influence from TLF. These opposing predictions provide a geological test that might shed light on the mechanisms that have stabilized Earth’s climate throughout planetary history. In the following section, we investigate Earth’s geologic record in the context of these findings.

To differentiate between the hypotheses described in the previous section, we analyzed the statistical relationships between the GMST reconstruction of 47 and continental fragmentation and TLF calculated from the paleogeographic reconstruction of 48 (see Fig. 5 ). We find that from 480 Ma to 295 ± 15 Ma (the range of possible transition times is shown as the rightmost error bar in Fig. 5 ), GMST displays a strong ( r < − 0.5) and significant ( p < 0.025) anti-correlation with TLF and no significant relationship to fragmentation. Then, at 295 ± 15 Ma, the apparent correlation switches, and subsequently GMST displays a strong, significant anti-correlation with continental fragmentation and no significant relationship to TLF (blue shaded region in Fig. 5 ) until 200 ± 10 Ma (leftmost error bar range in Fig. 5 ). Finally, from 200 ± 10 until the present, the relationships between variables revert back to their original behavior, with anti-correlation between GMST and TLF and no significant relationship between GMST and fragmentation. The period of anti-correlation with continental fragmentation notably overlaps with Pangea, which lasted from ≈ 325 Ma to ≈ 200 Ma[colored pink in Fig. 5 , 49 ]. The negative relationships between GMST and TLF and the fragmentation index during the three distinct periods are visible in the bottom three panels of Fig. 5 . The evolution of the relationships between GMST, TLF, and continental fragmentation is consistent with a dynamic scenario in which the main mechanism controlling the coupling between silicate weathering and climate has shifted across the Phanerozoic. Based on our GCM ensemble results, the anti-correlation between GMST and TLF at the beginning and end of the period under examination suggests temperature-controlled weathering, while the anti-correlation between GMST and fragmentation from ≈ 300 Ma to ≈ 200 Ma suggests that hydrology dominated the weathering response during that time span.

As a sensitivity test of our results, we repeated the analysis of correlations between surface temperature and exposed continental geometry over the Phanerozoic, replacing the paleogeographic reconstructions from ref. 48 with those of ref. 50 . The two sets of reconstructions differ primarily due to different underlying plate tectonic models 48 , although they are not entirely independent, since ref. 48 relied on some of the same data sources as ref. 50 . With the Scotese reconstruction (see Supplementary Fig. 2 ), our results are qualitatively similar, with a significant negative relationship between TLF and GMST from 480 to 300 Ma ( r = − 0.70, p = 2.7 × 10 −6 ) and a significant negative relationship between fragmentation and GMST from 300 Ma to 200 Ma ( r = − 0.62, p = 2.7 × 10 −3 ), but the anti-correlation between TLF and GMST from 200 Ma to present is weaker ( r = − 0.31) and marginally significant ( p = 0.054).

Analyzing reconstructed CO 2 may seem like a more direct route for demonstrating a relationship between climate and paleogeography, since changes to silicate weathering fluxes should manifest as changes to CO 2 levels. While there do exist a number of CO 2 records over the Phanerozoic based on modeling and data compilations 51 – 53 , pre-Cenozoic CO 2 estimates are poorly constrained and often inconsistent 54 . Given the large uncertainties associated with CO 2 paleo-records and the fact that Phanerozoic temperature variations are thought to mainly reflect CO 2 forcing 55 , 56 , we choose to focus on GMST in this study. In any case, the reconstructed GMST of 47 correlates strongly with (log-transformed) reconstructed CO 2 over most of the Phanerozoic [ r = 0.77, p < 0.01, 47 ], and our GCM ensemble displayed weak or non-existent relationships between global-mean surface temperature and both TLF and continental fragmentation (Fig. 4c, d ). This increases our confidence that it is a reasonable first-order assumption that CO 2 and temperature were tightly linked over most of the Phanerozoic and that variations in continental geometry were unlikely to have a large direct (non-carbon-cycle-mediated) effect on surface temperatures, consistent with previous GCM ensemble studies [e.g., refs. 33 , 57 ].

It is also important to note that our GCM simulations and weathering calculations are idealized in ways that could impact the results of this study. For example, the land topography is muted compared to Earth, with a maximum elevation of 100 m 40 . This means there are no mountain ranges, so our results do not include the potentially important impact of orographic precipitation 58 or possible interactions between uplift, erosion, and weathering 59 – 62 , which may vary systematically with continental fragmentation. We also did not attempt to explicitly represent variations in lithology, which could produce large variations in weathering parameters across the planet at any given time [e.g., refs. 22 , 63 , 64 ]. Additionally, the weathering calculations do not account for the potential biotic acceleration of silicate weathering by land plants [e.g., refs. 65 – 67 ], though it is unclear what impact the rise of forested ecosystems ≈ 385 Ma had on chemical weathering 68 , 69 . Furthermore, glacial weathering may be an important component of CO 2 drawdown 70 , so since ice extent has varied during the past 485 Ma, glacial cover could provide another co-varying modulator of weathering rates that could impart spurious correlations to our data, with glacial periods during the Ordovician-Silurian, end-Carboniferous, and late Cenozoic 71 . Seafloor weathering is also absent from our model, despite indications that it may play a crucial role in Earth’s climate stabilization similar to that of silicate weathering on the land 2 , 72 , 73 . Similarly, we do not consider authigenic clay formation ("reverse weathering”) which consumes alkalinity and could impact climate equilibria and the response of the carbon cycle to perturbations [e.g., refs. 74 – 77 ].

More generally, given the interconnected and recursive nature of the Earth system, it is difficult to establish causality when analyzing relationships between geological quantities. Although we observe correlations between the variables of interest in this study (i.e., GMST, TLF, and continental fragmentation), it is possible that these relationships are being driven by other mechanisms or variables that are co-varying simultaneously. For example, we excluded variations in CO 2 outgassing rate from our study even though such variations could have played a role in dictating the equilibrium weathering rate and climate state at any given time in Earth history. This is justified given the major uncertainty in reconstructions, with large inconsistencies in the magnitude and direction of outgassing changes depending on the set of processes considered and the methodology used for estimation 30 , 31 , 48 , 71 , 78 – 82 . Still, theoretical arguments and some data suggest outgassing may vary systematically across the supercontinent cycle, with periods of enhanced rifting corresponding to increases in the flux of CO 2 from Earth’s interior [e.g., refs. 83 – 85 ]. If CO 2 outgassing increases when continental fragmentation increases, then this may systematically bias the system away from displaying an anti-correlation between the degree of fragmentation and global surface temperature, since increased weathering could be partially or completely offset by increased outgassing. If that is the case, then the imprint of hydrologically controlled weathering on the geologic record might be reduced, biasing our analysis.

One potential geologic test of the hypothesis that the climate stabilization mechanism has shifted from temperature-dependence to hydrology-dependence and back during the Phanerozoic would be to examine global spatial and temporal trends in correlations between paleosol-based precipitation and temperature proxies with weathering proxies like chemical index of alteration 86 , 87 or the weathering index of Parker 88 . Deng et al. 15 used this method (except with direct temperature and precipitation measurements rather than proxies) to infer a strong temperature control on silicate weathering and a weak hydrologic control for the modern Earth, consistent with the results of our study. It is an open question whether geologic proxies would reveal the same pattern on Earth throughout the Phanerozoic across the period our analysis suggests may have displayed hydrologically-dominated weathering. Paleosols 89 and GCM simulations 29 , 90 of Earth during Pangea [which existed from ~ 325 Ma to ≈ 200 Ma, 49 ] suggest that this would have been a period of unusually low global precipitation and runoff, which would tend to push weathering zones toward hydrologic control by reducing water fluxes and allowing solutes to build to higher concentrations 12 , 64 . This observation suggests that the aridity of the Pangea supercontinent might explain the potential shift to hydrologic control described in this study.

Beyond Earth’s history, if Earth’s thermostat oscillates between temperature control and hydrology control over time due to the supercontinent cycle (or because of some other driver), then in addition to being crucial for understanding Earth’s past, this effect could be important for accurately predicting the future lifespans of various components of Earth’s biosphere 91 , 92 . This is because (in the absence of unpredictable biotechnological intervention) Earth’s far future climate state will be determined by the interplay between the gradually brightening Sun and the behavior of atmospheric CO 2 in response to this forcing, as dictated by the carbonate-silicate cycle, so the details of silicate weathering processes will be a primary control 91 – 93 . Similarly, the classical “circumstellar habitable zone” is typically defined as the band of orbits around a star where rocky exoplanets with CO 2 -N 2 -H 2 O atmospheres can in principle sustain liquid water oceans with the appropriate quantity of CO 2 in the atmosphere 94 , 95 , and this concept is rooted in the idea that sufficiently Earth-like planets will have carbonate-silicate cycles capable of regulating their CO 2 within bounds that allow for liquid water like Earth 96 . Some even propose to limit the width of the habitable zone based on simulations that suggest that silicate weathering behavior can cause periodic global glaciations for planets receiving somewhat less sunlight than Earth, but the precise details of the weathering parameterization used strongly impact the resulting climate behavior [e.g., refs. 97 – 99 ]. Therefore, the question of whether temperature or hydrology controls weathering on Earth directly affects predictions for the climates of potentially habitable exoplanets 19 , 22 , 100 , 101 .

In this study, we used weathering trends inferred from post-processing a large ensemble of GCM simulations to propose a pair of relationships between components of Earth’s continental geometry and silicate weathering behavior: If silicate weathering is primarily controlled by the local temperature in the weathering zone, then weathering should correlate strongly with tropical land fraction, but if weathering is controlled by hydrology, then it should correlate strongly with continental fragmentation. In turn, those relationships imply that temperature-controlled weathering should result in an anti-correlation between global-mean surface temperature and tropical land fraction, while hydrology-controlled weathering should result in an anti-correlation between global-mean surface temperature and fragmentation. We then analyzed Earth’s geologic record over the past 480 Myr and found that these relationships between continental geometry and climate seem to manifest in distinct periods: From 480 to 295 ± 15 Ma, surface temperature and tropical land fraction are anti-correlated, then from 295 ± 15 to 200 ± 10 Ma surface temperature and continental fragmentation are anti-correlated, and finally from 200 ± 10 Ma to the present surface temperature and tropical land fraction appear anti-correlated once again. The apparent shift in the mechanism stabilizing Earth’s climate overlaps with the existence of Pangea, suggesting a potential relationship between Earth’s dominant weathering mode and the mode of Earth’s supercontinent cycle, perhaps mediated by large changes in continental aridity.

We use an ensemble of Community Earth System Model (CESM) global climate model (GCM) simulations originally presented by ref. 40 and available for download at ref. 102 to analyze the sensitivity of silicate weathering rates to tropical land fraction (TLF) and continental fragmentation, represented by the ratio of non-submerged continental perimeter to continental area, which we denote the “continental fragmentation index” following 103 . The GCM simulations were all carried out at T31 resolution ( ≈ 4 ∘ by 4 ∘ ), and all have an identical top-of-atmosphere subsolar insolation of 1285 W m −2 , global land fraction of 30%, atmospheric CO 2 concentration of 1000 ppm (parts per million by volume), obliquity of 23.5 ∘ , eccentricity of 0, and lack of vegetation. They differ only in their continental geometries, which are stochastically generated spherical harmonics truncated at degree 12. ( 2 ).

Baum et al. 40 calculated weathering rates with a fixed set of sensitivity parameters ( α = 1 and k = 0.09 K −1 ), which limits the applicability of their results due to the large uncertainties in temperature- and hydrology-dependence for silicate weathering. We extend their work by varying α across the range α ∈ [0, 1] with α = 0 corresponding to no runoff-dependence for silicate weathering (except if q = 0, we assume weathering shuts off, even if α = 0) and α = 1 corresponding to a linear dependence. We vary k across the range k ∈ [10 −2 , 10 −1 ] K −1 , corresponding to a range of e -folding temperatures T e ∈ [100, 10] K, which encompasses the wide range of weathering temperature sensitivity values that have recently been suggested in the literature 4 , 5 , 15 . This wide range of weathering parameters allows us to probe how variations in strength for different forms of coupling between climate and weathering interact with TLF and fragmentation index, two large-scale aspects of continental geometry that may impact global weathering rates. TLF is defined as the land fraction between 15 ∘ N/S for consistency with 40 , with results insensitive to variations in latitude range. The fragmentation index is defined as the continental perimeter divided by the continental area. To quantify these relationships, we calculate the coefficient of determination (R 2 ) between weathering rates and both TLF and fragmentation across the GCM simulations in our ensemble as functions of α and k to measure the proportion of variance in weathering rate that is explained by variations in TLF and fragmentation index.

The weathering parameterization we use in this study is based on the common formulation first suggested in ref. 1 , sometimes referred to as the WHAK model[e.g., refs. 19 , 40 , 111 ]. An alternative or extension to the WHAK model presented by ref. 12 (MAC) allows for mechanistic transitions between the weathering regimes explored here, with a temperature-controlled regime dominated by silicate dissolution kinetics and a hydrologically regulated regime that occurs when secondary mineral precipitation in the weathering zone prevents solutes from accumulating to higher concentrations. Calculations with the MAC model display very similar patterns to results calculated with WHAK: parameter values with temperature-dependent weathering result in a strong correlation between global weathering and TLF, while hydrology-dependent weathering results in a strong correlation with continental fragmentation (see Supplementary Information Section A.3 , Supplementary Fig. 3 ).

Positive correlations between silicate weathering and TLF or fragmentation index, respectively, would imply, all else being equal, anti-correlations between global temperature and TLF or fragmentation index. This is because with a given CO 2 outgassing rate, an increase in global weathering should cause a drawdown in CO 2 and a corresponding reduction in temperature until the weathering rate is reduced back to equilibrium with outgassing. Further, the GCM/weathering results imply large differences between weathering regimes controlled by temperature and hydrology in terms of their responses to changes in TLF or changes in continental fragmentation. Therefore, by comparing proxy data for the evolution of global mean surface temperature (GMST) with reconstructed global continental geometry during the Phanerozoic and combining this information with the results from our GCM/weathering experiments, we can use the geologic record to gain insight into the relative strength of temperature vs. hydrology in stabilizing Earth’s climate through time.

To allow for the possibility that the Earth system may have shifted between hydrologically-controlled and temperature-controlled weathering at different times, we calculate the correlation coefficients across all time spans from 485 million years ago (Ma) to the present between a recent data-assimilation-based reconstruction of the Phanerozoic GMST record 47 and the TLF and fragmentation index from a recent tectonic reconstruction of exposed land across the Phanerozoic 48 using GPlates 112 . We converted the ShapeFiles from GPlates into NetCDF4 files encoding the exposed land from the 48 reconstructions at every 10 Myr interval from 480 Ma to present on a latitude-longitude grid resolution of 1 ∘ by 1 ∘ . Fragmentation index (total perimeter of exposed land divided by total area) only accounts for the outer boundary of land masses to avoid counting the boundaries of interior lakes and seas.

These calculations help differentiate between the competing hypotheses about the silicate weathering feedback described above by quantifying the statistical relationships between reconstructions of Earth’s paleogeography and surface temperature. See Supplementary Information Section A.1 for more detailed description of the correlation calculations.
