articles.title: Robust biexciton preparation for entangled photon-pair generation by single-shot Floquet driving.
articles.authors: Yan JY, Hagen PCA, Ge HY, Li FY, Babin HG, Sha WEI, Wang B, Gan ZH, Wieck AD, Ludwig A, Jin CY, Axt VM, Wang DW, Cygorek M, Liu F.
articles.abstract: Abstract Quantum emitters driven by resonant two-photon excitation are a leading source for deterministically generated entangled photon pairs, essential for scalable photonic quantum technologies. However, conventional excitation schemes pose various constraints, limiting their scalability and practicability. Here, we demonstrate how biexciton preparation schemes with significantly improved robustness and reduced experimental demands can be identified using a novel design principle: ultrafast single-shot Floquet driving . This is achieved by employing two strongly and symmetrically detuned pulses, whose superposition generates a stroboscopic Hamiltonian that enables direct coupling between ground and biexciton states. Moreover, a pulse delay serves as a tuning knob, introducing an effective magnetic field making biexciton preparation particularly robust. Experimentally, we achieve a biexciton occupation exceeding 96% and preserve photon-pair entanglement with a fidelity of 93.4%. Our work opens avenues for the design of quantum control protocols with superior performance across diverse quantum emitters and qubit platforms. Subject terms: Single photons and quantum effects, Quantum dots, Quantum optics
paragraphs: Quantum emitters driven by resonant two-photon excitation are a leading source for deterministically generated entangled photon pairs, essential for scalable photonic quantum technologies. However, conventional excitation schemes pose various constraints, limiting their scalability and practicability. Here, we demonstrate how biexciton preparation schemes with significantly improved robustness and reduced experimental demands can be identified using a novel design principle: ultrafast single-shot Floquet driving . This is achieved by employing two strongly and symmetrically detuned pulses, whose superposition generates a stroboscopic Hamiltonian that enables direct coupling between ground and biexciton states. Moreover, a pulse delay serves as a tuning knob, introducing an effective magnetic field making biexciton preparation particularly robust. Experimentally, we achieve a biexciton occupation exceeding 96% and preserve photon-pair entanglement with a fidelity of 93.4%. Our work opens avenues for the design of quantum control protocols with superior performance across diverse quantum emitters and qubit platforms.
Subject terms: Single photons and quantum effects, Quantum dots, Quantum optics

Deterministic generation of entangled photon pairs from quantum dots requires robust preparation of the biexciton state. Here, the authors demonstrate single-shot Floquet driving using symmetrically detuned optical pulses to prepare the biexciton with high efficiency and reduced sensitivity to pulse-area fluctuations, enabling the generation of polarization-entangled photon pairs with high fidelity.

Quantum entanglement, one of the most intriguing phenomena in the quantum world, lies at the heart of quantum information science. A deterministic source of entangled photons is a fundamental building block for modern quantum photonics applications, such as quantum communications 1 , 2 , optical quantum computing 3 , 4 , quantum imaging and sensing 5 , 6 . A semiconductor quantum dot (QD), often referred to as an artificial atom due to its three-dimensional electronic confinement and discrete energy levels, is a well-established source of highly entangled photons 7 – 9 . The on-demand high-fidelity preparation of the biexciton state is the starting point for the radiative cascade decay process that generates entangled photon pairs. Moreover, cascade-emitted photons have been shown to induce simultaneous excitation of two independent quantum emitters 10 , enabling the synthesis of effective multi-qubit interactions and coherent generation of entangled states 11 .

A degenerate resonant two-photon excitation (TPE) scheme, where two photons with identical frequencies are absorbed simultaneously, is commonly used to coherently prepare the biexciton state with minimal dephasing and time jitter 12 (see Fig. 1 b). This excitation scheme has shown significant potential in generating polarization-entangled photon pairs 13 – 15 , time-bin entangled photons 16 , 17 and indistinguishable single photons 18 – 20 . However, conventional TPE relies on Rabi oscillations of biexciton populations, making its excitation efficiency highly sensitive to variations in the excitation laser power and the dipole moment of the emitters. Furthermore, tuning the laser to the average frequency of the biexciton ( BX ) and exciton ( X ) photons is unfavorable for QDs with small or negative BX binding energy. In the former case 21 , 22 , the tiny detuning between the laser and the entangled photon pairs makes it particularly difficult to perform effective laser filtering. In the latter case, the TPE process competes with phonon-assisted excitation of X , reducing the preparation efficiency of B X 23 . These limitations hinder the performance and scalability of on-demand entangled photon sources. Although several alternative approaches based on a single excitation pulse, such as rapid adiabatic passage 24 – 26 and LA-phonon-assisted excitation 27 – 29 , have been explored, the simultaneous realization of robust state preparation and the generation of high-fidelity entangled photon pairs has not yet been achieved. Moreover, while multi-colour excitation schemes such as the swing-up of quantum emitter (SUPER) 30 – 32 for biexciton preparation have been proposed, their experimental implementation for entangled-photon generation has not yet been demonstrated.

a Biexciton state prepared by FTPE emits pairs of entangled photons. b Schematic of the TPE process. c Laser excitation spectrum under TPE, where the energy of the TPE pulse is set at the average energy of the BX and X photons. d Schematic of FTPE. e Laser excitation spectrum under FTPE, where the blue and red pulses are detuned symmetrically to meet the two-photon resonance condition.

Floquet engineering, which employs periodic driving to achieve desired quantum dynamics, offers a fundamentally different route for overcoming the limitations of existing excitation schemes. According to Floquet’s theorem 33 , when a quantum system is periodically driven with a period T , the time evolution operator evaluated at stroboscopic times (integer multiples of T ) takes the same form as for a time-independent Hamiltonian (see Methods Section). This stroboscopic Hamiltonian governs the behaviour of the quantum system on a coarse-grained time scale ≳ T . Moreover, if the driving oscillates periodically within a slowly varying envelope, the system approximately follows the instantaneous stroboscopic Hamiltonian, which is then time-dependent on the scale of the envelope 34 . The ability to control and tune the properties of quantum systems by Floquet engineering has enabled the realization of photonic topological insulators 35 and synthetic gauge fields in photonic systems 36 and in ultracold atomic systems 37 .

Existing Floquet engineering approaches typically utilize modulated continuous-wave laser fields or repetitive laser pulse trains. In the context of on-demand semiconductor quantum light sources, Floquet engineering has focused mainly on engineering excitonic wave functions by periodic microwave driving 38 . Despite these advances, all-optical Floquet engineering with single-cycle pulses to manipulate the optical excitation dynamics remains unexplored.

In this article, we propose and demonstrate a scheme for robust on-demand biexciton preparation and entangled photon generation enabled by all-optical single-shot Floquet driving [Fig. 1 a]. Our key observation is that one can realize a time-dependent stroboscopic Hamiltonian that directly drives the ground-to-biexciton transition of a semiconductor quantum dot simply by dichromatic excitation with laser pulses symmetrically detuned from the degenerate two-photon resonance by a detuning δ [Fig. 1 d, e]. Further requirements are that the detuning is large enough so that oscillations with frequency δ are fast compared to changes in the pulse envelope and that the pulses overlap temporally. Control of the phase relation between the pulses is not required (see Supplementary Sect. XI ). These requirements are well achievable within current state-of-the-art experimental techniques for two-colour excitation 39 – 42 . Moreover, the dichromatic pulses can be detuned far from the X and B X photons, relaxing the requirement for laser filtering, especially for QDs with small or negative B X binding energy. Hence, our proposed excitation scheme, which we refer to as Floquet-engineered Two-Photon Excitation (FTPE), can be readily implemented for a wide range of QDs. In our experiments, we demonstrate a B X preparation efficiency of 96.6% and a polarization-entanglement fidelity of 93.4%, proving its reliability.

Figure 1 a illustrates the proposed FTPE scheme applied to a semiconductor QD. A pair of temporally partially overlapping pulses (depicted in blue and red) generates a periodic driving field (indicated by gray lines). This periodic driving deterministically and reliably creates a biexciton in the QD, which subsequently emits entangled photon pairs via the cascade decay process.

To model the FTPE process, we consider a ladder system composed of a ground state ∣ 0 ⟩ , a vertically (V) polarized exciton X V ⟩ , and a biexciton state B X ⟩ . We assume that both driving lasers are vertically polarized such that the horizontally (H) polarized exciton is not involved in the excitation process. The energy of B X ⟩ is E B X = 2 E X − E b , where E X is the energy of the X state and E b is the biexciton binding energy. Figure 1 b shows the schematic of conventional TPE, where the laser is tuned to be strictly in resonance with the virtual state of the 0 ⟩ to B X ⟩ degenerate two-photon transition and Rabi oscillations can be observed 12 . A representative TPE laser excitation spectrum is presented in Fig. 1 c. The laser frequency is tuned to the midpoint between the B X and X emission lines. In contrast, as shown in Fig. 1 d, the two colour lasers used in FTPE are detuned to lie outside the B X and X lines. Thus, a large range of laser detunings is allowed as long as the two-photon resonance is maintained 43 , i.e., E blue + E red = E B X . The higher- and lower-energy lasers are labeled as blue and red pulses, respectively. Since the B X ⟩ to X V ⟩ and X V ⟩ to 0 ⟩ transitions have the same optical polarization selection rule, each laser pulse simultaneously couples to both transitions [Fig. 1 d]. Figure 1 e shows a representative laser excitation spectrum under FTPE. The detuning of either laser from conventional TPE resonance is labeled as δ . Some ripples in the excitation pulse spectra are attributed to the polarization optics used in the setup. In the frame rotating with the frequency of resonant TPE ( E B X /(2 ℏ )), the Hamiltonian in the basis { B X , X V , 0} is given by

where the light-matter interaction term contains two equally strong laser pulses Ω ( t ) = f ( t − τ /2) e − i δ ( t − τ /2) + f ( t + τ /2) e i δ ( t + τ /2) , which can be delayed relative to each other by a time τ . The individual pulse envelopes are Gaussian f ( t ) = Θ 2 π s e − t 2 / 2 s 2 with single-photon transition pulse area Θ and Gaussian standard deviation s = τ 0 2 2 ln 2 related to the FWHM duration of the electric field τ 0 = 12.49 ps. The pulse area is defined as Θ = μ ℏ ∫ − ∞ + ∞ E 0 ( t ) d t , where μ is the transition dipole moment for each single-photon transition, and E 0 ( t ) is the electric-field amplitude of either the blue- or red-detuned pulse. The full quantum dynamics of the driven QD including phonon effects 44 , 45 is simulated using the numerically exact process tensor method 46 , 47 (see Methods Section).

The working principle of our FTPE scheme can be understood by Floquet theory with respect to the period T = 2 π / δ . For detunings δ large enough so that T ≪ τ 0 , fast oscillations can be eliminated and H is replaced by a stroboscopic Hamiltonian H eff. . If moreover δ is the dominant energy scale in the Hamiltonian, δ ≫ E b / ℏ , f , the effective Hamiltonian H eff. can be obtained by systematic expansion in 1/ δ 48 , 49 . This procedure yields a term that directly couples the ground to the biexciton state. The residual impact of the excitonic state is further eliminated by a Schrieffer-Wolff transformation, and we arrive at an effective Hamiltonian involving only ground and biexciton-like states with slowly varying driving envelopes. The details of this calculation can be found in the methods section. Formally, such a two-level system can be regarded as a spin precessing in a fictitious time-dependent effective magnetic field B ( t ), which is described by the Hamiltonian

Here σ x and σ z are Pauli matrices acting in the reduced two-level subspace spanned by the ground and biexciton states. The σ x describes the effective coupling between these states, while the σ z represents their effective detuning.

The effective fields are shaped by a combination of parameters of the exciting lasers, the biexciton binding energy and the detuning. In the special case of zero delay τ = 0 between the pulses [Fig. 2 a, c], we find B z ( t ) = 0 and thus a Rabi-like dynamics with an effective pulse area ∫ − ∞ t B x ( t ′ ) d t ′ in the two-level system, which is a nonlinear function of the pulse area Θ of the original excitation pulses. Interestingly, to leading order, the effective pulse area Λ scales as ~ Θ 2 instead of the usual linear scaling (cf. Eq. ( 10 ) in the Methods Section). For finite delay τ , B z ( t ) becomes nonzero [Fig. 2 b, d], which facilitates the engineering of more complex dynamics.

The detuning ℏ δ = 3.75 meV was chosen. e , f Simulated time evolution of the QD state occupations for the optimal pulse areas corresponding to τ = 0 and −2.9 ps, respectively. ( 2 ). g , h Corresponding trajectories on the Bloch sphere of the effective two-level system composed of ground and biexciton states.

The time evolution of ground, exciton, and biexciton occupations is shown in Fig. 2 e, f for FTPE without and with time delay, respectively, at the optimal pulse area ( Θ opt. ), which is defined as the pulse area corresponding to the first maximum of the final B X occupation. The solid faded lines correspond to the solution of the full Hamiltonian Eq. ( 1 ), whereas the dashed lines describe the evolution according to the stroboscopic model of Eq. ( 2 ). Except for small-amplitude oscillations, the full numerical solution is well reproduced by the effective stroboscopic model. Thus, the behaviour of the physical system is indeed governed by the engineered effective magnetic field components B x ( t ) and B z ( t ). Finally, Fig. 2 g, h show the respective behaviour on the Bloch sphere, of which the south pole corresponds to the ground state 0 ⟩ and the north pole to the B X state B X ⟩ . To analyze the robustness of FTPE, we consider not only the optimal driving strengths Θ opt. but also driving with increased pulse areas 1.25 Θ opt. by scaling the envelopes f ( t ) correspondingly. Without delay, τ = 0, (left panel) the Bloch sphere trajectories run along a great circle (due to B z = 0). Thus, if the driving strength deviates from Θ opt. , the B X population decreases maximally, as the great circle describes the straightest line on the Bloch sphere. With finite delay τ = −2.9 ps, the component B z ( t ) is found to be antisymmetric in time. This component twists the trajectories out of the y z -plane. Nevertheless, the B X state is reached for pulse area Θ opt. . Further increasing the driving strength not only increases the off-diagonal elements B x of the stroboscopic model but also the effective detuning B z . The enhanced twisting leads to an elongation of the trajectory from the ground to the B X state, such that overshooting, as found for τ = 0 ps, is compensated. This mechanism is responsible for the significantly enhanced robustness found for certain delays τ .

To verify the experimental feasibility of the proposed FTPE scheme, we carry out the experiment with a single neutral droplet-etched GaAs/AlGaAs QD 50 . The sample is placed in a closed-cycle cryostat and cooled to 3.6 K. Transform-limited Gaussian pulses are generated from a femtosecond laser and stretched into two tunable 12.49-ps pulses using 4- f pulse shapers. The time delay τ between blue and red pulses is controlled by an optical delay line with a resolution of ~ 15 fs. The exciton fine-structure splitting (FSS) 51 due to the QD’s natural anisotropy is effectively eliminated by a continuous-wave (CW) laser via the ac Stark effect 8 . As considered in the theoretical model, the polarizations of lasers are all aligned with the QD’s V dipole orientation, thereby minimizing coupling with the H-polarized exciton X H . More experimental details are provided in the Supplementary Section I .

We first perform a two-dimensional simulation by scanning over the laser pulse area Θ and detuning δ to map the B X state preparation dynamics (Fig. 3 a). This allows us to identify parameter regimes that enable efficient and robust B X state preparation. Qualitatively different parameter regimes can be identified: For TPE with small detunings, biexciton population is found at certain spots but the results are very sensitive to parameter fluctuations. At larger detunings, cusps at ℏ δ = E b /2 indicate the simultaneous resonance of the lasers with the 0 ⟩ to X V ⟩ and X V ⟩ to B X ⟩ transitions. Increasing the detuning further to about ℏ δ ≈ E b , one reaches the FTPE regime. We note that low-order Magnus expansion captures only the FTPE regime well. The stroboscopic Floquet Hamiltonian describes the dynamics appropriately, down to small detunings where the pulse envelope no longer changes slowly with respect to 1/ δ (see Supplementary Section VII ). Notably, TPE theory 12 involves an adiabatic approximation that breaks down for the large detunings required for FTPE (see Supplementary Section X A ).

a Calculated B X occupation versus per-pulse area Θ and detuning δ with τ = −2.9 ps. The horizontal line is where ℏ δ = 3.75 meV as used in b , c . Inset: calculated values without phonon interaction. b Theoretically calculated B X occupation as a function of the area of each pulse Θ , where exciton-phonon interaction and radiative decay are taken into account. c Measured intensity of B X emission as a function of Θ under TPE and FTPE. The experimental B X occupation and per-pulse area are normalized with two scaling factors by fitting the TPE curve to simulations (see details in Supplementary Fig. 4 ).

The FTPE results show that near-unity preparation efficiency is achievable despite the presence of phonons, and high efficiency ( > 90%) can be maintained across a wide range of excitation conditions, demonstrating the robustness of the scheme. FTPE can also be robust against spectral shifts, as we show in Supplementary Section IX B . The theoretical model is described in the Methods Section, and it includes the full time-dependent Hamiltonian, radiative decay, as well as non-Markovian phonon effects, which are captured within the numerically exact process tensor framework ACE 46 , 47 . The inset of Fig. 3 a shows calculated results without phonon effects, confirming that phonon assistance is not essential for B X preparation. We attribute detrimental effects due to phonon coupling to phonon-assisted population of the exciton state, which are significant for detunings below about 3 meV, where the coupling to phonons is strongest. Choosing a larger detuning is therefore advisable to decouple from phonon effects. Without phonons, the reachable biexciton occupations are even higher, making the scheme even more attractive for emitters not affected by phonons, such as atomic systems.

Having identified the suitable laser pulse parameters, we next perform an experimental demonstration of FTPE. Figure 3 c shows experimentally measured B X emission (red dots) obtained under FTPE with ℏ δ = 3.75 meV. With increasing laser pulse area, the B X emission exhibits a gradual increase followed by a slightly fluctuating plateau. As a comparison, the B X emission (black dots) obtained under conventional TPE shows the well-known Rabi oscillation. The main damping source of the Rabi oscillations comes from the QD-phonon coupling 52 . The experimentally achieved occupations and pulse area are calibrated by fitting the TPE Rabi oscillation data to numerical results with two scaling factors, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 4 . Both excitation schemes are well reproduced by our model [Fig. 3 b]. As shown in Fig. 3 c, the first maximum of the B X occupation under TPE (black dots, 96.8%) occurs at a per-pulse area of 2.7 π . The maximum B X occupation achieved under FTPE is 96.6% and appears at a per-pulse area of 15.9 π . Importantly, the achieved final occupation shows significantly reduced sensitivity to variations in laser amplitude. This robustness to experimental fluctuations underscores the advantages of the FTPE scheme for practical quantum information applications. The small discrepancy between the theoretical and experimental peak occupations may arise from the uncertainty in the effective phonon-coupling coefficient extraction, as discussed in Supplementary Section IV . The slight decrease of the experimental curve in the high-power regime may be related to additional excited-state channels, such as hole-state excitation (Supplementary Section VI ), that are not included in the present model.

The temporal separation between the two pulses plays a key role in achieving the robustness of FTPE. To comprehensively investigate the influence of this delay on FTPE performance, we simulate and measure the dependence of B X occupation on the pulse area for various two-pulse delays. Figure 4 a presents a simulated two-dimensional colour map of B X occupation as a function of pulse area and time delay. The detuning ℏ δ is fixed at 3.75 meV, consistent with the experimental condition. The asymmetry with respect to zero delay observed in the colour map arises from the LA-phonon-assisted excitation of the exciton 27 . For delays τ > 0, the blue pulse arrives first, populating the exciton state and thereby hindering the two-photon excitation process. A simulation excluding phonon effects is shown in Supplementary Fig. 2 , where the delay dependence recovers a symmetric pattern. The corresponding experimentally measured two-dimensional map is presented in Fig. 4 b, which reproduces the main features predicted by the simulation. Figure 4 c, d show line cuts taken from Fig. 4 a, b, respectively, at selected delays. For τ < 0, the red-detuned pulse arrives first, such that competition from phonon-assisted excitation becomes negligible. In contrast to the pronounced Rabi-oscillation behavior observed near τ = 0 ps, the B X occupation becomes more robust against variations in pulse area over a finite range of negative delay. From the experimental results in Fig. 4 d, we identify τ = −2.5 to −4.2 ps as the experimentally optimal delay range.

a , b Two-dimensional maps of the calculated a and measured b B X occupation as functions of the per-pulse area Θ and pulse delay τ , with ℏ δ = 3.75 meV. c Line cuts extracted from the calculated map in a , showing the calculated B X occupation as a function of the per-pulse area for selected pulse delays ranging from 4.60 to −4.70 ps. d Line cuts extracted from the measured map in b , showing the measured B X occupation as a function of the per-pulse area for selected pulse delays ranging from 4.58 to −4.67 ps.

One promising application of our FTPE scheme is to deterministically generate entangled photon pairs. To assess the practicality, it is crucial to examine both the entanglement fidelity of the FTPE-generated photon pairs and the compatibility of the FTPE scheme with experimental techniques required for the collection and verification of entangled photons. To this end, we investigate the cascade emission from the B X state prepared by FTPE, which is operated as a source of polarization-entangled photon pairs [Fig. 5 a, b inset]. Since the FTPE pulses are far detuned from B X and X photon emission peaks, they can be removed simply by spectral filters without affecting the polarization state of entangled photons. The entanglement fidelity is then characterized by separating B X and X photons using a polarization-insensitive grating, followed by the measurement of the polarization-dependent second-order correlation functions. The intrinsic FSS of 3.4(2) μeV is eliminated by the ac Stark effect induced by the 13.5 μW CW laser with a red detuning of 300 μeV 8 . Figure 5 shows six cross-correlation measurements in the rectilinear [HH and HV, Fig. 5 b], diagonal [DD and DA, Fig. 5 c], and circular [RR and RL, Fig. 5 d] polarization bases under FTPE, with each histogram composed of 500-ps time bins. By analyzing the degrees of polarization correlation ( C μ , where μ is the polarization basis), the fidelity to the Bell state ψ + = 1 2 H B X H X + V B X V X is obtained as:

The uncertainties are calculated using error propagation, assuming Poisson statistics for the coincidence counts. In the idealized calculation without FSS and the CW laser, the fidelity reaches 97.7% (Supplementary Section VIII ), with the remaining 2.3 percentage-point reduction from unity caused by the pulse-induced transient spectral shift. Including the CW laser reduces the calculated fidelity further to 95.3%, close to the experimentally measured value of 93.4%. This additional reduction is associated with CW-induced state dressing, which is also supported by the power dependence of the autocorrelation measurements (see Supplementary Section III ). Importantly, the FTPE protocol is compatible with other established FSS-erasure techniques, such as strain 7 , magnetic-field 53 , and static electric-field 54 tuning, which could avoid the associated state dressing and thereby enable higher entanglement fidelity. These results demonstrate that the FTPE protocol is a reliable method for generating highly entangled photon pairs.

a Schematic of polarization entangled photon pairs generated by FTPE. b Detected B X - X photon cross-correlation coincidence counts under FTPE in linear basis (H, horizontal; V, vertical). Inset: The cascade radiative recombination of B X state provides two polarization-entangled photons. c In diagonal basis (D, diagonal; A, anti-diagonal). d In circular basis (R, right circular; L, left circular).

We have demonstrated the design and implementation of a robust biexciton state preparation scheme for a semiconductor quantum dot based on our concept of ultrafast all-optical Floquet engineering. Appropriately choosing the parameters of two differently coloured laser pulses lets us arrange a situation where the quantum dot experiences periodic driving within the laser duration. This allows us to engineer a stroboscopic Hamiltonian connecting the initial state with the target state of the protocol and to control the effective time-dependent driving between them. Thereby, we can identify a suitable parameter regime where FTPE is robust against fluctuations in the laser power and where detrimental phonon effects are also of minor importance. In particular, we have identified the delay between the two pulses to be a pivotal tuning knob for reaching the robust regime. The theoretical predictions are well reproduced in our experiments.

The selectable laser detuning of FTPE can provide greater experimental flexibility and relax the demand for laser filtering. In the present weakly confined GaAs/AlGaAs QD, the practical detuning window is finite but remains sizable ( ≳ 1 meV, Supplementary Section VI ). This restriction is specific to the present QD system rather than an intrinsic limitation of FTPE. Moreover, the high entanglement fidelity achieved suggests that the FTPE scheme does not induce additional dephasing channels, further validating its practicality for quantum information applications. Notably, the laser pulse parameters used in this work, such as duration, waveform, and chirp, can be further optimized. Future improvements could be realized through quantum optimal control 55 by systematically tailoring these parameters to enhance the efficiency and robustness of state preparation.

In Table 1 , we provide a comparison of FTPE with representative excitation schemes used for entangled-photon generation in QDs. FTPE offers a highly robust and filtering-friendly route for generating entangled photon pairs, while maintaining high fidelity and preparation efficiency comparable to those of conventional TPE. As also detailed in the Supplementary Section X , the proposed FTPE scheme is distinct from other excitation schemes: the parameter regime for FTPE with detuning δ > E b /(2 ℏ ) is opposite to the limit of resonant TPE, which can be generalized to small but nonzero detuning δ ≪ E b /(2 ℏ ). FTPE works almost the same when the binding energy is negative. As binding energy decreases, more laser power is needed and for zero binding energy no robust excitation can be obtained. Moreover, although robustness is also a feature found in adiabatic protocols, especially in the most robust region of finite pulse delays, FTPE is not adiabatic on an instantaneous eigenstate basis. The optical selection rules differ from stimulated Raman adiabatic passage (STIRAP), and the resonance conditions of FTPE differ from those in other two-colour excitation schemes such as SUPER. These unique characteristics collectively highlight the distinctions of FTPE. Hence, the concept of all-optical single-shot Floquet driving provides a basis for developing platform-tailored excitation protocols for quantum emitters with suitable ladder-type structure, whenever one wants to drive transitions between states that are only indirectly coupled via off-resonant intermediate states. The essential requirements are compatible optical selection rules, sufficiently large but experimentally accessible detunings to suppress real occupation of the intermediate state while retaining effective coupling, and coherence times long compared with the single-shot driving window. Beyond the semiconductor QD system demonstrated here, this concept may also be applicable to selected molecular 56 , atomic 57 , colour-center 58 , and superconducting artificial-atom systems 59 .

The radius of the electronic wavefunction is determined by fitting the calculated pulse-area dependence of the B X -occupation for TPE to the experimental TPE results, which are displayed in Fig. 3 b, c. We solve the combined QD-phonon Hamiltonian using a state-of-the-art process tensor method 47 , 61 , 62 . articles.title: Effect of liposome rigidity on corona formation and its implications for uptake by cells.
articles.authors: Ma X, Zhao F, Cantero-Reviejo M, de Weerd S, Squillante I, Portale G, Roos WH, Salvati A.
articles.abstract: Abstract Nanoparticle rigidity influences cellular uptake and in vivo behavior, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here we used lipids with identical head groups but different acyl chains to prepare liposomes with comparable surface composition, size and zeta potential, but distinct mechanical properties. Rigid liposomes showed much higher uptake than soft ones, mediated by distinct endocytic mechanisms. Proteomic analysis revealed that rigid and soft liposomes adsorbed very different coronas upon dispersion in serum. RNA interference and competition studies indicated that the enhanced uptake of rigid liposomes is likely driven by the lower abundance of multiple apolipoproteins in their corona, and possibly the higher abundance of apolipoprotein H and of a pattern of low-abundant corona proteins. Importantly, a strong difference in uptake was observed only when liposomes were added to cells in the presence of serum. Hence, the different uptake efficiency is not solely due to the different mechanical properties, but results from the effect of liposome mechanical properties on corona formation. Subject terms: Drug delivery, Endocytosis, Nanobiotechnology

Subject terms: Drug delivery, Endocytosis, Nanobiotechnology

Nanoparticle rigidity affects their cell uptake and in vivo behaviour, but the mechanisms remain unclear. Here, the authors show that rigid and soft liposomes form different coronas in serum and only when the corona is present does the uptake differ.

Nanomedicine uses nanomaterials of different physico-chemical properties, such as size and surface charge, to deliver drugs to their target 1 , 2 . Nanoparticle mechanical properties, particularly rigidity, have recently drawn significant attention, as they affect in vivo distribution, circulation time, and cellular uptake efficiency 3 – 5 . Theoretical studies show that rigidity affects membrane bending and wrapping during internalization by cells. Rigid nanoparticles can enforce membrane wrapping more easily, whereas softer ones deform along the membrane before inducing bending, requiring higher energy for internalization 3 , 5 , 6 . Many studies reported enhanced phagocytic uptake of rigid nanoparticles in vivo, leading to faster clearance and shorter circulation time 4 , 7 , 8 . Instead, results regarding the effect of rigidity on the uptake by cancer cells remain inconsistent and often appear contradictory 4 , 9 – 11 . This is likely due to the fact that many factors that can affect uptake efficacy are varied across different studies, such as the explored range of nanoparticle rigidity, nanoparticle material, size, surface charge, and incubation conditions. Overall, a clear fundamental understanding of how nanoparticle rigidity affects nanoparticle interactions at the cell and organism level is still lacking.

Within this context, one aspect that remains largely unexplored is whether corona formation is affected by nanoparticle mechanical properties. Once exposed to biological environments, nanoparticles are known to rapidly adsorb a corona of proteins and other biomolecules, which critically shapes their biological identity 12 . The corona can promote interactions with specific cell receptors and potentially endow nanoparticles with endogenous targeting capabilities, as reported for Onpattro, the first RNA therapeutic, as well as the so-called SORT (selective organ targeting) lipid nanoparticles and several other systems 13 – 18 . While nanomaterial properties such as size and surface charge are known to modulate corona composition 12 , 19 , 20 , surprisingly little is known on whether nanoparticle rigidity affects it as well 21 , 22 .

To address this question, here we selected liposomes as a model to obtain nanoparticles of different mechanical properties but comparable surface composition, size, and zeta potential. Modulating nanoparticle mechanical properties without affecting other physico-chemical parameters is very challenging. Different models have been developed and used for this purpose, each presenting some advantages and some limitations 11 , 23 – 25 . Here, liposomes composed of lipids with different lipid chain saturation were selected as a model system because they allow to modulate nanoparticle mechanical properties without affecting some of the other key physico-chemical properties known to affect nanoparticle biological behavior. In fact, depending on their composition and transition temperature, lipid bilayers can form different phases: solid ordered phase (S o ) bilayers are rigid, while liquid disordered (L d ) phase bilayers are soft 26 , 27 . By selecting lipid mixtures with different lipid chain length and saturation, liposome transition temperature can be modulated 24 , 28 . Hence, by varying lipid chain saturation and bilayer phase, liposomes of very different mechanical properties can be formed, while keeping their size, charge, and surface composition comparable.

Of note, liposomes with saturated lipids can often agglomerate and are usually stabilized by addition of pegylated lipids. However, inclusion of pegylated lipids reduces corona formation, hence interfering with the aim of this study. Therefore, extensive optimization was performed by tuning liposome charge and lipid mixture composition in order to vary the transition temperature of the bilayers, and obtain two non-pegylated liposomes of distinct mechanical properties that were stable in biological fluids. Next, atomic force microscopy (AFM) was used to quantify nanoparticle deformation under varying imaging forces, providing a direct comparison of their relative rigidity. The cellular uptake of the two liposomes was determined, and their uptake mechanisms were characterized. Mass spectrometry (MS) was used to compare the composition of the coronas formed on the two liposomes. RNA interference, competition experiments, and chemical inhibitors were combined in order to determine whether differences in corona composition could lead to the involvement of different receptors in the uptake of the two formulations. Finally, liposomes were dispersed in biological media of different composition in order to determine the effect of the resulting coronas on uptake efficiency. In this way, we disentangled how nanoparticle mechanical properties affect corona formation and their consequences on uptake by cells.

To obtain liposomes of same size, zeta potential and surface composition but different rigidity, lipids with identical head groups but varied chain lengths and saturation were selected. Liposomes of ~100 nm were prepared by thin layer hydration and extrusion. Initially, pure zwitterionic liposomes were prepared, with same surface properties but different phase transition temperature (Supplementary Fig. 1 ) 29 . Uptake was higher for the liposomes with saturated lipids, however, they were not stable in the biological medium used for cell studies (MEM supplemented with 10% v/v fetal bovine serum, hereafter referred to as complete medium, cMEM, Supplementary Fig. 1 ).

Liposomes agglomeration in biological medium was observed also for formulations where saturated lipids were mixed with increasing amounts of unsaturated lipids in order to lower the transition temperature, T m , below 37 °C (Supplementary Fig. 1B ). Next, we incorporated negatively charged phosphatidylglycerol (PG) lipids with identical acyl chains to increase the particle charge for improved stability, but without altering the T m . Stability in cMEM was achieved only when incorporating high amount of PG lipids (30–50%, see Supplementary Fig. 2 for details). However, possibly because of the strongly negative charge, uptake of the saturated and unsaturated charged liposomes was comparable (Supplementary Fig. 2 ).

Based on these results, we modulated both T m and charge by mixing DPPC or DOPC with unsaturated negatively charged DOPG at the minimum ratio necessary to obtain liposomes that remained stable in biological conditions and still showed different uptake efficiency. This led to a final formulation of DOPC/G and DPPC/G liposomes with an 85:15 PC:PG ratio (Fig. 1A, B ). The two liposomes had comparable size, (~110 nm in water and PBS, as measured by DLS and Nanoparticle Tracking Analysis), and were stable over time (Fig. 1C, D & Supplementary Fig. 3A-B ). Their zeta potential was also comparable (around −43 mV in H 2 O and −12 mV in PBS, Fig. 1C, E ). Importantly, the optimized liposomes were stable upon dispersion in medium with serum, where a second small peak at around 10 nm was also visible from the free serum proteins in solution (Fig. 1D and Supplementary Fig. 3B for results up to 24 h at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 , hence in the conditions used for cell experiments). Interestingly, the zeta potential in medium with serum further decreased towards neutrality as expected upon corona formation, but was slightly different for the two liposomes (−3.6 ± 0.8 mV for DPPC/G and −8.9 ± 0.5 mV for DOPC/G), suggesting potential differences in corona composition (Fig. 1E ).

In order to further characterize the optimized liposomes, DLS was employed to determine their transition temperature (T m ) 30 by monitoring the count rate (the number of photons detected per second) of the liposome dispersions at increasing temperature (Fig. 1F and Supplementary Fig. 3C for raw data). A discontinuity in the count rate can be observed when there is a change in the optical properties of the liposome, and this indicates a phase transition 30 . The corresponding temperature T m can be calculated by fitting the curve with a Boltzmann model (see Eq. 1 in the “Methods”). The results showed that DPPC/G liposomes exhibited a broader transition with a T m of 38.2 °C, slightly lower than that of pure DPPC liposomes (42.8 °C). In line with this, Differential Scanning Calorimeter (DSC) showed that pure DPPC liposomes exhibited a main transition peak at 41.2 °C. Instead, a much broader peak at around 37.3 °C was observed for DPPC/G liposomes (Fig. 1G and raw data in Supplementary Fig. 3D ). Overall, these results confirmed that the T m of DPPC/G liposomes is slightly lower than that of pure DPPC liposomes, as expected due to the addition of 15% DOPG.

We next compared the fluidity of the two formulations upon incorporation of laurdan in the bilayer 31 . Changes in laurdan fluorescence emission are commonly used to characterize membrane fluidity and this is often used as an indicator of membrane rigidity and of the different mechanical properties of liposomes with bilayers in different phases 26 . In fact, when laurdan is incorporated in bilayers in the ordered phase (S o , L o ), it shows maximum emission at around 440 nm, while when inserted in bilayers in the liquid disordered phase (L d ) the maximum emission is at around 490 nm. Based on this, a Generalized Polarization ratio (GP 340 ) can be calculated (as shown in Eq. 2 in the “Methods”). It is important to keep in mind that as a consequence of the different bilayer phase both the mechanical properties, as well as the hydration level of the bilayer are affected. In fact the laurdan GP ratio is also used as an indicator of the bilayer hydration at the liposome surface 32 , 33 . In the gel phase, tight lipid packing excludes water from the interface, while in the liquid disordered phase, looser packing permits greater water penetration. Therefore, in this model, nanoparticle mechanical properties and the bilayer hydration level are both varied, because they are strongly intertwined and cannot be separated, since they are both consequences of the different bilayer phase.

The results obtained with laurdan fluorescence showed that in line with literature 31 , 34 , pure DPPC liposomes at 30 °C displayed a high GP 340 value of 0.1, consistent with laurdan inclusion into a solid ordered phase. The GP 340 value dropped to below -0.1 (liquid disordered phase) when the temperature increased above 41 °C, consistent with the T m of pure DPPC (Fig. 1H ). DOPC/G liposomes instead showed GP 340 values lower than –0.2 at all temperatures tested, as expected for unsaturated lipids in the liquid disordered phase. In contrast, for DPPC/G liposomes the GP 340 value decreased gradually at increasing temperature. Watanabe previously reported that laurdan in multiple hydration status shows a more gradual GP 340 decrease, and suggested this is due to membrane region heterogeneity and/or incomplete phase segregation 35 . It would be interesting to determine whether inclusion of a small fraction of DOPG lipids in the liquid phase into the solid DPPC bilayer indeed leads to the formation of clusters of lipids and phase segregation. Consistent with these results, at 37 °C (as used for cell studies) the GP 340 value for DPPC/G liposomes was slightly lower than that for DPPC, but considerably higher than for DOPC/G liposomes. Overall, these results confirmed that DPPC/G and DOPC/G liposomes exhibit distinct bilayer fluidity, influenced by their respective T m values.

Next, atomic force microscopy (AFM) was employed to compare the mechanical properties of the two liposomes. Representative topographic images are shown in Fig. 2A (images at all imaging forces are shown in Supplementary Fig. 4A ). By imaging individual liposomes at increasing imaging forces, the decrease in height can be directly measured and provides a comparison of the difference in mechanical properties between samples. At low imaging force (70 pN), the heights of the DPPC/G and DOPC/G liposomes were generally lower than the diameters detected by DLS (Fig. 1D ), as typically observed because of liposome deformation upon surface attachment 36 . Notably, even at such low imaging force, DOPC/G liposomes showed a lower height, indicating higher deformability, as well as a greater number of lipid patches (Fig. 2A, B ). The presence of these patches further indicated a higher deformability and consequently a higher rate of collapse upon adsorption onto the glass. At increased forces only a few liposomes remained intact. Conversely, DPPC/G liposomes demonstrated greater resilience (see all images in Supplementary Fig. 4A ). We next tracked the height change of individual DPPC/G liposomes that withstood at least three consecutive imaging forces (Fig. 2C, D and Supplementary Fig. 4B for raw data) and their survival rates (Fig. 2E ). Even after using forces up to 200 pN, 73% of the DPPC/G liposomes remained intact. Analysis of the height vs force at 200 pN indicates a reduction of 10% of the original height measured at 70 pN. Gradually increasing the force further, up to 700 pN, resulted in total collapse of most DPPC/G liposomes, with an estimated survival population of 23%. These results clearly demonstrated the distinct mechanical properties of the two liposome formulations, with DOPC/G liposomes being much softer and brittle than DPPC/G liposomes. To further compare liposome mechanical properties, an analysis of indentation curves was performed. Due to—among others—pressure built up of the adhered vesicles and fluidity of bilayers, it is challenging to obtain elastic parameters 36 , 37 . Supplementary Fig. S5 shows a relative comparison of the elasticity, denoted as the apparent modulus M app , of the two liposomes. The results confirmed that the M app of the DPPC/G liposomes is higher than that of the DOPC/G liposomes, consistent with results of increased imaging force experiments. Based on the two methods for the quantitative characterization of nanoparticle mechanical properties by AFM, we refer hereafter to the two liposomes as “soft” and “rigid” liposomes, for simplicity.

Having confirmed the different mechanical properties of the optimized liposomes, we compared their cellular uptake behavior on HeLa cells. Results at different liposome concentrations and over time showed that uptake of the rigid liposomes was much higher than for the soft ones (Fig. 3A, B , up to 15-fold higher at 30 h incubation). Similar outcomes were observed in a range of cell lines, including A549 epithelial cells, SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells, THP-1 monocyte (mTHP-1) and PMA-stimulated THP-1 (sTHP-1) as a common model for human macrophages (Fig. 3C ), suggesting the higher uptake of rigid liposomes may be a general behavior across different cell types.

Confocal fluorescence microscopy (Fig. 3D ) confirmed liposome internalization and the overall higher uptake for the rigid liposomes, consistent with the results obtained by flow cytometry. LysoTracker staining showed that both liposomes were trafficked to the lysosomes, as usual for most nanomaterials. Other studies suggested that some liposomes may enter cells by passive fusion to the cell membrane 9 . Here instead, energy depletion by incubation with the metabolic inhibitor sodium azide (NaN 3 ) confirmed that for the liposomes used in this work uptake was energy-dependent rather than by passive fusion (Fig. 3E, F ). The strong drop of cell fluorescence in energy depleted cells also indicated that liposome adhesion to the cell membrane was minimal. Consistent with this, no membrane associated staining was observed by confocal microscopy in cells incubated with the liposomes in standard conditions (Supplementary Fig. 7 ). This was also a confirmation that the fluorescent lipid DiI used for liposome tracing remained associated within the liposomes inside endocytic compartments. Similarly, no membrane-associated staining was observed in energy-depleted cells either (Supplementary Fig. 7 ). These results confirmed that the lower fluorescence of cells incubated with the soft liposomes was not due to effects of DiI dilution in fused cell membranes on its fluorescence emission, but rather due to a lower uptake efficiency.

As a next step, a panel of common transport inhibitors was used to determine whether the different uptake efficiency observed for the soft and rigid liposomes could be explained by the involvement of different uptake mechanisms. Importantly, additional DLS studies were performed to confirm that the liposome dispersions in medium with serum remained stable also upon addition of the different inhibitors (Supplementary Fig. 8 ). Agglomeration in the presence of the inhibitors could strongly affect uptake studies and impair their interpretation. The results showed that inhibition of clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) with chlorpromazine strongly increased uptake of the rigid liposomes, potentially due to activation of compensatory mechanisms, while for the soft liposomes it reduced uptake of around 30–40% in the first hours (Fig. 4 and Supplementary Fig. S8 for raw data). Similarly, blocking macropinocytosis with EIPA increased uptake of the rigid liposomes, while it reduced uptake of the soft liposomes up to 40%. Incubation with the dynamin inhibitor hydroxydynasore and with nystatin to deplete cholesterol from the cell membrane indicated that for both liposomes endocytosis was dynamin dependent, but not cholesterol dependent, respectively. Finally, blocking actin polymerization with cytochalasin D reduced the uptake of soft liposomes up to ~60–70%, while for the rigid liposomes effects were visible only at shorter incubation times. Overall, the observed reduction of uptake upon incubation with different transport inhibitors confirmed once more that the liposomes were internalized by cells via active mechanisms of endocytosis (as opposed to passive fusion to the cell membrane). More specifically, the results suggested that for both liposomes uptake was actin- and dynamin-dependent, but cells likely internalize the two liposomes via different mechanisms, with macropinocytosis and (at short time) clathrin-mediated endocytosis involved in the uptake of the soft liposomes (Fig. 4B provides a schematic summary of these results).

To correlate the differences in uptake behavior with potential differences in the protein corona formed upon dispersion in serum, corona-coated liposomes were isolated using size exclusion chromatography (SEC) 38 . During SEC, nanoparticles with their strongly associated proteins (the so-called hard corona) elute first through the column, while the loosely associated proteins (soft corona) and the excess free proteins elute later. Hence, SEC is a common method to separate nanoparticles with their hard corona from the loosely bound soft corona proteins and the free serum proteins in solution 12 , 38 . FBS samples eluted by SEC were also tested to exclude contamination by particles of size and density comparable to liposomes in FBS (e.g., protein aggregates, lipid nanoparticles, exosomes, etc., Supplementary Fig. 9A ) 39 . The isolated hard corona-coated liposomes were well dispersed (Fig. 5A ), and—interestingly—displayed slightly different zeta potential (Fig. 5B ), suggesting differences in their corona composition. Protein quantification indicated that comparable amount of proteins were absorbed on both rigid and soft liposomes (Fig. 5C ). Next, SDS-PAGE was used to separate the isolated corona proteins (Fig. 5D and additional results in Supplementary Fig. S9B ). Interestingly, despite having the same size, surface properties and similar amount of adsorbed proteins, the two liposomes adsorbed very different corona proteins, particularly in the low molecular weight range below 50 kDa, where multiple bands with stronger intensity were detected for the soft liposomes (Fig. 5D, E ). These results clearly indicated that the two liposomes adsorbed different protein coronas upon dispersion in serum. The different coronas likely resulted from the observed differences in nanoparticle mechanical properties (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 5 ), as well as potential additional contributions due to differences in bilayer fluidity and bilayer hydration levels, that in this model are strongly intertwined.

When comparing the different samples, the majority of identified proteins were shared by both rigid and soft liposomes. Near 200 proteins were identified only in the corona samples but not in FBS, where they fell below detection limits, likely due to their low abundance. This is consistent with what is usually reported upon corona formation, where typically a very strong enrichment of low abundant proteins is observed. The top 20 most abundant proteins accounted for around 85% of the total protein corona abundance in both rigid and soft liposomes. While these proteins were present in both coronas, they were generally more enriched in the soft liposomes (Fig. 6C, D , and Supplementary Fig. 10D ). This confirmed that nanoparticle rigidity leads to selective enrichment of specific corona proteins on the surface of the two liposomes.

Among 528 overlapping proteins detected in both coronas, 25 proteins were significantly depleted in the corona formed on the rigid liposomes in respect to the soft liposomes, and 6 proteins were significantly enriched. However, the enriched proteins had very low abundance (individual log 2 (LFQ intensity) lower than 20, and combined abundance of only 0.26% of total recovered proteins) (Fig. 6B & Supplementary Table 1 ). Instead, 11 of the 25 significantly depleted proteins in the rigid corona were relatively highly abundant on the soft liposomes (log 2 (LFQ intensity) higher than 20), and 7 of them ranked within the top 21 abundant proteins in the soft liposome corona (Fig. 6C , and Supplementary Table 1 ). Given the lower uptake of the soft liposomes in respect to the rigid liposomes, it is likely that these include proteins with a stealth effect and “don’t eat me” signals, as reported for proteins such as clusterin, CD47 or histidine-rich glycoprotein (HRG) 40 – 42 . Among the most abundant proteins in the soft liposome corona, 6 were apolipoproteins, including APOA2, APOC3 and APOE, that collectively accounted for 33% of the total protein abundance in the soft liposome corona, compared to only 4% in rigid liposomes. Apolipoproteins are known to be commonly enriched in the corona forming on many different types of nanomaterials 12 , 14 , 15 , 43 . Conversely, the most abundant proteins in rigid liposomes were largely comparable to those in the soft liposomes, expect for apolipoprotein H (APOH, also known as beta-2-glycoprotein 1). Despite a strong variability among replicates, APOH was highly enriched in the rigid liposome corona, making up—on average—28.5% of the total proteins (rank 1), compared to only 2.9% in soft liposomes (rank 11). Its abundance in the rigid liposome corona was ~190-fold higher than in FBS (0.15%), being the most enriched protein in the corona formed on the rigid liposomes (Fig. 6C , Supplementary Fig. 10D ). When instead looking at proteins that were uniquely detected in either rigid or soft liposomes (Supplementary Table 2 , 3 ), 40 proteins were exclusive to soft liposomes and 7 to rigid liposomes. However, their overall abundance was minimal, contributing <0.3% and <0.1% in the rigid and soft liposome corona, respectively.

Overall, proteomic analysis confirmed that the two liposomes adsorbed very different coronas. The top 20 most abundant corona proteins were common, although most of them were more abundant on the soft liposomes, except for APOH, which was the most abundant protein in the rigid liposome corona. Instead, the unique proteins distinguishing the two coronas included a set of low-abundance proteins, contributing—for both liposomes—to only less than 0.3% of the corona.

Given the selective enrichment of several apolipoproteins in the corona formed on the two liposomes, as a next step we investigated whether some apolipoprotein receptors were involved in the uptake of soft and rigid liposomes. These included the low-density lipoprotein receptor LDLR and the scavenger receptor class B member 1, SRB1, that were already identified as corona receptors for different nanomaterials 11 , 13 , 18 , 44 , 45 . In addition, we tested whether known APOH receptors were involved in liposome uptake, especially for the rigid liposomes. APOH has been reported to bind to heparin 45 , a structure analog of heparan sulfate, which is one of the most common glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) on the cell surface 18 . GAGs, especially heparan sulfate, are frequently reported as co-receptors together with lipid particle receptors and are emerging as nanoparticle receptors in multiple studies, including for exosomes 18 , 46 – 48 . To investigate the role of heparan sulfate in the uptake of the two liposomes, exostosin glycosyltransferase 1 ( EXT1 ), a gene involved in glycosaminoglycan metabolism, was also silenced to deplete heparan sulfate on the cell membrane 18 . LRP1B and LRP8 were also included, since APOH is known to bind receptors of the LDL receptor-related protein (LRP) family (Fig. 7A, B ) 49 . When silencing EXT1 and LRP8 , around 30–40% uptake reduction was observed for both liposomes, while no reduction was observed for LRP1B . Silencing SCARB1 expression, which encodes SRB1, slightly reduced the uptake of soft liposomes (~30% reduction). Instead, silencing LDLR reduced uptake of both liposomes, but with much stronger effects for the rigid liposomes (~80% reduction versus 30%). Competition with dextran sulfate (Fig. 7C ), commonly used to test the role of heparan sulfate in uptake, reduced the uptake of rigid liposomes up to 80% in the first hour, with decreasing effects over time (up to 40% reduction after 5 h), while instead it had only minor effects on the uptake of soft liposomes. Of note, DLS analysis showed that for the rigid liposomes incubation with dextran sulfate induced agglomeration (Supplementary Fig. 11A ), hence complicating interpretation of these results.

Given the different response upon LDLR silencing for the two liposomes, we further investigated its role via competition experiments with LDL (Supplementary Fig. 11B ). When incubating cells with liposomes in the presence of increasing amounts of LDL, for the soft liposomes a small uptake reduction was observed, consistent with the results obtained after LDLR silencing. In contrast, addition of LDL increased uptake of the rigid liposomes. Similar results were obtained when changing the design and experimental conditions used for the competition study (Supplementary Fig. 11C ). DLS results confirmed that both liposomes remained stable after incubation with LDL (Supplementary Fig. 11D ), thus excluding confounding effects on nanoparticle stability.

To assess whether the enrichment of APOH in the rigid liposome corona could explain their higher uptake, we compared the uptake of liposomes pre-coated with either BSA or APOH and then added to cells in cMEM or in serum free MEM. In serum free medium, uptake of the two liposomes pre-coated with BSA or APOH was comparable and overall much lower than what was observed for the rigid liposomes in cMEM (Supplementary Fig. 11E ), suggesting that APOH alone cannot explain the higher uptake observed for rigid liposomes. Instead, in cMEM uptake was higher for the rigid liposomes regardless the pre-coating. Furthermore, when adding increasing concentrations of APOH to block its receptors (Supplementary Fig. 11F ), the uptake of corona-coated liposomes in serum free medium was not reduced, while in cMEM it was reduced to comparable extent for both liposomes (30–40% reduction, Supplementary Fig. 11G ).

Overall, no clear differences were observed in the role of the tested receptors in the uptake of the two liposomes, except for the stronger effect of LDLR silencing on the uptake of the rigid ones. Similarly, it was not possible to confirm whether enrichment of APOH in corona and uptake via APOH receptors were responsible for the higher uptake of the rigid liposomes. Indeed, competition experiments are challenging when testing families of receptors which are clearly connected with each other, as the lipoprotein receptor family 18 . For the same reason, silencing their expression can induce upregulation of other receptors in the same family, making it difficult to disentangle their roles 50 . Additionally, competition experiments for nanoparticles can be complicated by the potential binding of the competitor to the nanoparticle corona, further complicating interpretation.

As a further step to understand whether the differences in the corona adsorbed on the two liposomes could explain their different uptake efficiency, we compared the uptake of liposomes added to cells in different media. When liposomes were added to cells in serum free medium, thus in the absence of a serum corona on their surface, their uptake was comparable and generally rather low (Fig. 8A ). This demonstrates that the mechanical properties alone cannot explain the higher uptake observed for rigid liposomes. When added to cells in a solution of BSA, uptake levels remained rather low, but the rigid liposomes had roughly 5 times higher uptake than the soft ones. Instead, when the liposomes were added to cells in the presence of FBS, where a full corona can form on their surface, uptake levels increased substantially and in these conditions uptake of the rigid liposomes was around 12 times higher than for the soft liposomes (Fig. 8A ). Consistent with this, in cells incubated with the liposomes in energy depleted conditions, a comparable difference was observed on liposome adhesion to the cell membrane (around 16 time higher for the rigid liposomes). This suggests that the corona formed in serum promotes stronger adhesion to the cell membrane and this is likely to lead to the higher uptake observed. Similar uptake differences were observed for the two liposomes added to cells in human serum, although overall uptake efficiency was much lower, as typically observed for particles added to cells in human serum 51 . Finally, when hard corona-coated liposomes were first isolated by SEC and then added to cells in either serum free medium or reintroduced back in a medium with FBS, the uptake difference further increased to around 22 and 39-fold respectively (Fig. 8C ). These results suggest that while soft corona proteins (which are lost upon corona isolation by SEC) and the excess free FBS proteins in solution also affect uptake, it is primarily the nature of the adsorbed hard corona layer formed in FBS which drives the higher uptake observed for the rigid liposomes.
