At the core of this regulatory architecture lies MaoP, whose expression is controlled by the transcriptional regulator HdfR. In this hierarchy, HdfR links temperature-dependent host-associated cues to maoP expression, whereas MaoP acts downstream as a central effector, and its effects depend on both its expression level and the environmental condition. Through this arrangement, the HdfR-MaoP module couples biofilm formation required for flea-borne transmission with envelope-associated adaptations that enhance resistance to innate immune defenses in the mammalian host. These coordinated outputs support a role for HdfR-MaoP as a regulatory hub for integrating the opposing selective pressures inherent to vector-borne life cycles.

Our mechanistic analyses clarify MaoP’s molecular function within this framework. MaoP is a small, highly abundant protein with a basic central region and the capacity to autoregulate its own expression. It binds DNA without detectable sequence specificity and alters DNA conformation in vitro, as shown by MST and AFM. By contrast, Hi-C contact maps and contact-probability decay analyses did not reveal major changes in chromosome folding in vivo. This difference likely reflects the different scales probed by the two approaches, with AFM detecting local single-molecule DNA conformational changes, whereas Hi–C reports population-averaged chromosomal contacts at kilobase resolution, as well as potentially dynamic or heterogeneous MaoP-DNA interactions, as previously reported for H-NS 33 . Thus, transient, heterogeneous, or sub-kilobase MaoP-DNA interactions may not produce detectable changes in global Hi-C profiles. This scale-dependent behavior is consistent with MaoP acting as a local architectural DNA-binding factor rather than as a global nucleoid organizer, a role classically associated with abundant NAPs such as HU or IHF 34 , 35 . Together, these biochemical and functional properties place MaoP within the NAP functional spectrum. However, rather than acting as an autonomous global nucleoid organizer, MaoP appears to function as a quantitatively tuned architectural effector embedded in an HdfR-controlled, temperature-responsive regulatory module. How MaoP functionally interfaces with established nucleoid-associated proteins and DNA-binding regulators remains to be defined. These factors may act together with MaoP to modulate virulence-associated gene expression under specific conditions.

The difference between MaoP’s broad DNA-binding capacity in vitro and its promoter occupancy in vivo helps reconcile its sequence-agnostic DNA binding in vitro with its discrete promoter occupancy in vivo. Controlled maoP expression in the Δ hdfR background restores all tested phenotypes, indicating that HdfR is not required as a promoter-specific cofactor for MaoP activity. Instead, HdfR appears to coordinate the module by tuning MaoP abundance, thereby linking MaoP’s broad DNA-binding capacity to vector- and host-aligned molecular programs. Consistent with this model, MaoP binds DNA in vitro without detectable sequence specificity, its ChIP-seq peaks lack a clear consensus motif, and bacterial two-hybrid assays detected no interaction with the RNA polymerase subunits or sigma factors tested. These findings argue against strict sequence-specific recognition or protein-mediated recruitment as the main determinants of MaoP occupancy. Rather, MaoP occupancy at discrete promoters likely emerges from broad DNA binding constrained by local chromosomal accessibility, topology, and physiological state, as described for NAPs such as H-NS 34 , 36 . In this view, MaoP illustrates how architectural DNA-binding proteins can be integrated into environmentally responsive regulatory circuits to coordinate adaptive outputs across changing host-associated niches. In this context, HdfR-mediated tuning of MaoP abundance may ensure that MaoP-dependent phenotypes are expressed under appropriate temperature conditions. Autoregulatory loops at both the HdfR and MaoP levels may further reinforce this robustness.

Beyond immune evasion per se, the HdfR-MaoP module coordinates anticipatory adaptations across host transitions. Through this regulatory axis, envelope properties are preconfigured under flea-like conditions and selectively reinforced upon entry into the mammalian host, supporting resistance to distinct arms of innate immunity. By limiting exposure of immunogenic surface determinants while strengthening membrane robustness under host-associated conditions, HdfR-MaoP enables Y. pestis to withstand both complement-mediated attack and antimicrobial peptide stress. This temperature-gated coordination may allow the bacterium to anticipate, rather than merely react to, host-associated immune pressures during transmission and early infection.

The HdfR-MaoP module also illustrates how conserved regulators can incorporate horizontally acquired virulence genes. In S. enterica , HdfR directly regulates the horizontally acquired std fimbrial operon 37 , showing that conserved regulators can be wired to species-specific virulence programs. In Y. pestis , HdfR-MaoP-dependent regulation similarly extends beyond chromosomal loci to selected plasmid-borne virulence-associated genes, including the pMT1-encoded caf locus. Thus, horizontally acquired functions can be incorporated into host-responsive regulatory architectures governed by conserved modules.

The widespread conservation of the hdfR - maoP locus across Enterobacterales indicates that this regulatory architecture predates the specialized flea-mammal life cycle of Y. pestis . In diverse bacterial species, components of this module have been linked to distinct physiological outputs, including virulence, biofilm-associated traits, motility and mutagenic repair of DNA breaks 38 – 43 . Consistent with this functional diversification, HdfR has been shown to bind directly to promoters controlling adaptive traits in other Enterobacterales , including the flagellar master regulator flhDC in E. coli and the std fimbrial operon in S. enterica 37 , 44 . Our data connect these observations by showing that the organization and regulatory hierarchy of HdfR-MaoP have been retained despite substantial sequence divergence. The functional conservation of this scaffold is supported by prior evidence that MaoP expression is HdfR-dependent in E. coli 45 , and by our cross-species complementation experiments showing that HdfR and MaoP from E. coli restore all tested phenotypes in the corresponding Y. pestis mutants. Conversely, HdfR and MaoP from Y. pestis restore biofilm formation in the corresponding E. coli mutants, despite the absence of the HdfR-MaoP-regulated Y. pestis hmsHFRS biofilm genes in E. coli . Together, these findings suggest that HdfR-MaoP is an ancient regulatory module whose outputs have diversified across ecological contexts, with downstream outputs shaped by species-specific physiology and niche-associated pressures. In Y. pestis , this scaffold appears to have been integrated into regulatory programs that coordinate flea-borne transmission and mammalian host adaptation.

In conclusion, the HdfR-MaoP module functions as a compact regulatory architecture that resolves how opposing host-specific programs are integrated during vector-borne life cycles characterized by abrupt transitions between ectothermic and mammalian environments. Through this mechanism, Y. pestis can efficiently navigate transitions between its arthropod vector and mammalian host. By coupling biofilm-mediated transmission with anticipatory envelope-associated programs that limit complement recognition, while reinforcing resistance to antimicrobial peptides, this circuitry provides a mechanistic link between transmission-associated biofilm formation and host-associated envelope adaptation, allowing Y. pestis to meet the conflicting demands imposed by alternating vector and mammalian environments. The widespread conservation of this architecture across Gammaproteobacteria highlights an ancient and versatile strategy for physiological plasticity and positions HdfR-MaoP as a conserved regulatory hub coordinating adaptation across distinct ecological contexts. Consistent with this view, the identification of flunixin as a chemical probe provides a means to experimentally manipulate this conserved regulatory architecture, offering tractable entry points to modulate host- and environment-associated physiological states in Gram-negative bacteria.

All bacterial strains and plasmids used in this study are listed in Supplementary Data 3 . Y. pestis strains were grown in Brain Heart Infusion (BHI) or Lysogeny Broth (LB) at 21 °C or 37 °C for 15 h without shaking unless otherwise specified. When required, media were supplemented with MgCl 2 (4 mM), CaCl 2 (4 mM), and carbenicillin (100 µg/mL), kanamycin (50 µg/mL), trimethoprim (25 µg/mL) or streptomycin (50 µg/mL). Mutations were generated using the λ Red recombinase system as previously described 46 . Briefly, the target sequence was replaced with an antibiotic resistance cassette amplified from the vectors listed in Supplementary Data 3 using the primer pairs shown in Supplementary Data 4 . All constructs were verified by PCR. Complementation strategies were adapted to the experimental purpose. For in vitro assays, the gene of interest under its native promoter was cloned using the CloneJET PCR Cloning Kit (ThermoFisher Scientific), and the primer sets are listed in Supplementary Data 4 . Alternatively, the coding sequence without its promoter was cloned into the pBAD30 expression vector for arabinose-inducible expression. For flea infection experiments, the gene under the control of its native promoter was integrated at the chromosomal attTn 7 site. For this, PCR products were first cloned into the suicide vector pUC18R6KT-mini-Tn 7 T in E. coli DH5α λ -pir. Recombinant constructs were then co-electroporated with the helper plasmid pTNS2 into Y. pestis , enabling site-specific integration at the att Tn 7 site 47 . Correct integration was confirmed by PCR.

For both assays, 5 × 10 5 bioluminescent Y. pestis grown in LB at 21 °C or 37 °C were suspended in 10 µL of PBS (serum assay) or LB (antimicrobial peptide assay) and added to white 96-well plates (Fisher Scientific) containing 90 µL of the appropriate test solution, for a final volume of 100 µL per well. Plates were immediately sealed with a transparent film (ThinSeal™ ClearLine) and incubated at 21 °C or 37 °C without shaking. Luminescence was recorded at different incubation times using a Centro XS³ LB 960 luminometer (Berthold) and the Microwin 2010 5.24 software or a Victor™ X3 multilabel plate reader (PerkinElmer) and the PerkinElmer 2030 Manager 4.0. For the antimicrobial peptide assay, the test solution consisted of LB supplemented with increasing concentrations of polymyxin B (0–84 µg/mL; Sigma-Aldrich). For the serum resistance assay, the test solution consisted of either normal human serum, heat-inactivated serum (56 °C, 30 min) 48 ; serum was purchased from the Établissement Français du Sang (EFS).

Biofilm formation was quantified by crystal violet staining. A total of 2 × 10 6 Y. pestis from overnight cultures grown at 21 °C with shaking were inoculated into 24-well flat-bottom plates containing 1 mL of LB supplemented with 4 mM MgCl 2 and 4 mM CaCl 2 per well. After 24 h incubation at 21 °C with shaking, the medium was removed, and the wells were washed three times with water. Adherent biofilms were stained with 0.01% crystal violet for 15 min at room temperature, washed three times, and bound dye was solubilized with 1.5 mL ethanol-acetone (80:20). Aliquots were transferred to transparent 96-well round-bottom plates, and absorbance was measured at 540 nm using a Biotek ELx800 spectrophotometer. Exopolysaccharide production was quantified by Congo red binding as previously described 49 . Bacteria grown at 21 °C with shaking in LB supplemented with 4 mM MgCl 2 and 4 mM CaCl 2 were centrifuged and resuspended in the same medium containing 0.2% galactose and 3% Congo red to reach 10 9 CFU/mL. After 2.5 h of incubation at 21 °C without shaking, cultures were centrifuged, and the optical density of the supernatant was measured at 490 nm to quantify unbound dye.

The Xenopsylla cheopis fleas used in this study were originally obtained from the Rocky Mountain Laboratories, National Institutes of Health (RML/NIH, USA), and have been maintained in our laboratory. Flea infections were performed as previously described 8 . Starved X. cheopis were randomly selected from the same laboratory colony and allowed to feed for 1 h on heparinized male OF-1 mouse blood (Charles River Laboratories) containing 5 × 10 8 CFU/mL of Y. pestis grown overnight at 37 °C in BHI, using an artificial feeding system. Immediately after feeding, fully engorged fleas were randomly selected to generate cohorts of 100 fleas, either composed of equal numbers of males and females or of females only, and were selected and maintained in the dark at 21 °C and 75% relative humidity in a climatic chamber (Eratis). Fleas were fed twice weekly for 1 h on 2–5 day-old NMRI mouse neonates for up to 4 weeks. Neonates were obtained from an in-house breeding colony maintained under standard animal facility conditions: 12-h light/12-h dark cycle, 22 ± 2°C ambient temperature and 55 ± 10% relative humidity. Mouse sex was not determined because it could not be reliably assessed at this developmental stage. Mixed-sex cohorts were monitored twice weekly immediately after feeding to determine the blockage rate; blockage being defined as the presence of fresh red blood in the foregut but not in the midgut. Cohorts composed of females only were used to quantify the time course of gut colonization. At selected time points post-infection, fleas were surface-sterilized by sequential immersion in 1 mL of 3% hydrogen peroxide and 1 mL of absolute ethanol for 2 min each, rinsed in 10 mL of sterile PBS, and air-dried. Each flea was transferred into a Lysing Matrix H tube (MP Biomedicals) containing 1 mL of PBS and homogenized using a FastPrep-24 instrument (30 s, speed 6.0 m/s). Homogenates were mixed with LB agar supplemented with 1 µg/mL Irgasan and 10 µg/mL hemin and poured onto a base layer of the same medium. After drying, a second agar layer was added. Plates were incubated for 48 h at 28 °C before CFU enumeration. For co-infection experiments, fleas were infected with an equal mixture of two Y. pestis strains. Individual fleas were processed as described above, and homogenates were plated on non-selective supplemented LB agar to determine total bacterial loads and on selective supplemented LB agar to enumerate the antibiotic-resistant strain. The abundance of the competing strain was inferred by subtracting selective CFU counts from total CFU counts, and bacterial competition was quantified as the relative proportion of each strain within the total bacterial population recovered from each individual flea. All animal procedures were approved by the local Animal Care and Use Committee (Comité d’éthique en expérimentation animale n°75; reference: 2015102609372221 and 2022020316019750) and notified to the relevant French authorities, in accordance with current national legislation (Government Decree No. 2017-1411; Articles R.214-87 to R.214-126).

Wild-type and Δ hdfR Y. pestis strains grown in LB at 21 °C or 37 °C were harvested by centrifugation at 4 °C, washed twice with cold PBS, resuspended in PBS supplemented with an EDTA-free protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche) and then lysed by sonication using a Branson Digital Sonifier (2 cycles, 45 s on / 5 s off, 70% power, 4 °C). Lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 10,000 g for 20 min at 4 °C, and the supernatants were ultracentrifuged at 100,000 g for 40 min at 4 °C (Beckman Colter Optima XE-90). Protein concentrations were determined using the Bradford assay (Bio-Rad). Samples were dried in a SpeedVac™ concentrator (Thermo Scientific) and processed at the PISSARO proteomics platform (Université de Rouen Normandie, France) as already described 50 . Peptides were analyzed by nLC-MS/MS (RSLC Ultimate 3000 system coupled to an Eclipse mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific)). MS/MS spectra were exported for peptide identification against the Y. pestis KIM10+ proteome (4079 proteins, Uniprot UP000002490) and containing 4079 sequences) using Proteome Discoverer 1.4 and Mascot 2.6.0 (Matrix Science). Database searches were performed with the following parameters: 1 missed trypsin cleavage site allowed; variable modifications: carbamidomethylation of cysteine and oxidation of methionine. Mass tolerances for precursor and fragment ions were set at 5 ppm and 0.02 Da respectively. The FDR was set at 1%. Quantification was performed using Progenesis 4.1 LC-MS/MS software (Waters) under a label-free quantification workflow. Peptides and proteins with P -value and q-value 0.8 were retained. Only proteins identified with ≥2 peptides and showing a fold change >2 between conditions were considered significant. Five biological replicates per strain and condition were analyzed.
Functional annotation and pathway classification of differentially regulated proteins were performed using the KEGG, NCBI, and UniProt databases.

Metabolite profiling of Y. pestis strains was performed as described previously 51 . Briefly, bacteria grown in LB at 21 °C or 37 °C were harvested by centrifugation at 4 °C, and pellets were snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen. Metabolites were extracted at −20 °C using methanol/acetonitrile/water (50:30:20). Extracts were vortexed for 5 min at 4 °C, centrifuged at 16,000 g for 15 min at 4 °C, and supernatants were analyzed by LC-MS using a SeQuant ZIC-pHILIC column (Millipore). Chromatographic separation was performed using a linear gradient from 80% organic to 80% aqueous over 15 min at 200 µL/min, with the column maintained at 48 °C. The aqueous mobile phase contained 20 mM ammonium carbonate with 0.1% ammonium hydroxide, and the organic phase was acetonitrile. Mass spectrometry was performed on a Q-Exactive Plus instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operating in electrospray ionization with polarity switching, at 35,000 resolution at m/z 200 over an m/z range of 75-1000. Lock masses ensured mass accuracy <5 ppm. Peak areas were extracted using TraceFinder (Thermo Fisher Scientific) based on the exact mass of the singly charged ion and known retention times on the HPLC column. Statistical analyses were performed using MetaboAnalyst 4.0 52 . Hierarchical clustering was performed using a Pearson correlation-based distance metric and Ward linkage to group metabolites according to abundance patterns.

Promoter activity was quantified using luciferase- or GFP-based transcriptional reporters. For the luciferase assay, a Y. pestis strain harboring at the att Tn 7 site a promoterless luxCDABE operon downstream of a kanamycin-resistance cassette preceded by a single I- Sce I restriction site was used 53 . The promoters of interest were amplified by PCR and inserted in place of the kanamycin cassette and the I- SceI restriction site using the λ Red recombinase system with I- Sce I counter-selection 8 , employing the plasmids and primer pairs listed in Supplementary Data 3 and 4 . All constructs were verified by PCR and sequencing. Cultures grown in LB at 21 °C or 37 °C were transferred into white 96-well plates (Fisher), and luminescence was recorded for 1s using a Centro XS³ LB 960 luminometer (Berthold). Luminescence values were normalized to OD 600 . For the GFP assay, the promoters amplified by PCR were cloned into the pPromX-GFP plasmid. Y. pestis harboring the recombinant plasmids were grown in LB at 21 °C or 37 °C, washed three times in PBS and transferred into black 96-well plates (Fisher) using excitation/emission settings of 488/535 nm. GFP fluorescence was immediately recorded for 1s using a Victor™ X3 multilabel plate reader (PerkinElmer) and normalized to OD 600 measured after the final wash.

Y. pestis was directly resuspended in Laemmli sample buffer (Bio-Rad) containing β-mercaptoethanol after being grown in LB or after three washes with PBS when grown in human serum. Samples were boiled at 95 °C for 10 min and whole-cell lysates were separated by SDS-PAGE. Proteins were transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes (Amersham), which were then blocked in PBS containing 0.5% Tween-20 (PBS-T) and 5% skim milk. Membranes were incubated with the appropriate primary antibody (Supplementary Data 5 ), washed four times in PBS-0.5% Tween-20 and incubated for 45 min at room temperature with the corresponding HRP-conjugated secondary antibody (Supplementary Data 5 ). After four additional washes, signals were detected using SuperSignal West Pico (Thermo Fisher). Images were acquired using a LAS-3000 imager (Fujifilm) or an ImageQuant 800 system (Cytiva) and analyzed with the Multigauge 2.1.1 and ImageQuant TL 10.2, respectively (Supplementary Data 5 ). Band intensities were normalized to the RNA polymerase alpha subunit, to Ponceau or Coomassie blue-stained gels. Specific antibody conditions are provided in Supplementary Data 5 .

DOC-PAGE was performed as previously described 54 . A total of 7.5 × 10 8 Y. pestis grown at 21 °C or 37 °C were harvested by centrifugation, washed once in PBS, and resuspended in DOC lysis buffer (2% sodium deoxycholate, 4% 2-mercaptoethanol, 10% glycerol, and 0.002% bromophenol blue in 1 M Tris-HCl buffer, pH 6.8). Suspensions were heated for 10 min at 100 °C, treated with Proteinase K (80 μg/mL) for 3 h at 55 °C, and the reaction was stopped by an additional 10 min incubation at 100 °C. Equivalent amounts of material equivalent to 2 × 10 7 bacteria per lane were loaded onto DOC-PAGE gels, and LOS was visualized by silver staining.

Outer membrane permeability was assessed using the 1-N-phenylnaphthylamine (NPN) uptake assay as previously described 55 . Y. pestis grown in LB at 21 °C or 37 °C was harvested, washed three times in PBS, and adjusted to 10 9 CFU/mL. NPN (10 µM final) was added to the suspension and fluorescence was recorded after 30 min incubation in the dark at 21 °C or 37 °C (excitation 350 nm, emission 420 nm) using a Victor™ X3 multilabel plate reader (PerkinElmer). Background fluorescence (PBS + NPN) was subtracted from all readings, and values were normalized to the bioluminescence of the same suspensions, used as a proxy for bacterial load.

Deposition of complement factors and serum proteins (C3b, C4, C4BP, factor H, factor B, vitronectin, C1q and MBL) on the bacterial surface was assessed by Western blot as previously described 56 , using the antibodies listed in Supplementary Data 5 . Y. pestis was incubated with normal or heat-inactivated human serum at a final concentration of 90% (50% for assays involving factor H) using ~7.5 × 10 6 bacteria per reaction (~10 9 for factor H because higher bacterial input was required for detection). At the indicated time points, samples were chilled on ice and centrifuged at 4 °C, washed three times in cold PBS, resuspended in Laemmli sample buffer containing β-mercaptoethanol, and analyzed by Western blot as described above.

Total RNA was extracted by resuspending Y. pestis pellets in TRI Reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific), followed by the addition of chloroform (20% final; vortexed and incubated at room temperature for 10 min). After phase separation, the aqueous phase was mixed 1:1 with ethanol, and RNA was pelleted by centrifugation. Pellets were washed with 75% ethanol, centrifuged again, air-dried and resuspended in RNase-free water. Residual genomic DNA was removed by DNase I treatment (Merck). RNA concentration and purity were measured spectrophotometrically, and RNA integrity was verified by agarose gel electrophoresis. cDNA synthesis was performed using SuperScript III Reverse Transcriptase (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and random hexamers. Quantitative PCR was carried out using Takyon Rox SYBR MasterMix dTT Blue (Eurogentec) on a Stratagene Mx3005P instrument (Agilent Technologies), with fluorescence acquisition and Ct determination performed using MxPro 4.10 software. Relative transcript levels were calculated using the ΔΔCt method with proC as the internal reference 57 . Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Data 4 .

Y. pestis (Δ pla ) cells crosslinking and Hi-C library preparation were performed as described in 58 . Hi-C sequencing data were processed starting with adapter trimming using Cutadapt 3.2. Paired-end reads were then aligned to the Y. pestis KIM10+ genome (accession number: PRJNA288) using Bowtie2 (v2.4.2). Hi-C data were further analyzed using the OCHA pipeline in R ( https://github.com/js2264/OHCA ), as described in 59 . For visualization, the contact maps were displayed at 1 kb bin resolution. To qualitatively compare normalized contact maps, we performed a ratio of matrices. This ratio is computed for each bin of the map by dividing the amount of contacts it presents in Δ maoP by the amount of contacts in the WT, and applying a log2 transformation to the resulting matrix. The log2 of the ratio is plotted with a Gaussian filter (H = 1). The color code reflects a decrease or an increase in contacts in one condition compared to the other (blue or red signal, respectively). No change is represented by a white signal. To quantitatively compare chromosome organization between strains, contact probability was calculated as a function of genomic distance from normalized Hi–C contact matrices. Contact-probability decay curves were compared between WT Δ pla and Δ maoP Δ pla strains to assess potential changes in short- and long-range chromosomal contacts.

ChIP-seq was performed as previously described with minor modifications 60 , using three independent biological replicate cultures per strain. Y. pestis lacking pCD1 and pla , while expressing a C-terminal FLAG-tagged MaoP protein (MaoP-FLAG), together with the corresponding untagged parental strains (negative controls) were grown in LB at 37 °C; MaoP-FLAG were being functional (Supplementary Fig. 4a, b ). Cultures were crosslinked with 1% formaldehyde for 30 min at 37 °C under gentle agitation, quenched with glycine, washed with TBS, pelleted and resuspended in IP buffer. Chromatin was sheared to 100–300 bp fragments using a Bioruptor sonicator (40 cycles, 30 s on / 30 s off, high power, 4 °C). Complete compositions of buffers are provided in Supplementary Data 6 . Lysates were incubated overnight at 4 °C with anti-FLAG magnetic beads (GenScript). Beads were washed, and bound DNA was eluted with alkaline elution buffer prior to reverse-crosslinking Protein-DNA complexes overnight at 65 °C. DNA was purified by phenol:chloroform:isoamyl alcohol (25:24:1, pH 4.0) extraction, precipitated in precipitation buffer (30:1, v/v) overnight at −20 °C, washed with ethanol 70% and resuspended in TE buffer. 50 ng of fragmented double-stranded DNA was used for library preparation using the MicroPlex Library Preparation kit v3 (Diagenode). Dual-indexed libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 500 sequencer. Reads were processed using the Galaxy server 61 , mapped to the Y. pestis KIM genome with Bowtie2 2.5.5 + galaxy0 62 , and peaks were called with MACS2 2.2.9.1 + galaxy0 63 using default settings.

The maoP and zur genes from Y. pestis were amplified by PCR and cloned into the pET24d or pET28a vectors to generate 6His-tag fusion constructs, using the primers and plasmids listed in Supplementary Data 3 and 4 . Complete compositions of TNTI, TNI, and TN buffers, as well as all reagent formulations used for expression and purification, are provided in Supplementary Data 6 . The recombinant plasmids were transformed into E. coli C41(DE3). Cultures were grown in LB at 37 °C to an OD 600 of ~0.4, induced with 1 mM IPTG for 3 h at 37 °C, harvested, resuspended in PBS and lysed using a French press (Constant Systems). Clarified lysates were loaded onto HisPur™ affinity columns (Thermo Fisher) packed with complete His-Tag Purification Resin (Roche). Proteins were washed with TNTI and TNI buffers, and eluted with TNI containing 500 mM imidazole. Proteins were concentrated and exchanged into TN or TN AFM buffer using Amicon Ultra-15 devices (Merck). Purity was verified by SDS-PAGE.

MST measurements were performed on a Monolith NT.115 Pico instrument (NanoTemper Technologies). Purified MaoP and Zur proteins were exchanged into TNG buffer (Supplementary Data 6 ) and quantified by BCA assay. Proteins were diluted to 200 nM in PBS-T (NanoTemper) and labeled with 100 nM RED-tris-NTA dye for 30 min at room temperature in the dark, then diluted to a final concentration of 10 nM. DNA ligands consisted of purified PCR products (amplified from sequences listed in Supplementary Data 4 ). PCR products were purified using a PCR cleanup kit (Macherey Nagel), quantified by spectrophotometry, and serially diluted in a 1:1 ratio across 16 concentrations to generate the ligand titration series. Equal volumes of labeled protein and diluted DNA were mixed and incubated for 5 min at room temperature before loading into standard capillaries. Thermophoresis was recorded using medium MST power and 20% LED. Data were acquired with MO. Control 1.6.1 and analyzed with MO.Affinity Analysis 2.3 (NanoTemper) (Supplementary Data 6 ).

RIP was performed on Y. pestis lacking pPla and expressing the E. coli MaoP-3×FLAG from the pAK004 plasmid. Cultures were grown overnight in LB at 37 °C supplemented with 10 mM arabinose, harvested, washed once in cold PBS and lysed by bead beating (Biospec) in ice-cold lysis buffer (Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 0.5% Triton X-100). Lysates were clarified by centrifugation and incubated with anti-FLAG magnetic beads (GenScript) for 2 h at 4 °C with gentle rotation. Beads were washed four times with TBS, and MaoP-RNA complexes were eluted with RIP elution buffer using a thermomixer (70 °C, 800 rpm, 5 min). RNA was extracted with phenol:chloroform:isoamyl alcohol (25:24:1, pH 4.0), precipitated overnight at -20°C with precipitation buffer, washed with 70% ethanol, air-dried, then resuspended in nuclease-free water. RNA samples were treated with DNase I (Merck) prior to being assessed for integrity by agarose gel electrophoresis and quantity with a Qubit RNA High Sensitivity kit (Thermo Fisher). Details on buffer compositions, washing conditions, and centrifugation parameters are provided in Supplementary Data 6 .

c-di-GMP was extracted and quantified by HPLC as described previously 64 , with minor modifications. Briefly, bacterial cultures were fixed with 0.18% formaldehyde, pelleted, washed, and resuspended in distilled water. An aliquot was used for protein normalization by BCA assay, while the remaining sample was heated at 99 °C and extracted sequentially with 95% and 70% ethanol. Dried extracts were resuspended in nanopure water and analyzed on a Dionex Chromeleon 7 HPLC system equipped with a reverse-phase C18 column. c-di-GMP was eluted using ammonium acetate-based water/methanol solvents, detected at 253 nm, quantified using a commercial c-di-GMP standard curve, and normalized to total protein content. Details on buffer compositions are provided in Supplementary Data 6 .

MaoP copy number per bacterium was estimated by quantitative immunoblotting. Clarified lysates were incubated with anti-FLAG magnetic beads (GenScript) for 2 h at 4 °C with gentle rotation. Beads were washed four times with Wash buffer, and MaoP-FLAG was eluted using the Alkaline elution buffer. After neutralization as recommended by the manufacturer, the purified proteins were quantified by BCA assay. Purified MaoP-FLAG was used as a calibration standard and loaded alongside whole-cell extracts prepared from 2.5 × 10 8 Y. pestis grown at 21 °C or 37 °C. Samples were resolved by electrophoresis, transferred, and probed with an anti-FLAG antibody. Band intensities were quantified and compared with the purified MaoP-FLAG standard curve to determine the amount of MaoP-FLAG in each extract. Molecule numbers were derived using the predicted molecular weight of MaoP-FLAG (14,065 kDa) and Avogadro’s constant, then normalized to bacterial cell counts. Details on magnetic beads and Antibody Supplementary Data 5 , as well as buffer compositions, are provided in Supplementary Data 6 .

Protein-protein interactions were assessed using the adenylate cyclase-based BACTH system (Euromedex) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Candidate genes were cloned into the pKT25 vector, and maoP was cloned into the pUT18 vector using the primers listed in Supplementary Data 4 . The resulting plasmid pairs were co-transformed into E. coli DHM01 (Δ cyaA ). Transformants were plated on MacConkey agar supplemented with maltose 1%, ampicillin and kanamycin, and incubated at 30 °C until colony color discrimination was evident. The pKT25-Zip and pUT18C-Zip plasmid pair was used as the positive control.

DNA and protein samples were prepared and imaged in liquid according to a previously published protocol 65 . DNA was obtained after PCR using primer sets in Supplementary Data 4 , and subsequently was extracted with phenol:chloroform:isoamyl alcohol (25:24:1, pH 4.0), precipitated overnight at −20 °C, washed with ethanol 70% and resuspended in nuclease-free water. Purified MaoP in TN AFM buffer was obtained as described above. Samples were immobilized onto freshly cleaved mica (10 mm, Ted Pella, US) by incubating 4 µl of 10 ng/µl solution in a 70 µl drop of divalent cations buffer during 10 min for DNA or 30 min for DNA mixed with purified MaoP. Samples were then washed four times in the same buffer to remove unbound material and rinsed in Ni buffer to stabilize DNA-protein complexes during AFM scanning. Imaging was conducted on a FastScan Bio microscope (Bruker, US) operating NanoScope 9.4 software in Peak Force Tapping mode, using FastScan-D probes (Bruker, US). Engage and Peak Force imaging setpoints were minimized to [40–100] pN. Peak Force parameters were as follows: 2 kHz PF frequency, [10–20] nm PF amplitude, [150–1000] μm scan size, [256–512] pixels, [1–3] Hz scan rate, [5–10] nm lift height, [2–5] gain. Sync distances were adjusted at engagement and kept constant throughout imaging. Images were plane-fitted, cropped (if needed), and exported using NanoScope Analysis 1.9. Complete compositions of divalent cations buffer, Ni Buffer and TN AFM buffers, as well as all reagent formulations used, are provided in Supplementary Data 6 . For DNA Bend angles analysis, only DNA molecules that were completely visible on the image and could be unambiguously traced were taken for analysis. DNA bend angles were measured using ImageJ 1.52, a software. The angles were defined by manually determining the path of the DNA segments. By convention, the DNA bend angle is defined as the deviation from straight.

Inhibitors of the HdfR-MaoP module were identified using Y. pestis carrying a chromosomal maoP - luxCDABE reporter integrated at the attTn 7 site. Approximately 10 6 bacteria were dispensed into 384-well plates containing 50 µL of LB medium with or without individual compounds from an FDA-approved compound library (Tocris and Prestwick). Plates were incubated at 37 °C, and luminescence (RLU) and optical density (OD 595 ) were measured at 0, 4, and 8 h using a Victor™ X3 plate reader (PerkinElmer). Luminescence values were normalized to OD 595 to control for bacterial growth. Compounds that reduced maoP promoter activity by at least twofold relative to DMSO controls, without affecting OD 595 , were selected for dose-response analyses. Selected compounds were tested at concentrations ranging from 6 nM to 50 µM, performed in triplicate. The lead compound was validated by assessing Y. pestis survival after exposure to polymyxin B (1.25 µg/mL) and the lead compound (25 µM), alone or in combination (in the presence of the DMSO vehicle control), as described in the antimicrobial peptide susceptibility assays section.

Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 10 (GraphPad Software). For experiments comparing multiple groups to a single control, an ordinary one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test was used. For antimicrobial peptide resistance assays, comparisons between strains across tested doses were analyzed using a two-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple comparisons test. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). n values correspond to distinct biological samples or independent experimental units, not repeated measurements of the same sample. A P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. ns, not significant; * P < 0.05.

articles.title: Regulatory mechanisms of maternal imprinting at the murine Dlk1-Dio3 domain.
articles.authors: Weinberg-Shukron A, Dearden FL, Moreno-Barriga A, New LTN, Müller M, Rancourt RC, Edwards CA, Ferguson-Smith AC.
articles.abstract: Abstract Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic process causing parent-of-origin specific gene expression. The Dlk1-Dio3 domain is one of the largest imprinted clusters. While DNA methylation at an intergenic CpG-island (IG-CGI) within the imprinting control region (ICR) controls expression from the paternal chromosome, mechanisms regulating the unmethylated maternal chromosome remain unknown. Within the transcriptional regulatory element (IG-TRE) of the ICR, deletions identified a minimal region in vitro exhibiting both silencing and enhancing activity, with SOX2 and ZFP281 contributing to enhancer function on the maternal chromosome. In vivo, however, this deletion did not affect maternal expression in mouse embryos; instead it activated Dlk1 on both parental chromosomes. Combining deletion of this IG-TRE with the lethal IG-CGI deletion rescued lethality in mice by balancing Dlk1 expression, despite persistent maternal gene upregulation. These results demonstrate that loss of expression at this domain is more detrimental than gain, highlighting the importance of in vivo analysis. Identification of active regulatory factors on the unmethylated maternal chromosome challenges the prevailing view that imprinting is primarily a methylation-driven phenomenon, further revealing the sophisticated hierarchical mechanisms governing imprinting control. Subject terms: Imprinting, Gene expression, Dosage compensation, Transcriptional regulatory elements
paragraphs: Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic process causing parent-of-origin specific gene expression. The Dlk1-Dio3 domain is one of the largest imprinted clusters. In vivo, however, this deletion did not affect maternal expression in mouse embryos; instead it activated Dlk1 on both parental chromosomes. Subject terms: Imprinting, Gene expression, Dosage compensation, Transcriptional regulatory elements

Researchers reveal that genomic imprinting is regulated by mechanisms beyond DNA methylation, identifying key transcription factors acting on the unmethylated maternal chromosome and providing insights into gene dosage control during development.

Genome function is regulated temporally and tissue-specifically through the orchestrated interplay of regulatory factors, genomic features, and epigenetic states. Epigenetic modifications are dynamic during development and across the cell cycle. A hierarchy of successive epigenetic states, including DNA methylation, ensures the creation of healthy individuals. In mammals, extensive epigenetic reprogramming events occur during germ cell development, fertilization, and early embryogenesis 1 .

One major process that maintains epigenetic memory in the germline is that of mammalian genomic imprinting 2 , 3 . Genomic imprinting is an epigenetically regulated process causing genes to be expressed according to the parent-of-origin. Imprinting is highly conserved in eutherian mammals, with mouse studies providing insights into the repertoire of developmental and physiological pathways regulated by imprinted genes 4 , 5 .

Differentially DNA methylated regions (DMRs) at imprinting control regions (ICRs) are established in the parental germlines 6 . They are protected from the global wave of demethylation in the early embryo by the KRAB zinc finger proteins ZFP57 and ZFP445 in order to maintain the epigenetic memory of parental origin 7 . Failure to correctly establish and maintain imprints is associated with developmental syndromes, including growth abnormalities, neurological and metabolic disorders, and numerous forms of cancer 8 , 9 . The extreme dosage sensitivity of imprinted genes highlights the complex and dynamic nature of their gene expression and importance in human biology.

Genomic imprinting is a tractable model for studying epigenetic regulation, as the two genetically identical parental genomes within the same nucleus express a different repertoire of genes according to their parental origin. However, the dynamic hierarchy of events initiated by the ICR, which leads to the long-range, domain-wide, temporal, and tissue-specific behavior of imprinted genes, is not fully understood. By employing a systemic set of mutants at a single imprinted domain, we can dissect the relationship between allelic expression, dosage, epigenetic control, and phenotypic outcomes.

The developmentally regulated Dlk1-Dio3 imprinted domain, is conserved between mouse and human, spans 1.2 Mb and is one of the largest imprinted clusters. Failure to correctly imprint genes in this cluster in mice causes prenatal lethality, and in humans leads to Temple or Kagami–Ogata Syndromes, both exhibiting neurological, developmental, and behavioral impairments 10 , 11 .

Four protein-coding genes: Dlk1 , Rtl1 , Dio3 , and one isoform of Begain are preferentially expressed from the paternally inherited chromosome, and the maternally inherited chromosome expresses multiple imprinted noncoding transcripts, including Gtl2 (also known as Meg3 ), Rian , and Mirg (Fig. 1A ) 12 . Gtl2 also forms a long polycistronic transcript along with its associated transcripts Rian and Mirg , acting as a host for multiple snoRNAs and miRNAs, including the miR-379/miR-410 cluster, all of which are driven by the Gtl2 promoter 13 – 15 . Appropriate expression of genes in this region is essential for the lifelong health of mammals and understanding their epigenetic regulation has significant biomedical relevance for a diverse range of processes 16 – 19 .

A The paternally inherited chromosome expresses Dlk1 , Rtl1 , Dio3 , and one isoform of Begain (blue). The maternally inherited chromosome expresses Gtl2 / Meg3 , antiRtl1 , and arrays of snoRNAs and miRNAs (red). The IG-DMR is methylated in sperm and unmethylated in oocytes and is the imprinting control region for the domain. DMRs are indicated by circles: black (methylated), white (unmethylated). B The IG-DMR contains a CpG island (IG-CGI) that binds ZFP57 (turquoise) on the methylated paternal copy and a transcriptional regulatory element (IG-TRE) that has an enhancer-like function on the unmethylated maternal copy (green). The IG-DMR also binds AFF3 (purple) through ZFP57 at the IG-CGI on the methylated paternal chromosome and co-bound with ZFP281 (yellow) at the IG-TRE on the unmethylated maternal chromosome. C The secondary somatic Gtl2-DMR is methylated in cis according to the methylation pattern of the IG-DMR. D Maternal deletion of the entire IG-DMR results in a maternal-to-paternal epigenotype switch 20 . E Paternal deletion of the IG-CGI results in a paternal-to-maternal epigenotype switch 30 . F Maternal deletion of the IG-TRE is hypothesized to result in a maternal-to-paternal epigenotype switch, similar to deletion of the entire IG-DMR. Created in BioRender. Edwards, C. (2026) https://BioRender.com/g67o4d9 .

Imprinting at the Dlk1-Dio3 domain is regulated by the germline-derived intergenic DMR (IG-DMR) 20 , which spans approximately 5 kb between Dlk1 and Gtl2 and is required for regulating parent-specific expression across the locus 21 . The IG-DMR is normally methylated in sperm and unmethylated in oocytes and maintains this parent-specific pattern throughout development (Fig. 1A, B ). After implantation, a secondary somatic DMR is established at the promoter of the Gtl2 gene (the Gtl2-DMR), which is also hypermethylated on the paternal chromosome 22 (Fig. 1C ).

The IG-DMR was recently established as a bipartite element comprised of two distinct functional elements 23 (Fig. 1B ). The first, termed the IG-CGI, is a small CpG island comprising seven tandemly repeated sequences of which five contain a ZFP57 binding motif 24 . The sequence-specific zinc finger protein, ZFP57, only binds to the methylated paternal chromosome, where it interacts with TRIM28, which recruits the repressive epigenetic machinery, including DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs) and heterochromatin-associated proteins, thereby maintaining the methylation memory of the germline imprint in early development at the time when most epigenetic modifications are being erased 25 , 26 . The IG-CGI has also been shown to bind AFF3, a component of the super elongation complex-like 3 (SEC-L3), on the methylated allele in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) where it is thought to interact with the ZFP57/TRIM28 complex 27 (Fig. 1B ).

Maternal deletion of the IG-DMR leads to paternalization of the maternal chromosome and mice die between E16.5 and birth 20 , 28 (Fig. 1D ). Surprisingly, in contrast to the full IG-DMR deletion, paternal deletion of only the IG-CGI results in the reciprocal paternal-to-maternal epigenotype switch with the Gtl2-DMR becoming hypomethylated on the paternal chromosome 29 , 30 (Fig. 1E ). These data indicate that the IG-CGI is required to maintain a repressive chromatin landscape on the paternal chromosome, while the same element is dispensable on the maternal copy 30 – 32 . The experiments therefore indicate that the maternal epigenotype must be regulated by elements within the IG-DMR, independent of the CpG island. Together, the paradoxical effects imposed by distinct deletions within the IG-DMR represent an attractive experimental framework for dissecting the impact of changes in gene dosage on embryonic phenotypes.

The remaining part of the IG-DMR, located downstream of the IG-CGI, has the potential to be an enhancer. It binds pluripotency transcription factors in mESCs, exhibiting active enhancer marks (H3K27ac) and nascent transcription 27 , 33 . It was therefore termed the transcriptional regulatory element (IG-TRE) and suggested to drive expression of the maternally inherited genes within the domain (Fig. 1B ) 23 .

The transcription factor AFF3 also binds to the 3′ side of the IG-DMR at the IG-TRE. There, AFF3 is co-bound with the zinc finger protein 281 (ZFP281/ZNF281), a zinc finger protein that has previously been reported to act as both a transcriptional activator and a repressor 34 (Fig. 1B ). In the Dlk1-Dio3 locus, depletion of ZFP281 from mESCs leads to decreased AFF3 binding at this downstream region. Since depletion of AFF3 leads to decreased expression of Gtl2 , Mirg , and Rian , this suggests that the downstream bound region is relevant for AFF3 function and that it also acts as an enhancer for maternally expressed genes 35 . Whether this region is acting in concert with the IG-TRE to control expression of Gtl2 and its associated transcripts remains to be established.

Recently, Hara et al. demonstrated that deletion of a 2.7 kb segment containing the IG-TRE results in postnatal lethality when maternally inherited 36 . However, smaller deletions of the IG-TRE subregions, including the AFF3/ZFP281-binding site alone, did not produce any obvious phenotype, suggesting the involvement of multiple elements spanning the IG-TRE in the regulation of the maternal epigenotype.

There is evidence suggesting a role for pluripotency-associated transcription factors such as OCT4, SOX2, and KLF4 in maintaining the unmethylated state of the maternal allele at imprints, potentially by forming a regulatory complex that promotes enhancer activity in pluripotent cells. For example, at the Igf2-H19 imprinted locus, SOX2 and OCT4 bind to the H19-ICR, and preserve the hypomethylated status of the maternal allele 37 , 38 . Whether this is a feature of these factors at other imprinted loci such as the IG-DMR is useful to ascertain. However, while the multiple transcription factor binding motifs suggest that the IG-TRE is most likely a positive regulator for Gtl2 , it is possible that the IG-TRE also contains a silencer element that is capable of directly repressing the paternally expressed genes on the maternally inherited chromosome. Experiments dissecting this region further are necessary to tease apart these options (Fig. 1F ).

Here, we defined the minimal region of activity at the IG-TRE in vitro, generated an in vivo knockout mouse model to dissect the function of the IG-TRE during mouse development, and pieced these together with the previous deletion models to understand how the parental-origin-specific epigenetic landscapes, genetic elements, and transcription are exquisitely coordinated to regulate genome function at this domain.

The IG-DMR knockout in mice demonstrated that it regulates the activity and repression of multiple imprinted genes in cis and influences differential methylation at the Gtl2-DMR in the Dlk1-Dio3 domain 20 but, though studies have shown it contains two features (IG-CGI and IG-TRE) acting individually on the paternally and maternally inherited imprinted gene cluster respectively, a systematic dissection of the regulatory features within the IG-DMR has not been conducted, making it unclear how it works. In order to address this, we used an in vitro luciferase reporter gene assay in a manner described for other imprinted clusters 39 , 40 .

A 6.125 kb region of the IG-DMR was divided into four overlapping fragments (Fig. 2A ). The first 2 kb of the IG-DMR knockout region is referred to as the 5′ fragment, which encompasses the IG-CGI and contains tandem repeat arrays identified by Paulsen et al. 41 The next fragment, referred to as Mid, overlaps the 5′ fragment and is located in the core of the differentially methylated region. It is 1.2 kb and also contains the CpG island and the tandem repeat array. At the end of the original knockout region 18 is the 3′1 fragment, which is 1.3 kb and located within the differentially methylated region. Finally, the 3′2 fragment spanning 2.2 kb includes the 3′ sequence downstream of the IG-DMR knockout region. All fragments were cloned in both orientations, with the sense (S) referring to the direction towards Gtl2 and antisense (AS) referring to the direction towards Dlk1 .

The 1.2 kb Mid fragment (mid IG-DMR in Fig. 2 ) revealed promoter-like and some enhancer activity in mESCs only in the sense orientation compared to the empty vectors (Figs. 2B,C and S1A , P Basic = 0.004; P Promoter = 0.05; P Enhancer = 0.04). Activity was not detected from any of the antisense constructs.

In order to narrow down the positive regulatory region, the Mid fragment was divided into smaller sections. The original 1.2 kb Mid fragment was first separated into two fragments: 471 bp (Mid-471) and 724 bp (Mid-724), and assayed in ES cells. The results showed that the promoter-like activity was present in the Mid-724 (sense orientation) while the Mid-471 fragment had no activity (Figs. 2B,C and S1A , P Basic =3.2E −05 , 0.0003; P Promoter =2.9E −05 , 8.9E −17 ; P Enhancer =8.8E −09 ,9.04E −06 ). Next, to further test the minimal region of activity, the 724 bp Mid region was divided into two additional fragments: 210 bp (Mid-210) and 510 bp (Mid-510). No activity was observed from Mid-210, while promoter-like activity was seen in Mid-510. However, Mid-510 had a lower level of activity than that of Mid-724 (Figs. 2B, C and S1A , P Basic =1.1E −08 ,6.4E −06 ). These results reveal that the 724 bp fragment is the minimal region for effective positive regulation, which the smaller fragments alone could not achieve.

To determine the role of the transcriptional regulatory element in the regulation of expression at the Dlk1-Dio3 locus, we created mESCs deleted for the IG-TRE (Fig. 3A ). We targeted 1.3 kb downstream of the IG-CGI, with two guide RNAs flanking this region, as defined by Aronson et al. 23 . Using SNPs between C57BL/6 and CAST/EiJ alleles in hybrid mESCs, we screened for clones with maternal, paternal, or biallelic deletions. In addition to the full 1.3 kb deletion, by chance we also obtained a smaller maternal deletion of 315 bp (Fig. 3B ).

Maternal deletion of the entire 1.3 kb resulted in loss of maternal expression of Gtl2 , Rian , and Mirg (Figs. 3D,E and S2A–D , Gtl2 P ∆M = 0.0002, Rian P ∆M = 0.02, Mirg P ∆M = 0.003), indicating that this region positively regulates the imprinted genes on the maternal chromosome. The same deletion on the paternal chromosome did not result in any change to gene expression at the Dlk1-Dio3 locus.

Furthermore, methylation analysis showed that loss of the maternal 1.3 kb IG-TRE resulted in increased methylation at the downstream Gtl2-DMR, while no change was observed in the upstream CpG island (IG-CGI) (Figs. 3F and S3A–C , P ∆M = 1.3E −05 ), suggesting that the IG-TRE normally contributes to protection of the maternal chromosome from DNA methylation.

Deleting only 315 bp at the 5′ end of the TRE, had the same effect on maternal gene expression and methylation at the Gtl2-DMR as deleting the entire 1.3 kb on the maternal chromosome (Figs. 3D–F , S2A–D and S3A–C , Gtl2 P ∆M-315bp = 4.1E −06 , Rian P ∆M-315bp = 0.01, Mirg P ∆M-315bp = 3.02E −05 , Gtl2-DMR P ∆M-315bp = 8.9E −05 ) indicating that the regulatory function of the IG-TRE is controlled by elements within that minimal 315 bp region.

To investigate which elements within the IG-TRE are responsible for maintaining the maternal epigenotype, we scanned the 315 bp region for transcription factor binding sites and identified highly conserved predicted binding sites for the SRY-Box Transcription Factor 2 (SOX2) and for the zinc finger protein 281 (ZFP281) (Fig. 3B, C ).

We created mESC clones with targeted deletions for these transcription factor binding sites within the 315 bp of the IG-TRE (Fig. 3B ). As a control, we also deleted the transcription factor binding site for PRDM14 (PR/SET Domain 14) from within the 315 bp of the IG-TRE, but found no change in expression or methylation at the region (Fig. S4 ).

Deletion of the SOX2-binding site on the maternal chromosome resulted in dysregulation of the maternal epigenotype, with decreased maternal gene expression (Figs. 3G, H and S2E–H , Gtl2 P ∆M = 0.004; P ∆Bi = 0.004, Rian P ∆M = 0.001; P ∆Bi = 0.001, Mirg P ∆M = 0.003; P ∆Bi = 0.007) and increased methylation at the IG-TRE and Gtl2-DMR (Figs. 3I and S3D–F , IG-TRE P ∆M = 0.02; P ∆Bi = 0.03; Gtl2-DMR P ∆M = 8.7E −06 ; P ∆Bi = 0.001). No effect was observed with the deletion on the paternal chromosome.

Deletion of the ZFP281-binding site on the maternal chromosome also resulted in similar dysregulation of the maternal epigenotype, with decreased maternal gene expression (Figs. 3J, K and S2I–L , Gtl2 P ∆M = 0.0002, Rian P ∆M = 0.01, Mirg P ∆M = 0.004) and increased methylation at the Gtl2-DMR (Figs. 3L and S3G–I , P ∆M = 0.05). No effect was observed with the deletion on the paternal chromosome.
These results indicate that SOX2 and ZFP281 binding play a key role in the cis -regulation of the maternally expressed genes in mESCs.

We dissected the previously identified 724 bp fragment into the 315 bp fragment, identified by our CRISPR deletion experiments, and 235 bp, which includes the rest of the downstream sequence, as well as a 550 bp fragment which encompasses both the 315 bp and 235 bp regions (Fig. 2A ), and conducted luciferase assays in vitro to validate the ES cells' findings.

Similar to the 724 bp fragment, the minimal 315 bp fragment exhibited significant activity in the sense direction, indicating promoter-like function, as well as enhancer-like function in the promoter vector (Figs. 2D, E and S1B, C , P Basic =1.01E −07 ,0.002; P Promoter =1.4E −06 , 0.005; P Enhancer =2.6E −06 , 0.002). However, when the SOX2-binding site was deleted from this minimal 315 bp fragment, this activity was lost (Figs. 2D, E and S1B,C , P Basic =1.1E −07 , 2.3E −06 ; P Promoter =1.5E −06 , 0.0003; P Enhancer =5.9E −06 , 0.001).

Strikingly, the 235 bp fragment, located downstream of the 315 bp region, exhibited the opposite silencing activity (Figs. 2D, E and S1B, C , P Basic =6.2E −16 , 1.03E −16 ; P Promoter =0.003,0.003; P Enhancer =9.95E −11 , 3.04E −09 ). Finally, the 550 bp fragment exhibited a partially enhancing function, reflecting a combination of the enhancing elements from the 315 bp region and silencing from the 235 bp region (Figs. 2D, E and S1B, C , P Basic =1.3E −06 , 7.6E −07 ; P Promoter =0.0004; P Enhancer =3.02E −13 , 5.7E −08 ).

We concluded that the 315 bp region at the IG-TRE is functionally important for expression of the imprinted noncoding RNAs from the maternal chromosome, and that this function is mediated by SOX2 binding. In contrast, the 235 bp region downstream of the 315 bp region contains a silencing element, and the combined 550 bp region is the minimal region of activity containing both regulatory elements at the IG-TRE.

In order to verify SOX2 and ZFP281 binding at the IG-TRE, and to determine whether they bind to one or both chromosomes, we performed chromatin immunoprecipitation and quantitative polymerase chain reactions (ChIP-qPCR) in wild-type, SOX2-BS mutant, and ZFP281-BS mutant hybrid mESCs (Fig. 4A ).

Surprisingly, we found that in mESCs, SOX2 binds to both the maternal and paternal copies of the IG-TRE at the 315 bp region, with the maternal and paternal SOX2-binding site deletions resulting in loss of binding on the corresponding copy (Fig. 4B , P SOX2-BS-∆P = 0.008, P SOX2-BS-∆M = 0.01; and Fig. 4C , P SOX2-BS-∆P = 0.0001, P SOX2-BS-∆M = 0.0001). SOX2 binding was unchanged when the ZFP281-binding site was deleted from within the 315 bp of the IG-TRE. SOX2 binding at Ceacam1 and the H19-ICR were assayed as negative and positive controls, respectively (Fig. 4B ).

Since we found that SOX2 bound both parental chromosomes, we hypothesized that the maternal activity of the IG-TRE is combined with ZFP281 to confer allele specificity and regulate expression of the Gtl2 polycistron 35 . We identified several ZFP281 predicted binding sites across the region in addition to the binding site we deleted from within the IG-TRE (predicted binding site#2, Fig. 4A ): At the 3′ end of the IG-CGI, upstream of the IG-TRE (predicted binding site #1), downstream of the IG-TRE where it has previously been shown to bind and recruit AFF3 (predicted binding site #3) 35 , downstream to the IG-DMR (predicted binding site #4) and at the Gtl2-DMR (predicted binding sites #5,6) 35 . We assayed ZFP281 binding at these predicted binding sites and at two control regions in the Otx2 gene (negative and positive controls).

We observed no binding at sites 3, 4, or 5 (Fig. S5 ), but that ZFP281 did bind at sites 1 and 2, upstream and in the 315 bp region, and at site 6 in the Gtl2-DMR (Fig. 4D ), and that this binding was maternal-specific (Fig. 4E ). As expected, ZFP281 binding was depleted at site#2 upon deletion of its binding site from within the 315 bp of the IG-TRE (Fig. 4D , P site2 =0.02; Fig. 4E , P site2 =0.003). Importantly, we found that ZFP281 binding was also lost upon deletion of the maternal SOX2-binding site at the 315 bp region (Fig. 4D , P site1 =0.002, P site2 =0.001, P site6 =0.04; Fig. 4E , P site2 =0.04), indicating that ZFP281 binding is dependent on SOX2 binding, but not the other way around, and together they regulate expression of the genes on the maternal chromosome. No change in ZFP281 binding was observed upon deletion of the paternal ZFP281 or SOX2-binding sites at the 315 bp region (Fig. 4D, E ).

To elucidate the functional roles of the SOX2 and ZFP281 binding at the IG-TRE in vivo during mouse development, we created knockout mice deleted for 550 bp of the IG-TRE, containing both functional elements that we identified in vitro: the minimal 315 bp enhancing region, and the 235 bp silencing region. Reciprocally, crossing IG-TRE ∆550 F1 deletion animals with C57BL/6 or CAST/EiJ wild-type partners allowed us to determine parent-of-origin effects of this deletion at different developmental stages in a highly controlled and reproducible manner (Fig. 5A ).

Consistent with recent results 36 , we found that both maternal and paternal inheritance of the IG-TRE ∆550 deletion produced viable and fertile offspring. At 9 weeks of age, the weights and lengths of both maternal and paternal deleted animals were indistinguishable from their wild-type littermates (Fig. 5B, C ). No difference was observed in brain and fat weight either (Fig. S6A, C, D, F ), however, maternal IG-TRE ∆550 animals and paternal IG-TRE ∆550 males had reduced liver weight (Fig. S6B , P ∆P-males =0.05; P ∆M-males =0.05; P ∆M-females =0.04 and Fig. S6E , P ∆P-males =0.01; P ∆M-males =0.02; P ∆M- females =0.03).

We performed allele-specific expression analysis on brains from 9-week-old hybrid animals harboring the maternal IG-TRE ∆550 and their wild-type littermates (Fig. 5D ). Expression of Dlk1 from the maternally inherited chromosome, though low, was significantly increased when the IG-TRE ∆550 deletion was on the maternally inherited chromosome compared to wild-type, where Dlk1 is predominantly expressed from the paternal chromosome (Fig. 5E, F , P = 3.5E −10 ). Reciprocally, Gtl2 , Rian , and Mirg were downregulated when the deletion was on the maternal chromosome compared to controls, similar to our observations in vitro (Fig. 5E , P Gtl2 =0.001; P Rian =1.3E −06 ; P Mirg =0.002). No change in expression was observed in the brains of paternal IG-TRE ∆550 animals, or in the liver of either maternal or paternal IG-TRE ∆550 and their wild-type littermates (Fig. S7A–D ). We next analyzed methylation levels associated with the three regulatory elements at the Dlk1-Dio3 region, the IG-CGI, IG-TRE and Gtl2-DMR, and found that they maintained normal levels of methylation in maternal and paternal IG-TRE ∆550 adult brains compared to their wild-type littermates (Fig. S7E, F ), indicating that the 550 bp on the maternally inherited IG-TRE is involved in regulating expression from the maternal chromosome in vivo, but that this function is tissue-specific, and its deletion neither changes the imprint at the ICR nor is detrimental for embryonic development.

To further elucidate the effect of the IG-TRE ∆550 deletion in a time-dependent manner, we crossed IG-TRE ∆550 heterozygote animals with CAST/EiJ partners to dissect mutant embryos at E15.5 and analyzed gene expression and methylation in E15.5 embryonic brains upon maternal and paternal transmission of the deletion (Fig. 6A, B ). We found that maternal IG-TRE ∆550 E15.5 embryos were smaller than their wild-type littermates, while their placenta weight was unchanged (Fig. 6C–F , P embryo-weight) =0.003, P embryo-length =0.002, P embryo/placenta-weight-ratio = 0.02, and Fig. S8A–D ). Similar to our observations from adult brains, we found that Dlk1 expression was increased in maternal IG-TRE ∆550 E15.5 brains compared to controls (Fig. 6G , P = 0.05) and that strikingly this expression came from both chromosomes (Fig. 6H , P = 0.005). Furthermore, surprisingly, and unlike adult brains and mESCs, there was no change in expression of the maternally expressed genes. Dlk1 expression was also increased in maternal IG-TRE ∆550 E15.5 liver (Fig. S8E , P = 0.04). No expression change of any gene at the Dlk1-Dio3 domain was observed in paternal IG-TRE ∆550 E15.5 tissues compared to hybrid wild-type littermates (Figs. 6I, J and S8G, H ). Lastly, and consistent with the adult findings, we found no change in methylation at the IG-CGI, IG-TRE, or Gtl2-DMRs in E15.5 brains with either maternal or paternal deletion of the IG-TRE ∆550 (Fig. S8I, J ).

Taken together, these results indicate that the IG-TRE functions in a tissue and developmental stage-specific manner that may be associated with a requirement for exquisite Dlk1 dosage control. For example, as opposed to its role as an enhancer of maternal Gtl2 expression in mESCs and in adult brains where Dlk1 is not strongly expressed, in vivo during embryonic development, where Dlk1 expression is high in the brain, the IG-TRE has a more pronounced silencing effect on Dlk1 expression, and its absence results in changes to Dlk1 expression from both chromosomes (Figs. S8 and S9 ).

To explain the observed differences between the functionality of our IG-TRE ∆550 deletion in embryonic and adult brains, we assayed the binding of SOX2 and ZFP281 in vivo. We found that both SOX2 and ZFP281 bind to the IG-TRE in 9-week-old brains, but that binding is weak in embryonic brains (Fig. 7A, C , P SOX2 = 0.0001, P ZFP281-site1 =0.0005, P (ZFP281-site2) =0.003). Furthermore, as opposed to the biallelic binding of SOX2 that we observed in ESCs, in vivo both SOX2 and ZFP281 binding was primarily maternal, and binding of both was lost in IG-TRE ∆550 maternal deletion brains (Fig. 7A , P SOX2 = 0.001; Fig. 7B , P E15.5 = 3.8E −05 , P 9w =3.3E −05 ; Fig. 7C , P ZFP281-site1 =0.0001, P ZFP281-site2 =0.001; Fig. 7D , P E15.5 = 1.2E −12 , P 9w =1.3E −10 ).

Together, these findings support a model in which SOX2 binding at the IG-TRE contributes to ZFP281 recruitment and maternal gene regulation in the adult brain, whereas this regulatory mechanism appears to be absent, less prominent, or not yet established in the embryonic brain. While the maternal silencing of Dlk1 is already functional in utero, it is probably mediated by other elements within the 235 bp of the IG-TRE.

In light of our findings that the IG-TRE 550 bp deletion from the maternal chromosome results in increased Dlk1 expression, but that the animals have no apparent phenotype, we asked whether this increased expression was significant enough to rescue a postnatal phenotype that arises from loss of Dlk1 expression on the opposite chromosome. Previously we described that deleting the IG-CGI from the paternal chromosome results in an epigenotype switch from paternal to maternal like properties 30 , with downregulation of Dlk1 and upregulation of the maternal transcripts Gtl2 , Rian , and Mirg (Fig. 8A ). Furthermore, we showed that balancing the gene dosage, through flipping expression of paternally expressed genes from the maternal chromosome and maternally expressed genes from the paternal chromosome, was sufficient for normal development and viability. However, it remains unknown whether this is due to a balanced dosage of a specific gene or a combination of multiple/all genes at the Dlk1-Dio3 domain. The IG-TRE ∆550 model described here offers a rare opportunity to address the possibility that the paternal or maternal genes at the Dlk1-Dio3 domain are not equally essential for viability. Specifically, crossing IG-TRE ∆550 heterozygote females (increased Dlk1 ) with IG-CGI ∆ heterozygote males (loss of Dlk1 ) is expected to produce double deletion embryos with a balance of Dlk1 expression, while the maternal genes will remain dysregulated (Fig. 8A ). We hypothesized that inheritance of both deletions, would rescue the postnatal lethality of the paternal IG-CGI deletion if balancing Dlk1 expression was sufficient for development, but not if balance of the maternal transcripts was essential.
